## A Reminiscence of Dr. Samuel Johnson / 塞缪尔·约翰逊博士的回忆
===Original===

Humphry Littlewit, Esq.

The Privilege of Reminiscence, however rambling or tiresome, is one generally allow’d to the very aged; indeed, ’tis frequently by means of such Recollections that the obscure occurrences of History, and the lesser Anecdotes of the Great, are transmitted to Posterity.

Though many of my readers have at times observ’d and remark’d a Sort of antique Flow in my Stile of Writing, it hath pleased me to pass amongst the Members of this Generation as a young Man, giving out the Fiction that I was born in 1890, in **America**. I am now, however, resolv’d to unburden myself of a secret which I have hitherto kept thro’ Dread of Incredulity; and to impart to the Publick a true knowledge of my long years, in order to gratifie their taste for authentick Information of an Age with whose famous Personages I was on familiar Terms. Be it then known that I was born on the family Estate in **Devonshire**, of the 10th day of August, 1690, (or in the new **Gregorian** Stile of Reckoning, the 20th of August) being therefore now in my 228th year. Coming early to **London**, I saw as a Child many of the celebrated Men of King **William’s** Reign, including the lamented Mr. **Dryden**, who sat much at the Tables of **Will’s** Coffee-House. With Mr. **Addison** and Dr. **Swift** I later became very well acquainted, and was an even more familiar Friend to Mr. **Pope**, whom I knew and respected till the Day of his Death. But since it is of my more recent Associate, the late Dr. **Johnson**, that I am at this time desir’d to write; I will pass over my Youth for the present.

I had first Knowledge of the Doctor in May of the year 1738, though I did not at that Time meet him. Mr. **Pope** had just compleated his Epilogue to his Satires, (the Piece beginning: “Not twice a Twelvemonth you appear in Print.”) and had arrang’d for its Publication. On the very Day it appear’d, there was also publish’d a Satire in Imitation of **Juvenal**, entituled “**London**,” by the then unknown **Johnson**; and this so struck the Town, that many Gentlemen of Taste declared, it was the Work of a greater Poet than Mr. **Pope**. Notwithstanding what some Detractors have said of Mr. **Pope’s** petty Jealousy, he gave the Verses of his new Rival no small Praise; and having learnt thro’ Mr. **Richardson** who the Poet was, told me, “that Mr. **Johnson** wou’d soon be **deterre**.”

===Chinese===

汉弗莱·利特尔维特先生（Humphry Littlewit, Esq.）

回忆之特权，无论怎样散漫、怎样惹人厌烦，世人通常总肯赐予高龄之人；确实，历史上那些晦暗的事迹、伟人们的细枝逸闻，往往正是靠这类追忆才得以传于后世。

尽管我的读者中不少人在我的文字风格里时而察见并论及一种古旧的流风，我却乐于以一个年轻人的身份行走于这一代人中间，散布虚构，说自己生于一八九〇年的**美洲**。然而我如今决意卸下一桩秘密——我至今讳它，只因怕人不信——并向公众透露我漫长岁月的真数，好满足他们对一个时代的可靠见闻的胃口，那个时代的名人，我都过从甚密。那么请知晓：我生于**德文郡**的祖传田宅，时在一六九〇年八月十日（依**格列高利**新历，则为八月二十日），如此算来，今年已是我的第二百二十八岁。我早年到了**伦敦**，孩提时便见过**威廉**王朝许多名人，包括那位令人悼念的**德莱顿**先生，他常坐在**威尔**咖啡馆的桌旁。后来我同**艾迪生**先生与**斯威夫特**博士十分相熟，同**蒲柏**先生更是莫逆，直到他去世那日，我始终敬重他。只是我此刻想写的，是我较晚的伙伴、已故的**约翰逊**博士，故少年时事，姑且从略。

我初知博士，是在一七三八年五月，虽则当时并未谋面。**蒲柏**先生刚写完他的《讽刺诗集》跋（即以“你一年上不了两回印刷所”起句的那篇），并已安排刊行。刊出的当天，又有一篇仿**尤文纳尔**的讽刺诗问世，题作《**伦敦**》，作者便是当时尚无声名的**约翰逊**；此诗轰动京城，许多有鉴赏力的绅士宣称，其作者比**蒲柏**先生更伟大。尽管有些诋毁者说**蒲柏**先生如何小气嫉妒，他对这位新对手的诗句却嘉许不少；又经**理查森**先生打听到诗人是谁之后，对我说：“**约翰逊**先生不久便会**名世**。”

===Original===

I had no personal Acquaintances with the Doctor till 1763, when I was presented to him at the **Mitre** Tavern by Mr. **James Boswell**, a young **Scotchman** of excellent Family and great Learning, but small Wit, whose metrical Effusions I had sometimes revis’d.

Dr. **Johnson**, as I beheld him, was a full, pursy Man, very ill drest, and of slovenly Aspect. I recall him to have worn a bushy Bob-Wig, untyed and without Powder, and much too small for his Head. His Cloaths were of rusty brown, much wrinkled, and with more than one Button missing. His Face, too full to be handsom, was likewise marred by the Effects of some scrofulous Disorder; and his Head was continually rolling about in a sort of convulsive way. Of this Infirmity, indeed, I had known before; having heard of it from Mr. **Pope**, who took the Trouble to make particular Inquiries.

Being nearly seventy-three, full nineteen Years older than Dr. **Johnson**, (I say Doctor, though his Degree came not till two Years afterward) I naturally expected him to have some Regard for my Age; and was therefore not in that Fear of him, which others confess’d. On my asking him what he thought of my favourable Notice of his Dictionary in **The Londoner**, my periodical Paper, he said: “Sir, I possess no Recollection of having perus’d your Paper, and have not a great Interest in the Opinions of the less thoughtful Part of Mankind.” Being more than a little piqued at the Incivility of one whose Celebrity made me solicitous of his Approbation, I ventur’d to retaliate in kind, and told him, I was surpris’d that a Man of Sense shou’d judge the Thoughtfulness of one whose Productions he admitted never having read. “Why, Sir,” reply’d **Johnson**, “I do not require to become familiar with a Man’s Writings in order to estimate the Superficiality of his Attainments, when he plainly shows it by his Eagerness to mention his own Productions in the first Question he puts to me.” Having thus become Friends, we convers’d on many Matters. When, to agree with him, I said I was distrustful of the Authenticity of **Ossian’s** Poems, Mr. **Johnson** said: “That, Sir, does not do your Understanding particular Credit; for what all the Town is sensible of, is no great Discovery for a **Grub-Street** Critick to make. You might as well say, you have a strong Suspicion that **Milton** wrote *Paradise Lost*!”

===Chinese===

直到一七六三年，我才与博士本人相识，是**詹姆斯·鲍斯韦尔**先生在**米特**酒馆引见的。鲍斯韦尔是个出身上等门第、学问渊博的**苏格兰**青年，只是机锋不足，他的诗稿我时有代为斟酌。

**约翰逊**博士，在我眼中是个肥硕臃肿的人，衣冠不整，仪容邋遢。我记得他戴一顶浓密的短假发，不系带，不敷粉，而且比他的头小了许多。他的衣裳是锈棕色，皱皱巴巴，不止一粒纽扣失落。他的脸因过于肥满而谈不上俊雅，又因瘰疬之症的后遗症而更受损；他的头还不住地以一种抽搐的样子左右滚动。这毛病我原有所闻，是**蒲柏**先生费心特意打听过告诉我的。

我时年将近七十三，比**约翰逊**博士足足年长十九岁（我称他博士，虽说他的学位还是两年之后的事），自然指望他对我这年纪存几分敬意，因此也不像旁人自认的那样怕他。我问他，对我在自己的期刊《伦敦人》上对他的字典的嘉评有何高见，他说：“先生，我不记得读过您的刊物，对人类中较少深思的那部分人的意见，也不大有兴味。”此人名望正盛，他的赞许为我所渴仰，这般无礼不免叫我着恼，我便斗气以其人之道还治，对他说，一个明白人，既承认从未读过人家的文章，却去断断人家的深浅，实在出我意外。“哎呀，先生，”**约翰逊**答道，“用不着熟悉一个人的著作，也能估量他学问的浅薄——他见我第一问，便急着自陈其大作，这浅薄已自招供了。”我们就这样成了朋友，纵谈了许多事。有一回为附和他，我说我不信**莪相**那些诗是真品，**约翰逊**博士说：“先生，这话并不为您的见识添什么光彩；全城人都明白的事，**格拉布街**（Grub-Street）的批评家再发现一回，算不得高明。您何不说，您强烈疑心**弥尔顿**的《失乐园》是**弥尔顿**写的！”

===Original===

I thereafter saw **Johnson** very frequently, most often at Meetings of **The Literary Club**, which was founded the next Year by the Doctor, together with Mr. **Burke**, the parliamentary Orator, Mr. **Beauclerk**, a Gentleman of Fashion, Mr. **Langton**, a pious Man and Captain of Militia, Sir **J. Reynolds**, the widely known Painter, Dr. **Goldsmith**, the Prose and poetick Writer, Dr. **Nugent**, father-in-law to Mr. **Burke**, Sir **John Hawkins**, Mr. **Anthony Chamier**, and my self. We assembled generally at seven o’clock of an Evening, once a Week, at the **Turk’s-Head**, in **Gerrard-Street**, **Soho**, till that Tavern was sold and made into a private Dwelling; after which Event we mov’d our Gatherings successively to **Prince’s** in **Sackville-Street**, **Le Tellier’s** in **Dover-Street**, and **Parsloe’s** and the **Thatched House** in **St. James’s-Street**. In these Meetings we preserv’d a remarkable Degree of Amity and Tranquillity, which contrasts very favourably with some of the Dissensions and Disruptions I observe in the literary and amateur Press Associations of today. This Tranquillity was the more remarkable, because we had amongst us Gentlemen of very opposed Opinions. Dr. **Johnson** and I, as well as many others, were high Tories; whilst Mr. **Burke** was a Whig, and against the **American** War, many of his Speeches on that Subject having been widely publish’d. The least congenial Member was one of the Founders, Sir **John Hawkins**, who hath since written many misrepresentations of our Society. Sir **John**, an eccentrick Fellow, once declin’d to pay his part of the Reckoning for Supper, because ’twas his Custom at Home to eat no Supper. Later he insulted Mr. **Burke** in so intolerable a Manner, that we all took Pains to show our Disapproval; after which Incident he came no more to our Meetings. However, he never openly fell out with the Doctor, and was the Executor of his Will; though Mr. **Boswell** and others have Reason to question the genuineness of his Attachment. Other and later Members of the **Club** were Mr. **David Garrick**, the Actor and early Friend of Dr. **Johnson**, Messieurs **Tho.** and **Jos. Warton**, Dr. **Adam Smith**, Dr. **Percy**, Author of the “Reliques,” Mr. **Edw. Gibbon**, the Historian, Dr. **Burney**, the Musician, Mr. **Malone**, the Critick, and Mr. **Boswell**. Mr.

此后我常常见到**约翰逊**，多半是在**文学俱乐部**的聚会上。那是次年博士一手创立的，同创者有议会雄辩家**伯克**先生、时髦绅士**博克莱尔**先生、虔信之人兼民团上尉**兰顿**先生、声名远播的画家**雷诺兹**爵士、散文与韵文兼工的**哥尔德斯密斯**博士、**伯克**先生的岳丈**纽金特**博士、**约翰·霍金斯**爵士、**安东尼·尚米耶**先生，以及在下。我们通常每星期一晚，晚七点，在**索霍**区**杰拉德街**的**土耳其人头**酒馆聚会，直到那酒馆易主改作私宅；此后我们的聚会相继移到**萨克维尔街**的**普林斯**、**多佛街**的**勒泰利耶**，以及**圣詹姆斯街**的**帕斯洛**和**茅屋**。在那些聚会上，我们保持着一种可观的和睦与安谧，比起今日文学界和业余报界那些内讧与破裂，实在体面得多。这安谧尤为难得，因为我们中间有意见极相左的君子。**约翰逊**博士和我，以及许多同人，是坚决的托利党；**伯克**先生却是辉格党，又反对**美洲**战争，他在那个题目上的许多演说流传甚广。最不投机的一位会员是创会人之一的**约翰·霍金斯**爵士，他后来写了许多歪曲本会的话。**霍金斯**爵士是个乖僻的人，有一回不肯出他那份晚饭的账，理由是在他自己家里向来不进晚饭。后来他又以不可容忍的方式侮辱**伯克**先生，我们全体特意表示了反感；此事之后他再不来赴会了。然而他同博士从未公开闹翻，还是博士遗嘱的执行人；虽说**鲍斯韦尔**先生等人有理由怀疑这份情谊的真伪。俱乐部较晚的会员有演员、**约翰逊**博士的早年挚友**大卫·加里克**先生，**托·**与**约·沃顿**二位先生，**亚当·斯密**博士，《英诗拾遗》的作者**珀西**博士，史家**爱德华·吉本**先生，音乐家**伯尼**博士，批评家**马隆**先生，还有**鲍斯韦尔**先生。至於

===Original===

**Garrick** obtain’d Admittance only with Difficulty; for the Doctor, notwithstanding his great Friendship, was for ever affecting to decry the Stage and all Things connected with it. **Johnson**, indeed, had a most singular Habit of speaking for **Davy** when others were against him, and of arguing against him, when others were for him. I have no Doubt but that he sincerely lov’d Mr. **Garrick**, for he never alluded to him as he did to **Foote**, who was a very coarse Fellow despite his comick Genius. Mr. **Gibbon** was none too well lik’d, for he had an odious sneering Way which offended even those of us who most admir’d his historical Productions. Mr. **Goldsmith**, a little Man very vain of his Dress and very deficient in Brilliancy of Conversation, was my particular Favourite; since I was equally unable to shine in the Discourse. He was vastly jealous of Dr. **Johnson**, though none the less liking and respecting him. I remember that once a Foreigner, a **German**, I think, was in our Company; and that whilst **Goldsmith** was speaking, he observ’d the Doctor preparing to utter something. Unconsciously looking upon **Goldsmith** as a meer Encumbrance when compar’d to the greater Man, the Foreigner bluntly interrupted him and incurr’d his lasting Hostility by crying, “Hush, Toctor **Shonson** iss going to speak!”

In this luminous Company I was tolerated more because of my Years than for my Wit or Learning; being no Match at all for the rest. My Friendship for the celebrated Monsieur **Voltaire** was ever a Cause of Annoyance to the Doctor; who was deeply orthodox, and who us’d to say of the **French** Philosopher: “*Vir est acerrimi Ingenii et paucarum Literarum.*”

===Chinese===

**加里克**先生获准入会，颇费了一番周折；因为博士虽与他交谊极笃，却总爱作践戏台和同它沾边的一切。**约翰逊**确实有个极古怪的习惯：别人贬**戴维**时他偏替他说话，别人捧**戴维**时他偏同他抬杠。我毫不怀疑他真心爱**加里克**先生，因为他提到他从不像提到**富特**那样——富特虽有滑稽天才，为人却极粗俗。**吉本**先生不怎么讨人喜欢，他那种可憎的讥诮腔，连我们中间最佩服他史学的人也要被冒犯。**哥尔德斯密斯**先生，一个小个子，极自负于衣著，谈吐又殊欠光彩，却是我的心头至好；因为谈锋之上我也一样发不出亮。他对**约翰逊**博士怀有强烈的妒意，却仍旧喜欢他、敬重他。我记得有一回，一位外国人——我想是个**德国**人——在我们中间；**哥尔德斯密斯**正说话时，他瞧见博士要开言了。那外国人下意识把**哥尔德斯密斯**同那位大人物一比，只当他是个赘物，便鲁莽地打断了他，喊道：“嘘，**琼森**博士要说话了！”从此结下了他永久的仇恨。

在这群煌煌的人物中间，我所以被容忍，多半是为着我的年纪，而非我的机锋或学问；同其余诸公相比，我全然不济。我对著名的**伏尔泰**先生的友谊，历来是博士的一桩烦恼；他信教极诚，常这样论那位**法兰西**哲学家：“*Vir est acerrimi Ingenii et paucarum Literarum*。”（其人锐敏绝伦，而学殖甚浅。）

===Original===

Mr. **Boswell**, a little teazing Fellow whom I had known for some Time previously, us’d to make Sport of my aukward Manners and old-fashion’d Wig and Cloaths. Once coming in a little the worse for Wine (to which he was addicted) he endeavour’d to lampoon me by means of an Impromptu in verse, writ on the Surface of the Table; but lacking the Aid he usually had in his Composition, he made a bad grammatical Blunder. I told him, he shou’d not try to pasquinade the Source of his Poesy. At another Time **Bozzy** (as we us’d to call him) complain’d of my Harshness toward new Writers in the Articles I prepar’d for *The Monthly Review*. He said, I push’d every Aspirant off the Slopes of Parnassus. “Sir,” I reply’d, “you are mistaken. They who lose their Hold do so from their own Want of Strength; but desiring to conceal their Weakness, they attribute the absence of Success to the first Critick that mentions them.” I am glad to recall that Dr. **Johnson** upheld me in this Matter.

Dr. **Johnson** was second to no Man in the Pains he took to revise the bad Verses of others; indeed, ’tis said that in the book of poor blind old Mrs. **Williams**, there are scarce two lines which are not the Doctor’s. At one Time **Johnson** recited to me some lines by a Servant to the Duke of **Leeds**, which had so amus’d him, that he had got them by Heart. They are on the Duke’s Wedding, and so much resemble in Quality the Work of other and more recent poetick Dunces, that I cannot forbear copying them:

“When the Duke of **Leeds** shall marry’d be

To a fine young Lady of high Quality

How happy will that Gentlewoman be

In his Grace of **Leeds’** good Company.”

I ask’d the Doctor, if he had ever try’d making Sense of this Piece; and upon his saying he had not, I amus’d myself with the following Amendment of it:

When Gallant **Leeds** auspiciously shall wed

The virtuous Fair, of antient Lineage bred,

How must the Maid rejoice with conscious Pride

To win so great an Husband to her Side!

On showing this to Dr. **Johnson**, he said, “Sir, you have straightened out the Feet, but you have put neither Wit nor Poetry into the Lines.”

===Chinese===

**鲍斯韦尔**先生，一个小小的促狭鬼，我认识他有些时日了，惯爱拿我笨拙的举止和过时的假发衣著取笑。有一回他带着几分酒意（他嗜酒）进来，想在桌面上一首即兴打油诗里挖苦我；但少了平日起草捉刀的帮手，他犯了个糟糕的语法错。我对他说，他不该去讥诮他那些诗的源头。又有一回，**博齐**（我们常这样叫他）抱怨我在《每月评论》上写的文章里对新起作家太苛刻，说我把每一个攀爬者都从帕纳索斯山坡上推了下去。“先生，”我答道，“您错了。抓不住的人，是自家力气不济；他们想遮掩这软弱，便把不成名归咎于第一个提到他们的批评家。”我很欣慰地记得，在这件事上**约翰逊**博士是站在我这一边的。

**约翰逊**博士肯费心替人改劣诗，天下无人能出其右；据说可怜的瞎眼**威廉斯**老太太那本诗集里，几乎没有两行不是博士的手笔。有一回**约翰逊**背给我听**利兹**公爵一个仆人的几句诗，那诗叫他乐不可支，都记熟了。诗咏公爵的婚事，其成色同近来别的一些诗中蠢才的作品如此相像，我忍不住抄在这里：

“当**利兹**公爵娶亲成家

娶一位高贵门第的娇娃

那位淑女该多么快活

有**利兹**大人陪她过活。”

我问博士可曾设法把这首诗读通；他说不曾，我便自娱，替它改成了下面这样：

当豪侠的**利兹**喜结良缘，

娶淑女出自名门世系，

那闺秀该怎样自豪欣然，

赢得如此夫婿相守不离！

拿给**约翰逊**博士看，他说：“先生，您把音步理顺了，可诗行里仍旧没有机智，也没有诗。”

===Original===

It wou’d afford me Gratification to tell more of my Experiences with Dr. **Johnson** and his circle of Wits; but I am an old Man, and easily fatigued. I seem to ramble along without much Logick or Continuity when I endeavour to recall the Past; and fear I light upon but few Incidents which others have not before discuss’d. Shou’d my present Recollections meet with Favour, I might later set down some further Anecdotes of old Times of which I am the only Survivor. I recall many Things of **Sam Johnson** and his Club, having kept up my Membership in the Latter long after the Doctor’s Death, at which I sincerely mourn’d. I remember how **John Burgoyne**, Esq., the General, whose Dramatick and Poetical Works were printed after his Death, was blackballed by three Votes; probably because of his unfortunate Defeat in the **American** War, at **Saratoga**. Poor **John**! His Son fared better, I think, and was made a Baronet. But I am very tired. I am old, very old; it is Time for my Afternoon Nap.

===Chinese===

我原愿再讲讲我同**约翰逊**博士及其智士圈子交往的经历；无奈我已老朽，极易困倦。我一回忆往昔，便像信步乱走，谈不上多少条理和连贯；而且恐怕撞见的逸事，多是别人早已谈过的。倘若这一番回忆竟蒙青睐，我日后或可再写下几则旧日掌故——那些事的亲历者，如今只剩我一人了。我记得**塞姆·约翰逊**和他的俱乐部的许多事，博士身后，我在后者的会籍还维持了许多年，他的死，我是真心哀恸过的。我记得**约翰·伯戈因**将军——他的戏剧和诗作都在身后印行——以三票之差被黑球拒于门外；多半是因为他在**美洲**战争的**萨拉托加**不幸败绩。可怜的**约翰**！他的儿子倒走运些，我记得，得了从男爵封号。可是我乏了。我老了，老得很；该睡午觉了。

## Beyond the Wall of Sleep / 梦墙之外
===Original===

“I have an exposition of sleep come upon me.”

> Shakespeare

I have often wondered if the majority of mankind ever pause to reflect upon the occasionally titanic significance of dreams, and of the obscure world to which they belong. Whilst the greater number of our nocturnal visions are perhaps no more than faint and fantastic reflections of our waking experiences﻿—Freud to the contrary with his puerile symbolism﻿—there are still a certain remainder whose immundane and ethereal character permits of no ordinary interpretation, and whose vaguely exciting and disquieting effect suggests possible minute glimpses into a sphere of mental existence no less important than physical life, yet separated from that life by an all but impassable barrier. From my experience I cannot doubt but that man, when lost to terrestrial consciousness, is indeed sojourning in another and uncorporeal life of far different nature from the life we know; and of which only the slightest and most indistinct memories linger after waking. From those blurred and fragmentary memories we may infer much, yet prove little. We may guess that in dreams life, matter, and vitality, as the earth knows such things, are not necessarily constant; and that time and space do not exist as our waking selves comprehend them. Sometimes I believe that this less material life is our truer life, and that our vain presence on the terraqueous globe is itself the secondary or merely virtual phenomenon.

===Chinese===

“一场睡眠不知不觉临到了我身上。”

> 莎士比亚

我常常纳闷，世人大多数可曾停下来想一想梦的偶发的巨大意义，想一想梦所隶属的那个幽昧世界。我们的夜见幻象，多半不过是清醒经验的微弱而奇幻的反照——弗洛伊德那一套幼稚的象征说且随他去——然而总还剩下一类，其超凡出尘的性质容不得寻常的解释，其隐约令人激动又不寒而栗的效果，暗示着我们或许对一种精神存在的领域略窥了一斑——那领域绝不比肉体生命次要，只是被一道几乎不可逾越的屏障同这生命隔开。凭我的经验，我不能不信：人一旦失去尘世的知觉，确乎是旅居在另一种无形的生命里，同我们所知的生命性质迥异；醒来之后，只有最微弱、最模糊的记忆残留。从那些模糊残缺的记忆里，我们可以推想很多，证明的却极少。我们可以猜想：在梦中，生命、物质与活力——如地球所理解的这些东西——未必恒定；时间与空间，也不像我们清醒的自我所理解的那样存在。有时我相信，这较少物质性的生命才是我们更真实的生命，而我们在这水陆星球上的虚浮存在，反而是次要的、近乎虚象的东西。

===Original===

It was from a youthful reverie filled with speculations of this sort that I arose one afternoon in the winter of 1900﻿–﻿01, when to the state psychopathic institution in which I served as an interne was brought the man whose case has ever since haunted me so unceasingly. His name, as given on the records, was Joe Slater, or Slaader, and his appearance was that of the typical denizen of the Catskill Mountain region; one of those strange, repellent scions of a primitive Colonial peasant stock whose isolation for nearly three centuries in the hilly fastnesses of a little travelled countryside has caused them to sink to a kind of barbaric degeneracy, rather than advance with their more fortunately placed brethren of the thickly settled districts. Among these odd folk, who correspond exactly to the decadent element of “white trash” in the south, law and morals are nonexistent; and their general mental status is probably below that of any other section of the native American people.

Joe Slater, who came to the institution in the vigilant custody of four state policemen, and who was described as a highly dangerous character, certainly presented no evidence of his perilous disposition when I first beheld him. Though well above the middle stature, and of somewhat brawny frame, he was given an absurd appearance of harmless stupidity by the pale, sleepy blueness of his small watery eyes, the scantiness of his neglected and never-shaven growth of yellow beard, and the listless drooping of his heavy nether lip. His age was unknown, since among his kind neither family records nor permanent family ties exist; but from the baldness of his head in front, and from the decayed condition of his teeth, the head surgeon wrote him down as a man of about forty.

===Chinese===

一九〇〇至〇一年间的那个冬天，一天下午，我正从满脑这路玄想的少年白日梦里回过神来，我们那所州立精神病院——我在那里当实习医生——收下了那个从此无休无止纠缠着我的病例。病历上写的名字是乔·斯莱特，或作斯莱德，长相是卡兹奇山区的典型土人：殖民时代农夫血统的一支古怪而讨嫌的余孽，将近三百年闭锁在一片人迹罕至的乡野山塞里，非但没有进步，反倒堕落回某种野蛮状态，同住在富庶平川、运气较好的同宗愈离愈远。在这些怪人中间——他们同南方的“白垃圾”败类恰好对应——法律与道德是不存在的，其总体心智状况，多半低于美洲土生白人的任何别一支。

乔·斯莱特由四名州警戒备森严地押进院来，档案上说他是个极端危险的人物，可我初见他时，他全无一点凶险的迹象。他高出中等身材，筋骨相当粗壮，但那双水汪汪的小眼睛泛着苍白困倦的蓝色，黄胡子又稀又乱从不刮，厚下唇没精打采地耷拉着，合成一副愚蠢无害的滑稽相。年纪无从知晓，因为他那类人既无家谱，也无恒久的家庭纽带；但看他前顶的秃和一口烂牙，外科主任把他记作四十岁上下的人。

===Original===

From the medical and court documents we learned all that could be gathered of his case: This man, a vagabond, hunter, and trapper, had always been strange in the eyes of his primitive associates. He had habitually slept at night beyond the ordinary time, and upon waking would often talk of unknown things in a manner so bizarre as to inspire fear even in the hearts of an unimaginative populace. Not that his form of language was at all unusual, for he never spoke save in the debased patois of his environment; but the tone and tenor of his utterances were of such mysterious wildness, that none might listen without apprehension. He himself was generally as terrified and baffled as his auditors, and within an hour after awakening would forget all that he had said, or at least all that had caused him to say what he did; relapsing into a bovine, half amiable normality like that of the other hill-dwellers.

===Chinese===

从医疗和法庭文书里，我们得知了关于他案情所能收集到的一切：此人是个流浪汉、猎户和设陷阱的，在他那些原始同伴眼里从来古怪。他夜里惯常睡得超过常度，醒来又常说些不知名的东西，说法之诡异，连没有想象力的乡民也要心惊。倒不是他的语言本身有什么特别，他开口从来只用他那环境里的下等土话；而是他言谈的腔调和内容带着那种神秘的野性，听者无不惴惴。他自己往往同听众一样惊恐、一样惶惑，醒后不到一个钟头，便把说过的话忘个干净——至少把使他那样说话的原因忘个干净——重新跌回一种牛一样的、半和善的常态，同别的山人一般无二。

===Original===

As Slater grew older, it appeared, his matutinal aberrations had gradually increased in frequency and violence; till about a month before his arrival at the institution had occurred the shocking tragedy which caused his arrest by the authorities. One day near noon, after a profound sleep begun in a whiskey debauch at about five of the previous afternoon, the man had roused himself most suddenly; with ululations so horrible and unearthly that they brought several neighbours to his cabin﻿—a filthy sty where he dwelt with a family as indescribable as himself. Rushing out into the snow, he had flung his arms aloft and commenced a series of leaps directly upward in the air; the while shouting his determination to reach some “big, big cabin with brightness in the roof and walls and floor and the loud queer music far away.” As two men of moderate size sought to restrain him, he had struggled with maniacal force and fury, screaming of his desire and need to find and kill a certain “thing that shines and shakes and laughs.” At length, after temporarily felling one of his detainers with a sudden blow, he had flung himself upon the other in a daemonic ecstasy of bloodthirstiness, shrieking fiendishly that he would “jump high in the air and burn his way through anything that stopped him.” Family and neighbours had now fled in a panic, and when the more courageous of them returned, Slater was gone, leaving behind an unrecognisable pulp-like thing that had been a living man but an hour before. None of the mountaineers had dared to pursue him, and it is likely that they would have welcomed his death from the cold; but when several mornings later they heard his screams from a distant ravine they realised that he had somehow managed to survive, and that his removal in one way or another would be necessary. Then had followed an armed searching party, whose purpose (whatever it may have been originally) became that of a sheriff’s posse after one of the seldom popular state troopers had by accident observed, then questioned, and finally joined the seekers.

===Chinese===

据称，斯莱特年岁渐长，这晨起的怪病发作愈频愈烈；直到入院前约一个月，出了那桩叫他被官府拿下的骇人惨剧。那一天近正午，他从头天下午五点来钟开始的威士忌烂醉中沉沉睡去之后，忽然惊起，发出的嚎叫可怕得不似人声，把几个邻居引到了他的木屋——那是个肮脏的猪圈似的所在，同他住在一处的家人也同他一样无法形容。他冲进雪地里，双臂高举，开始一连串直上直下的蹦跳，嘴里喊着他决心要到达某一处“顶大顶大的木屋，屋顶、墙壁、地板都亮堂堂的，还有老远老远又响又怪的音乐”。两个中等身材的人想拦住他，他疯子般又挣又打，尖声嚷着他要找到并杀掉某一个“亮闪闪、直发抖、爱笑的东西”的欲望和必要。最后，他一拳暂时摃倒了其中一个看守，便怀着嗜血的魔性狂喜扑向另一个，狞声厉叫说他要“跳到半天空里，烧穿一切拦他的东西”。家人和邻居这时已吓作鸟兽散，等胆大的几个回来，斯莱特已不知去向，身后留下一摊认不出的肉泥——一个钟头之前那还是个活人。山民们没人敢追，他们多半巴不得他冻死才好；可是几天后的一个早晨，他们听见一条远谷里传来他的尖叫，才明白他居然活了下来，不设法弄走他是不行的。随后便来了一支带枪的搜山队，其目的（原本是什么且不管它）在一名难得受人待见的州骑警无意中撞见、盘问、终于入伙之后，变成了副警长率领的民团。

===Original===

On the third day Slater was found unconscious in the hollow of a tree, and taken to the nearest gaol; where alienists from Albany examined him as soon as his senses returned. To them he told a simple story. He had, he said, gone to sleep one afternoon about sundown after drinking much liquor. He had awakened to find himself standing bloody-handed in the snow before his cabin, the mangled corpse of his neighbour Peter Slader at his feet. Horrified, he had taken to the woods in a vague effort to escape from the scene of what must have been his crime. Beyond these things he seemed to know nothing, nor could the expert questioning of his interrogators bring out a single additional fact. That night Slater slept quietly, and the next morning he wakened with no singular feature save a certain alteration of expression. Dr. Barnard, who had been watching the patient, thought he noticed in the pale blue eyes a certain gleam of peculiar quality; and in the flaccid lips an all but imperceptible tightening, as if of intelligent determination. But when questioned, Slater relapsed into the habitual vacancy of the mountaineer, and only reiterated what he had said on the preceding day.

===Chinese===

第三天，人们在一条树洞里找到了昏迷的斯莱特，送往最近的监狱；奥尔巴尼来的精神病专家等他神志一恢复便做了检查。他向他们讲了一个简单的故事。他说，一天下午日落时分，他喝了好多酒睡去。醒来时，发现自己立在木屋前的雪地里，双手是血，脚下躺着邻居彼得·斯莱德血肉模糊的尸首。他吓坏了，钻进树林，糊里糊涂想逃离那必是他罪案的现场。除这些之外他似乎一无所知，审讯者的老到盘问也没能再榨出一条事实。当夜斯莱特睡得安稳，次晨醒来也无异状，只是神情有了某种变化。巴纳德医生一直守着病人，觉得他注意到那双淡蓝的眼睛里有一道特质特别的光，松懈的嘴唇几乎不可察觉地绷紧了，像是一种有智能的决心。可一问，斯莱特又跌回山人惯常的茫然，只把头一天的话重说了一遍。

===Original===

On the third morning occurred the first of the man’s mental attacks. After some show of uneasiness in sleep, he burst forth into a frenzy so powerful that the combined efforts of four men were needed to bind him in a straitjacket. The alienists listened with keen attention to his words, since their curiosity had been aroused to a high pitch by the suggestive yet mostly conflicting and incoherent stories of his family and neighbours. Slater raved for upward of fifteen minutes, babbling in his backwoods dialect of green edifices of light, oceans of space, strange music, and shadowy mountains and valleys. But most of all did he dwell upon some mysterious blazing entity that shook and laughed and mocked at him. This vast, vague personality seemed to have done him a terrible wrong, and to kill it in triumphant revenge was his paramount desire. In order to reach it, he said, he would soar through abysses of emptiness, *burning* every obstacle that stood in his way. Thus ran his discourse, until with the greatest suddenness he ceased. The fire of madness died from his eyes, and in dull wonder he looked at his questioners and asked why he was bound. R. Barnard unbuckled the leather harness and did not restore it till night, when he succeeded in persuading Slater to don it of his own volition, for his own good. The man had now admitted that he sometimes talked queerly, though he knew not why.

Within a week two more attacks appeared, but from them the doctors learned little. On the *source* of Slater’s visions they speculated at length, for since he could neither read nor write, and had apparently never heard a legend or fairy tale, his gorgeous imagery was quite inexplicable. That it could not come from any known myth or romance was made especially clear by the fact that the unfortunate lunatic expressed himself only in his own simple manner. He raved of things he did not understand and could not interpret; things which he claimed to have experienced, but which he could not have learned through any normal or connected narration. The alienists soon agreed that abnormal dreams were the foundation of the trouble; dreams whose vividness could for a time completely dominate the waking mind of this basically inferior man. With due formality Slater was tried for murder, acquitted on the ground of insanity, and committed to the institution wherein I held so humble a post.

===Chinese===

第三个早晨，此人的第一次精神发作来了。他在睡眠中先有些不安的迹象，随即爆发出一阵狂乱，力气大得四个人合力才把他捆进约束衣。精神病专家们屏息细听他的话，因为家属和邻居那些启人疑窦又多半互相矛盾、语无伦次的陈述，早把他们的好奇吊到了极处。斯莱特狂言了十五分钟以上，用他那林间土话呓语着光的碧色巨厦、太空的海洋、奇异的音乐，和影影绰绰的群山与谷地。而他说得最多的，是某个发光的神秘存在，那东西发着抖，笑着，嘲弄他。这个巨大而模糊的个性像是害他吃了天大的亏，把它杀掉、痛快报仇，便是他压倒一切的愿望。他说，为了够到它，他要穿越空虚的深渊翱翔，*烧掉*一切拦路的东西。他的话就这样流下去，直到极突然地戛然而止。疯狂的火从他眼里熄了，他懵懵地问他的问话人，为什么把他绑起来。R·巴纳德解开皮带，直到夜里才重新给他系上——他好说歹说劝得斯莱特为了自己好自愿穿上。此人如今承认自己有时说话古怪，虽然不知道为什么。

一周之内又发了两次，可医生们从中所得甚少。关于斯莱特幻象的*来源*，他们推敲了很久，因为此人既不能读也不能写，显然从未听过什么传说或童话，他那绚烂的意象便全然无从解释。它不可能出自任何已知的神话或传奇——这一点尤其清楚，因为那不幸的疯子只用他自己那套简单的方式表达。他呓语着他不理解也不能解释的东西；他声称亲身经历过、却绝非任何正常连贯的叙述所能教给他的东西。专家们不久便一致认为，反常的梦是这病症的根；那些梦的鲜明程度，一时竟能完全支配这个素质低下者的清醒头脑。斯莱特经正式程序以杀人罪受审，以精神失常获无罪，投入了我供职的那所病院——我在那里职位卑微。

===Original===

I have said that I am a constant speculator concerning dream life, and from this you may judge of the eagerness with which I applied myself to the study of the new patient as soon as I had fully ascertained the facts of his case. He seemed to sense a certain friendliness in me; born no doubt of the interest I could not conceal, and the gentle manner in which I questioned him. Not that he ever recognised me during his attacks, when I hung breathlessly upon his chaotic but cosmic word-pictures; but he knew me in his quiet hours, when he would sit by his barred window weaving baskets of straw and willow, and perhaps pining for the mountain freedom he could never again enjoy. His family never called to see him; probably it had found another temporary head, after the manner of decadent mountain folk.

By degrees I commenced to feel an overwhelming wonder at the mad and fantastic conceptions of Joe Slater. The man himself was pitiably inferior in mentality and language alike; but his glowing, titanic visions, though described in a barbarous and disjointed jargon, were assuredly things which only a superior or even exceptional brain could conceive. How, I often asked myself, could the stolid imagination of a Catskill degenerate conjure up sights whose very possession argued a lurking spark of genius? How could any backwoods dullard have gained so much as an idea of those glittering realms of supernal radiance and space about which Slater ranted in his furious delirium? More and more I inclined to the belief that in the pitiful personality who cringed before me lay the disordered nucleus of something beyond my comprehension; something infinitely beyond the comprehension of my more experienced but less imaginative medical and scientific colleagues.

===Chinese===

我说过，我对梦的生命素来是个执着的玄想着，由此你们可以想见，一查明他的案情，我便以怎样的热忱扑到对新病人的研究上。他像是觉出我身上某种友好——无疑生自我掩饰不住的兴趣和我问话的温和。倒不是他发作时认得我，虽然那时我屏息悬在他那混乱而宏茫的话语图景上；可他安静时是认得我的，那时他会坐在铁窗边编麦秆和柳条的篮子，多半还在渴念他再不能享受的山中自由。他的家人从不来看他；按堕落山民的做派，那一家多半已另立了一个临时的头目。

渐渐地，我开始对乔·斯莱特疯狂而奇妙的构想生出压倒性的惊叹。这人本身，心智与语言都可怜地低下；可他那发光的、巨灵般的幻象，虽是用粗野支离的黑话描述的，确乎是唯有优越乃至异禀的头脑才能构想的东西。我常自问：一个卡兹奇退化者那呆滞的想象力，怎么变出这些光景？单是占有它们，便证明天才的火花还在暗处藏著。一个山林的蠢材，又怎么会得到关于那些辉煌境界的哪怕一点概念——那些超凡的光与空间，斯莱特在暴怒的谵妄里吼叫着的？我越来越倾向于相信：在这个缩在我面前的可怜人格里，藏着一个超出我理解力的、错乱的核；某种东西，无限超出我那些更有经验、却较少想象力的医学与科学同侪的理解。

===Original===

And yet I could extract nothing definite from the man. The sum of all my investigation was, that in a kind of semi-corporeal dream life Slater wandered or floated through resplendent and prodigious valleys, meadows, gardens, cities, and palaces of light; in a region unbounded and unknown to man. That there he was no peasant or degenerate, but creature of importance and vivid life; moving proudly and dominantly, and checked only by a certain deadly enemy, who seemed to be a being of visible yet ethereal structure, and who did not appear to be of human shape, since Slater never referred to it as a *man*, or as aught save a *thing*. This *thing* had done Slater some hideous but unnamed wrong, which the maniac (if maniac he were) yearned to avenge. From the manner in which Slater alluded to their dealings, I judged that he and the luminous *thing* had met on equal terms; that in his dream existence the man was himself a luminous *thing* of the same race as his enemy. This impression was sustained by his frequent references to *flying through space* and *burning* all that impeded his progress. Yet these conceptions were formulated in rustic words wholly inadequate to convey them, a circumstance which drove me to the conclusion that if a true dream world indeed existed, oral language was not its medium for the transmission of thought. Could it be that the dream soul inhabiting this inferior body was desperately struggling to speak things which the simple and halting tongue of dullness could not utter? Could it be that I was face to face with intellectual emanations which would explain the mystery if I could but learn to discover and read them? I did not tell the older physicians of these things, for middle age is sceptical, cynical, and disinclined to accept new ideas. Besides, the head of the institution had but lately warned me in his paternal way that I was overworking; that my mind needed a rest.

===Chinese===

可我从这人身上榨不出任何确切的东西。我全部调查的总和是：在一种半实体的梦的生命里，斯莱特游荡或漂浮过光的辉煌浩大的谷地、草甸、园囿、城池和宫殿；在一个无垠的、人所不知的地界。在那里，他不是农夫也不是退化者，而是个要紧而鲜活的生命；他骄傲而威严地行动，只受一个致命的仇敌牵制——那似乎是一个可见而缥缈结构的存在，而且不像人形，因为斯莱特从不称它为*人*，只称它为一个*东西*。这*东西*害斯莱特吃了一桩可怕而无名的亏，这疯子（如果他是疯子）渴欲报仇。从斯莱特提到他们交往的口气，我判断他和那发光的*东西*是平等相会的；在梦的存在里，这人自己也是一个发光的*东西*，同他仇敌同族。他屡屡提到*穿越太空飞翔*和*烧掉*一切阻碍，也印证了这印象。然而这些构想都披着全然不配传达它们的村野字眼，这一情势使我得出结论：倘若真有一个梦的世界存在，口头语言并不是它传递思想的媒介。会不会是，栖居在这具下等躯体里的梦之魂，正拼命挣扎着要说一些迟钝者简单结巴的舌头说不出的事？会不会是，我正面对着智慧的流射，只要我学会发现并解读它们，那谜便可解？这些我没有告诉年长的医生们，因为中年是多疑的、玩世的、不肯接受新想法的。再说，院长新近还以父辈的口气警告过我，说我劳碌过度，脑子需要歇息。

===Original===

It had long been my belief that human thought consists basically of atomic or molecular motion, convertible into ether waves of radiant energy like heat, light, and electricity. This belief had early led me to contemplate the possibility of telepathy or mental communication by means of suitable apparatus, and I had in my college days prepared a set of transmitting and receiving instruments somewhat similar to the cumbrous devices employed in wireless telegraphy at that crude, pre-radio period. These I had tested with a fellow-student; but achieving no result, had soon packed them away with other scientific odds and ends for possible future use. Now, in my intense desire to probe into the dream life of Joe Slater, I sought these instruments again; and spent several days in repairing them for action. When they were complete once more I missed no opportunity for their trial. At each outburst of Slater’s violence, I would fit the transmitter to his forehead and the receiver to my own; constantly making delicate adjustments for various hypothetical wavelengths of intellectual energy. I had but little notion of how the thought-impressions would, if successfully conveyed, arouse an intelligent response in my brain; but I felt certain that I could detect and interpret them. Accordingly I continued my experiments, though informing no one of their nature.

---

===Chinese===

我久已相信，人的思想基本上由原子或分子的运动构成，可以转化为热、光、电一类辐射能的以太波。这信念早早引我设想，凭借适当的器械，或有心灵感应或思想通信的可能；大学时代我便备了一套收发仪器，同那个粗糙的、前无线电时代无线电极笨重的装置颇有几分相像。我曾同一个同学试验过；毫无结果，不久便连同别的科学零碎一起收起，以备将来或有用处。如今，出于探究乔·斯莱特梦之生命的强烈愿望，我把这些仪器又找了出来，花了好几天修整待用。它们重新齐备之后，我不放过任何一试的机会。斯莱特每次狂乱发作，我便把发射器贴上他的前额，接收器贴上我自己的，不断为思想能量的种种假想波长做着细微的调校。思想印象倘若真传送成功，会怎样在我脑中唤起智性的回应，我几乎无从想象；但我确信我能侦到并解读它们。于是我把实验继续下去，没有告诉任何人它们的性质。

---

===Original===

It was on the twenty-first of February, 1901, that the thing occurred. As I look back across the years I realise how unreal it seems; and sometimes half-wonder if old Dr. Fenton was not right when he charged it all to my excited imagination. I recall that he listened with great kindness and patience when I told him, but afterward gave me a nerve-powder and arranged for the half-year’s vacation on which I departed the next week. That fateful night I was wildly agitated and perturbed, for despite the excellent care he had received, Joe Slater was unmistakably dying. Perhaps it was his mountain freedom that he missed, or perhaps the turmoil in his brain had grown too acute for his rather sluggish physique; but at all events the flame of vitality flickered low in the decadent body. He was drowsy near the end, and as darkness fell he dropped off into a troubled sleep. I did not strap on the straitjacket as was customary when he slept, since I saw that he was too feeble to be dangerous, even if he woke in mental disorder once more before passing away. But I did place upon his head and mine the two ends of my cosmic “radio” hoping against hope for a first and last message from the dream world in the brief time remaining. In the cell with us was one nurse, a mediocre fellow who did not understand the purpose of the apparatus, or think to inquire into my course. As the hours wore on I saw his head droop awkwardly in sleep, but I did not disturb him. I myself, lulled by the rhythmical breathing of the healthy and the dying man, must have nodded a little later.

===Chinese===

那件事发生在一九〇一年二月二十一日。如今回望隔着这些年，我觉出它多么不真实；有时几乎要疑心，老芬顿医生把它一股脑归给我的兴奋的想象，未尝不对。我记得我讲给他听时，他和气耐心地听着，随后却给了我一包镇静药粉，又安排了半年假期，我下星期便动身走了。那决定命运的一夜，我心乱如麻，因为尽管护理周到，乔·斯莱特分明是快死了。也许他渴念的是山中的自由，也许他脑中的骚乱已长得他那迟钝的体格受不住；总之，生命的火苗在那具败坏的身体里摇曳欲熄。临了时他昏昏沉沉，天一黑便坠入烦乱睡眠。我没有照惯例在他睡时系上约束衣，因为我看得出他虚弱得已无危险，即便去世前再一次精神错乱地醒来。但我确实把我那“宇宙无线电”的两端安放在他的头和我的头上，抱着万一的希望，指望在剩下的短促时间里，收到来自梦世界的第一道、也是最后一道讯息。同在病房里的还有一名护士，一个平庸的家伙，既不懂器械的用意，也没想到要过问我的行止。时辰一点点过去，我看见他的头在睡眠中别扭地垂下，我没有惊动他。我自己，被病人那垂死之人均匀的呼吸催眠，想必稍后也打起了盹。

===Original===

The sound of weird lyric melody was what aroused me. Chords, vibrations, and harmonic ecstasies echoed passionately on every hand; while on my ravished sight burst the stupendous spectacle of ultimate beauty. Walls, columns, and architraves of living fire blazed effulgently around the spot where I seemed to float in air; extending upward to an infinitely high vaulted dome of indescribable splendour. Blending with this display of palatial magnificence, or rather, supplanting it at times in kaleidoscopic rotation, were glimpses of wide plains and graceful valleys, high mountains and inviting grottoes; covered with every lovely attribute of scenery which my delighted eye could conceive of, yet formed wholly of some glowing, ethereal plastic entity, which in consistency partook as much of spirit as of matter. As I gazed, I perceived that my own brain held the key to these enchanting metamorphoses; for each vista which appeared to me, was the one my changing mind most wished to behold. Amidst this elysian realm I dwelt not as a stranger, for each sight and sound was familiar to me; just as it had been for uncounted aeons of eternity before, and would be for like eternities to come.

===Chinese===

把我唤醒的是奇异如歌的旋律。和弦、震颤与和声的狂喜，在四面八方激荡回响；而扑进我被劫夺的视界的，是极致之美的壮丽奇观。活的火焰筑成的墙、柱和楣梁，在我仿佛凌空漂浮的地方周围辉煌地燃烧，向上延展成一座不可名状之壮丽的、无限高拱的穹顶。同这场宫殿式的豪华交织在一起——或者说，在万花筒般的轮转中不时取而代之的——是宽阔的平原和秀美的山谷、高山和诱人的洞窟的种种矄见；覆着我这双欣喜的眼睛所能想望的风景的一切美妙属性，却全由某种发光的、缥缈的可塑实体构成，其质地既是物质，也是精神。我凝望时，察觉我自己的脑掌握着这些迷人形变的钥匙；因为每幅展现给我的远景，正是我变动的心最想看见的那一幅。在这极乐的境域里，我居留得并不像个生客，因为每一景每一声我都熟稔；正如在那之前的无法计数的永恒纪元里一样，也将在此后同样漫长的永恒里一样。

===Original===

Then the resplendent aura of my brother of light drew near and held colloquy with me, soul to soul, with silent and perfect interchange of thought. The hour was one of approaching triumph, for was not my fellow-being escaping at last from a degrading periodic bondage; escaping forever, and preparing to follow the accursed oppressor even unto the uttermost fields of ether, that upon it might be wrought a flaming cosmic vengeance which would shake the spheres? We floated thus for a little time, when I perceived a slight blurring and fading of the objects around us, as though some force were recalling me to earth﻿—where I least wished to go. The form near me seemed to feel a change also, for it gradually brought its discourse towards a conclusion, and itself prepared to quit the scene; fading from my sight at a rate somewhat less rapid than that of the other objects. A few more thoughts were exchanged, and I knew that the luminous one and I were being recalled to bondage, though for my brother of light it would be the last time. The sorry planet shell being well-nigh spent, in less than an hour my fellow would be free to pursue the oppressor along the Milky Way and past the hither stars to the very confines of infinity.

===Chinese===

随后，我那光的兄弟的辉煌光晕临近了，同我交谈起来，魂对魂，沉默而完美的思想交换。那是一个临近胜利的时辰，因为我的同伴不正终于逃脱一场卑贱的、周期性的枷锁么？永远地逃脱，并准备追踪那受咒的压迫者，直赶到以太的最远田野，好在那里施行一场撼动诸天的、烈焰般的宇宙复仇？我们这样漂浮了片刻，我察觉我们周围的事物微微模糊、褪色，仿佛有种力量在把我召回地球——我最不愿去的地方。我身边的那形体像是也感到了变化，因为它渐渐把话引向收束，自己也准备离场，从我眼前消隐，速率比其余事物略缓。又交换了几缕思想，我知道那发光者和我都在被召回顾缚，虽然对我的光之兄弟，这将是最后一次。这可悲的行星躯壳将近用尽，不出一个钟头，我的同伴便将自由，可以沿着银河、越过近侧的群星，追踪那压迫者直趋无限的边界。

===Original===

A well-defined shock separates my final impression of the fading scene of light from my sudden and somewhat shamefaced awakening and straightening up in my chair as I saw the dying figure on the couch move hesitantly. Joe Slater was indeed awaking, though probably for the last time. As I looked more closely, I saw that in the sallow cheeks shone spots of colour which had never before been present. The lips, too, seemed unusual; being tightly compressed, as if by the force of a stronger character than had been Slater’s. The whole face finally began to grow tense, and the head turned restlessly with closed eyes. I did not rouse the sleeping nurse, but readjusted the slightly disarranged headbands of my telepathic “radio” intent to catch any parting message the dreamer might have to deliver. All at once the head turned sharply in my direction and the eyes fell open, causing me to stare in blank amazement at what I beheld. The man who had been Joe Slater, the Catskill decadent, was now gazing at me with a pair of luminous, expanding eyes whose blue seemed subtly to have deepened. Neither mania nor degeneracy was visible in that gaze, and I felt beyond a doubt that I was viewing a face behind which lay an active mind of high order.

At this juncture my brain became aware of a steady external influence operating upon it. I closed my eyes to concentrate my thoughts more profoundly, and was rewarded by the positive knowledge that *my long-sought mental message had come at last*. Each transmitted idea formed rapidly in my mind, and though no actual language was employed, my habitual association of conception and expression was so great that I seemed to be receiving the message in ordinary English.

===Chinese===

一道清晰的震荡，把我对那渐渐隐没的光之景象的最后印象，同我猛然而带愧色的惊醒分开——我在椅子上直起身，看见沙发上垂死的身形迟疑地动了。乔·斯莱特确实在醒来，虽然多半是最后一次。我细看时，看见那蜡黄的双颊上闪着从未有过的色斑。嘴唇也不寻常：紧紧抿着，像被一个比斯莱特更强的性格的力气抿住。整张脸终于开始绷紧，头闭着眼不安地转动。我没有唤醒打盹的护士，只把我那心灵感应“无线电”微微挪歪的头带重新正了正，一心要接住这梦者临别时或有的任何讯息。骤然间，那头猛地转向我这方，眼睛睁开了，叫我茫然惊愕地瞪着我所看见的。方才还是乔·斯莱特、那个卡兹奇退化者的人，此刻正用一双发光的、扩大着的眼睛望我，那蓝色像是微妙地深了。那凝视里没有疯狂，也没有退化，我毫不怀疑，我正望着一张脸，其后卧着一个高级的、活跃的心智。

正在这时，我的脑察觉到一股持续的外来影响作用其上。我闭上眼，好把思想凝得更深，随即得了确凿的认知：*我久觅的心灵讯息终于到了*。每个传送来的观念迅速在我心中成形，虽没有使用任何实际的语言，我那概念与表达的惯常联结如此之强，我仿佛是在用寻常的英语接收讯息。

===Original===

“*Joe Slater is dead*,” came the soul-petrifying voice or agency from beyond the wall of sleep. My opened eyes sought the couch of pain in curious horror, but the blue eyes were still calmly gazing, and the countenance was still intelligently animated. “He is better dead, for he was unfit to bear the active intellect of cosmic entity. His gross body could not undergo the needed adjustments between ethereal life and planet life. He was too much of an animal, too little a man; yet it is through his deficiency that you have come to discover me, for the cosmic and planet souls rightly should never meet. He has been my torment and diurnal prison for forty-two of your terrestrial years. I am an entity like that which you yourself become in the freedom of dreamless sleep, I am your brother of light, and have floated with you in the effulgent valleys. It is not permitted me to tell your waking earth-self of your real self, but we are all roamers of vast spaces and travellers in many ages. Next year I may be dwelling in the Egypt which you call ancient, or in the cruel empire of Tsan Chan which is to come three thousand years hence. You and I have drifted to the worlds that reel about the red Arcturus, and dwelt in the bodies of the insect-philosophers that crawl proudly over the fourth moon of Jupiter. How little does the earth-self know life and its extent! How little, indeed, ought it to know for its own tranquillity! Of the oppressor I cannot speak. You on earth have unwittingly felt its distant presence﻿—you who without knowing idly gave the blinking beacon the name of *Algol, the Daemon-Star*. It is to meet and conquer the oppressor that I have vainly striven for aeons, held back by bodily encumbrances. Tonight I go as a Nemesis bearing just and blazingly cataclysmic vengeance. *Watch me in the sky close by the Daemon-Star.* I cannot speak longer, for the body of Joe Slater grows cold and rigid, and the coarse brains are ceasing to vibrate as I wish. You have been my friend in the cosmos; you have been my only friend on this planet﻿—the only soul to sense and seek for me within the repellent form which lies on this couch. We shall meet again﻿—perhaps in the shining mists of Orion’s Sword, perhaps on a bleak plateau in prehistoric Asia.

===Chinese===

“*乔·斯莱特死了*，”睡眠之墙的那一边传来那使魂魄僵固的声音或作用。我睁开的眼睛带着奇异的恐怖去寻那张病榻，可那双蓝眼睛仍在平静地凝望，那张脸仍在智性地生动着。“他死了倒好，因为他那具躯壳，当不起宇宙实体的活跃心智。他粗劣的身体经不起以太生命与行星生命之间必需的调适。他兽性太多，人性太少；然而正因他的欠缺，你才得以发现我，因为宇宙的灵魂同行星的灵魂，本不该相会。四十二个你们的地球年，他一直是我的酷刑和昼夜的牢狱。我是一个实体，同你自己在不梦的睡眠的自由中所变成的那个一样；我是你的光之兄弟，曾同你一起漂浮在辉煌的谷地里。我不获准向你清醒的尘世之我讲述你真实的自我，但我们都是浩瀚空间的漫游者，许多纪元的旅人。明年，我或许住在你们称为古代的埃及，或许住在三千年后将有的残暴的禅占帝国。你和我曾漂流到绕着红色大角星旋转的那些世界，住过骄傲地爬行于木星第四颗卫星上的昆虫哲学家们的身体。尘世之我对生命及其边界知道得何其少！的确，为了它自己的安宁，又何其应当少知道！至于那压迫者，我不能说。你们在地球上曾无意间感到它遥远的存在——你们不知情地、随意地把那颗眨眼的灯塔命名作*大陵五，魔星*。正是为遭遇并征服那压迫者，我才徒然挣扎了亿万年，总被身体的拖累所阻。今夜我去当一位复仇女神，带着正义的、烈焰般灾变的复仇。*在魔星近旁的天上望着我*。我不能再说了，因为乔·斯莱特的躯体正在变冷变僵，那粗劣的脑子就要停止我所愿的振动。你在宇宙中做过我的朋友；你在这行星上做过我唯一的朋友——唯一在这张卧榻上、这具可憎形骸里察觉我、寻找我的灵魂。我们还会再见——也许在猎户座之剑的辉光雾霭里，也许在史前亚洲的一块荒凉高原上。

===Original===

Perhaps in unremembered dreams tonight; perhaps in some other form an aeon hence, when the solar system shall have been swept away.”

At this point the thought-waves abruptly ceased, and the pale eyes of the dreamer﻿—or can I say dead man?﻿—commenced to glaze fishily. In a half-stupor I crossed over to the couch and felt of his wrist, but found it cold, stiff, and pulseless. The sallow cheeks paled again, and the thick lips fell open, disclosing the repulsively rotten fangs of the degenerate Joe Slater. I shivered, pulled a blanket over the hideous face, and awakened the nurse. Then I left the cell and went silently to my room. I had an instant and unaccountable craving for a sleep whose dreams I should not remember.

The climax? What plain tale of science can boast of such a rhetorical effect? I have merely set down certain things appealing to me as facts, allowing you to construe them as you will. As I have already admitted, my superior, old Dr. Fenton, denies the reality of everything I have related. He vows that I was broken down with nervous strain, and badly in need of the long vacation on full pay which he so generously gave me. He assures me on his professional honour that Joe Slater was but a low-grade paranoic, whose fantastic notions must have come from the crude hereditary folktales which circulate in even the most decadent of communities. All this he tells me﻿—yet I cannot forget what I saw in the sky on the night after Slater died. Lest you think me a biased witness, another pen must add this final testimony, which may perhaps supply the climax you expect. I will quote the following account of the star *Nova Persei* verbatim from the pages of that eminent astronomical authority, Prof. Garrett P. Serviss:

“On February 22, 1901, a marvelous new star was discovered by Dr. Anderson of Edinburgh, *not very far from Algol*. No star had been visible at that point before. Within 24 hours the stranger had become so bright that it outshone Capella. In a week or two it had visibly faded, and in the course of a few months it was hardly discernible with the naked eye.”

===Chinese===

也许就在今夜不被记忆的梦里；也许亿万年后的另一种形骸里，等太阳系已被扫荡一空。”

话到这里，思想波戛然而止，梦者那双苍白的眼睛——或者说，那死人的眼睛？——开始发鱼一般呆滞的光。我半呆半醒地走到床边摸他的腕，却是冷的、硬的、没有脉。蜡黄的双颊又灰下去，厚嘴唇张开，露出退化者乔·斯莱特那口烂得叫人恶心的牙。我打了个寒噤，拉过一条毯子盖上那张可怕的脸，唤醒了护士。随后我走出病房，默默回到自己屋里。我有一种即刻的、无从解释的对睡眠的渴求——一场我不该记得其梦的睡眠。

高潮？科学的平淡叙述，哪一篇敢夸这样的修辞效果？我不过记下几件在我看来是事实的东西，任凭你们随自己的意思去解。我已承认，我的上司老芬顿医生，否认我讲的一切的真实性。他发誓说我是神经劳损垮了，急需他慷慨给我的那段带全薪的长假。他以职业名誉向我保证，乔·斯莱特不过是个低等的偏执狂，他那套奇想必出自粗劣的遗传民间故事——哪怕最败坏的村落里也流传的那种。这些他都对我说了——可我忘不了斯莱特死后那夜我在天上看见的东西。免得你们当我是偏心的证人，另一支笔必须补上这最后的证词，它也许恰好供给你所期待的高潮。我从那位杰出的天文权威加勒特·P·瑟维斯教授的书页上，逐字抄下关于英仙座新星（*Nova Persei*）的这段记载：

“一九〇一年二月二十二日，爱丁堡的安德森博士发现一颗奇异的新星，*离大陵五不远*。此前那一点上本无可见之星。二十四小时之内，这陌生者亮得超过了五车二。一两周后它肉眼可见地转暗，几个月之后，肉眼已几乎分辨不出。”

## Celephaïs / 塞勒菲斯
===Original===

In a dream Kuranes saw the city in the valley, and the seacoast beyond, and the snowy peak overlooking the sea, and the gaily painted galleys that sail out of the harbour toward distant regions where the sea meets the sky. In a dream it was also that he came by his name of Kuranes, for when awake he was called by another name. Perhaps it was natural for him to dream a new name; for he was the last of his family, and alone among the indifferent millions of London, so there were not many to speak to him and to remind him who he had been. His money and lands were gone, and he did not care for the ways of the people about him, but preferred to dream and write of his dreams. What he wrote was laughed at by those to whom he showed it, so that after a time he kept his writings to himself, and finally ceased to write. The more he withdrew from the world about him, the more wonderful became his dreams; and it would have been quite futile to try to describe them on paper. Kuranes was not modern, and did not think like others who wrote. Whilst they strove to strip from life its embroidered robes of myth, and to show in naked ugliness the foul thing that is reality, Kuranes sought for beauty alone. When truth and experience failed to reveal it, he sought it in fancy and illusion, and found it on his very doorstep, amid the nebulous memories of childhood tales and dreams.

There are not many persons who know what wonders are opened to them in the stories and visions of their youth; for when as children we listen and dream, we think but half-formed thoughts, and when as men we try to remember, we are dulled and prosaic with the poison of life. But some of us awake in the night with strange phantasms of enchanted hills and gardens, of fountains that sing in the sun, of golden cliffs overhanging murmuring seas, of plains that stretch down to sleeping cities of bronze and stone, and of shadowy companies of heroes that ride caparisoned white horses along the edges of thick forests; and then we know that we have looked back through the ivory gates into that world of wonder which was ours before we were wise and unhappy.

===Chinese===

在梦里，库拉尼斯看见了谷中的城，看见城外远处的海岸，俯临大海的雪峰，还有那些驶出海港、航向海天相接之远方的、漆得鲜亮的大帆船。也是在梦里，他得了库拉尼斯这个名字，因为醒着的时候，人们叫他另一个名字。他给自己梦出一个新名字，也许是自然的：他是家族最后一人，独自混在伦敦冷漠的几百万中国人间，没有几个人同他说话，提醒他曾经是谁。他的钱和田产都完了，他也不屑于身边人的营生，宁可做梦，再写下他的梦。他写下的东西，给他看的人都要笑，于是过了一个时期，他把文稿藏起来只给自己，最后干脆不写了。他从周遭的世界退得越远，梦就变得越奇妙；想用纸笔描画它们，已是全然徒劳。库拉尼斯不现代，也不像别的写作人那样思想。他们拼命剥去生活那绣满神话的锦袍，要把“现实”这秽物以赤裸的丑态示人，库拉尼斯却单单求美。当真实与经验不肯把它显露，他便到幻想和幻境里去寻，并在自家的门槛上寻到了它——在童年故事与童年之梦的朦胧回忆中间。

没有多少人知道，他们少年时代的故事和幻景为他们敞开过怎样的奇迹；因为孩提时我们听着、梦着，思想只成形一半；成人后想回忆，却已被生活的毒液弄得迟钝而乏味。但我们中间有些人，会在夜里醒来，带着种种怪异的幻象——着魔的山丘和花园，阳光下歌唱的泉水，临着低语大海的金色悬崖，一路铺展到青铜与石头沉睡之城的平原，还有沿着密林边缘、骑着披挂彩衣的白马的英雄们的朦胧行列；于是我们知道，我们已从象牙之门回望了那个奇迹世界——在我们变聪明、变不幸之前，它本是我们的。

===Original===

Kuranes came very suddenly upon his old world of childhood. He had been dreaming of the house where he had been born; the great stone house covered with ivy, where thirteen generations of his ancestors had lived, and where he had hoped to die. It was moonlight, and he had stolen out into the fragrant summer night, through the gardens, down the terraces, past the great oaks of the park, and along the long white road to the village. The village seemed very old, eaten away at the edge like the moon which had commenced to wane, and Kuranes wondered whether the peaked roofs of the small houses hid sleep or death. In the streets were spears of long grass, and the windowpanes on either side were either broken or filmily staring. Kuranes had not lingered, but had plodded on as though summoned toward some goal. He dared not disobey the summons for fear it might prove an illusion like the urges and aspirations of waking life, which do not lead to any goal. Then he had been drawn down a lane that led off from the village street toward the channel cliffs, and had come to the end of things﻿—to the precipice and the abyss where all the village and all the world fell abruptly into the unechoing emptiness of infinity, and where even the sky ahead was empty and unlit by the crumbling moon and the peering stars. Faith had urged him on, over the precipice and into the gulf, where he had floated down, down, down; past dark, shapeless, undreamed dreams, faintly glowing spheres that may have been partly dreamed dreams, and laughing winged things that seemed to mock the dreamers of all the worlds. Then a rift seemed to open in the darkness before him, and he saw the city of the valley, glistening radiantly far, far below, with a background of sea and sky, and a snow-capped mountain near the shore.

===Chinese===

库拉尼斯是猛然撞回他童年的旧世界的。他梦见了出生的宅子；那座爬满常春藤的大石宅，他家十三代先人住过，他也曾希望死在里面。月光之下，他悄悄溜进芬芳的夏夜，穿过花园，下了层层台地，绕过园里的大橡树，沿长长的白色大路向村子去。村子显得很老，边缘像开始亏蚀的月亮一样残缺，库拉尼斯暗想，那些尖顶小屋里藏着的，是睡眠还是死亡。街上长着一丛丛长草，两侧的窗玻璃要么破了，要么蒙着薄膜似的琚视。库拉尼斯没有流连，只管向前跋涉，像被什么召唤着奔向一个目标。他不敢违抗这召唤，唯恐它也像清醒生活里那些冲动和渴望一样，结果是幻象，引不到任何目标。随后他被引下村街旁一条小巷，那巷子通向海峡悬崖，他走到了万物的尽头——悬崖和深渊，整个村子、整个世界在那里陡然跌进无穷的、不回声的空虚，连头顶的天空也是空的，残月和窥视的星照不亮它。信念推着他向前，越过悬崖，进入深湾，在那里他向下、向下、向下地漂浮；掠过黑暗的、无形无状的、未经梦过的梦，掠过微微发光、或许半是被梦过的球体，掠过长着翅膀、笑着、像在嘲弄一切世界的梦者的东西。随后，黑暗在他面前裂开一道口子，他看见了谷中之城，在极远极远的下方灿烂生辉，衬着海与天的背景，近岸处一座雪顶的山。

===Original===

Kuranes had awaked the very moment he beheld the city, yet he knew from his brief glance that it was none other than Celephaïs, in the Valley of Ooth-Nargai beyond the Tanarian Hills, where his spirit had dwelt all the eternity of an hour one summer afternoon very long ago, when he had slipt away from his nurse and let the warm sea-breeze lull him to sleep as he watched the clouds from the cliff near the village. He had protested then, when they had found him, waked him, and carried him home, for just as he was aroused he had been about to sail in a golden galley for those alluring regions where the sea meets the sky. And now he was equally resentful of awaking, for he had found his fabulous city after forty weary years.

But three nights afterward Kuranes came again to Celephaïs. As before, he dreamed first of the village that was asleep or dead, and of the abyss down which one must float silently; then the rift appeared again, and he beheld the glittering minarets of the city, and saw the graceful galleys riding at anchor in the blue harbour, and watched the ginkgo trees of Mount Aran swaying in the sea-breeze. But this time he was not snatched away, and like a winged being settled gradually over a grassy hillside till finally his feet rested gently on the turf. He had indeed come back to the Valley of Ooth-Nargai and the splendid city of Celephaïs.

===Chinese===

库拉尼斯望见城的那一瞬便醒了，可就凭那一瞥他知道，那不是别的，正是塞勒菲斯，在塔纳里亚丘陵之外的奥斯-纳尔盖谷地里。很久以前一个夏日午后，他的魂曾在那里栖居过整整一个钟头的永恒——那时他从保姆身边溜开，任温暖的海风把自己催眠，在村边悬崖上看云。后来人们找到他、唤醒他、抱他回家，他还抗议来着，因为被惊醒的那一刻，他正要乘一艘金色的单桅帆船，驶向那些海天相接的迷人地方。此刻他同样怨恨这醒来，因为寻了四十个疲惫的年头，他终于寻到了他传说的城。

但三夜之后，库拉尼斯又来到了塞勒菲斯。同先前一样，他先梦见那座睡着或死了的村子，梦见人须默默漂浮而下的深渊；随后裂口又现，他望见城中闪光的宣礼塔，看见优雅的大帆船泊在蓝色的港里，看着阿兰山的银杏在海风里摇曳。可这一次他没有被拽走，而像一个有翼的存在，缓缓降落在一片草坡上，末了双脚轻轻踏上草皮。他果真回到了奥斯-纳尔盖谷地，回到了辉煌的塞勒菲斯城。

===Original===

Down the hill amid scented grasses and brilliant flowers walked Kuranes, over the bubbling Naraxa on the small wooden bridge where he had carved his name so many years ago, and through the whispering grove to the great stone bridge by the city gate. All was as of old, nor were the marble walls discoloured, nor the polished bronze statues upon them tarnished. And Kuranes saw that he need not tremble lest the things he knew be vanished; for even the sentries on the ramparts were the same, and still as young as he remembered them. When he entered the city, past the bronze gates and over the onyx pavements, the merchants and camel-drivers greeted him as if he had never been away; and it was the same at the turquoise temple of Nath-Horthath, where the orchid-wreathed priests told him that there is no time in Ooth-Nargai, but only perpetual youth. Then Kuranes walked through the Street of Pillars to the seaward wall, where gathered the traders and sailors, and strange men from the regions where the sea meets the sky. There he stayed long, gazing out over the bright harbour where the ripples sparkled beneath an unknown sun, and where rode lightly the galleys from far places over the water. And he gazed also upon Mount Aran rising regally from the shore, its lower slopes green with swaying trees and its white summit touching the sky.

===Chinese===

库拉尼斯沿山而下，穿过香草和繁花，跨过翻腾的纳拉克萨河上的小木桥——多年前他曾在桥上刻下自己的名字——再穿过低语的树丛，到城门边的大石桥。一切都同旧时一样，大理石的墙没有变色，墙上擦亮的铜像没有失光。库拉尼斯明白，他不必再战栗，唯恐他熟知的事物已经消逝；连城垛上的哨兵都是旧人，仍同他记忆里一样年轻。进了城，穿过铜门，踏着缟玛瑙铺的路面，商人和赶骆驼的向他招呼，仿佛他从不曾离开；绿松石的纳斯-霍塔斯神庙里也是一样，戴兰花花环的祭司告诉他：奥斯-纳尔盖没有时间，只有永远的青春。随后库拉尼斯沿石柱大街走到临海的城墙边，那里聚着商人、水手，和来自海天相接之地的怪人。他在那里流连良久，眺望明亮的港湾，涟漪在一轮不知名的太阳下闪光，远方来的大帆船轻盈地浮在水面。他也眺望阿兰山，帝王一般从岸边升起，低坡绿着摇曳的树，白色的山顶触着天空。

===Original===

More than ever Kuranes wished to sail in a galley to the far places of which he had heard so many strange tales, and he sought again the captain who had agreed to carry him so long ago. He found the man, Athib, sitting on the same chest of spices he had sat upon before, and Athib seemed not to realise that any time had passed. Then the two rowed to a galley in the harbour, and giving orders to the oarsmen, commenced to sail out into the billowy Cerenarian Sea that leads to the sky. For several days they glided undulatingly over the water, till finally they came to the horizon, where the sea meets the sky. Here the galley paused not at all, but floated easily in the blue of the sky among fleecy clouds tinted with rose. And far beneath the keel Kuranes could see strange lands and rivers and cities of surpassing beauty, spread indolently in the sunshine which seemed never to lessen or disappear. At length Athib told him that their journey was near its end, and that they would soon enter the harbour of Serannian, the pink marble city of the clouds, which is built on that ethereal coast where the west wind flows into the sky; but as the highest of the city’s carven towers came into sight there was a sound somewhere in space, and Kuranes awaked in his London garret.

===Chinese===

库拉尼斯比任何时候都渴望乘一艘大帆船，去那些他听过许多怪谈的远方，他重新寻找多年前答应载他的那位船长。他找到了那人，阿西布，还坐在他从前坐过的那口香料箱上，阿西布像是根本不觉得光阴流过。两人划到港中一艘大帆船上，向桨手下过令，便扬帆驶入通往天空的、涌着波涛的塞雷纳利亚海。好几天，他们在水上起伏滑行，终于来到地平线，海与天相接的地方。大帆船毫不迟疑，径自浮进天空的蓝色里，浮在染着玫瑰色的絮云之间。龙骨底下极深处，库拉尼斯望得见奇异的大地、河流和美得超绝的城池，慵懒地铺在永不衰减、永不消逝的阳光里。末了，阿西布告诉他，旅程将尽，他们马上要进塞拉尼安的港了——云中的粉红大理石之城，建在以太的海岸上，西风在那里流入天空；可正当城中最高的雕塔映入眼帘，太空里某处响起一个声音，库拉尼斯在他伦敦的阁楼里醒了。

===Original===

For many months after that Kuranes sought the marvellous city of Celephaïs and its sky-bound galleys in vain; and though his dreams carried him to many gorgeous and unheard-of places, no one whom he met could tell him how to find Ooth-Nargai, beyond the Tanarian Hills. One night he went flying over dark mountains where there were faint, lone campfires at great distances apart, and strange, shaggy herds with tinkling bells on the leaders; and in the wildest part of this hilly country, so remote that few men could ever have seen it, he found a hideously ancient wall or causeway of stone zigzagging along the ridges and valleys; too gigantic ever to have risen by human hands, and of such a length that neither end of it could be seen. Beyond that wall in the grey dawn he came to a land of quaint gardens and cherry trees, and when the sun rose he beheld such beauty of red and white flowers, green foliage and lawns, white paths, diamond brooks, blue lakelets, carven bridges, and red-roofed pagodas, that he for a moment forgot Celephaïs in sheer delight. But he remembered it again when he walked down a white path toward a red-roofed pagoda, and would have questioned the people of that land about it, had he not found that there were no people there, but only birds and bees and butterflies. On another night Kuranes walked up a damp stone spiral stairway endlessly, and came to a tower window overlooking a mighty plain and river lit by the full moon; and in the silent city that spread away from the riverbank he thought he beheld some feature or arrangement which he had known before. He would have descended and asked the way to Ooth-Nargai had not a fearsome aurora sputtered up from some remote place beyond the horizon, showing the ruin and antiquity of the city, and the stagnation of the reedy river, and the death lying upon that land, as it had lain since King Kynaratholis came home from his conquests to find the vengeance of the gods.

===Chinese===

此后好几个月，库拉尼斯徒劳地追寻着奇妙的塞勒菲斯城和它驶向天空的大帆船；他的梦虽把他带到许多瑰丽而闻所未闻的地方，遇见的人却没一个说得清怎样找到塔纳里亚丘陵外的奥斯-纳尔盖。一夜，他飞过黑暗的群山，山间远远地隔着一点一点微弱孤单的篝火，还有怪模怪样、毛茸茸的兽群，领头者颈上铃铛可当；在这山区最荒僻、少有人见过的深处，他发现一道骇人地古老的石墙，或者说是石砌长堤，沿山脊和谷地之字而行；它巨大得绝非人手所能筑起，又长得两端都望不见。灰色黎明里，过了那道墙，他来到一片古雅的花园和樱桃树之地；太阳升起时，他看见红花白花、绿荫草地、白色小径、钻石似的溪流、蓝色的小湖、雕花的桥和红顶的宝塔，那样一种美，叫他一时纯粹出于欢喜竟忘了塞勒菲斯。可当他沿一条白径走向一座红顶宝塔时，他又记起了它，本想向那地方的人打听，却发现那里没有人，只有鸟、蜜蜂和蝴蝶。又一夜，库拉尼斯沿一道潮湿的石旋梯无休止地向上走，走到一扇塔窗前，俯瞰月光照亮的辽阔平原和大河；在那条自河岸铺展开去的寂静之城里，他以为认出了某种他从前熟识的面貌或格局。他本想下去问一问去奥斯-纳尔盖的路，不料一团可怕的极光从地平线外某个远方噼啪腾起，照出城的倾颓与古老，照出芦苇塞河道的一潭死水，照出覆在那片土地上的死亡——自基纳拉索利斯王远征归来、遭了诸神报复的那天起，它就一直这样躺着。

===Original===

So Kuranes sought fruitlessly for the marvellous city of Celephaïs and its galleys that sail to Serannian in the sky, meanwhile seeing many wonders and once barely escaping from the high-priest not to be described, which wears a yellow silken mask over its face and dwells all alone in a prehistoric stone monastery on the cold desert plateau of Leng. In time he grew so impatient of the bleak intervals of day that he began buying drugs in order to increase his periods of sleep. Hashish helped a great deal, and once sent him to a part of space where form does not exist, but where glowing gases study the secrets of existence. And a violet-coloured gas told him that this part of space was outside what he had called infinity. The gas had not heard of planets and organisms before, but identified Kuranes merely as one from the infinity where matter, energy, and gravitation exist. Kuranes was now very anxious to return to minaret-studded Celephaïs, and increased his doses of drugs; but eventually he had no more money left, and could buy no drugs. Then one summer day he was turned out of his garret, and wandered aimlessly through the streets, drifting over a bridge to a place where the houses grew thinner and thinner. And it was there that fulfillment came, and he met the cortege of knights come from Celephaïs to bear him thither forever.

===Chinese===

就这样，库拉尼斯徒劳地寻找着奇妙的塞勒菲斯城和它驶向云中塞拉尼安的大帆船，其间见识了许多奇迹，还有一回险些没躲开那位不可名状的大祭司——它脸罩黄色丝面具，独居在冷原（Leng）寒冷荒漠高原上一座史前的石头修道院里。渐渐地，他再也受不了白昼那凄凉的间隔，开始买药，好延长睡眠。大麻脂帮了大忙，有一回把他送进了太空的一隅，那里没有形体，只有发光的气体研究存在的秘密。一团紫色的气体告诉他，太空的这一隅在他所谓的“无穷”之外。那气体从前没听说过行星和生物，只把库拉尼斯认作来自“物质、能量和引力皆存在的那重无穷”的来客。库拉尼斯如今急欲回到宣礼塔林立的塞勒菲斯，把药量一加再加；可到头来钱花光了，药也买不成了。随后一个夏日，他被赶出阁楼，在街上游荡，漫无目的，飘过一座桥，到了房屋越来越稀的地方。就在那里，成全来了——他遇上了从塞勒菲斯来的骑士的仪仗，来接他永远归去。

===Original===

Handsome knights they were, astride roan horses and clad in shining armour with tabards of cloth-of-gold curiously emblazoned. So numerous were they, that Kuranes almost mistook them for an army, but their leader told him they were sent in his honour; since it was he who had created Ooth-Nargai in his dreams, on which account he was now to be appointed its chief god forevermore. Then they gave Kuranes a horse and placed him at the head of the cavalcade, and all rode majestically through the downs of Surrey and onward toward the region where Kuranes and his ancestors were born. It was very strange, but as the riders went on they seemed to gallop back through Time; for whenever they passed through a village in the twilight they saw only such houses and villagers as Chaucer or men before him might have seen, and sometimes they saw knights on horseback with small companies of retainers. When it grew dark they travelled more swiftly, till soon they were flying uncannily as if in the air. In the dim dawn they came upon the village which Kuranes had seen alive in his childhood, and asleep or dead in his dreams. It was alive now, and early villagers curtsied as the horsemen clattered down the street and turned off into the lane that ends in the abyss of dreams. Kuranes had previously entered that abyss only at night, and wondered what it would look like by day; so he watched anxiously as the column approached its brink. Just as they galloped up the rising ground to the precipice a golden glare came somewhere out of the east and hid all the landscape in effulgent draperies. The abyss was a seething chaos of roseate and cerulean splendour, and invisible voices sang exultantly as the knightly entourage plunged over the edge and floated gracefully down past glittering clouds and silvery coruscations. Endlessly down the horsemen floated, their chargers pawing the aether as if galloping over golden sands; and then the luminous vapours spread apart to reveal a greater brightness, the brightness of the city Celephaïs, and the seacoast beyond, and the snowy peak overlooking the sea, and the gaily painted galleys that sail out of the harbour toward distant regions where the sea meets the sky.

===Chinese===

那是些英俊的骑士，骑着花斑马，甲胄鲜亮，罩着绣工奇诡的金锦罩袍。人数之多，库拉尼斯几乎错当成一支大军，可领队告诉他，他们是奉他的荣誉派来的；因为正是在他的梦里，奥斯-纳尔盖被创造出来，为此，他如今要被立为它永远的主神。他们给了库拉尼斯一匹马，请他走在队伍最前，一行人威严地驰过萨里的丘陵，朝着库拉尼斯和他祖先出生的地方去。事情非常奇怪：骑士们一路走着，仿佛在沿着时间往回疾驰；因为每当他们在暮色里穿过一座村子，所见到的只是乔叟或乔叟之前的人可能见过的屋舍和村民，有时还看见带着小小一队随从的骑马骑士。天黑之后，他们行得更快，不久便邪门地飞起来，像在空中。朦胧的黎明里，他们来到库拉尼斯童年见过它活着、梦里见它睡着或死了的那个村子。此刻它是活的，早起的村民屈膝行礼，马队嘚嘚地驰下街道，拐进那条尽头是梦之深渊的小巷。库拉尼斯先前只在夜里进过那深渊，不知它在白日是什么模样，便急切地望着队伍走近崖沿。正当他们驰上悬崖前的缓坡，一道金光从东方某处迸出，把全部风景藏进辉煌的帷幔。深渊是一片玫瑰色与天青色的壮丽沸腾，无形的嗓音欢畅地高唱，骑士的扈从冲过崖沿，优雅地漂浮而下，掠过闪光的云和银色的光浪。骑士们无止境地向下漂浮，坐骑刨着以太，像驰过金色的沙原；随后发光的雾气向两边分开，露出更大的光亮——塞勒菲斯城的光亮，和城外远处的海岸，俯临大海的雪峰，还有那些驶出海港、航向海天相接之远方的、漆得鲜亮的大帆船。

===Original===

And Kuranes reigned thereafter over Ooth-Nargai and all the neighbouring regions of dream, and held his court alternately in Celephaïs and in the cloud-fashioned Serannian. He reigns there still, and will reign happily forever, though below the cliffs at Innsmouth the channel tides played mockingly with the body of a tramp who had stumbled through the half-deserted village at dawn; played mockingly, and cast it upon the rocks by ivy-covered Trevor Towers, where a notably fat and especially offensive millionaire brewer enjoys the purchased atmosphere of extinct nobility.

===Chinese===

此后，库拉尼斯统治了奥斯-纳尔盖和梦域所有毗邻的地方，朝廷轮流设在塞勒菲斯和云造的塞拉尼安。他至今仍在那里为王，并将永远快乐地为王；虽然在印斯茅斯的悬崖下，海峡的潮水戏弄着一具流浪汉的尸体——黎明时分，他踉跄穿过了那半空的村子；潮水戏弄着它，把它抛在爬满常春藤的特雷弗塔楼旁的礁石上——那里，一位格外肥胖、尤其讨嫌的百万富翁酿酒商，正享用着他买来的、绝了种的贵族气。

## Cool Air / 冷气
===Original===

You ask me to explain why I am afraid of a draft of cool air; why I shiver more than others upon entering a cold room, and seem nauseated and repelled when the chill of evening creeps through the heat of a mild autumn day. There are those who say I respond to cold as others do to a bad odor, and I am the last to deny the impression. What I will do is to relate the most horrible circumstance I ever encountered, and leave it to you to judge whether or not this forms a suitable explanation of my peculiarity.

It is a mistake to fancy that horror is associated inextricably with darkness, silence, and solitude. I found it in the glare of midafternoon, in the clangor of a metropolis, and in the teeming midst of a shabby and commonplace rooming-house with a prosaic landlady and two stalwart men by my side. In the spring of 1923 I had secured some dreary and unprofitable magazine work in the city of New York; and being unable to pay any substantial rent, began drifting from one cheap boarding establishment to another in search of a room which might combine the qualities of decent cleanliness, endurable furnishings, and very reasonable price. It soon developed that I had only a choice between different evils, but after a time I came upon a house in West Fourteenth Street which disgusted me much less than the others I had sampled.

The place was a four-story mansion of brownstone, dating apparently from the late forties, and fitted with woodwork and marble whose stained and sullied splendor argued a descent from high levels of tasteful opulence. In the rooms, large and lofty, and decorated with impossible paper and ridiculously ornate stucco cornices, there lingered a depressing mustiness and hint of obscure cookery; but the floors were clean, the linen tolerably regular, and the hot water not too often cold or turned off; so that I came to regard it as at least a bearable place to hibernate until one might really live again. The landlady, a slatternly, almost bearded Spanish woman named Herrero, did not annoy me with gossip or with criticisms of the late-burning electric light in my third floor front hall room; and my fellow-lodgers were as quiet and uncommunicative as one might desire, being mostly Spaniards a little above the coarsest and crudest grade. Only the din of streetcars in the thoroughfare below proved a serious annoyance.

===Chinese===

你要我解释，为什么我怕一缕冷气；为什么走进寒冷的房间，我比别人抖得更凶；为什么温和秋日的余温里一旦渗入傍晚的凉意，我便像闻见什么似的恶心、退避。有人说我对冷的反应，就像别人对臭气的反应，这一点我绝不否认。我只想讲一讲我平生遭遇的最骇人的境况，让你们自己判断，它能否充分解释我这怪癖。

以为恐怖必定与黑暗、寂静、孤独难解难分，那是一种误解。我是在午后耀眼的白光里、在大都会的喧嚣里、在一间寒侖而俗气的公寓里撞上它的，身边有一位平庸的女房东，还有两条壮汉。一九二三年春，我在纽约城里谋到几份沉闷而无利可图的杂志差事；付不起像样的房租，便从一家廉价寄宿处漂到另一家，想找一间兼有像样的干净、过得去的家具和极低廉价格的屋子。不久就明白，我不过是在各种坏处里挑拣，但过了一阵，我在西十四街撞见一所房子，比我采样过的其余几家都不那么叫我作呕。

那是一座褐石的四层楼房，看样子建于四十年代末，木作与大理石虽已污损，那份气派仍看得出是从风雅豪奢的高处跌落下来的。房间宽大高敞，糊着不堪入目的墙纸，装着俗艳得可笑的粉檐，屋里滞着一股闷人的霉味，还有一丝来历不明的烹饪气；但地板干净，床单换得还算勤，热水也不常冷、不常断；于是我把它当作至少可以蛰伏一阵的地方，捱到真正重新生活的日子。女房东埃雷罗是个邋遢得几乎长胡子的西班牙女人，不同我啖舌根，也不挑剔我三楼临街那间屋里电灯点得太晚；同住的房客安静而寡言，正合人意，多半是西班牙人，比最粗鄙的那一等稍高一点。唯一真正搅扰人的，是楼底下大街上有轨电车的喧声。

===Original===

I had been there about three weeks when the first odd incident occurred. One evening at about eight I heard a spattering on the floor and became suddenly aware that I had been smelling the pungent odor of ammonia for some time. Looking about, I saw that the ceiling was wet and dripping; the soaking apparently proceeding from a corner on the side toward the street. Anxious to stop the matter at its source, I hastened to the basement to tell the landlady, and was assured by her that the trouble would quickly be set right.

“Doctair Muñoz,” she cried as she rushed upstairs ahead of me, “he have speel hees chemicals. He ees too seeck for doctair heemself﻿—seecker and seecker all the time﻿—but he weel not have no othair for help. He ees vairy queer in hees seeckness﻿—all day he take funnee-smelling baths, and he cannot get excite or warm. All hees own housework he do﻿—hees leetle room are full of bottles and machines and he do not work as doctair. But he was great once﻿—my fathair in Barcelona have hear of heem﻿—and only joost now he feex a arm of the plumber that get hurt of sudden. He nevair go out, only on roof, and my boy Esteban he breeng heem hees food and laundry and mediceens and chemicals. My God, the sal-ammoniac that man use for to keep heem cool!”

Mrs. Herrero disappeared up the staircase to the fourth floor, and I returned to my room. The ammonia ceased to drip, and as I cleaned up what had spilled and opened the window for air, I heard the landlady’s heavy footsteps above me. Doctor Muñoz I had never heard, save for certain sounds as of some gasoline-driven mechanism; since his step was soft and gentle. I wondered for a moment what the strange affliction of this man might be, and whether his obstinate refusal of outside aid were not the result of a rather baseless eccentricity. There is, I reflected tritely, an infinite deal of pathos in the state of an eminent person who has come down in the world.

---

I might never have known Doctor Muñoz had it not been for the heart attack that suddenly seized me one forenoon as I sat writing in my room. Physicians had told me of the danger of those spells, and I knew there was no time to be lost; so, remembering what the landlady had said about the invalid’s help of the injured workman, I dragged myself upstairs and knocked feebly at the door above mine.

===Chinese===

我在那里住了大约三个星期，头一桩怪事来了。一天晚上八点来钟，我听见地板上啪嗒作响，忽然察觉自己闻氨水的刺鼻味已有一阵了。四下一看，天花板湿了，正滴着水；渗水显然来自靠街那一面的一个角落。我想从源头止住它，急忙下到地下室去告诉房东，她满口应承说马上就修好。

“穆尼奥什大夫，”她抢在我前头奔上楼去，一面喊，“他把药水打翻拉。他病得太厉害，当不成大夫给自己瞧——一天重似一天——可他谁的帮也不要。他这病古怪得很——成天价洗怪味的澡，还不能激动，不能受热。屋里的事全自己干——他那小屋摆满瓶瓶罐罐和机器，早就不行医了。可他从前是了不得的人物——我父亲在巴塞罗那都听说过他——就在前两天，他还接好了一个水管工突然砸坏的胳膊。他从来不出门，只上屋顶，我儿子埃斯特万给他送饭、送换洗衣裳、送药、送化学品。我的天，那个人为了叫自己凉快，用的氯化铵可没数！”

埃雷罗太太消失在通往四楼的楼梯上，我回到自己房里。氨水不再滴了，我收拾了泼洒的东西，开窗透气，听见头顶上房东沉重的脚步。那位穆尼奥斯大夫我从未听见过动静，除了某种汽油机般的声响；因为他的脚步又轻又缓。我一时纳闷，这人害的是什么怪病，他那样固执地拒绝外援，会不会只是一种毫无来由的乖僻。我平庸地想道，一个显赫人物落到这般田地，其中自有无限的凄凉。

---

若不是有天上午我正坐在屋里写字，心脏病突然发作，我也许永远不会认识穆尼奥斯大夫。医生们早警告过我这种发作的危险，我知道一刻也耽误不得；于是想起房东说过的、这位病人给受伤工人治伤的事，我拖着自己上楼，有气无力地敲响了头顶那扇门。

===Original===

My knock was answered in good English by a curious voice some distance to the right, asking my name and business; and these things being stated, there came an opening of the door next to the one I had sought.

A rush of cool air greeted me; and though the day was one of the hottest of late June, I shivered as I crossed the threshold into a large apartment whose rich and tasteful decoration surprised me in this nest of squalor and seediness. A folding couch now filled its diurnal role of sofa, and the mahogany furniture, sumptuous hangings, old paintings, and mellow bookshelves all bespoke a gentleman’s study rather than a boardinghouse bedroom. I now saw that the hall room above mine﻿—the “leetle room” of bottles and machines which Mrs. Herrero had mentioned﻿—was merely the laboratory of the doctor; and that his main living-quarters lay in the spacious adjoining room whose convenient alcoves and large contiguous bathroom permitted him to hide all dressers and obtrusively utilitarian devices. Doctor Muñoz, most certainly, was a man of birth, cultivation, and discrimination.

The figure before me was short but exquisitely proportioned, and clad in somewhat formal dress of perfect fit and cut. A high-bred face of masterful though not arrogant expression was adorned by a short iron-gray full beard, and an old-fashioned pince-nez shielded the full, dark eyes and surmounted an aquiline nose which gave a Moorish touch to a physiognomy otherwise dominantly Celt-Iberian. Thick, well-trimmed hair that argued the punctual calls of a barber was parted gracefully above a high forehead; and the whole picture was one of striking intelligence and superior blood and breeding.

Nevertheless, as I saw Doctor Muñoz in that blast of cool air, I felt a repugnance which nothing in his aspect could justify. Only his lividly inclined complexion and coldness of touch could have afforded a physical basis for this feeling, and even these things should have been excusable considering the man’s known invalidism. It might, too, have been the singular cold that alienated me; for such chilliness was abnormal on so hot a day, and the abnormal always excites aversion, distrust, and fear.

===Chinese===

敲门声换来一口字正腔圆的英语，从右手一段距离外的什么地方问我的姓名和来意；我答过了，我敲的那扇门旁边一扇门开了。

一股冷气扑面而来；虽是六月末最热的日子之一，我跨进门槛时还是打了个寒噤。那是一套宽大的房间，陈设的富丽雅致在这窝肮脏寒酸里叫我吃了一惊。折叠卧榻此刻充作白天的沙发，桃花心木的家具、华美的帏帘、古画和温润的书架，处处是一间绅士的书斋，而不是寄宿舍的卧室。我这才明白，我楼上那间临街屋——埃雷罗太太嘴里摆瓶瓶罐罐和机器的“小屋”——不过是大夫的实验室；他的起居重地在与它相通的宽大里间，间间有妥帖的凹室，还有一间相连的大浴室，好让他把五斗柜和一切扎眼的实用物件都藏起来。这位穆尼奥斯大夫，无疑是个有出身、有教养、有品位的人。

我眼前这个人个子不高，身材却精美匀称，穿一身剪裁贴体的半正式服装。一张高贵的脸，神情专断而不倨傲，蓄着短短的铁灰连鬓胡；一副老式夹鼻眼镜遮着饱满的黑眼睛，架在一座鹰钩鼻上，给那张主要属于凯尔特-伊比利亚的脸添了一分摩尔气。浓密而修剪齐整的头发——看得出理发师按时光顾——在高额头上优雅地分开；整个形象透着惊人的智慧、优越的血统和教养。

然而，在那一股冷气里看见穆尼奥斯大夫的那一刻，我感到一种厌恶，他的仪表没有一处配得上它。唯有那微微泛青的脸色和指尖的冰冷，能为这感觉提供一点生理依据；而即便这两样，念在他有病之身，也本该得到谅解的。再说，使我疏离的也许是那反常的冷；这样的大热天里冷到这个地步，是反常的，而反常的东西总要激起嫌恶、猜疑和恐惧。

===Original===

But repugnance was soon forgotten in admiration, for the strange physician’s extreme skill at once became manifest despite the ice-coldness and shakiness of his bloodless-looking hands. He clearly understood my needs at a glance, and ministered to them with a master’s deftness; the while reassuring me in a finely modulated though oddly hollow and timbreless voice that he was the bitterest of sworn enemies to death, and had sunk his fortune and lost all his friends in a lifetime of bizarre experiment devoted to its bafflement and extirpation. Something of the benevolent fanatic seemed to reside in him, and he rambled on almost garrulously as he sounded my chest and mixed a suitable draft of drugs fetched from the smaller laboratory room. Evidently he found the society of a wellborn man a rare novelty in this dingy environment, and was moved to unaccustomed speech as memories of better days surged over him.

His voice, if queer, was at least soothing; and I could not even perceive that he breathed as the fluent sentences rolled urbanely out. He sought to distract my mind from my own seizure by speaking of his theories and experiments; and I remember his tactfully consoling me about my weak heart by insisting that will and consciousness are stronger than organic life itself, so that if a bodily frame be but originally healthy and carefully preserved, it may through a scientific enhancement of these qualities retain a kind of nervous animation despite the most serious impairments, defects, or even absences in the battery of specific organs. He might, he half-jestingly said, some day teach me to live﻿—or at least to possess some kind of conscious existence﻿—without any heart at all! For his part, he was afflicted with a complication of maladies requiring a very exact regimen which included constant cold. Any marked rise in temperature might, if prolonged, affect him fatally; and the frigidity of his habitation﻿—some fifty-five or fifty-six degrees Fahrenheit﻿—was maintained by an absorption system of ammonia cooling, the gasoline engine whose pumps I had often heard in my room below.

===Chinese===

不过厌恶很快被叹服淹没，因为这位古怪医生的绝技立刻显了出来，尽管他那双看上去毫无血色的手冰冷而微颤。他一眼就看透我的需要，以大师的轻巧一一看料；一面用一种调子优雅、却古怪地空洞、没有音色的嗓音安慰我，说他是死亡不共戴天的死敌，为挫败它、铲除它，倾尽了家财、失尽了朋友，做了一辈子古怪的实验。他身上似乎住着一种慈善的狂热者，一面听我的胸腔，一面从小实验室取药配剂，几乎是絮叨地谈个不停。显然，在这片昏暗的环境里，一个出身良好的男子的来访于他是难得的新鲜事，昔日好时光的记忆涌上来，引得他破例健谈。

他的嗓音虽然古怪，至少是抚慰的；那一串流利的句子从容吐出时，我甚至察觉不出他在呼吸。他谈他的理论和实验，好教我忘了自己的病；我还记得他委婉地安慰我那衰弱的心脏，坚持说意志和意识比有机的生命本身更强固，所以只要躯体生来健康、又得到精心的保养，纵使那一整套具体器官损毁、残缺、甚至全然阙如，凭借对这两种品质的科学强化，躯体仍能保有一种神经性的存活。他半开玩笑地说，也许哪一天，他能教我根本没有心脏也活下去——至少保有某种有意识的存在！至于他自己，他患着一串纠缠的痼疾，需要一套极其精确的养生法，其中就包括持续的寒冷。体温若有显著升高，又持续不退，便可能致命；他那居所的严寒——大约恒定在华氏五十五六度——靠一套氨制冷的吸收系统维持，那台汽油机的泵声，我在楼下房里时常听见。

===Original===

Relieved of my seizure in a marvelously short while, I left the shivery place a disciple and devotee of the gifted recluse. After that I paid him frequent overcoated calls, listening while he told of secret researches and almost ghastly results, and trembling a bit when I examined the unconventional and astonishingly ancient volumes on his shelves. I was eventually, I may add, almost cured of my disease for all time by his skilful ministrations. It seems that he did not scorn the incantations of the medievalists, since he believed these cryptic formulae to contain rare psychological stimuli which might conceivably have singular effects on the substance of a nervous system from which organic pulsations had fled. I was touched by his account of the aged Doctor Torres of Valencia, who had shared his earlier experiments and nursed him through the great illness of eighteen years before, whence his present disorders proceeded. No sooner had the venerable practitioner saved his colleague than he himself succumbed to the grim enemy he had fought.
