Let them prosecute and persecute above ground﻿—things went on every day that they couldn’t reach, and voices laughed at night that they couldn’t place!

===Chinese===

“艺术家该爱的地方是北端。哪个审美家若有真心，就该为那聚拢的传统忍受贫民窟。天哪，老兄！你不明白，那样的地方不单是*造*出来的，简直是*长*出来的？一代又一代人在那里活、感、死，而且是在人们不怕活、不怕感、不怕死的年代。你不知道科普山一六三二年就有了磨坊，如今一半的街道一六五〇年前就画定了吗？我能指给你看两世纪半以上的老屋；看过足以叫现代房子碎成粉末的事情。现代人懂得什么生命和生命背后的力量？你说塞勒姆的巫术是妄想，可我赌我的上五代祖母能讲些东西给你听。他们把她绞死在绞刑架山上，科顿·马瑟在一旁假正经地看着。马瑟，该死的，是怕有人真挣脱出这单调的该死牢笼——我巴不得有人给他下了咒，或是夜里吸了他的血！

“我能指给你看他住过的房子，还能指给你看另一处，他吹足了牛皮也不敢进的。他知道一些事情，不敢写进他那本愚蠢的《美洲基督教大事》，或那部幼稚的《无形世界的奇观》。听着，你可知道整个北端从前有一套地道，叫某些人的各家各户、墓园和海边都通着气？让他们在地面上起诉、迫害吧——他们够不着的事情天天在办，他们定位不了的声音夜里在笑！

===Original===

“Why, man, out of ten surviving houses built before 1700 and not moved since I’ll wager that in eight I can show you something queer in the cellar. There’s hardly a month that you don’t read of workmen finding bricked-up arches and wells leading nowhere in this or that old place as it comes down﻿—you could see one near Henchman Street from the elevated last year. There were witches and what their spells summoned; pirates and what they brought in from the sea; smugglers; privateers﻿—and I tell you, people knew how to live, and how to enlarge the bounds of life, in the old times! This wasn’t the only world a bold and wise man could know﻿—faugh! And to think of today in contrast, with such pale-pink brains that even a club of supposed artists gets shudders and convulsions if a picture goes beyond the feelings of a Beacon Street tea-table!

“The only saving grace of the present is that it’s too damned stupid to question the past very closely. What do maps and records and guidebooks really tell of the North End? Bah! At a guess I’ll guarantee to lead you to thirty or forty alleys and networks of alleys north of Prince Street that aren’t suspected by ten living beings outside of the foreigners that swarm them. And what do those Dagoes know of their meaning? No, Thurber, these ancient places are dreaming gorgeously and overflowing with wonder and terror and escapes from the commonplace, and yet there’s not a living soul to understand or profit by them. Or, rather, there’s only one living soul﻿—for I haven’t been digging around in the past for nothing!

“See here, you’re interested in this sort of thing. What if I told you that I’ve got another studio up there, where I can catch the night-spirit of antique horror and paint things that I couldn’t even think of in Marlborough Street? Naturally I don’t tell those cursed old maids at the club﻿—with Reid, damn him, whispering even as it is that I’m a sort of monster bound down the toboggan of reverse evolution. Yes, Thurber, I decided long ago that one must paint terror as well as beauty from life, so I did some exploring in places where I had reason to know terror lives.

===Chinese===

“哎呀老兄，现存的、一七〇〇年前造、又没挪过窝的房子，十座里我赌八座，我能在地窖里指给你看古怪的东西。隔不了一个月，你就读到新闻，说哪个老宅拆除时，工人发现砌死的拱门和通不到哪里的井——去年你在高架道上还能看见亨奇曼街附近的一个。有女巫，和她们咒来的东西；有海盗，和他们从海上带回来的东西；有走私贩，有私掠船——我告诉你，从前的人懂得怎么活，懂得怎么扩开生命的边界！对大胆而聪明的人，这不是唯一可知道的世界——呸！再想想今天，粉红脑子苍白到这般地步，连一个号称艺术家的俱乐部，画一出比肯街茶桌的感情深一点的东西都要发抖抽风！

“现在唯一的可取之处，是它蠢得该死，不大会细问过去。地图、档案、导游书，对北端到底讲了什么？呸！随口我就能担保，领你到普林斯街以北三四十条巷子和巷网去，除了挤在里面的外国人，外面十个活人也不知道它们。那些南欧佬又懂它们的意思几分？不，瑟伯，这些古老的地方正做着辉煌的梦，满溢着奇妙、恐怖和对凡庸的逃逸，却没有一个活人懂得它们、受益于它们。或者说，只有一个活人——因为我在过去这番挖掘，不是白挖的！

“你听着，你对这类东西有兴趣。要是我告诉你，我在那边还有一间画室，在那儿我能捕到古昔恐怖的夜之精魂，画出在马尔伯勒街连想都想不出的东西，怎么样？我自然不告诉俱乐部那班可咒的老处女——里德，该死的，已经在嚏咕我是什么反向演化滑道上滑下去的怪物了。是的，瑟伯，我早就断定，恐怖同美一样，必须从生人写生，所以我去了一些地方探察——我有理由知道恐怖住在那里的地方。

===Original===

“I’ve got a place that I don’t believe three living Nordic men besides myself have ever seen. It isn’t so very far from the elevated as distance goes, but it’s centuries away as the soul goes. I took it because of the queer old brick well in the cellar﻿—one of the sort I told you about. The shack’s almost tumbling down, so that nobody else would live there, and I’d hate to tell you how little I pay for it. The windows are boarded up, but I like that all the better, since I don’t want daylight for what I do. I paint in the cellar, where the inspiration is thickest, but I’ve other rooms furnished on the ground floor. A Sicilian owns it, and I’ve hired it under the name of Peters.

“Now if you’re game, I’ll take you there tonight. I think you’d enjoy the pictures, for as I said, I’ve let myself go a bit there. It’s no vast tour﻿—I sometimes do it on foot, for I don’t want to attract attention with a taxi in such a place. We can take the shuttle at the South Station for Battery Street, and after that the walk isn’t much.”

---

Well, Eliot, there wasn’t much for me to do after that harangue but to keep myself from running instead of walking for the first vacant cab we could sight. We changed to the elevated at the South Station, and at about 12 o’clock had climbed down the steps at Battery Street and struck along the old waterfront past Constitution Wharf. I didn’t keep track of the cross streets, and can’t tell you yet which it was we turned up, but I know it wasn’t Greenough Lane.

When we did turn, it was to climb through the deserted length of the oldest and dirtiest alley I ever saw in my life, with crumbling-looking gables, broken small-paned windows, and archaic chimneys that stood out half-disintegrated against the moonlit sky. I don’t believe there were three houses in sight that hadn’t been standing in Cotton Mather’s time﻿—certainly I glimpsed at least two with an overhang, and once I thought I saw a peaked roof-line of the almost forgotten pre-gambrel type, though antiquarians tell us there are none left in Boston.

===Chinese===

“我有个地方，除了我，活着的人里，我不信还有三个北欧人见过。论路程离高架道不算远，论灵魂却隔了几个世纪。我租它，就为地窖里那口古怪的砖井——我同你讲过的那一种。那棚屋快塌了，没人肯住，我付的租金少得不好开口告诉你。窗子全钉了板，我倒更喜欢，因为我干的事用不着日光。我在地窖里画画，那儿灵感最浓，但底层我也布置了几间屋。房东是个西西里人，我用彼得斯的名字租的。

“你要是有胆，今晚我就带你去。我想你会喜欢那些画，因为我说过，我在那边放开了手脚。路不算远——我有时走着去，因为不想在那地方叫出租惹眼。咱们在南站坐联轨车到巴特里街，剩下的路不多。”

---

唉，埃利奥特，听了那一通演讲，我没别的可做，只有按住自己，别跑着去寻我们望见的第一辆空车。我们在南站换上高架，约莫十二点，从巴特里街的台阶下来，沿着老滨水街，过了宪法码头。交叉的街我没数，至今说不出我们拐上的是哪一条，只知道不是格里诺巷。

拐上之后，是穿行一条荒巷的全长，我生平所见最老最脏的一条，看来要塌的山墙，破了小格的窗，古式的烟囱半颓着衬在月光的天上。视野里的房子，我说不信有三座不是科顿·马瑟时代就立着的——肯定捄见了至少两座带出挑层的，还有一回，我以为是望见了几乎被遗忘的前复斜式的尖顶线，虽然古物家告诉我们，波士顿一处也不剩了。

===Original===

From that alley, which had a dim light, we turned to the left into an equally silent and still narrower alley with no light at all; and in a minute made what I think was an obtuse-angled bend toward the right in the dark. Not long after this Pickman produced a flashlight and revealed an antediluvian ten-paneled door that looked damnably worm-eaten. Unlocking it, he ushered me into a barren hallway with what was once splendid dark-oak paneling﻿—simple, of course, but thrillingly suggestive of the times of Andros and Phips and the Witchcraft. Then he took me through a door on the left, lighted an oil lamp, and told me to make myself at home.

Now, Eliot, I’m what the man in the street would call fairly “hard-boiled,” but I’ll confess that what I saw on the walls of that room gave me a bad turn. They were his pictures, you know﻿—the ones he couldn’t paint or even show in Marlborough Street﻿—and he was right when he said he had “let himself go.” Here﻿—have another drink﻿—I need one anyhow!

There’s no use in my trying to tell you what they were like, because the awful, the blasphemous horror, and the unbelievable loathsomeness and moral fetor came from simple touches quite beyond the power of words to classify. There was none of the exotic technique you see in Sidney Sime, none of the trans-Saturnian landscapes and lunar fungi that Clark Ashton Smith uses to freeze the blood. The backgrounds were mostly old churchyards, deep woods, cliffs by the sea, brick tunnels, ancient paneled rooms, or simple vaults of masonry. Copp’s Hill Burying Ground, which could not be many blocks away from this very house, was a favorite scene.

===Chinese===

出了那条有一点昏灯的巷，我们左拐，进了一条同样寂静、更窄、全无灯光的巷；一分钟后，在黑暗里朝右来了个我猜是钝角的转弯。此后不久，皮克曼摸出一只手电，照出一扇洪荒前的十格老门，蛀得不像话。他开了锁，引我进一条空落的门厅，护壁板从前是气派的深橡木——自然是简朴的，却动人心魄地令人想起安德罗斯、菲普斯和巫术的时代。随后他领我进了左边一道门，点上一盏油灯，叫我别拘束。

这么跟你说吧，埃利奥特，我是街面上人叫做“煮硬了”的那种，可我承认，我在那间屋的墙上所见，给了我好一下。那是他的画，你知道——马尔伯勒街画不出、也拿不出的那些——他说他“放开了手脚”，说得一点不错。来——再喝一杯——反正我也需要！

我试着给你讲它们像什么，毫无用处，因为那可怕、那渎神的恐怖，那难以置信的恶心和道德的恶臭，全来自几笔简单的点触，远非言语所能归类。没有你在西德尼·赛姆笔下见到的那种异域技巧，没有克拉卡·阿什顿·史密斯用来冻人血液的外土星风景和月面菌类。背景多半是老教堂墓地、密林、海边断崖、砖砌隧道、古老的护壁房间，或简单的砖石墓窖。科普山墓园——离这房子想必没有几个街区——是他爱用的场景。

===Original===

The madness and monstrosity lay in the figures in the foreground﻿—for Pickman’s morbid art was preeminently one of demoniac portraiture. These figures were seldom completely human, but often approached humanity in varying degrees. Most of the bodies, while roughly bipedal, had a forward slumping, and a vaguely canine cast. The texture of the majority was a kind of unpleasant rubberiness. Ugh! I can see them now! Their occupations﻿—well, don’t ask me to be too precise. They were usually feeding﻿—I won’t say on what. They were sometimes shown in groups in cemeteries or underground passages, and often appeared to be in battle over their prey﻿—or rather, their treasure-trove. And what damnable expressiveness Pickman sometimes gave the sightless faces of this charnel booty! Occasionally the things were shown leaping through open windows at night, or squatting on the chests of sleepers, worrying at their throats. One canvas showed a ring of them baying about a hanged witch on Gallows Hill, whose dead face held a close kinship to theirs.

But don’t get the idea that it was all this hideous business of theme and setting which struck me faint. I’m not a three-year-old kid, and I’d seen much like this before. It was the *faces*, Eliot, those accursed *faces*, that leered and slavered out of the canvas with the very breath of life! By God, man, I verily believe they *were* alive! That nauseous wizard had waked the fires of hell in pigment, and his brush had been a nightmare-spawning wand. Give me that decanter, Eliot!

There was one thing called *The Lesson*﻿—heaven pity me, that I ever saw it! Listen﻿—can you fancy a squatting circle of nameless doglike things in a churchyard teaching a small child how to feed like themselves? The price of a changeling, I suppose﻿—you know the old myth about how the weird people leave their spawn in cradles in exchange for the human babes they steal. Pickman was showing what happens to those stolen babes﻿—how they grow up﻿—and then I began to see a hideous relationship in the faces of the human and nonhuman figures. He was, in all his gradations of morbidity between the frankly nonhuman and the degradedly human, establishing a sardonic linkage and evolution. The dog-things were developed from mortals!

===Chinese===

疯狂和怪诞卧在前景的人形里——因为皮克曼的病态艺术，首先是一门魔性的肖像术。这些人形很少是全然的人，却常常在不同程度上接近人。大多数躯体虽大致双足，却向前佝偻，带着一种模糊的犬相。质地多半是一种叫人不快的胶皮感。呢！我如今还看得见它们！它们的营生——唉，别叫我讲得太细。它们常在进食——我不说吃什么。有时成群出现在墓地或地下通道里，常像是在为猎物——或者说它们的窖藏——厮打。皮克曼有时给这停尸房赃物的无目的脸孔何等该死的表现力啊！偶尔，那些东西被画成夜里跃进敞开的窗，或蹲在睡者胸口折腾他们的喉咙。有一幅，画它们围成一圈，对绞刑架山上一个吊死的女巫狂吠，那具死脸同它们的脸，亲缘得紧。

可你别以为，叫我发昏的全是这题材和布景的狰狞营生。我不是三岁的孩子，这一类我从前见得多了。是那些*脸*，埃利奥特，那些可咒的*脸*，带着活的呼吸，从画布上斜睨着、淌着涎！上帝作证，老兄，我真信它们*是活的*！那个作呕的巫师在颜料里点着了地狱之火，他的笔是一根孳生噩梦的魔杖。把细颈瓶递给我，埃利奥特！

有一幅叫《授课》的——上天怜我，叫我看见过它！听着——你能想象吗：墓园里蹲着一圈无名的犬形之物，正教一个小孩子怎样像它们那样进食？换一个婴孩的代价吧，我想——你知道那个老传说，怪种把自己的崽放进摇篮，换走偷来的人婴。皮克曼画的是那些偷走的孩子后来怎样了——他们怎样长大——于是我开始在人和非人形象的脸上看出一层可憎的亲缘。他以其病态的种种浓淡——从公然非人到堕落近人——在建立一条讥诮的链和一套演化。那些犬形之物，是从人变来的！

===Original===

And no sooner had I wondered what he made of their own young as left with mankind in the form of changelings, than my eye caught a picture embodying that very thought. It was that of an ancient Puritan interior﻿—a heavily beamed room with lattice windows, a settle, and clumsy Seventeenth Century furniture, with the family sitting about while the father read from the Scriptures. Every face but one showed nobility and reverence, but that one reflected the mockery of the pit. It was that of a young man in years, and no doubt belonged to a supposed son of that pious father, but in essence it was the kin of the unclean things. It was their changeling﻿—and in a spirit of supreme irony Pickman had given the features a very perceptible resemblance to his own.

By this time Pickman had lighted a lamp in an adjoining room and was politely holding open the door for me; asking me if I would care to see his “modern studies.” I hadn’t been able to give him much of my opinions﻿—I was too speechless with fright and loathing﻿—but I think he fully understood and felt highly complimented. And now I want to assure you again, Eliot, that I’m no mollycoddle to scream at anything which shows a bit of departure from the usual. I’m middle-aged and decently sophisticated, and I guess you saw enough of me in France to know I’m not easily knocked out. Remember, too, that I’d just about recovered my wind and gotten used to those frightful pictures which turned colonial New England into a kind of annex of hell. Well, in spite of all this, that next room forced a real scream out of me, and I had to clutch at the doorway to keep from keeling over. The other chamber had shown a pack of ghouls and witches overrunning the world of our forefathers, but this one brought the horror right into our own daily life!

Gad, how that man could paint! There was a study called *Subway Accident*, in which a flock of the vile things were clambering up from some unknown catacomb through a crack in the floor of the Boylston Street subway and attacking a crowd of people on the platform. Another showed a dance on Copp’s Hill among the tombs with the background of today. Then there were any number of cellar views, with monsters creeping in through holes and rifts in the masonry and grinning as they squatted behind barrels or furnaces and waited for their first victim to descend the stairs.

===Chinese===

我刚在想，他又是怎样处理它们自己那些换成换婴留在人间的崽种的，眼睛就撞上一幅画，画的正是这个念头。那是一幅清教徒的古内室——粗梁的屋子，格子窗，高背长椅，笨重的十七世纪家具，一家人围坐着，父亲在读《圣经》。除了一张，每张脸都显出高贵和虔敬，唯独那一张，映着深渊的嘲弄。那是一张年轻的脸，无疑属于那位虔诚父亲名义上的儿子，骨子里却是那班不洁之物的亲族。那是他们的换婴——皮克曼怀着至高的讥诮，给那张脸添了同他自己相当可辨的相似。

这时，皮克曼已在隔壁房间点起一盏灯，客气地为我拉着门，问我可愿看看他的“现代习作”。我没能给他多少意见——我怕憎得说不出话——可我想他全懂了，而且觉得极受恭维。现在我要再向你保证一遍，埃利奥特，我不是那种见到一点出格的东西就叫唤的娘气人。我人到中年，见过的世面像样，你在法国也见够了我，知道我不容易放倒。还要记住，我方才差不多缓过气来，也看惯了那些把殖民时代的新英格兰变成地狱一角的可怕画。可尽管如此，隔壁那间屋还是逼出我一声真正的尖叫，我抓住门框才没栽倒。前一间屋画的是一群食尸鬼和女巫蹂躚我们祖辈的世界，这一间却把恐怖直接搬进了我们自己的日常！

天哪，那人多会画！有一幅叫《地铁事故》，一群可憎之物正从什么不知名的地下墓窟，顺着博伊尔斯顿街地铁地板的一道裂缝爬上来，袭击月台上的人群。另一幅画科普山墓丛间的今天的背景之下的舞蹈。还有数不清的地窖图，怪物从砖石的孔洞和裂缝里爬进来，狞笑着蹲在木桶或炉子后面，等头一个下楼梯的牺牲。

===Original===

One disgusting canvas seemed to depict a vast cross-section of Beacon Hill, with antlike armies of the mephitic monsters squeezing themselves through burrows that honeycombed the ground. Dances in the modern cemeteries were freely pictured, and another conception somehow shocked me more than all the rest﻿—a scene in an unknown vault, where scores of the beasts crowded about one who held a well-known Boston guidebook and was evidently reading aloud. All were pointing to a certain passage, and every face seemed so distorted with epileptic and reverberant laughter that I almost thought I heard the fiendish echoes. The title of the picture was, *Holmes, Lowell, and Longfellow Lie Buried in Mount Auburn*.

As I gradually steadied myself and got readjusted to this second room of deviltry and morbidity, I began to analyze some of the points in my sickening loathing. In the first place, I said to myself, these things repelled because of the utter inhumanity and callous cruelty they showed in Pickman. The fellow must be a relentless enemy of all mankind to take such glee in the torture of brain and flesh and the degradation of the mortal tenement. In the second place, they terrified, because of their very greatness. Their art was the art that convinced﻿—when we saw the pictures we saw the demons themselves and were afraid of them. And the queer part was, that Pickman got none of his power from the use of selectiveness or bizarrerie. Nothing was blurred, distorted, or conventionalized; outlines were sharp and lifelike, and details were almost painfully defined. And the faces!

It was not any mere artist’s interpretation that we saw; it was pandemonium itself, crystal-clear in stark objectivity. That was it, by heaven! The man was not a *fantaisiste* or romanticist at all﻿—he did not even try to give us the churning, prismatic ephemera of dreams, but coldly and sardonically reflected some stable, mechanistic, and well-established horror-world which he saw fully, brilliantly, squarely, and unfalteringly. God knows what that world can have been, or where he ever glimpsed the blasphemous shapes that loped and trotted and crawled through it; but whatever the baffling source of his images, one thing was plain. Pickman was in every sense﻿—in conception and in execution﻿—a thorough, painstaking, and almost scientific *realist*.

===Chinese===

一幅叫人作呕的画，画的像是灯塔山的一个巨大剖面，蚁群似的恶臭怪物挤着钻过蜂窝般遍布地下的洞穴。现代墓园里的舞会画了不少，还有一幅立意不知怎么比其余所有的更震我：一间无名的墓窖里，几十头畜生围着其中一头，那头手里捧着一册人人认得的波士顿导游书，分明在朗读。全体指着某一段，每一张脸都笑得癫痫般抽搐回响，我几乎以为自己听见了那魔鬼的回声。画的题目是：《霍姆斯、洛厄尔与朗费罗长眠奥本山》。

等我渐渐站稳、重新适应了这第二间恶魔与病态之屋，我开始剖析我那作呕的憎恶中的几个要点。首先我对自己说，这些东西叫人反感，是因为皮克曼在画里显露的十足的非人性和冷酷的残忍。这家伙必是全人类死心塌地的仇敌，才会在对脑与肉的折磨、对凡人躯壳的糟践里取这样的乐。其次，它们吓人，恰因为它们的伟大。它们的艺术是叫人信服的艺术——看到那些画，我们便是看见了魔鬼本身，便怕了它们。而古怪的是，皮克曼的魔力一点也不靠选材的冷僻或古怪。没有什么是模糊、变形、程式化的；轮廓锐利如生，细节清楚得几乎叫人痛。还有那些脸！

我们看见的，不是随便哪个艺术家的诠释；那是群魔殿本身，在赤裸的客观里水晶般清晰。就是这个，老天在上！这人根本不是什么*幻想家*或浪漫派——他甚至不打算给我们梦的那种翻搅的、棱镜似的蜉蝣，而是冷冷地、讥诮地，映出一个稳定的、机械的、根基牢固的恐怖世界，他把它看得完全、灿烂、端端正正、毫不动摇。天知道那是个什么世界，他在哪里捄见那些又跳又跑又爬、亵渎地穿过它的形骸；可无论他的图像来源如何费解，有一点是明白的。皮克曼在每一层意义上——在构想与执行上——都是一个彻底、细密、近乎科学的*写实主义者*。

===Original===

My host was now leading the way down cellar to his actual studio, and I braced myself for some hellish effects among the unfinished canvases. As we reached the bottom of the damp stairs he turned his flashlight to a corner of the large open space at hand, revealing the circular brick curb of what was evidently a great well in the earthen floor. We walked nearer, and I saw that it must be five feet across, with walls a good foot thick and some six inches above the ground level﻿—solid work of the Seventeenth Century, or I was much mistaken. That, Pickman said, was the kind of thing he had been talking about﻿—an aperture of the network of tunnels that used to undermine the hill. I noticed idly that it did not seem to be bricked up, and that a heavy disk of wood formed the apparent cover. Thinking of the things this well must have been connected with if Pickman’s wild hints had not been mere rhetoric, I shivered slightly; then turned to follow him up a step and through a narrow door into a room of fair size, provided with a wooden floor and furnished as a studio. An acetylene gas outfit gave the light necessary for work.

The unfinished pictures on easels or propped against the walls were as ghastly as the finished ones upstairs, and showed the painstaking methods of the artist. Scenes were blocked out with extreme care, and penciled guide lines told of the minute exactitude which Pickman used in getting the right perspective and proportions. The man was great﻿—I say it even now, knowing as much as I do. A large camera on a table excited my notice, and Pickman told me that he used it in taking scenes for backgrounds, so that he might paint them from photographs in the studio instead of carting his outfit around the town for this or that view. He thought a photograph quite as good as an actual scene or model for sustained work, and declared he employed them regularly.

===Chinese===

主人这时领路下地窖，去看他真正的画室，我振作精神，预备在那些未完成的画布中间再挨几记地狱的。走到潮湿的楼梯底，他把手电照向手边那片开敞大空间的一角，照出泥地上一口大井的圆形砖口。我们走近了，我看出井口必得有五英尺宽，井壁足有一英尺厚，高出地面约六英寸——十七世纪的结实活计，不然我大错特错。皮克曼说，这正是他讲的那种东西——从前在山底下纵横的地道网的一个口子。我漫不经心地注意到它似乎没有砌死，木制的大圆盘像是盖子。想到这口井必曾连着些什么——倘若皮克曼那些狂放的暗示不只是修辞——我微微一凛；随后跟了他上一级台阶，穿过一道窄门，进了一间不小、铺着木地板、布置成画室的屋子。一套乙炔气灯供着作画必需的光。

画架上和靠墙立着的未完成之作，同楼上那些完成品一样骇人，显出这位画家的不惿烦。场景都划得极细，铅笔的基准线诉说着皮克曼在取准透视和比例时的分毫必究。这人是伟大的——如今我知道了这许多，我还是这样说。桌上一架大照相机引起我注意，皮克曼说，他用它拍背景，这样便可照着相片在画室里画，不必扛着一套家伙满城找景。他认为对持续的创作，相片同实景或模特儿一样好，还说他有规律地使用它们。

===Original===

There was something very disturbing about the nauseous sketches and half-finished monstrosities that leered around from every side of the room, and when Pickman suddenly unveiled a huge canvas on the side away from the light I could not for my life keep back a loud scream﻿—the second I had emitted that night. It echoed and echoed through the dim vaultings of that ancient and nitrous cellar, and I had to choke back a flood of reaction that threatened to burst out as hysterical laughter. Merciful Creator! Eliot, but I don’t know how much was real and how much was feverish fancy. It doesn’t seem to me that earth can hold a dream like that!

It was a colossal and nameless blasphemy with glaring red eyes, and it held in bony claws a thing that had been a man, gnawing at the head as a child nibbles at a stick of candy. Its position was a kind of crouch, and as one looked one felt that at any moment it might drop its present prey and seek a juicier morsel. But, damn it all, it wasn’t even the fiendish subject that made it such an immortal fountainhead of all panic﻿—not that, nor the dog face with its pointed ears, bloodshot eyes, flat nose, and drooling lips. It wasn’t the scaly claws nor the mold-caked body nor the half-hooved feet﻿—none of these, though any one of them might well have driven an excitable man to madness.

It was the technique, Eliot﻿—the cursed, the impious, the unnatural technique! As I am a living being, I never elsewhere saw the actual breath of life so fused into a canvas. The monster was there﻿—it glared and gnawed and gnawed and glared﻿—and I knew that only a suspension of nature’s laws could ever let a man paint a thing like that without a model﻿—without some glimpse of the nether world which no mortal unsold to the Fiend has ever had.

===Chinese===

屋子里四面八方斜睨过来的那些恶心素描和半成的怪物，本已叫人心神大乱，而皮克曼突然在背光那一面揭开一幅巨大的画布时，我豁出命也忍不住一声大喊——那一夜的第二声。它在古老而硝气弥漫的地窖的昏暗穹窿里荡了又荡，我不得不掐住一阵几乎要化作歇斯底里大笑的反潮。仁慈的造物主！埃利奥特，我说不上多少是真，多少是热病的幻。依我看，大地盛不下那样的一个梦！

那是一个巨大而无名的渎神之物，红眼睛瞪着，骨爪里攥着一个曾经是人的东西，正啃那颗头，像小孩啃一根棒糖。它的姿势是一种蹲踞，看着的人只觉得它随时会丢下眼前的猎物，另寻一块更多汁的。可是，该死的，叫它成为一切惊慌之不朽源泉的，甚至还不是那魔鬼的题材——不是那个，也不是那张狗脸：尖耳朵，充血的眼睛，塌鼻子，淌涎的嘴。不是那鳞爪，不是那霉壳的身子，也不是那半蹄的脚——这些都不是，虽然任何一样都尽够把一个易激的人逼疯。

是那技法，埃利奥特——那可咒的、渎神的、不自然的技法！我是活人，我在别处从没见过生命的实际呼吸这样熔进一块画布。那怪物就在那里——它瞪着、啃着、啃着、瞪着——我知道，只有叫自然的规律暂停，才能让一个人没有模特儿画出这样的东西——没有对下界的一瞥，那一瞥，没有把自己卖给恶魔的凡人得到过。

===Original===

Pinned with a thumbtack to a vacant part of the canvas was a piece of paper now badly curled up﻿—probably, I thought, a photograph from which Pickman meant to paint a background as hideous as the nightmare it was to enhance. I reached out to uncurl and look at it, when suddenly I saw Pickman start as if shot. He had been listening with peculiar intensity ever since my shocked scream had waked unaccustomed echoes in the dark cellar, and now he seemed struck with a fright which, though not comparable to my own, had in it more of the physical than of the spiritual. He drew a revolver and motioned me to silence, then stepped out into the main cellar and closed the door behind him.

I think I was paralyzed for an instant. Imitating Pickman’s listening, I fancied I heard a faint scurrying sound somewhere, and a series of squeals or bleats in a direction I couldn’t determine. I thought of huge rats and shuddered. Then there came a subdued sort of clatter which somehow set me all in gooseflesh﻿—a furtive, groping kind of clatter, though I can’t attempt to convey what I mean in words. It was like heavy wood falling on stone or brick﻿—wood on brick﻿—what did that make me think of?

It came again, and louder. There was a vibration as if the wood had fallen farther than it had fallen before. After that followed a sharp grating noise, a shouted gibberish from Pickman, and the deafening discharge of all six chambers of a revolver, fired spectacularly as a lion-tamer might fire in the air for effect. A muffled squeal or squawk, and a thud. Then more wood and brick grating, a pause, and the opening of the door﻿—at which I’ll confess I started violently. Pickman reappeared with his smoking weapon, cursing the bloated rats that infested the ancient well.

“The deuce knows what they eat, Thurber,” he grinned, “for those archaic tunnels touched graveyard and witch-den and seacoast. But whatever it is, they must have run short, for they were devilish anxious to get out. Your yelling stirred them up, I fancy. Better be cautious in these old places﻿—our rodent friends are the one drawback, though I sometimes think they’re a positive asset by way of atmosphere and color.”

===Chinese===

画布空处用图钉钉着一小片纸，已经卷得很厉害——我想，多半是张相片，皮克曼打算照它画一个背景，配那噩梦般的画面。我伸手要展开看，忽然看见皮克曼像中了枪似的跳起来。自从我那声惊叫在黑地窖里唤醒了不惯的回声，他就一直极异常地听着，此刻他像是被一种恐惧击中了——虽比不上我的，但那恐惧里肉体的成分多于灵魂的。他拔出左轮，示意我别作声，随后跨进外间地窖，把门带上了。

我想我有一瞬是瘫了。我学着他听，恍惚听见什么地方一阵细碎的疾行，还有一串尖叫或哀鸣，方向辨不出。我想到大老鼠，一凛。随后来了一种闷闷的磕碰，不知怎么叫我浑身起栗——一种鬼祟的、摸索的磕碰，尽管我没法用字眼说清我的意思。它像沉重的木头落在石头或砖上——木头落在砖上——这叫我想到什么？

它又响了，更响。有一种震动，像木头比先前落得更深。随后是一声锐利的摩擦，皮克曼一声喊出的怪话，六弹仓左轮震耳的一声齐发，放得像驯狮人朝天上放枪那样漂亮。一声闷叫或怪喘，一记撞击。随后又是木头擦砖，停顿，门开了——我承认我猛地一惊。皮克曼带着冒烟的枪回来了，咒骂着古井里成窝的肥老鼠。

“鬼才知道它们吃什么，瑟伯，”他到嘴道，“那些老地道通着墓地、巫窟和海岸。可不管吃什么，想必断了粮，才这么发了疯似的要出来。多半是你那嗓子把它们吵起来的。在这些老地方得小心——咱们这些啮齿朋友是唯一的毛病，不过我有时想，论气氛和色彩，它们倒是笔正资产。”

===Original===

Well, Eliot, that was the end of the night’s adventure. Pickman had promised to show me the place, and heaven knows he had done it. He led me out of that tangle of alleys in another direction, it seems, for when we sighted a lamppost we were in a half-familiar street with monotonous rows of mingled tenement blocks and old houses. Charter Street, it turned out to be, but I was too flustered to notice just where we hit it. We were too late for the elevated, and walked back downtown through Hanover Street. I remember that walk. We switched from Tremont up Beacon, and Pickman left me at the corner of Joy, where I turned off. I never spoke to him again.

Why did I drop him? Don’t be impatient. Wait till I ring for coffee. We’ve had enough of the other stuff, but I for one need something. No﻿—it wasn’t the paintings I saw in that place; though I’ll swear they were enough to get him ostracized in nine-tenths of the homes and clubs of Boston, and I guess you won’t wonder now why I have to steer clear of subways and cellars. It was﻿—something I found in my coat the next morning. You know, the curled-up paper tacked to that frightful canvas in the cellar; the thing I thought was a photograph of some scene he meant to use as a background for that monster. That last scare had come while I was reaching to uncurl it, and it seems I had vacantly crumpled it into my pocket. But here’s the coffee﻿—take it black, Eliot, if you’re wise.

Yes, that paper was the reason I dropped Pickman; Richard Upton Pickman, the greatest artist I have ever known﻿—and the foulest being that ever leaped the bounds of life into the pits of myth and madness. Eliot﻿—old Reid was right. He wasn’t strictly human. Either he was born in strange shadow, or he’d found a way to unlock the forbidden gate. It’s all the same now, for he’s gone﻿—back into the fabulous darkness he loved to haunt. Here, let’s have the chandelier going.

Don’t ask me to explain or even conjecture about what I burned. Don’t ask me, either, what lay behind that mole-like scrambling Pickman was so keen to pass off as rats. There are secrets, you know, which might have come down from old Salem times, and Cotton Mather tells even stranger things. You know how damned lifelike Pickman’s paintings were﻿—how we all wondered where he got those faces.

===Chinese===

唉，埃利奥特，那晚的奇遇就此收场。皮克曼答应带我看看那地方，天知道他做绝了。他领我出那片乱巷，像是换了方向，因为望见灯柱时，我们已在一条半熟的街上，一排排单调的公寓楼和旧宅混杂。后来查明是查特街，可我当时太慌，没留意我们撞上它的位置。高架赶不上了，我们步行穿汉诺威街回城。那段路我记得。我们从特里蒙特拐上灯塔街，皮克曼在乔伊街口把我摞下，我在那里拐弯。我再没同他说过话。

我为什么甩了他？别急。等我按铃叫咖啡。那玩意儿够了，我反正得换换。不——不是我在那地方见的那些画；虽然我可以起誓，光那些就够叫波士顿十分之九的人家和俱乐部把他扫地出门，我想你如今也不奇怪我为什么躲着地铁和地窖了。是——第二天早晨我在大衣里发现的一件东西。你知道，就是地窖里那幅可怕画布上钉着的卷纸；我原以为是张相片，是他打算给那怪物作背景用的。最后一惊来时我正要展开它，看来我失神地把它揉进了口袋。咖啡来了——喝黑的吧，埃利奥特，你若识货。

是的，那张纸就是我甩掉皮克曼的原因；理查德·厄普顿·皮克曼，我所知的最伟大的艺术家——也是跳跃了生命之界、坠进神话与疯狂之坑的至秽的存在。埃利奥特——老里德是对的。他不严格是人。要么他生在怪影里，要么他找到了开那扇禁门的法子。如今都一样了，因为他去了——回到他爱出没的神话的黑暗里去了。来，把枝形吊灯点上。

别求我解释、甚至猜测我烧掉的是什么。也别问我，皮克曼急急地想栽作老鼠的那阵鼹鼠似的扑腾背后是什么。世上有种种秘密，你知道，也许是从老塞勒姆时代传下来的，科顿·马瑟还讲过更怪的。你知道皮克曼的画画得多么该死地像活的——我们都纳闷他从哪里得来那些脸。

===Original===

Well﻿—that paper wasn’t a photograph of any background, after all. What it showed was simply the monstrous being he was painting on that awful canvas. It was the model he was using﻿—and its background was merely the wall of the cellar studio in minute detail. But by God, Eliot, *it was a photograph from life*.

===Chinese===

唉——那张纸终究不是什么背景的相片。它上面的，就是他画在那幅可怕画布上的那个怪物本身。那是他用的模特儿——它的背景，不过是地窖画室那面墙的纤毫细节。可是上帝作证，埃利奥特，*那是一张从实物拍来的照片*。

## Polaris / 北极星
===Original===

Into the north window of my chamber glows the Pole Star with uncanny light. All through the long hellish hours of blackness it shines there. And in the autumn of the year, when the winds from the north curse and whine, and the red-leaved trees of the swamp mutter things to one another in the small hours of the morning under the horned waning moon, I sit by the casement and watch that star. Down from the heights reels the glittering Cassiopeia as the hours wear on, while Charles’ Wain lumbers up from behind the vapour-soaked swamp trees that sway in the night wind. Just before dawn Arcturus winks ruddily from above the cemetery on the low hillock, and Coma Berenices shimmers weirdly afar off in the mysterious east; but still the Pole Star leers down from the same place in the black vault, winking hideously like an insane watching eye which strives to convey some strange message, yet recalls nothing save that it once had a message to convey. Sometimes, when it is cloudy, I can sleep.

Well do I remember the night of the great Aurora, when over the swamp played the shocking coruscations of the daemon light. After the beam came clouds, and then I slept.

And it was under a horned waning moon that I saw the city for the first time. Still and somnolent did it lie, on a strange plateau in a hollow betwixt strange peaks. Of ghastly marble were its walls and its towers, its columns, domes, and pavements. In the marble street, were marble pillars, the upper parts of which were carven into the images of grave bearded men. The air was warm and stirred not. And overhead, scarce ten degrees from the zenith, glowed that watching Pole Star. Long did I gaze on the city, but the day came not. When the red Aldebaran, which blinked low in the sky but never set, had crawled a quarter of the way around the horizon, I saw light and motion in the houses and the streets. Forms strangely robed, but at once noble and familiar, walked abroad and under the horned waning moon men talked wisdom in a tongue which I understood, though it was unlike any language I had ever known. And when the red Aldebaran had crawled more than halfway around the horizon, there were again darkness and silence.

===Chinese===

北极星带着邪异的光，照进我房间的北窗。在黑夜那漫长的地狱时辰里，它始终在那里亮着。到了一年中的秋天，当北风咒骂着呼啸，沼泽里的红叶树在凌晨时分、在长角的残月下彼此低语，我便坐在窗边，守着那颗星。随着时辰流转，闪光的仙后座从高处摇坠而下，查理的马车从水汽浸透、在夜风里摇摆的沼树后面隆隆驶上来。拂晓之前，大角星在矮丘上墓地上方红红地眨眼，后发座在神秘的东方远处诡异地微光闪烁；而北极星依旧从黑色穹窿的同一处斜睨下来，可憎地眨着，像一只疯狂的守视的眼，拼命想传达什么古怪的讯息，却只记得自己曾有一个讯息要传达。有时天阴，我睡得着。

我清楚地记得大极光的那一夜，魔光骇人的回闪在沼泽上空嬉戏。光束过后来了云，随后我睡了。

正是在一个长角的残月下，我第一次看见了那座城。它静静卧着，睡意沉沉，卧在一道怪峰之间洼地里的一片奇怪的高原上。它的墙和塔、柱、穹顶和路面，都是惨白的大理石。大理石的街上立着大理石柱，柱的上半截雕成神情肃穆的须眉男子的立像。空气温暖，一动不动。头顶上，离天顶不足十度，那颗守视的北极星发着光。我久久凝望那座城，白昼却不来。红色的毕宿五在天边低处眨着眼、从不落下，当它沿地平线爬过四分之一圈，我看见屋里和街上有了光和动静。装束古怪却一下便觉高贵而熟稔的身影走出门来，在长角的残月下，男人们用一种我听得懂的话谈论智慧，虽然它同我认识的任何语言都不像。待到红色的毕宿五爬过地平线一半还多，重又是黑暗与寂静。

===Original===

When I awaked, I was not as I had been. Upon my memory was graven the vision of the city, and within my soul had arisen another and vaguer recollection, of whose nature I was not then certain. Thereafter, on the cloudy nights when I could sleep, I saw the city often; sometimes under that horned waning moon, and sometimes under the hot yellow rays of a sun which did not set, but which wheeled low around the horizon. And on the clear nights the Pole Star leered as never before.

Gradually I came to wonder what might be my place in that city on the strange plateau betwixt strange peaks. At first content to view the scene as an all-observant uncorporeal presence, I now desired to define my relation to it, and to speak my mind amongst the grave men who conversed each day in the public squares. I said to myself, “This is no dream, for by what means can I prove the greater reality of that other life in the house of stone and brick south of the sinister swamp and the cemetery on the low hillock, where the Pole Star peeps into my north window each night?”

One night as I listened to the discourse in the large square containing many statues I felt a change; and perceived that I had at last a bodily form. Nor was a stranger in the streets of Olathoe, which lies on the plateau of Sarkis, betwixt the peaks Noton and Kadiphonek. It was my friend Alos who spoke, and his speech was one that pleased my soul, for it was the speech of a true man and patriot. That night had the news come of Daikos’ fall, and of the advance of the Inutos; squat, hellish yellow fiends who five years ago had appeared out of the unknown west to ravage the confines of our kingdom and finally to besiege our towns. Having taken the fortified places at the foot of the mountains, their way now lay open to the plateau, unless every citizen could resist with the strength of ten men. For the squat creatures were mighty in the arts of war, and knew not the scruples of honour which hold back our tall, grey-eyed men of Lomar from ruthless conquest.

===Chinese===

醒来之后，我已不是原先的我。那座城的景象刻上了我的记忆，我灵魂里又升起另一重更模糊的回想，其性质我当时还不确知。此后，凡阴得能睡的夜里，我常常见到那座城：有时在长角的残月下，有时在一轮不落、只低低绕着地平线转圈的太阳的灼黄光线下。而晴夜里，北极星斜睨得比以往任何时候都厉害。

渐渐地，我开始想：在那座怪峰之间高原上的城里，我算是什么。起初我只满足于做一个全盘旁观的无形临在，如今我却想确定自己同它的关系，想在那班每天在公共广场上谈论的肃穆男子中间说出我的想法。我对自己说：“这不是梦，因为我凭什么证明，那另一种生活——在凶险沼泽和矮丘墓地之南、石头砖头的房子里、北极星每夜窥进北窗的生活——更真实呢？”

一夜，我在那座立着许多雕像的大广场上听人们谈论，忽觉一种变化；我察觉自己终于有了一个身体。在奥拉索厄的街上，我并非陌生人——那城坐落在萨基斯高原上，在诺顿峰与卡迪福内克峰之间。说话的是我的朋友阿洛斯，他的话悦我的魂，因为那是真正的男子汉和爱国者的话。那夜传来了戴科斯陷落的消息，传来了伊努托人逼近的消息——矮墩墩的、地狱般的黄色魔鬼，五年前从无人知晓的西方出现，蹂躏我们王国的边境，终于围困我们的城镇。山脚下的要塞既失，他们通向高原的路已敞开，除非每一个公民都能以十人之力抵挡。因为那些矮墩墩的家伙精通战阵，而且不懂得我们洛马尔灰眼高个子男子的荣誉顾忌——正是那顾忌，拦住我们不去做无情的征服。

===Original===

Alos, my friend, was commander of all the forces on the plateau, and in him lay the last hope of our country. On this occasion he spoke of the perils to be faced and exhorted the men of Olathoe, bravest of the Lomarians, to sustain the traditions of their ancestors, who when forced to move southward from Zobna before the advance of the great ice sheet, (even as our descendants must some day flee from the land of Lomar) valiantly and victoriously swept aside the hairy, long-armed, cannibal Gnophkehs that stood in their way. To me Alos denied a warrior’s part, for I was feeble and given to strange faintings when subjected to stress and hardships. But my eyes were the keenest in the city, despite the long hours I gave each day to the study of the Pnakotic manuscripts and the wisdom of the Zobnarian Fathers; so my friend, desiring not to doom me to inaction, rewarded me with that duty which was second to nothing in importance. To the watchtower of Thapnen he sent me, there to serve as the eyes of our army. Should the Inutos attempt to gain the citadel by the narrow pass behind the peak Noton and thereby surprise the garrison, I was to give the signal of fire which would warn the waiting soldiers, and, save the town from immediate disaster.

Alone I mounted the tower, for every man of stout body was needed in the passes below. My brain was sore dazed with excitement and fatigue, for I had not slept in many days; yet was my purpose firm, for I loved my native land of Lomar, and the marble city Olathoe that lies betwixt the peaks of Noton and Kadiphonek.

But as I stood in the tower’s topmost chamber, I beheld the horned waning moon, red and sinister, quivering through the vapours that hovered over the distant valley of Banof. And through an opening in the roof glittered the pale Pole Star, fluttering as if alive, and leering like a fiend and tempter. Methought its spirit whispered evil counsel, soothing me to traitorous somnolence with a damnable rhythmical promise which it repeated over and over:

“Slumber, watcher, till the spheres,

Six and twenty thousand years

Have revolv’d, and I return

To the spot where now I burn.

Other stars anon shall rise

To the axis of the skies;

Stars that soothe and stars that bless

With a sweet forgetfulness:

Only when my round is o’er

Shall the past disturb thy door.”

===Chinese===

我的朋友阿洛斯是高原上全军的统帅，我国的最后希望就在他身上。这一次，他讲说面临的危难，勉励奥拉索厄人——洛马尔人中最勇敢的——承住祖先的传统：当年大冰盖进逼，他们被迫从佐布纳南迁（正如我们的子孙有朝一日也必得逃离洛马尔之地），一路英勇而胜捷地扫开挡路的多毛、长臂、食人的诺夫克人。阿洛斯不许我充战士，因为我体弱，一受劳顿困苦就犯古怪的晕厥。可我的眼睛是全城最利的，尽管我每天把许多钟头花在研读普纳科提克手稿和佐布纳先哲的智慧上；于是我的朋友不愿判我无所事事，把一个重要性仅次于一切的职任给了我：他派我到塔普嫩的瞭望塔去，做我们大军的眼睛。倘若伊努托人企图从诺顿峰背后的窄道夺取卫城、奇袭守军，我便点起火信号，警告待命的士兵，救全城于旦夕之祸。

我独自登上塔，因为身强力壮的每一个人都需守在下面的山口。我的脑子被激动和疲乏搅得发昏，我已多日不眠；可我的意志坚定，因为我爱我的故土洛马尔，爱卧在诺顿峰与卡迪福内克峰之间的大理石之城奥拉索厄。

可当我立在塔顶的小室里，我望见长角的残月，红而凶险，在远方的巴诺夫谷上浮起的水汽里颤动。屋顶的一处开孔里，闪着惨白的北极星，扑动如活物，斜睨如魔鬼和诱引者。我仿佛觉得它的精魂在低语恶毒的劝告，用一个该咒的有节律的许诺，一遍又一遍，哄我坠入背叛的昏睡：

“睡吧，守望者，直到诸天

再转两万六千年，

我自回到此刻燃烧的地点。

别的星随后会升起

升到诸天的轴极；

有星抚慰，有星祝福，

给你甜美的忘却：

只等我这一圈转完，

往昔才会来叩你的门。”

===Original===

Vainly did I struggle with my drowsiness, seeking to connect these strange words with some lore of the skies which I had learnt from the Pnakotic manuscripts. My head, heavy and reeling, drooped to my breast, and when next I looked up it was in a dream; with the Pole Star grinning at me through a window from over the horrible swaying trees of a dream-swamp. And I am still dreaming.

In my shame and despair I sometimes scream frantically, begging the dream-creatures around me to waken me ere the Inutos steal up the pass behind the peak Noton and take the citadel by surprise; but these creatures are daemons, for they laugh at me and tell me I am not dreaming. They mock me whilst I sleep, and whilst the squat yellow foe may be creeping silently upon us. I have failed in my duty and betrayed the marble city of Olathoe; I have proven false to Alos, my friend and commander. But still these shadows of my dreams deride me. They say there is no land of Lomar, save in my nocturnal imaginings; that in those realms where the Pole Star shines high, and red Aldebaran crawls low around the horizon, there has been naught save ice and snow for thousands of years, and never a man save squat, yellow creatures, blighted by the cold, whom they call “Eskimo.”

And as I writhe in my guilty agony, frantic to save the city whose peril every moment grows, and vainly striving to shake off this unnatural dream of a house of stone and brick south of a sinister swamp and a cemetery on a low hillock; the Pole Star, evil and monstrous, leers down from the black vault, winking hideously like an insane watching eye which strives to convey some message, yet recalls nothing save that it once had a message to convey.

===Chinese===

我徒劳地同睡魔挣扎，想把这些奇怪的字句同我从普纳科提克手稿里学到的某种天文学问连起来。我那沉重的、晕眩的头垂到胸前，再抬眼时，已是在梦里；北极星隔着一扇窗朝我狞笑，窗外是梦的沼泽那些可怕的摇曳的树。而我至今仍在梦里。

羞惭与绝望之中，我有时狂乱地尖叫，哀求我梦里的那些造物，趁伊努托人还没偷偷摸上诺顿峰背后的山道、奇袭卫城，把我唤醒；可那些造物是魔鬼，它们笑我，说我并没有在做梦。我睡着，它们嘲弄我；那矮墩墩的黄色敌人，也许正悄悄向我们爬近。我失了职守，背叛了大理石的城奥拉索厄；我对不起阿洛斯，我的朋友和统帅。可我梦里的这些影子还是讥笑我。它们说，没有什么洛马尔之地，只在我的夜想里才有；说在北极星高照、红毕宿五低低绕行的那些地方，几千年除冰雪外一无所有，从没有过人，只有矮墩墩的、被寒冷毁了形的黄色造物——它们管他们叫“爱斯基摩人”。

而当我在罪疚的苦痛里翻滚，狂乱地想救那危殆每一刻都在加深的城，徒劳地想甩脱这场不自然的梦——凶险沼泽和矮丘墓地之南一座砖石房子的梦——北极星，邪恶而巨大，从黑色的穹窿里斜睨下来，可憎地眨着，像一只疯狂的守视的眼，拼命想传达什么讯息，却只记得自己曾有一个讯息要传达。

## The Alchemist / 炼金术士
===Original===

High up, crowning the grassy summit of a swelling mound whose sides are wooded near the base with the gnarled trees of the primeval forest, stands the old château of my ancestors. For centuries its lofty battlements have frowned down upon the wild and rugged countryside about, serving as a home and stronghold for the proud house whose honoured line is older even than the moss-grown castle walls. These ancient turrets, stained by the storms of generations and crumbling under the slow yet mighty pressure of time, formed in the ages of feudalism one of the most dreaded and formidable fortresses in all France. From its machicolated parapets and mounted battlements Barons, Counts, and even Kings had been defied, yet never had its spacious halls resounded to the footstep of the invader.

But since those glorious years all is changed. A poverty but little above the level of dire want, together with a pride of name that forbids its alleviation by the pursuits of commercial life, have prevented the scions of our line from maintaining their estates in pristine splendour; and the falling stones of the walls, the overgrown vegetation in the parks, the dry and dusty moat, the ill-paved courtyards, and toppling towers without, as well as the sagging floors, the worm-eaten wainscots, and the faded tapestries within, all tell a gloomy tale of fallen grandeur. As the ages passed, first one, then another of the four great turrets were left to ruin, until at last but a single tower housed the sadly reduced descendants of the once mighty lords of the estate.

===Chinese===

高高的，在一座隆起土丘的草顶上——丘脚一带覆着原始森林多节的古树——立着我祖先的古堡。几百年来，它高高的城垛俯临着周围荒凉崎岖的乡野，做着一个骄傲门第的家园和堡垒，那个尊贵的家系，甚至比生满青苔的城堡围墙还要古老。这些古老的角楼，被世世代代的风雨浸染，在时间缓慢而巨大的压力下剥蚀，在封建时代曾是全法兰西最可畏、最坚固的堡垒之一。从它带堞口的女儿墙和架着炮的城垛上，男爵、伯爵、甚至国王都曾被抗拒，可它宽敞的大厅，从不曾回响过入侵者的脚步。

可自那些辉煌岁月以来，一切都变了。一种仅高出赤贫一线的贫穷，加上一种不许靠经商来缓解的家门骄傲，使我们这一支的子孙无力维持产业的旧日光华；墙上的落石，园中疯长的草木，干涸积尘的壕沟，铺得糟糕的院子，外面倾颓的塔，加上里面下陷的地板、虫蛀的护壁板、褪色的挂毯，都在讲一个门庭败落的阴郁故事。随着世纪流过，四座大角楼一座接一座地任其倾颓，到末了，只剩一座塔，住着这份产业昔日威严领主们的、凄凉地减少了的后裔。

===Original===

It was in one of the vast and gloomy chambers of this remaining tower that I, Antoine, last of the unhappy and accursed Comtes de C﻿—﻿—, first saw the light of day, ninety long years ago. Within these walls, and amongst the dark and shadowy forests, the wild ravines and grottoes of the hillside below, were spent the first years of my troubled life. My parents I never knew. My father had been killed at the age of thirty-two, a month before I was born, by the fall of a stone somehow dislodged from one of the deserted parapets of the castle, and my mother having died at my birth, my care and education devolved solely upon one remaining servitor, an old and trusted man of considerable intelligence, whose name I remember as Pierre. I was an only child, and the lack of companionship which this fact entailed upon me was augmented by the strange care exercised by my aged guardian in excluding me from the society of the peasant children whose abodes were scattered here and there upon the plains that surround the base of the hill. At the time, Pierre said that this restriction was imposed upon me because my noble birth placed me above association with such plebeian company. Now I know that its real object was to keep from my ears the idle tales of the dread curse upon our line, that were nightly told and magnified by the simple tenantry as they conversed in hushed accents in the glow of their cottage hearths.

Thus isolated, and thrown upon my own resources, I spent the hours of my childhood in poring over the ancient tomes that filled the shadow-haunted library of the château, and in roaming without aim or purpose through the perpetual dusk of the spectral wood that clothes the sides of the hill near its foot. It was perhaps an effect of such surroundings that my mind early acquired a shade of melancholy. Those studies and pursuits which partake of the dark and occult in nature most strongly claimed my attention.

===Chinese===

正是在这仅存之塔一间巨大而阴暗的屋子里，我，安托万——不幸而受咒的德·C——伯爵家的最后一个——九十年前，第一次见到了天光。在这些墙内，在山下阴暗的森林、野谷和岩洞之间，我度过了我烦扰一生的最初岁月。我的父母我从不曾认识。我的父亲三十二岁上死了，在我出生前一个月，被城堡一处荒废女儿墙上不知怎么松动落下的一块石头砸死；母亲又死于生我，于是照管和教养我的事，全落在仅存的一个仆人身上——一个年迈而可信、相当有智性的男人，我记得他叫皮埃尔。我是独子，由此而来的孤伴之缺，又因年迈监护人对我的一种古怪看管而加深：他不许我同农家孩子来往，他们的住屋星星点点散在山脚四周的平原上。当时皮埃尔说，这约束加于我，是因为我高贵的出身使我不能同这等平民为伍。如今我知道，它真正的用意，是不叫我的耳朵沾上关于我家那可怕诅咒的闲话——淳朴的佃户们每夜在农舍炉火的光里压低嗓门交谈，把它讲得越来越大。

就这样与世隔绝，全凭自己，我把童年的时辰消磨在古堡闹鬼书房里满架古书的钻研中，消磨在山脚近处披覆山坡的幽灵之林的无尽暮色里的漫无目的的游荡中。多半是这种环境的作用，我的心早早染上一点忧郁。凡是带几分黑暗和玄秘性质的学问和嗜好，最强烈地吸引着我。

===Original===

Of my own race I was permitted to learn singularly little, yet what small knowledge of it I was able to gain, seemed to depress me much. Perhaps it was at first only the manifest reluctance of my old preceptor to discuss with me my paternal ancestry that gave rise to the terror which I ever felt at the mention of my great house, yet as I grew out of childhood, I was able to piece together disconnected fragments of discourse, let slip from the unwilling tongue which had begun to falter in approaching senility, that had a sort of relation to a certain circumstance which I had always deemed strange, but which now became dimly terrible. The circumstance to which I allude is the early age at which all the Comtes of my line had met their end. Whilst I had hitherto considered this but a natural attribute of a family of short-lived men, I afterward pondered long upon these premature deaths, and began to connect them with the wanderings of the old man, who often spoke of a curse which for centuries had prevented the lives of the holders of my title from much exceeding the span of thirty-two years. Upon my twenty-first birthday, the aged Pierre gave to me a family document which he said had for many generations been handed down from father to son, and continued by each possessor. Its contents were of the most startling nature, and its perusal confirmed the gravest of my apprehensions. At this time, my belief in the supernatural was firm and deep-seated, else I should have dismissed with scorn the incredible narrative unfolded before my eyes.

===Chinese===

关于我自己的一族，我只被许知道得出奇地少，而我勉力得来的那一点点，又似乎叫我极是消沉。起先，也许只是老监护人对谈论我父系家谱的明显勉强，养成了我一提及我伟大门第便感到的那种恐怖；可随着我长大，脱离了童年，我能把散漫的言语碎片拼凑起来了——它们从不情愿的、临近老朽而开始结巴的舌尖漏出，同某一件我一直觉得古怪、如今却隐约觉得可怕的事有某种关联。我所指的事，是我这一族历代伯爵全都早死的年纪。从前我只当这是短命家族的天然属性，后来我久久琢磨这些夭亡，开始把它们同老人的游荡联系起来——他常常说到一个诅咒，几百年来不许我家爵位的持有者活过三十二岁太多。我二十一岁生日那天，年迈的皮埃尔给了我一份家族文书，说它多少代以来父子相传，每一位持有者接着写下去。它的内容极其惊人，一读之下，证实了我最重的忧惧。那时我对超自然的信仰根深蒂固，否则我会嗤笑着抛开眼前展开的这难以置信的叙述。

===Original===

The paper carried me back to the days of the thirteenth century, when the old castle in which I sat had been a feared and impregnable fortress. It told of a certain ancient man who had once dwelt on our estates, a person of no small accomplishments, though little above the rank of peasant; by name, Michel, usually designated by the surname of Mauvais, the Evil, on account of his sinister reputation. He had studied beyond the custom of his kind, seeking such things as the Philosopher’s Stone, or the Elixir of Eternal Life, and was reputed wise in the terrible secrets of Black Magic and Alchemy. Michel Mauvais had one son, named Charles, a youth as proficient as himself in the hidden arts, and who had therefore been called Le Sorcier, or the Wizard. This pair, shunned by all honest folk, were suspected of the most hideous practices. Old Michel was said to have burnt his wife alive as a sacrifice to the Devil, and the unaccountable disappearances of many small peasant children were laid at the dreaded door of these two. Yet through the dark natures of the father and the son ran one redeeming ray of humanity; the evil old man loved his offspring with fierce intensity, whilst the youth had for his parent a more than filial affection.

One night the castle on the hill was thrown into the wildest confusion by the vanishment of young Godfrey, son to Henri, the Comte. A searching party, headed by the frantic father, invaded the cottage of the sorcerers and there came upon old Michel Mauvais, busy over a huge and violently boiling cauldron. Without certain cause, in the ungoverned madness of fury and despair, the Comte laid hands on the aged wizard, and ere he released his murderous hold his victim was no more. Meanwhile joyful servants were proclaiming aloud the finding of young Godfrey in a distant and unused chamber of the great edifice, telling too late that poor Michel had been killed in vain. As the Comte and his associates turned away from the lowly abode of the alchemists, the form of Charles Le Sorcier appeared through the trees. The excited chatter of the menials standing about told him what had occurred, yet he seemed at first unmoved at his father’s fate. Then, slowly advancing to meet the Comte, he pronounced in dull yet terrible accents the curse that ever afterward haunted the house of C﻿—﻿—.

“May ne’er a noble of thy murd’rous line

===Chinese===

这份文书把我带回十三世纪，那时我坐着的老堡是一座令人畏惧、攻不破的堡垒。它讲到一个曾经住在我们产业上的老人，一个虽只略高于农人品级、却颇有造诣的人；名叫米歇尔，通常以外号“恶人莫万”称之，因为他名声险恶。他的学问超出他那类人的惯例，寻求点金石、长生不老药一类东西，据说精通黑魔法和炼金术的可怕秘密。恶人米歇尔有一个儿子，名叫夏尔，一个在隐秘技艺上同他一样精熟的青年，因此被人称作“巫师”。这一对父子，正经人个个回避，被疑干着最见不得人的勾当。据说老米歇尔把活着的妻子烧死，献祭给魔鬼；许多农家小孩的无端失踪，也被记在这两个可怕的人的账上。然而，在父与子的黑暗天性里，也穿过一线救赎的人性：邪恶的老人爱他的后代爱得炽烈；那青年对父亲，怀着一种超出孝道的感情。

一夜，山上城堡陷入最大的骚乱：伯爵亨利的儿子、小戈弗雷失踪了。一队人由狂乱的父亲带领，闯进术士父子的农舍，撞见老恶人米歇尔，正忙着照看一口猛烈沸腾的大锅。没有确凿的缘由，在狂怒与绝望的失控疯狂中，伯爵掐住了年迈的巫师，不等松开那杀人的手，被害者已经没气了。与此同时，欢天喜地的仆人们正高声传报：小戈弗雷在宏伟府邸一间偏僻不用的屋里找到了——这消息来得太迟，可怜的米歇尔白死了。当伯爵一行人从炼金术士的低矮住处转开时，巫师夏尔的身形穿过树林显现。站在一旁的仆人们的兴奋絮语告诉他发生了什么，可他对父亲的命运起初像是无动于衷。随后，他缓缓走上前来迎着伯爵，用平板而可怕的声调，念出了从此永远纠缠着德·C——家的诅咒。

“愿你那杀人的一族

===Original===

Survive to reach a greater age than thine!”

spake he, when, suddenly leaping backwards into the black wood, he drew from his tunic a phial of colourless liquid which he threw in the face of his father’s slayer as he disappeared behind the inky curtain of the night. The Comte died without utterance, and was buried the next day, but little more than two and thirty years from the hour of his birth. No trace of the assassin could be found, though relentless bands of peasants scoured the neighboring woods and the meadow-land around the hill.

Thus time and the want of a reminder dulled the memory of the curse in the minds of the late Comte’s family, so that when Godfrey, innocent cause of the whole tragedy and now bearing the title, was killed by an arrow whilst hunting, at the age of thirty-two, there were no thoughts save those of grief at his demise. But when, years afterward, the next young Comte, Robert by name, was found dead in a nearby field from no apparent cause, the peasants told in whispers that their seigneur had but lately passed his thirty-second birthday when surprised by early death. Louis, son to Robert, was found drowned in the moat at the same fateful age, and thus down through the centuries ran the ominous chronicle; Henris, Roberts, Antoines, and Armands snatched from happy and virtuous lives when a little below the age of their unfortunate ancestor at his murder.

===Chinese===

再没有一个贵族活到比你更高的年纪！”

他说罢，骤然向后跃进黑色的树林，从袍下摸出一小瓶无色的液体，泼向他父亲的凶手脸上，随即消失在夜的黑幕后。伯爵没来得及出一句话就死了，次日下葬，离他出生的时辰不过三十二年多一点。刺客踪影全无，尽管一队队不肯罢休的农民搜遍了附近的树林和山周草地。

就这样，时间和没有提醒，把诅咒的记忆在后一代伯爵家人的心里磨钝了；于是当戈弗雷——整场悲剧的无辜肇因，如今承了爵位——三十二岁上狩猎时中箭而死，人们心里只有哀悼，再无别的念头。可多年以后，下一位年轻的伯爵，名叫罗贝尔，在附近一块田野里被发现死了，死因不明，佃户们便交头接耳：他们的领主遭横死时，刚过三十二岁生日不久。罗贝尔的儿子路易，在同一个命数的年纪，被发现淹死在壕沟里；就这样，不祥的编年史沿着世纪流下去：一代代亨利、罗贝尔、安托万、阿尔芒，在他们那位倒霉先人遇害时的年纪略往下一点，被从幸福而良善的生活里攝走。

===Original===

That I had left at most but eleven years of further existence was made certain to me by the words which I read. My life, previously held at small value, now became dearer to me each day, as I delved deeper and deeper into the mysteries of the hidden world of black magic. Isolated as I was, modern science had produced no impression upon me, and I laboured as in the Middle Ages, as wrapt as had been old Michel and young Charles themselves in the acquisition of demonological and alchemical learning. Yet read as I might, in no manner could I account for the strange curse upon my line. In unusually rational moments, I would even go so far as to seek a natural explanation, attributing the early deaths of my ancestors to the sinister Charles Le Sorcier and his heirs; yet having found upon careful inquiry that there were no known descendants of the alchemist, I would fall back to my occult studies, and once more endeavour to find a spell that would release my house from its terrible burden. Upon one thing I was absolutely resolved. I should never wed, for since no other branches of my family were in existence, I might thus end the curse with myself.

As I drew near the age of thirty, old Pierre was called to the land beyond. Alone I buried him beneath the stones of the courtyard about which he had loved to wander in life. Thus was I left to ponder on myself as the only human creature within the great fortress, and in my utter solitude my mind began to cease its vain protest against the impending doom, to become almost reconciled to the fate which so many of my ancestors had met. Much of my time was now occupied in the exploration of the ruined and abandoned halls and towers of the old château, which in youth fear had caused me to shun, and some of which old Pierre had once told me had not been trodden by human foot for over four centuries. Strange and awesome were many of the objects I encountered. Furniture, covered by the dust of ages and crumbling with the rot of long dampness met my eyes. Cobwebs in a profusion never before seen by me were spun everywhere, and huge bats flapped their bony and uncanny wings on all sides of the otherwise untenanted gloom.

===Chinese===

我至多还剩十一年可活，这一点，读到的文字叫我确凿无疑了。我这条先前本不看重性命，如今一天比一天更觉贵重，因为我越钻越深，钻进黑色魔法那个隐秘世界的神秘里。我既与世隔绝，现代科学不曾对我有过一点影响，我像在中世纪一样劳作，像老米歇尔和年轻的夏尔当年那样入迷地获取魔学和炼金的知识。可任凭我怎么读，我全然解释不了落在我家族上的奇怪诅咒。在格外理性的时刻，我甚至去寻一种自然的解释，把先人们的早死归给阴险的巫师夏尔和他的后人；可细查之下发现炼金术士并没有已知的后裔，我便又跌回玄秘的钻研，再一次设法找一道咒，解我的家门于那可怕的重负。有一件事我是铁了心的：我永不结婚，因为我的家族别无旁支，这样，诅咒便可终结在我身上。

临近三十岁时，老皮埃尔被召去了彼世。我独自把他葬在院中的石板下——生前他爱在那一带流连。就这样，我成了大堡垒里唯一的人，被撇下独自思量；在彻底的孤独里，我的心渐渐停止了对临头厄运的徒劳抗议，几乎同那许多先人共过的命运和解了。我的时光如今大半花在探察古堡废弃的大厅和角楼上——年轻时恐惧使我避开的地方，有几处，老皮埃尔曾告诉我，四百多年不曾有人踏过。我撞见的许多物件古怪而可畏。蒙着年代尘土、在长年潮湿里朽烂的家具扑进眼里。多得我从未见过的蛛网到处结着，巨大的蝙蝠在无人阴晦的四下拍着瘦骨嶙峋的可憎翅膀。

===Original===

Of my exact age, even down to days and hours, I kept a most careful record, for each movement of the pendulum of the massive clock in the library tolled off so much more of my doomed existence. At length I approached that time which I had so long viewed with apprehension. Since most of my ancestors had been seized some little while before they reached the exact age of the Comte Henri at his end, I was every moment on the watch for the coming of the unknown death. In what strange form the curse should overtake me, I knew not; but I was resolved at least that it should not find me a cowardly or a passive victim. With new vigour I applied myself to my examination of the old château and its contents.

===Chinese===

我连自己的确切年纪，精确到日和钟点，都仔细记录着，因为书房里那座大钟的钟摆每摆一下，便敲掉我命定存在的一分。终于，我逼近了那个长久以来心怀忧惧的时辰。我的先人们大多在未到伯爵亨利确切死龄之前不多时便被攝去，所以我时时刻刻提防着那未知之死的到来。诅咒会以怎样的怪样子追上我，我不知道；可我至少拿定主意，它找到的我，不该是一个懦怯或被动的牺牲。我以新的劲头，继续我对古堡及其藏物的查考。

===Original===

It was upon one of the longest of all my excursions of discovery in the deserted portion of the castle, less than a week before that fatal hour which I felt must mark the utmost limit of my stay on Earth, beyond which I could have not even the slightest hope of continuing to draw breath, that I came upon the culminating event of my whole life. I had spent the better part of the morning in climbing up and down half ruined staircases in one of the most dilapidated of the ancient turrets. As the afternoon progressed, I sought the lower levels, descending into what appeared to be either a medieval place of confinement, or a more recently excavated storehouse for gunpowder. As I slowly traversed the nitre-encrusted passageway at the foot of the last staircase, the paving became very damp, and soon I saw by the light of my flickering torch that a blank, water-stained wall impeded my journey. Turning to retrace my steps, my eye fell upon a small trapdoor with a ring, which lay directly beneath my feet. Pausing, I succeeded with difficulty in raising it, whereupon there was revealed a black aperture, exhaling noxious fumes which caused my torch to sputter, and disclosing in the unsteady glare the top of a flight of stone steps. As soon as the torch, which I lowered into the repellent depths, burned freely and steadily, I commenced my descent. The steps were many, and led to a narrow stone-flagged passage which I knew must be far underground. This passage proved of great length, and terminated in a massive oaken door, dripping with the moisture of the place, and stoutly resisting all my attempts to open it. Ceasing after a time my efforts in this direction, I had proceeded back some distance toward the steps, when there suddenly fell to my experience one of the most profound and maddening shocks capable of reception by the human mind. Without warning, *I heard the heavy door behind me creak slowly open upon its rusted hinges*. My immediate sensations are incapable of analysis. To be confronted in a place as thoroughly deserted as I had deemed the old castle with evidence of the presence of man or spirit, produced in my brain a horror of the most acute description. When at last I turned and faced the seat of the sound, my eyes must have started from their orbits at the sight that they beheld. There in the ancient Gothic doorway stood a human figure.

===Chinese===

那是我对城堡荒弃部分的一切探察中最长的一次，离那个我感到必是我留世极限的致命时辰不到一个星期——过了它，我再无一丝续喘的希望——就在那次，我撞上了我一生的高潮事件。那天上午的大半，我都在一座最破败的古角楼里，爬上爬下半塌的楼梯。下午渐深，我寻到较低的层，下到一个像是中世纪拘囚之地、或新近挖的火药库的地方。当我缓缓走过最末一道楼梯脚下那条硝壳斑斑的过道，铺石变得很湿，很快，凭着我那支摇曳火把的光，我看到一面渗着水渍的空墙拦住了去路。我转身要折回，眼睛落在脚下一个带环的小活板门上。我停下，费力地掀起了它，底下露出一个黑色的口子，呼出恶毒的烟气，呛得火把劈啪作响，在不稳的光焰里，照出一段石阶的顶。等降到那可憎深处的火把烧得畅旺稳定，我便开始下去。台阶很多，通到一条窄窄的铺石甬道，我知道必已在地下深处。这条甬道极长，尽头是一扇厚重的橡木门，滴着此地的水汽，我怎样弄也弄不开。在这个方向试了一阵之后，我已往回走了相当一段，突然，人类心智所能承受的最深重、最疯狂的震撼之一，落到了我身上。毫无预兆，*我听见身后那扇沉重的门，在锈蚀的铰链上缓缓地吱呀打开了*。我即刻的感觉无从分析。在我本以为彻底无人迹的老堡里，面对面撞上人或幽灵存在的证据，这在我脑中激起最尖锐的一种恐怖。等我终于转身，面向声音来处，我的眼睛见了那景象，准是从眼眶里突了出来。在古老的哥特式门洞里，立着一个人形。

===Original===

It was that of a man clad in a skullcap and long medieval tunic of dark colour. His long hair and flowing beard were of a terrible and intense black hue, and of incredible profusion. His forehead, high beyond the usual dimensions; his cheeks, deep sunken and heavily lined with wrinkles; and his hands, long, claw-like and gnarled, were of such a deathly, marble-like whiteness as I have never elsewhere seen in man. His figure, lean to the proportions of a skeleton, was strangely bent and almost lost within the voluminous folds of his peculiar garment. But strangest of all were his eyes; twin caves of abysmal blackness; profound in expression of understanding, yet inhuman in degree of wickedness. These were now fixed upon me, piercing my soul with their hatred, and rooting me to the spot whereon I stood. At last the figure spoke in a rumbling voice that chilled me through with its dull hollowness and latent malevolence. The language in which the discourse was clothed was that debased form of Latin in use amongst the more learned men of the Middle Ages, and made familiar to me by my prolonged researches into the works of the old alchemists and demonologists. The apparition spoke of the curse which had hovered over my house, told me of my coming end, dwelt on the wrong perpetrated by my ancestor against old Michel Mauvais, and gloated over the revenge of Charles Le Sorcier. He told me how the young Charles had escaped into the night, returning in after years to kill Godfrey the heir with an arrow just as he approached the age which had been his father’s at his assassination; how he had secretly returned to the estate and established himself, unknown, in the even then deserted subterranean chamber whose doorway now framed the hideous narrator; how he had seized Robert, son of Godfrey, in a field, forced poison down his throat and left him to die at the age of thirty-two, thus maintaining the foul provisions of his vengeful curse.

===Chinese===

那是一个男人，戴一顶无边小帽，穿一件深色的中世纪长袍。他的长发和飘拂的须，是一种可怕而浓烈的黑色，密得难以置信。他的额头，高得超出寻常的尺度；他的双颊，深深下陷，刻满皱纹；他的双手，细长，爪样，多节——都带着一种死一般的大理石似的白，我在别处的人身上从未见过。他的身形，瘦到骷髅的比例，古怪地佝偻着，几乎消失在那件独特袍子的宽大褶层里。而最古怪的是他的眼睛：两汪深渊似的黑色洞穴；深含着领悟的表情，其邪恶的程度却非人所有。此刻它们盯住我，用它们的憎恨穿透我的魂，把我钉在我站立的地方。那身影终于开口了，用一种隆隆的嗓音，那声音的单调空洞和潜藏的歹毒，把我凉透。谈话所用的语言，是中世纪较有学问的人们通用的那种下等拉丁语，我因长期研究老炼金术士和魔学家的著作而熟悉。那幽魂讲起笼罩我家的诅咒，讲了我的死期将至，细数我的先人对老恶人米歇尔犯下的冤业，为巫师夏尔的报复而得意。他告诉我，年轻的夏尔怎样逃进夜里，多年后回来，正当继承人戈弗雷逼近他父亲遇害的年纪时，用一支箭射死了他；他怎样悄悄回到产业，隐姓埋名，住进那间当时已废弃的地下室——它的门洞此刻正框着这可憎的叙述者；他怎样在一块田野里捉住戈弗雷的儿子罗贝尔，把毒药灌下他的喉咙，任他三十二岁死去，就这样维持着他复仇诅咒的恶毒条款。

===Original===

At this point I was left to imagine the solution of the greatest mystery of all, how the curse had been fulfilled since that time when Charles Le Sorcier must in the course of nature have died, for the man digressed into an account of the deep alchemical studies of the two wizards, father and son, speaking most particularly of the researches of Charles Le Sorcier concerning the elixir which should grant to him who partook of it eternal life and youth.

His enthusiasm had seemed for the moment to remove from his terrible eyes the hatred that had at first so haunted them, but suddenly the fiendish glare returned, and with a shocking sound like the hissing of a serpent, the stranger raised a glass phial with the evident intent of ending my life as had Charles Le Sorcier, six hundred years before, ended that of my ancestor. Prompted by some preserving instinct of self-defense, I broke through the spell that had hitherto held me immovable, and flung my now dying torch at the creature who menaced my existence. I heard the phial break harmlessly against the stones of the passage as the tunic of the strange man caught fire and lit the horrid scene with a ghastly radiance. The shriek of fright and impotent malice emitted by the would-be assassin proved too much for my already shaken nerves, and I fell prone upon the slimy floor in a total faint.

===Chinese===

讲到这里，最大的谜底便留给我自己去想象了——自巫师夏尔按自然之理必死之后，诅咒又何以始终得逞——因为那人岔了开去，讲起两个巫师父子的深奥炼金研究，特别说到巫师夏尔对那种药的钻研：谁服下它，谁便得永生和青春。

有一刻，他的热望似乎把他可怕眼睛里起初盘踞的恨意驱走了，可那魔鬼的凶光突然又回来，随着一声蛇嘶似的骇人声响，那陌生人举起一只玻璃小瓶，分明是要了结我的性命，一如六百年前巫师夏尔了结我祖先的性命。被某种自我保存的本能催动，我挣破了先前把我钉死的魔咒，把那截将熄的火把掷向威胁我存在的怪物。我听见小瓶无害地碎在甬道的石上，那怪人的长袍着了火，用一种坟墓般的光照亮这可怕的场景。那未遂刺客发出的恐惧而无力歹毒的尖叫，叫我本已动摇的神经再撑不住，我栽倒在黏滑的地上，彻底晕了过去。

===Original===

When at last my senses returned, all was frightfully dark, and my mind remembering what had occurred, shrank from the idea of beholding more; yet curiosity overmastered all. Who, I asked myself, was this man of evil, and how came he within the castle walls? Why should he seek to avenge the death of poor Michel Mauvais, and how had the curse been carried on through all the long centuries since the time of Charles Le Sorcier? The dread of years was lifted off my shoulders, for I knew that he whom I had felled was the source of all my danger from the curse; and now that I was free, I burned with the desire to learn more of the sinister thing which had haunted my line for centuries, and made of my own youth one long-continued nightmare. Determined upon further exploration, I felt in my pockets for flint and steel, and lit the unused torch which I had with me. First of all, the new light revealed the distorted and blackened form of the mysterious stranger. The hideous eyes were now closed. Disliking the sight, I turned away and entered the chamber beyond the Gothic door. Here I found what seemed much like an alchemist’s laboratory. In one corner was an immense pile of a shining yellow metal that sparkled gorgeously in the light of the torch. It may have been gold, but I did not pause to examine it, for I was strangely affected by that which I had undergone. At the farther end of the apartment was an opening leading out into one of the many wild ravines of the dark hillside forest. Filled with wonder, yet now realizing how the man had obtained access to the château, I proceeded to return. I had intended to pass by the remains of the stranger with averted face, but as I approached the body, I seemed to hear emanating from it a faint sound, as though life were not yet wholly extinct. Aghast, I turned to examine the charred and shrivelled figure on the floor.

===Chinese===

知觉终于回来时，四下一片可怕的黑，我的心记起了发生过的事，缩着不敢再见；可好奇压倒了一切。这个人是谁，我问自己，这恶人，他怎么进的城堡？他为什么要替可怜的恶人米歇尔复仇，而自巫师夏尔的时代以来，诅咒又怎样延续了这漫长的几个世纪？多年的惊惧从我肩头卸下了，因为我知道，我撂倒的这个，便是诅咒带给我的全部危险的源头；如今我自由了，我烧灼着渴望，想多知道一些那几个世纪纠缠我家族、把我自己的青春变作一场绵长噩梦的阴险之物。决意进一步探察，我在口袋里摸出火镰，点燃随身带着的备用火把。首先，新光照亮了那神秘陌生人扭曲焦黑的形体。那双可怕的眼睛闭着。我不愿多看，转身进了哥特式门内的屋子。这里的东西很像是炼金术士的实验室。一角堆着一大堆闪亮的黄色金属，在火把光里辉煌地闪烁。那也许是金子，可我没有停下来验看，因为我被方才的遭遇古怪地撼动了。屋子另一头有一个开口，通向黑暗山林诸多野谷中的一条。满怀着惊奇，又明白了那人如何进出古堡，我便动身返回。我本想偏过脸，从那陌生人的残骸旁边走过，可走近尸体时，我仿佛听见从那里发出一点微弱的声音，像生命还没有全然断绝。我惊骇地转身，去查看地上那具焦缩的躯体。

===Original===

Then all at once the horrible eyes, blacker even than the seared face in which they were set, opened wide with an expression which I was unable to interpret. The cracked lips tried to frame words which I could not well understand. Once I caught the name of Charles Le Sorcier, and again I fancied that the words “years” and “curse” issued from the twisted mouth. Still I was at a loss to gather the purport of his disconnected speech. At my evident ignorance of his meaning, the pitchy eyes once more flashed malevolently at me, until, helpless as I saw my opponent to be, I trembled as I watched him.

Suddenly the wretch, animated with his last burst of strength, raised his hideous head from the damp and sunken pavement. Then, as I remained, paralyzed with fear, he found his voice and in his dying breath screamed forth those words which have ever afterward haunted my days and my nights. “Fool,” he shrieked, “can you not guess my secret? Have you no brain whereby you may recognize the will which has through six long centuries fulfilled the dreadful curse upon your house? Have I not told you of the great elixir of eternal life? Know you not how the secret of Alchemy was solved? I tell you, it is I! I! *I! that have lived for six hundred years to maintain my revenge*, **for I am Charles Le Sorcier!**”

===Chinese===

骤然间，那双可怕的眼睛——比它们嵌着的焦脸还要黑——睁大了，带着一种我无法解读的表情。皲裂的嘴唇努力想拼出话来，我听不太懂。有一回我捉到了“巫师夏尔”的名字，又有一回，我恍惚觉得“年”和“诅咒”两个字从那扭曲的嘴里吐出来。可我仍旧抓不住他断续言语的要旨。见我显然不懂他的意思，那柏油似的眼睛又朝我凶恶地一闪，直到——明知我的对头已无力为害——我看着它仍旧发抖。

突然，那可怜虫被最后一股力气鼓动，从潮湿下陷的石地上抬起了他可憎的头。随后，当我僵立在那里、恐惧得动弹不得，他找回了嗓音，用垂死的呼吸，尖声喊出了那些从此日夜纠缠我的字句。“蠢货，”他厉叫，“你猜不出我的秘密么？你没有脑子，认不出那个意志么——六个漫长的世纪里，是它在你家身上履行着可怕的诅咒？我没有告诉过你那伟大的长生不老药么？你不知道炼金术的秘密早已解开么？我告诉你，是我！我！*我！六百年来维护我复仇的，就是我*，**因为我是巫师夏尔！**”

## The Call of Cthulhu / 克苏鲁的呼唤
===Original===

“Of such great powers or beings there may be conceivably a survival﻿ ﻿… a survival of a hugely remote period when﻿ ﻿… consciousness was manifested, perhaps, in shapes and forms long since withdrawn before the tide of advancing humanity﻿ ﻿… forms of which poetry and legend alone have caught a flying memory and called them gods, monsters, mythical beings of all sorts and kinds.﻿ ﻿…”

> Algernon Blackwood

===Chinese===

“这样的大力量或大存在，或许可能有残存者……残存自一个极其遥远的时期，那时……意识或许显现于一些形态和形体之中，早在推进中的人潮之前便已退隐……诗与传说仅捕捉到它们飞逝的记忆，称之为神、怪物、各类各样的神话造物。……”

> 阿尔杰农·布莱克伍德

## I / 一

## I / 
===Original===

The Horror in Clay

The most merciful thing in the world, I think, is the inability of the human mind to correlate all its contents. We live on a placid island of ignorance in the midst of black seas of infinity, and it was not meant that we should voyage far. The sciences, each straining in its own direction, have hitherto harmed us little; but some day the piecing together of dissociated knowledge will open up such terrifying vistas of reality, and of our frightful position therein, that we shall either go mad from the revelation or flee from the deadly light into the peace and safety of a new dark age.

Theosophists have guessed at the awesome grandeur of the cosmic cycle wherein our world and human race form transient incidents. They have hinted at strange survivals in terms which would freeze the blood if not masked by a bland optimism. But it is not from them that there came the single glimpse of forbidden eons which chills me when I think of it and maddens me when I dream of it. That glimpse, like all dread glimpses of truth, flashed out from an accidental piecing together of separated things﻿—in this case an old newspaper item and the notes of a dead professor. I hope that no one else will accomplish this piecing out; certainly, if I live, I shall never knowingly supply a link in so hideous a chain. I think that the professor, too, intended to keep silent regarding the part he knew, and that he would have destroyed his notes had not sudden death seized him.

===Chinese===

泥塑中的恐怖

世上最仁慈的事，我想，是人类心智无力把它的一切内容联成一体。我们住在一座平静的无知之岛上，四面是无穷的黑海，我们本不该远航。诸门科学各朝各的方向使劲，至今害我们还不多；可有朝一日，被拆散的知识一旦拼合，将敞开那样一些关于现实、关于我们在其中可怕位置的恐怖远景，我们要么被这启示逼疯，要么从那致命的光里逃进一个新的黑暗时代的平安。

神智学者们猜过宇宙大循环的骇人宏丽，我们的世界和人类在其中只是转瞬的事故。他们以一些字句暗示过怪异的残存者——若非罩着一层温和的乐观，那些字句会冻结血液。但叫我想到便寒、梦到便狂的、对禁锢时代的那唯一一瞥，并非来自他们。那一瞥，同一切对真理的可怖磎见一样，是从几件分离之物的偶然拼合中闪出的——本例中，是一则旧新闻和一位死去教授的笔记。我希望没有别的人再完成这番拼合；当然，只要我活着，我决不故意为这样一条可憎的链条供应任何一环。我想，那位教授也打算对他知道的那部分保持缄默，若不是猝死攝住了他，他早把笔记毁了。

===Original===

My knowledge of the thing began in the winter of 1926﻿–﻿27 with the death of my granduncle, George Gammell Angell, Professor Emeritus of Semitic languages in Brown University, Providence, Rhode Island. Professor Angell was widely known as an authority on ancient inscriptions, and had frequently been resorted to by the heads of prominent museums; so that his passing at the age of ninety-two may be recalled by many. Locally, interest was intensified by the obscurity of the cause of death. The professor had been stricken whilst returning from the Newport boat; falling suddenly, as witnesses said, after having been jostled by a nautical-looking negro who had come from one of the queer dark courts on the precipitous hillside which formed a shortcut from the waterfront to the deceased’s home in Williams Street. Physicians were unable to find any visible disorder, but concluded after perplexed debate that some obscure lesion of the heart, induced by the brisk ascent of so steep a hill by so elderly a man, was responsible for the end. At the time I saw no reason to dissent from this dictum, but latterly I am inclined to wonder﻿—and more than wonder.

As my granduncle’s heir and executor, for he died a childless widower, I was expected to go over his papers with some thoroughness; and for that purpose moved his entire set of files and boxes to my quarters in Boston. Much of the material which I correlated will be later published by the American Archeological Society, but there was one box which I found exceedingly puzzling, and which I felt much averse from showing to other eyes. It had been locked, and I did not find the key till it occurred to me to examine the personal ring which the professor carried always in his pocket. Then, indeed, I succeeded in opening it, but when I did so seemed only to be confronted by a greater and more closely locked barrier. For what could be the meaning of the queer clay bas-relief and the disjointed jottings, ramblings, and cuttings which I found? Had my uncle, in his latter years, become credulous of the most superficial impostures? I resolved to search out the eccentric sculptor responsible for this apparent disturbance of an old man’s peace of mind.

===Chinese===

我对这事的知识，始于一九二六至二七年的冬天，随着我的叔祖父乔治·加梅尔·安杰尔的死——他是罗得岛州普罗维登斯布朗大学的闪语系荣休教授。安杰尔教授是公认的古代铭文权威，各大博物馆的馆长们常去请教他；所以他九十二岁上的去世，许多人或许还记得。在本地，死因的模糊更加强了人们的兴味。教授是在从纽波特的班轮回来的路上出事的；据目击者说，一个水手模样的黑人从陡坡上那些古怪的黑巷子里出来——那是从滨水区到他威廉斯街住宅的近路——撞了他一下，他随即倒地。医生们找不到任何可见的病症，困惑地讨论之后断定：这样高龄的人快步爬上这样陡的山，引起了某种不明的心脏损伤，导致了死亡。当时我看不出有什么理由不同意这判词，可近来我倾向于怀疑——不止于怀疑。

作为叔祖父的继承人和遗嘱执行人——他死时是个无子的鳏夫——我须把他的文件相当彻底地过一遍；为此，我把他的全套档案箱笼都搬到了我在波士顿的住处。我整理的材料大多将由美国考古学会日后刊布，但有一只箱子叫我极为困惑，也极不愿给别的眼睛看。它是锁着的，直到我想起查看教授总揣在口袋里的私人钥匙环，才找到钥匙。开了之后，我却似乎只撞上一道更大、锁得更严的屏障。因为我找到的，是那块古怪的泥塑浮雕，和那些散乱的涂写、叹语和剪报，能有什么意义呢？莫非我叔父晚年被最浅薄的骗局骗信了？我决意去寻那位古怪的雕刻家——就是他，搅扰了一位老人的心境安宁。

===Original===

The bas-relief was a rough rectangle less than an inch thick and about five by six inches in area; obviously of modern origin. Its designs, however, were far from modern in atmosphere and suggestion; for, although the vagaries of cubism and futurism are many and wild, they do not often reproduce that cryptic regularity which lurks in prehistoric writing. And writing of some kind the bulk of these designs seemed certainly to be; though my memory, despite much familiarity with the papers and collections of my uncle, failed in any way to identify this particular species, or even hint at its remotest affiliations.

Above these apparent hieroglyphics was a figure of evidently pictorial intent, though its impressionistic execution forbade a very clear idea of its nature. It seemed to be a sort of monster, or symbol representing a monster, of a form which only a diseased fancy could conceive. If I say that my somewhat extravagant imagination yielded simultaneous pictures of an octopus, a dragon, and a human caricature, I shall not be unfaithful to the spirit of the thing. A pulpy, tentacled head surmounted a grotesque and scaly body with rudimentary wings; but it was the *general outline* of the whole which made it most shockingly frightful. Behind the figure was a vague suggestion of a Cyclopean architectural background.

===Chinese===

浮雕是一块粗糙的长方形，厚不到一英寸，面积约五乘六英寸；显然是现代的东西。它的图案，气氛和暗示上却全不现代；因为立体派和未来派的怪诞尽管又多又野，却不常复制那种潜藏在史前文字里的隐秘的规整。而这些图案的主体，看去确乎是某种文字；虽然我尽管熟悉叔父的文件和收藏，记忆却全然认不出这个特殊的种类，连它最疏远的亲缘也提示不出。

在这些似是而非的象形文字上方，有一个显然属图画意图的形象，虽然它印象派的手法叫人得不出清楚的概念。它像是一种怪物，或代表一个怪物的符号，其形态只有病态的幻想才能构想。如果我说，我那有点奢侈的想象力同时给出了一幅章鱼、一幅龙、一幅人的漫画的图景，我并没有背离这东西的精神。一个软块的、长触手的头，蹲在一具古怪的、覆鳞的、长着雏形翅膀的身体上；但最叫人震骇的是全体的*总体轮廓*。形象背后，隐隐有一个巨人族建筑背景的暗示。

===Original===

The writing accompanying this oddity was, aside from a stack of press cuttings, in Professor Angell’s most recent hand; and made no pretense to literary style. What seemed to be the main document was headed “**Cthulhu Cult**” in characters painstakingly printed to avoid the erroneous reading of a word so unheard-of. This manuscript was divided into two sections, the first of which was headed “1925﻿—Dream and Dream Work of H. A. Wilcox, 7 Thomas St., Providence, RI,” and the second, “Narrative of Inspector John R. Legrasse, 121 Bienville St., New Orleans, LA, at 1908 A.A.S. Mtg.﻿—Notes on Same, & Prof. Webb’s Acct.” The other manuscript papers were all brief notes, some of them accounts of the queer dreams of different persons, some of them citations from theosophical books and magazines (notably W. Scott-Eliott’s *Atlantis and the Lost Lemuria*), and the rest comments on long-surviving secret societies and hidden cults, with references to passages in such mythological and anthropological source-books as Frazer’s *Golden Bough* and Miss Murray’s *Witch-Cult in Western Europe*. The cuttings largely alluded to outré mental illnesses and outbreaks of group folly or mania in the spring of 1925.

---

The first half of the principal manuscript told a very peculiar tale. It appears that on March 1st, 1925, a thin, dark young man of neurotic and excited aspect had called upon Professor Angell bearing the singular clay bas-relief, which was then exceedingly damp and fresh. His card bore the name of Henry Anthony Wilcox, and my uncle had recognized him as the youngest son of an excellent family slightly known to him, who had latterly been studying sculpture at the Rhode Island School of Design and living alone at the Fleur-de-Lys Building near that institution. Wilcox was a precocious youth of known genius but great eccentricity, and had from childhood excited attention through the strange stories and odd dreams he was in the habit of relating. He called himself “psychically hypersensitive,” but the staid folk of the ancient commercial city dismissed him as merely “queer.” Never mingling much with his kind, he had dropped gradually from social visibility, and was now known only to a small group of esthetes from other towns. Even the Providence Art Club, anxious to preserve its conservatism, had found him quite hopeless.

===Chinese===

伴随着这件怪物的文字，除一摞剪报外，都出自安杰尔教授最晚近的手迹；毫不称意于文体。像是主文件的那份，标题是“**克苏鲁教团**”，用一笔一画印得仔细的字排成，免得这个闻所未闻的词被读错。手稿分两部，第一部题为“1925——H·A·威尔科克斯的梦与梦作，罗得岛普罗维登斯托马斯街7号”，第二部题为“约翰·R·勒格拉斯巡官的叙述，路易斯安那新奥尔良比安维尔街121号，1908年美国考古学会年会——及笔记与韦布教授的记述”。其余手稿都是简短的笔记，有的是各色人怪梦的记述，有的是神智学书刊的引文（特别是W·斯科特-埃利奥特的《亚特兰蒂斯与失落的利莫里亚》），其余是对长久残存的秘密会社和隐秘教团的评论，并引《金枝》（弗雷泽）和《西欧的巫术崇拜》（默里小姐）这类神话学和人类学源书中的段落。剪报大多暗指一九二五年春天离奇的精神病例和群体痴愚或癫狂的爆发。

---

主手稿的前半讲了一个非常古怪的故事。一九二五年三月一日，一个瘦削、黝黑、神经质而亢奋的青年，带着那块奇异的湿泥浮雕拜访了安杰尔教授。名片上印着亨利·安东尼·威尔科克斯，我叔父认得他是他略知的一家极好人家的幼子，近来在罗得岛设计学院学雕塑，独住在该学院附近的鸢尾花楼。威尔科克斯是个早熟的青年，天才已知而怪僻出名，从小就以他惯讲的怪故事和怪梦惹人注意。他自称“心灵过敏”，而这座古老商业城里古板的人们只把他归于“古怪”。他不大与同侪来往，渐渐从社交的视野里消失，如今只有一小群外来的审美家知道他。连一心要保持保守的普罗维登斯艺术俱乐部，也早觉得他无可救药。

===Original===

On the occasion of the visit, ran the professor’s manuscript, the sculptor abruptly asked for the benefit of his host’s archeological knowledge in identifying the hieroglyphics on the bas-relief. He spoke in a dreamy, stilted manner which suggested pose and alienated sympathy; and my uncle showed some sharpness in replying, for the conspicuous freshness of the tablet implied kinship with anything but archeology. Young Wilcox’s rejoinder, which impressed my uncle enough to make him recall and record it verbatim, was of a fantastically poetic cast which must have typified his whole conversation, and which I have since found highly characteristic of him. He said, “It is new, indeed, for I made it last night in a dream of strange cities; and dreams are older than brooding Tyre, or the contemplative Sphinx, or garden-girdled Babylon.”

It was then that he began that rambling tale which suddenly played upon a sleeping memory and won the fevered interest of my uncle. There had been a slight earthquake tremor the night before, the most considerable felt in New England for some years; and Wilcox’s imagination had been keenly affected. Upon retiring, he had had an unprecedented dream of great Cyclopean cities of Titan blocks and sky-flung monoliths, all dripping with green ooze and sinister with latent horror. Hieroglyphics had covered the walls and pillars, and from some undetermined point below had come a voice that was not a voice; a chaotic sensation which only fancy could transmute into sound, but which he attempted to render by the almost unpronounceable jumble of letters, “*Cthulhu fhtagn.*”

===Chinese===

教授的手稿里说，那次拜访中，雕刻家唐突地请求主人以考古学之识鉴别浮雕上的象形文字。他说话梦呓般、拿腔作调，透着做作，叫人无从同情；我叔父的答语便带了几分尖刻，因为石板那显眼的新鲜，同考古学毫无干系。小威尔科克斯的回答——它给我叔父的印象深到逐字回忆并记录下来——属于一种奇幻的诗体，想必代表了他全部的谈吐，我后来发现这正是他的本色。他说：“它确实是新的，因为我昨夜在一个怪城的梦里做了它；而梦比沉思的推罗更老，比冥想的斯芬克斯更老，比花园环抱的巴比伦更老。”

就是那时，他开始讲那篇散漫的故事，它忽然拨响了一段沉睡的记忆，赢去了我叔父发热的兴趣。前夜有过一次轻微的地震，是新英格兰几年来有感最强的一次；威尔科克斯的想象力被深深撼动了。就寝之后，他做了一个前所未有的梦，梦见巨人族的巨城，泰坦的巨石和抛上天空的独石，全都滴着绿色的黏液，潜伏的恐怖使它们阴森。象形文字覆满墙壁和柱子，从下方某个测定不出的地点，传来一个不是声音的声音；一种只有幻想才能化为声音的混沌感觉，而他试图用那几乎读不出的字母堆“*克苏鲁·弗塔格恩*”来描摹它。

===Original===

This verbal jumble was the key to the recollection which excited and disturbed Professor Angell. He questioned the sculptor with scientific minuteness; and studied with almost frantic intensity the bas-relief on which the youth had found himself working, chilled and clad only in his nightclothes, when waking had stolen bewilderingly over him. My uncle blamed his old age, Wilcox afterward said, for his slowness in recognizing both hieroglyphics and pictorial design. Many of his questions seemed highly out of place to his visitor, especially those which tried to connect the latter with strange cults or societies; and Wilcox could not understand the repeated promises of silence which he was offered in exchange for an admission of membership in some widespread mystical or paganly religious body. When Professor Angell became convinced that the sculptor was indeed ignorant of any cult or system of cryptic lore, he besieged his visitor with demands for future reports of dreams. This bore regular fruit, for after the first interview the manuscript records daily calls of the young man, during which he related startling fragments of nocturnal imagery whose burden was always some terrible Cyclopean vista of dark and dripping stone, with a subterrene voice or intelligence shouting monotonously in enigmatical sense-impacts uninscribable save as gibberish. The two sounds most frequently repeated are those rendered by the letters “*Cthulhu*” and “*R’lyeh*.”

===Chinese===

这堆字正是唤起那段回忆、搅动安杰尔教授的钥匙。他以科学的细密盘问雕刻家，并以近乎狂乱的专注研究那浮雕——青年醒来懵然发觉自己正在雕它，浑身发冷，只穿着睡衣。威尔科克斯后来说，我叔父把认不出象形文字和图画的迟缓归咎于自己的老迈。他的许多问题在来客看来全然文不对题，尤其是那些想把来客同怪异教团或会社连起来的问题；威尔科克斯不懂，为什么反复许诺缄默，只为换取他承认是某个广泛流传的神秘或异教团体的成员。安杰尔教授确信雕刻家当真不知任何教团或秘传体系之后，便缠着来访者索要日后的梦的报告。这结出了规律的果实：第一次面谈之后，手稿记录了青年每天的来访，讲述夜里意象的惊人片段，其主旨永远是某种可怕的多石滴水的巨人族远景，一个地下的声音或智慧，单调地以谜样的意义冲击呼喊，除却胡言无法记录。重复最多的两个音，是用字母“*克苏鲁*”和“*拉莱耶*”拼出的。

===Original===
