The moon no longer shone through the chinks and apertures above me, and with a sense of fateful alarm I heard the sinister and significant rumble of approaching thunder. A confusion of associated ideas possessed my brain, leading me to grope back toward the farthest corner of the cellar. My eyes, however, never turned away from the horrible opening at the base of the chimney; and I began to get glimpses of the crumbling bricks and unhealthy weeds as faint glows of lightning penetrated the woods outside and illumined the chinks in the upper wall. Every second I was consumed with a mixture of fear and curiosity. What would the storm call forth﻿—or was there anything left for it to call? Guided by a lightning flash I settled myself down behind a dense clump of vegetation, through which I could see the opening without being seen.

---

If heaven is merciful, it will some day efface from my consciousness the sight that I saw, and let me live my last years in peace. I can not sleep at night now, and have to take opiates when it thunders. The thing came abruptly and unannounced; a demon, ratlike scurrying from pits remote and unimaginable, a hellish panting and stifled grunting, and then from that opening beneath the chimney a burst of multitudinous and leprous life﻿—a loathsome night-spawned flood of organic corruption more devastatingly hideous than the blackest conjurations of mortal madness and morbidity. Seething, stewing, surging, bubbling like serpents’ slime it rolled up and out of that yawning hole, spreading like a septic contagion and streaming from the cellar at every point of egress﻿—streaming out to scatter through the accursed midnight forests and strew fear, madness, and death.

===Chinese===

我正踌躇——是立刻独自带手电钻进那条通道，还是先去纠集一队擅居者——犹豫被一阵外面突然灌进的风打断了：它吹灭了蜡烛，把我撇在纯粹的黑里。月亮已不再从我头顶的缝隙和窟窿里漏光，我怀着大难临头的警觉，听见那不祥而有分量的、愈来愈近的雷的轰鸣。一团乱麻似的联想占住了我的脑子，引着我摸索着退到地窖最远的角落。可我的眼睛始终没有离开烟囱根上那个可怕的洞口；当外面的电光穿过树林、照亮上墙的砖缝时，我开始瞥见剥落的碎砖和不健康的杂草。每一秒，我都被恐惧与好奇的混合吞噬着。这场暴风雨会召出什么——或者，还有什么留下的可召？借着一次闪电，我在一丛密密的草木后伏下身来，从那里我看得见洞口，却不被看见。

上天若是慈悲的，但愿有一天会把我看见的那一幕从我的意识里抹去，让我在平静里度过余年。如今我夜里睡不着，一打雷就得服鸦片剂。那东西来得突兀，没有预告：一个恶魔，老鼠似的从遥远而不可想象的深坑里窜出来，一阵地狱似的喘息和憋住的呼噜；随后，从烟囱底下那个洞口里，涌出一大群癞病似的生命——一股夜间滋生的、有机腐败的可憎洪流，比凡人疯狂与病态最黑的邪术还要狰狞。它翻滚着、沸腾着、汹涌着、冒着泡，像蛇的黏涎，从那张开的洞里滚上来、滚出来，像败血的传染铺展开去，从地窖的每一条出路往外流——流出去，散进受诅咒的午夜森林，撒播恐惧、疯狂和死亡。

===Original===

God knows how many there were﻿—there must have been thousands. To see the stream of them in that faint, intermittent lightning was shocking. When they had thinned out enough to be glimpsed as separate organisms, I saw that they were dwarfed, deformed hairy devils or apes﻿—monstrous and diabolic caricatures of the monkey tribe. They were so hideously silent; there was hardly a squeal when one of the last stragglers turned with the skill of long practise to make a meal in accustomed fashion on a weaker companion. Others snapped up what it left and ate with slavering relish. Then, in spite of my daze of fright and disgust, my morbid curiosity triumphed; and as the last of the monstrosities oozed up alone from that nether world of unknown nightmare, I drew my automatic pistol and shot it under cover of the thunder.

Shrieking, slithering, torrential shadows of red viscous madness chasing one another through endless, ensanguined corridors of purple fulgurous sky﻿ ﻿… formless phantasms and kaleidoscopic mutations of a ghoulish, remembered scene; forests of monstrous overnourished oaks with serpent roots twisting and sucking unnamable juices from an earth verminous with millions of cannibal devils; moundlike tentacles groping from underground nuclei of polypous perversion﻿ ﻿… insane lightning over malignant ivied walls and demon arcades choked with fungous vegetation.﻿ ﻿… Heaven be thanked for the instinct which led me unconscious to places where men dwell; to the peaceful village that slept under the calm stars of clearing skies.

---

===Chinese===

天知道它们有多少——必得上千。在微弱断续的闪电里看见它们那股人流，是触目惊心的。等它们稀疏到能一个个看清时，我看出那是一群侏儒的、畸形的、生毛的恶魔或类人猿——猴族的一幅副副狰狞的恶魔漫画。它们狰狞地无声；最后一批掉队的里头有一个，转身凭着久练的技巧，照惯常的方式拿一个较弱的同伴当了一餐，这时几乎没有一声尖叫。其余的抢食它剩下的，淌着馋涎大嚼。随后，尽管我又怕又恶心地发着懵，我那病态的好奇心还是占了上风；当最后一个怪物独自从那个无名梦魇的阴世里渗上来时，我拔出自动手枪，就着雷声的掩护，打死了它。

尖叫着、滑行着，红色的黏稠疯狂的一道道黑影，在紫电天空无尽染血的走廊里互相追逐……一场鬼气森森、记忆犹存的场景的无形幻影和万花筒般的突变；一片病肥巨橡的森林，蛇根扭绞着，从爬满百万食人恶魔的虫豸大地里吮吸无名的汁液；一座座丘似的触手，从多瘤的乖张的地下核心里摸索出来……疯狂的闪电，照着恶毒的常春藤墙和塞满菌草的恶魔拱廊。……感谢上天，凭那股本能，我在昏乱中被引到了有人住的地方；引到那座在放晴的天空平静星辰下入睡的安宁村子。

===Original===

I had recovered enough in a week to send to Albany for a gang of men to blow up the Martense mansion and the entire top of Tempest Mountain with dynamite, stop up all the discoverable mound-burrows, and destroy certain overnourished trees whose very existence seemed an insult to sanity. I could sleep a little after they had done this, but true rest will never come as long as I remember that nameless secret of the lurking fear. The thing will haunt me, for who can say the extermination is complete, and that analogous phenomena do not exist all over the world? Who can, with my knowledge, think of the earth’s unknown caverns without a nightmare dread of future possibilities? I can not see a well or a subway entrance without shuddering﻿ ﻿… why can not the doctors give me something to make me sleep, or truly calm my brain when it thunders?

What I saw in the glow of my flashlight after I shot the unspeakable straggling object was so simple that almost a minute elapsed before I understood and went delirious. The object was nauseous; a filthy whitish gorilla thing with sharp yellow fangs and matted fur. It was the ultimate product of mammalian degeneration; the frightful outcome of isolated spawning, multiplication, and cannibal nutrition above and below the ground; the embodiment of all the snarling chaos and grinning fear that lurk behind life. It had looked at me as it died, and its eyes had the same odd quality that marked those other eyes which had stared at me underground and excited cloudy recollections. One eye was blue, the other brown. They were the dissimilar Martense eyes of the old legends, and I knew in one inundating cataclysm of voiceless horror what had become of that vanished family; the terrible and thunder-crazed house of Martense.

===Chinese===

一个星期后我恢复得差不多了，便派人去奥尔巴尼调来一队人，用炸药炸掉马滕斯宅邸和风暴山的整个山顶，堵死一切找得到的丘洞，毁掉某些过肥的树——它们的存在本身就是对清醒的侮辱。他们干完之后，我能稍稍睡一睡了；可只要我还记得那潜伏的恐惧的无名秘密，真正的安息就永远不会来。那东西会缠着我，因为谁能说灭绝已是彻底，谁能说类似的现象不存在于全世界？有着我这份知识的人，想到大地那些不名的洞窟，谁能不感到梦魇般的畏惧？我看见一口井、一个地铁入口都要打颤……医生们为什么不能给我一点什么，让我睡得着，或者在打雷的时候，真正让我的脑子静下来？

我开枪打掉那个不可名状的掉队者之后，在电筒的光里看见的东西，简单得几乎过了一分钟我才明白过来，然后发起狂来。那东西令人作呕：一个污秽的、发白的、大猩猩似的东西，黄色的利牙，毡结的毛。它是哺乳类退化的终极产物；是地上地下隔绝的生育、增殖和同类相食的营养的可怕结局；是一切潜藏在生命背后的狂吠的混乱与狞笑的恐惧的化身。它死的时候看了我一眼，它那对眼睛带着的那种古怪的性质，同地下瞪过我的那对眼睛一模一样，也勾起过云雾般的记忆。一只眼睛是蓝的，另一只是褐的。那是古老传说里马滕斯家不相同的两只眼睛；于是在一场无声的、灭顶的恐怖里，我知道了那个消失的家庭的下落——知道了那个可怕的、被雷逼疯的马滕斯之家。

## The Moon-Bog / 月沼
===Original===

Somewhere, to what remote and fearsome region I know not, Denys Barry has gone. I was with him the last night he lived among men, and heard his screams when the thing came to him; but all the peasants and police in County Meath could never find him, or the others, though they searched long and far. And now I shudder when I hear the frogs piping in swamps, or see the moon in lonely places.

I had known Denys Barry well in America, where he had grown rich, and had congratulated him when he bought back the old castle by the bog at sleepy Kilderry. It was from Kilderry that his father had come, and it was there that he wished to enjoy his wealth among ancestral scenes. Men of his blood had once ruled over Kilderry and built and dwelt in the castle, but those days were very remote, so that for generations the castle had been empty and decaying. After he went to Ireland Barry wrote me often, and told me how under his care the gray castle was rising tower by tower to its ancient splendor; how the ivy was climbing slowly over the restored walls as it had climbed so many centuries ago, and how the peasants blessed him for bringing back the old days with his gold from over the sea. But in time there came troubles, and the peasants ceased to bless him, and fled away instead as from a doom. And then he sent a letter and asked me to visit him, for he was lonely in the castle with no one to speak to save the new servants and laborers he had brought from the North.

The bog was the cause of all these troubles, as Barry told me the night I came to the castle. I had reached Kilderry in the summer sunset, as the gold of the sky lighted the green of the hills and groves and the blue of the bog, where on a far islet a strange olden ruin glistened spectrally. That sunset was very beautiful, but the peasants at Ballylough had warned me against it and said that Kilderry had become accursed, so that I almost shuddered to see the high turrets of the castle gilded with fire. Barry’s motor had met me at the Ballylough station, for Kilderry is off the railway. The villagers had shunned the car and the driver from the North, but had whispered to me with pale faces when they saw I was going to Kilderry. And that night, after our reunion, Barry told me why.

===Chinese===

德尼斯·巴里去了什么地方，我不知道——某个遥远而可怕的疆域。他还在人间度过的最后一夜，我在他身边，听见那东西扑向他时他的尖叫；可米斯郡所有的农民和警察，搜寻了那么久、那么远，始终没有找到他，也没有找到其他人。如今我听见沼泽里青蛙啼鸣，或看见荒寂之地的月亮，便要发抖。

我在美国就熟识德尼斯·巴里，他在那里发了财；他买回沉睡的基尔德里泥炭沼旁那座老城堡时，我曾向他道贺。他父亲正是从基尔德里出去的，他也正想回祖先的故土享享清福。他血统里的人曾经统治基尔德里，建起城堡住在里面；可那些岁月太遥远了，城堡空置朽败已有好几代人。巴里到了爱尔兰后常给我写信，告诉我那灰色的城堡怎样在他手里一座塔楼接一座塔楼地恢复旧观；常春藤怎样慢慢爬上修缮的墙，同多少世纪前爬上的一样；农民们怎样为他祝福，因为他用海外带回的黄金唤回了旧日。可是后来麻烦来了，农民们不再祝福他，反倒像躲灾星一样逃光了。于是他来信请我去住些日子，因为城堡里只剩他从北方带来的新仆人和工人，没有一个说话的人。

那泥沼正是一切麻烦的根由，我到城堡的那晚巴里就这么告诉我。我抵达基尔德里时正值夏日黄昏，天空的金光点亮山峦和小树林的绿、点亮泥沼的蓝，远处一座小岛上，一爿古怪的远古废墟幽灵般闪着白。那黄昏真美；可巴利洛的农民警告我别去，说基尔德里受了诅咒，害得我望见城堡高塔被落火镀金时几乎打了个寒噤。巴里的汽车在巴利洛车站接我，因为基尔德里不通铁路。村里人躲着汽车和北方来的司机，见我要去基尔德里，却脸色发白地同我咬耳朵。当晚重聚之后，巴里把缘故讲给了我。

===Original===

The peasants had gone from Kilderry because Denys Barry was to drain the great bog. For all his love of Ireland, America had not left him untouched, and he hated the beautiful wasted space where peat might be cut and land opened up. The legends and superstitions of Kilderry did not move him, and he laughed when the peasants first refused to help, and then cursed him and went away to Ballylough with their few belongings as they saw his determination. In their place he sent for laborers from the North, and when the servants left he replaced them likewise. But it was lonely among strangers, so Barry had asked me to come.

When I heard the fears which had driven the people from Kilderry I laughed as loudly as my friend had laughed, for these fears were of the vaguest, wildest, and most absurd character. They had to do with some preposterous legend of the bog, and of a grim guardian spirit that dwelt in the strange olden ruin on the far islet I had seen in the sunset. There were tales of dancing lights in the dark of the moon, and of chill winds when the night was warm; of wraiths in white hovering over the waters, and of an imagined city of stone deep down below the swampy surface. But foremost among the weird fancies, and alone in its absolute unanimity, was that of the curse awaiting him who should dare to touch or drain the vast reddish morass. There were secrets, said the peasants, which must not be uncovered; secrets that had lain hidden since the plague came to the children of Partholan in the fabulous years beyond history. In the *Book of Invaders* it is told that these sons of the Greeks were all buried at Tallaght, but old men in Kilderry said that one city was overlooked save by its patron moon-goddess; so that only the wooded hills buried it when the men of Nemed swept down from Scythia in their thirty ships.

===Chinese===

农民们离开基尔德里，是因为德尼斯·巴里要排干那片大泥沼。他尽管爱爱尔兰，美国并没有白住，他恨那片美丽的荒地白白浪费，本可以挖泥炭、开田地。基尔德里传说与迷信打动不了他；农民们先是不肯帮忙，随后见他铁了心，便咒骂着卷起一点家当投奔巴利洛去了，他只觉好笑。他们的位置，他从北方招工来补；仆人走光了，也照样补上。只是身处生人堆里孤单，巴里才请了我来。

听说赶走基尔德里人的是这些恐惧时，我笑得同我朋友一样响，因为这些恐惧最空泛、最狂乱、最荒唐。它们同泥沼的某个荒诞传说有关，同住在远岛那座古怪远古废墟里的一个阴沉守护神有关。有黑月夜里跳舞的鬼火的传说，有暖夜里寒风的传说；有白影在水面上盘旋的传说，还有一座想象中的石头城深藏在沼泽底下的传说。可这一切怪想里居首的、唯一众口一词的，是那个等着胆敢触动或排干这片微红大沼的人的诅咒。农民们说，有些秘密揭不得；那是自瘟疫降临帕索兰的子孙——在历史之外那神话般的年代里——就一直藏着的秘密。《入侵者书》里说，这些希腊人的儿子都埋在塔拉赫特；可基尔德里老人们说，有一座城被漏掉了，只有它的守护月神没有漏掉；所以后来内梅德的人乘三十条船从斯基泰扫荡下来时，只有林木的山峦掩埋了它。

===Original===

Such were the idle tales which had made the villagers leave Kilderry, and when I heard them I did not wonder that Denys Barry had refused to listen. He had, however, a great interest in antiquities; and proposed to explore the bog thoroughly when it was drained. The white ruins on the islet he had often visited, but though their age was plainly great, and their contour very little like that of most ruins in Ireland, they were too dilapidated to tell the days of their glory. Now the work of drainage was ready to begin, and the laborers from the North were soon to strip the forbidden bog of its green moss and red heather, and kill the tiny shell-paved streamlets and quiet blue pools fringed with rushes.

After Barry had told me these things I was very drowsy, for the travels of the day had been wearying and my host had talked late into the night. A manservant showed me to my room, which was in a remote tower overlooking the village, and the plain at the edge of the bog, and the bog itself; so that I could see from my windows in the moonlight the silent roofs from which the peasants had fled and which now sheltered the laborers from the North, and too, the parish church with its antique spire, and far out across the brooding bog the remote olden ruin on the islet gleaming white and spectral. Just as I dropped to sleep I fancied I heard faint sounds from the distance; sounds that were wild and half musical, and stirred me with a weird excitement which colored my dreams. But when I awaked next morning I felt it had all been a dream, for the visions I had seen were more wonderful than any sound of wild pipes in the night. Influenced by the legends that Barry had related, my mind had in slumber hovered around a stately city in a green valley, where marble streets and statues, villas and temples, carvings and inscriptions, all spoke in certain tones the glory that was Greece. When I told this dream to Barry we both laughed; but I laughed the louder, because he was perplexed about his laborers from the North. For the sixth time they had all overslept, waking very slowly and dazedly, and acting as if they had not rested, although they were known to have gone early to bed the night before.

===Chinese===

使村人离开基尔德里，就是这样一些闲话；听罢我毫不奇怪德尼斯·巴里不肯听信。不过他对古物大有兴趣，打算排干泥沼后把它彻彻底底探一遍。岛上那白色废墟他常去；但废墟年月虽分明极古，轮廓又同爱尔兰多数废墟大不一样，却坍败得太狠，说不出它全盛的日子。如今排水的工程就要动工，北方来的工人不日就要剥去禁沼的绿苔和红石楠，弄死那些细沙铺底的小溪流和灯心草镶边的安静蓝水洼。

巴里讲完这些，我已经困极了，白天赶路乏透了，主人又聊到深夜。一名男仆领我到我的房间，在一座偏远的塔楼里，俯瞰着村子、泥沼边缘的平野和泥沼本身；于是我从窗口望得见月光下悄然无声的屋顶——农民们逃离的、如今住着北方工人的屋顶——也望得见教区教堂古色古香的尖顶，还有幽幽泥沼之外远处小岛上那座闪着幽白的远古废墟。将睡未睡之际，我恍惚听见远处飘来声音；那声音野而半含乐律，搅得我心头一种怪异的兴奋，给我的梦染了色。可次日早晨醒来，我觉得那全然是个梦，因为我看见的景象比夜里任何野笛的声音都更奇妙。受了巴里所述传说的影响，我的神魂在睡梦里萦绕着一座绿谷中的庄严之城，那里大理石的街道和雕像、别墅和神庙、雕刻和铭文，字字声声都在诉说希腊的荣光。我把这梦讲给巴里听，我们俩都笑了；可我笑得更响，因为他对北方来的工人正犯嘀咕——他们第六次全体睡过了头，醒得又慢又发懵，一个个像没歇过来似的，尽管谁都知道他们头晚早早便上了床。

===Original===

That morning and afternoon I wandered alone through the sun-gilded village and talked now and then with idle laborers, for Barry was busy with the final plans for beginning his work of drainage. The laborers were not as happy as they might have been, for most of them seemed uneasy over some dream which they had had, yet which they tried in vain to remember. I told them of my dream, but they were not interested till I spoke of the weird sounds I thought I had heard. Then they looked oddly at me, and said that they seemed to remember weird sounds, too.

In the evening Barry dined with me and announced that he would begin the drainage in two days. I was glad, for although I disliked to see the moss and the heather and the little streams and lakes depart, I had a growing wish to discern the ancient secrets the deep-matted peat might hide. And that night my dreams of piping flutes and marble peristyles came to a sudden and disquieting end; for upon the city in the valley I saw a pestilence descend, and then a frightful avalanche of wooded slopes that covered the dead bodies in the streets and left unburied only the temple of Artemis on the high peak, where the aged moon-priestess Cleis lay cold and silent with a crown of ivory on her silver head.

---

I have said that I awaked suddenly and in alarm. For some time I could not tell whether I was waking or sleeping, for the sound of flutes still rang shrilly in my ears; but when I saw on the floor the icy moonbeams and the outlines of a latticed gothic window I decided I must be awake and in the castle at Kilderry. Then I heard a clock from some remote landing below strike the hour of two, and knew I was awake. Yet still there came that monotonous piping from afar; wild, weird airs that made me think of some dance of fauns on distant Maenalus. It would not let me sleep, and in impatience I sprang up and paced the floor. Only by chance did I go to the north window and look out upon the silent village and the plain at the edge of the bog. I had no wish to gaze abroad, for I wanted to sleep; but the flutes tormented me, and I had to do or see something. How could I have suspected the thing I was to behold?

===Chinese===

那天上午和下午，我独自在阳光镀金的村子里溜达，不时同闲着的工人搭话，因为巴里忙着定夺排水开工的最后计划。工人们并不如本该的那样快活，多数人似乎被什么梦搅得不安，却又怎么也想不起来。我把我的梦讲给他们听，他们不感兴趣；直到我说起恍惚听见的那种怪声，他们才古怪地看我，说他们似乎也记得怪声。

傍晚巴里同我一起吃饭，宣布两天后开工排水。我挺高兴，因为尽管我不愿看苔藓、石楠和小溪小湖就此消失，我心里越来越想看清那深积的泥炭底下藏着的古老秘密。那一夜，我那笛声与大理石柱廊的梦戛然而止在一种不安里；因为我看见瘟疫降临谷中之城，随后林木的山坡雪崩般塌下，盖住街上横陈的尸首，只留高巅上阿耳忒弥斯的神庙没有掩埋——年迈的月之女祭司克勒斯躺在那里，冰冷，沉默，银发的头上戴着象牙冠。

---

我说过，我是在惊惶中突然醒来的。好一阵子我分不清自己是醒是睡，因为笛声还在耳边尖利地响；可等地板上现出清冷的月光和哥特式格子窗的轮廓，我断定自己是醒着的，在基尔德里的城堡里。随后我听见下面远处楼梯口一座钟敲了两点，知道自己确实醒着。可那单调的笛吹仍旧从远方传来；狂野、怪异的调子，叫我想起远方玛伊纳罗斯山上羊怪们的什么舞蹈。它不让我睡，我烦躁地跳起身，在地板上来回踱步。我也是碰巧才走到北窗前，望向寂静的村庄和泥沼边的平野。我本无心向外看，只想睡觉；可笛声折磨我，我总得做点什么、看点什么。我哪能料到即将望见的东西？

===Original===

There in the moonlight that flooded the spacious plain was a spectacle which no mortal, having seen it, could ever forget. To the sound of reedy pipes that echoed over the bog there glided silently and eerily a mixed throng of swaying figures, reeling through such a revel as the Sicilians may have danced to Demeter in the old days under the harvest moon beside the Cyane. The wide plain, the golden moonlight, the shadowy moving forms, and above all the shrill monotonous piping, produced an effect which almost paralyzed me; yet I noted amidst my fear that half of these tireless, mechanical dancers were the laborers whom I had thought asleep, whilst the other half were strange airy beings in white, half-indeterminate in nature, but suggesting pale wistful naiads from the haunted fountains of the bog. I do not know how long I gazed at this sight from the lonely turret window before I dropped suddenly in a dreamless swoon, out of which the high sun of morning aroused me.

===Chinese===

月光漫过空阔的平野，那里正是一幅凡人见了便永不能忘的景象。芦笛之声在泥沼上回荡，应和着笛声，一大群摇曳的身影无声而鬼气地滑行，跌跌撞撞地狂欢——西西里人古时在库阿涅泉边、收获月下献给得墨忒耳的，或许就是这样一场舞。空阔的平野、金色的月光、幢幢的暗影，尤其那尖利的单调笛吹，造出一种几乎把我瘫痪的效果；然而我在恐惧中还留意到：这些不知疲倦的、机械的舞者，一半是我以为睡熟了的工人，另一半是些白衣的、虚渺的存在，性质半明半昧，令人想到泥沼魔泉里苍白的、怅惘的水仙。我不知道自己从孤塔的窗口凝望了多久，随后蓦地跌入一场无梦的晕厥，直到早晨高高的太阳把我唤醒。

===Original===

My first impulse on awaking was to communicate all my fears and observations to Denys Barry, but as I saw the sunlight glowing through the latticed east window I became sure that there was no reality in what I thought I had seen. I am given to strange fantasms, yet am never weak enough to believe in them; so on this occasion contented myself with questioning the laborers, who slept very late and recalled nothing of the previous night save misty dreams of shrill sounds. This matter of the spectral piping harassed me greatly, and I wondered if the crickets of autumn had come before their time to vex the night and haunt the visions of men. Later in the day I watched Barry in the library poring over his plans for the great work which was to begin on the morrow, and for the first time felt a touch of the same kind of fear that had driven the peasants away. For some unknown reason I dreaded the thought of disturbing the ancient bog and its sunless secrets, and pictured terrible sights lying black under the unmeasured depth of age-old peat. That these secrets should be brought to light seemed injudicious, and I began to wish for an excuse to leave the castle and the village. I went so far as to talk casually to Barry on the subject, but did not dare continue after he gave his resounding laugh. So I was silent when the sun set fulgently over the far hills, and Kilderry blazed all red and gold in a flame that seemed a portent.

---

Whether the events of that night were of reality or illusion I shall never ascertain. Certainly they transcend anything we dream of in nature and the universe; yet in no normal fashion can I explain those disappearances which were known to all men after it was over. I retired early and full of dread, and for a long time could not sleep in the uncanny silence of the tower. It was very dark, for although the sky was clear the moon was now well in the wane, and would not rise till the small hours. I thought as I lay there of Denys Barry, and of what would befall that bog when the day came, and found myself almost frantic with an impulse to rush out into the night, take Barry’s car, and drive madly to Ballylough out of the menaced lands. But before my fears could crystallize into action I had fallen asleep, and gazed in dreams upon the city in the valley, cold and dead under a shroud of hideous shadow.

===Chinese===

醒来我的头一个冲动，是把全部的恐惧和所见告诉德尼斯·巴里；可当望见阳光透过格子东窗照进来，我便确信自己以为看见的东西并无其事。我这个人惯生幻象，却从不至于软弱到信以为真；于是这一回，我只满足于盘问工人。他们睡到很晚才醒，前夜的事除了一些尖利声响的模糊梦影，什么也不记得。这幽灵笛吹的事搅得我心烦，我纳闷是不是秋天的蟋蟀提早来了，来搅扰黑夜、缠住人的梦。当天晚些时候，我看巴里在书房里埋头推敲明日开工的大计划，头一回觉出一丝赶走农民的那种恐惧。不知为什么，一想到搅动这片古老的泥沼和它不见天日的秘密，我便心悸，想象着可怕的景象横陈在积年泥炭不可测度的深度底下，黑黑地躺着。把这些秘密翻到光天化日之下，似乎不合时宜；我开始想找个借口离开城堡和村子。我甚至煞有介事同巴里提了提这话题，可他放声一笑，我便不敢再提。于是日落时分，落日煌煌烧过远山，基尔德里通体赤金，在一片仿佛凶兆的火焰里烧着，我默然无语。

---

那一夜的事，究竟是实在还是幻象，我永远无从查证。它们当然越出了我们对自然与宇宙的一切梦想；可事情过后人人皆知的那几桩失踪，我用任何正常的法子也解释不了。我早早带着满心恐惧上了床，在塔里那说不出的寂静中久久睡不着。天很黑，因为夜空虽晴，月亮已残得很，要到后半夜才升。我躺在那里想着德尼斯·巴里，想着天亮之后泥沼会遭逢什么，发觉自己几乎按捺不住，想冲进黑夜里，开上巴里的车，疯了一样逃出这片受胁的土地，逃去巴利洛。可不等恐惧凝成行动，我已睡着，在梦里望见谷中之城，裹在可憎阴影的尸衣下，寒冷，死寂。

===Original===

Probably it was the shrill piping that awaked me, yet that piping was not what I noticed first when I opened my eyes. I was lying with my back to the east window overlooking the bog, where the waning moon would rise, and therefore expected to see light cast on the opposite wall before me; but I had not looked for such a sight as now appeared. Light indeed glowed on the panels ahead, but it was not any light that the moon gives. Terrible and piercing was the shaft of ruddy refulgence that streamed through the gothic window, and the whole chamber was brilliant with a splendor intense and unearthly. My immediate actions were peculiar for such a situation, but it is only in tales that a man does the dramatic and foreseen thing. Instead of looking out across the bog toward the source of the new light, I kept my eyes from the window in panic fear, and clumsily drew on my clothing with some dazed idea of escape. I remember seizing my revolver and hat, but before it was over I had lost them both without firing the one or donning the other. After a time the fascination of the red radiance overcame my fright, and I crept to the east window and looked out whilst the maddening, incessant piping whined and reverberated through the castle and over all the village.

===Chinese===

多半是那尖利的笛吹把我唤醒的，可睁眼时头一样注意到的并不是笛声。我背朝俯瞰泥沼的东窗躺着——残月将从那里升起——料定前方对面墙上会先映来光；可我没料到此刻显现的这一幕。前方壁板上的确亮着光，却不是月亮给得出的任何光。透过哥特式窗口涌进的那道赤红辉煌的光柱，可怕而刺目；整间屋子被一种浓烈而非人间的光辉照得通明。在那样一种处境里，我紧接着的举动是古怪的；可只有故事里的人才会做出戏剧性的、料得到的事。我没有朝泥沼方向、朝那新光源望出去，反而惊惶地把眼睛避开窗口，迷迷瞪瞪地穿戴起来，带着一个逃跑的念头。我记得抓起了左轮枪和帽子，可等到一切结束，两样都丢了，枪一枪未发，帽子一顶未戴。过了一阵，那红色辉光的魅惑压过了恐惧，我爬向东窗，向外望去——那发狂的、无休无止的笛吹，正穿过城堡、漫过全村，呜呜地回荡。

===Original===

Over the bog was a deluge of flaring light, scarlet and sinister, and pouring from the strange olden ruin on the far islet. The aspect of that ruin I can not describe﻿—I must have been mad, for it seemed to rise majestic and undecayed, splendid and column-cinctured, the flame-reflecting marble of its entablature piercing the sky like the apex of a temple on a mountaintop. Flutes shrieked and drums began to beat, and as I watched in awe and terror I thought I saw dark saltant forms silhouetted grotesquely against the vision of marble and effulgence. The effect was titanic﻿—altogether unthinkable﻿—and I might have stared indefinitely had not the sound of the piping seemed to grow stronger at my left. Trembling with a terror oddly mixed with ecstasy I crossed the circular room to the north window from which I could see the village and the plain at the edge of the bog. There my eyes dilated again with a wild wonder as great as if I had not just turned from a scene beyond the pale of nature, for on the ghastly red-litten plain was moving a procession of beings in such a manner as none ever saw before save in nightmares.

===Chinese===

泥沼上空是一片火光的洪流，猩红而狰狞，从远岛那座古怪的远古废墟里倾泻出来。那废墟的模样我没法描画——我当时必定疯了，因为它仿佛巍峨而全无朽坏地立着，辉煌，环柱耸峙，檐部映火的理石直刺天心，像山顶神庙的尖顶。笛声尖啸，鼓声擂动；我敬畏而恐惧地望着，恍惚看见黑黑的跳跃身影，衬着那理石与辉光的幻景，怪诞如剪影。那效果是泰坦式的——全然不可思议——若不是笛声仿佛在我左边越来越强，我也许会一直瞪下去。我战栗着，恐惧里古怪地掺着迷狂，穿过圆形的房间走到北窗，从那里望得见村庄和泥沼边的平野。我的眼睛再一次因狂野的惊异而睁大，仿佛方才不曾从超乎自然的景象前转过身来——在那被鬼光映红的骇人平野上，行进着一队存在，那样行进，除却噩梦谁也不曾见过。

===Original===

Half gliding, half floating in the air, the white-clad bog-wraiths were slowly retreating toward the still waters and the island ruin in fantastic formations suggesting some ancient and solemn ceremonial dance. Their waving translucent arms, guided by the detestable piping of those unseen flutes, beckoned in uncanny rhythm to a throng of lurching laborers who followed doglike with blind, brainless, floundering steps as if dragged by a clumsy but resistless demon-will. As the naiads neared the bog, without altering their course, a new line of stumbling stragglers zigzagged drunkenly out of the castle from some door far below my window, groped sightlessly across the courtyard and through the intervening bit of village, and joined the floundering column of laborers on the plain. Despite their distance below me I at once knew they were the servants brought from the North, for I recognized the ugly and unwieldy form of the cook, whose very absurdness had now become unutterably tragic. The flutes piped horribly, and again I heard the beating of the drums from the direction of the island ruin. Then silently and gracefully the naiads reached the water and melted one by one into the ancient bog; while the line of followers, never checking their speed, splashed awkwardly after them and vanished amidst a tiny vortex of unwholesome bubbles which I could barely see in the scarlet light. And as the last pathetic straggler, the fat cook, sank heavily out of sight in that sullen pool, the flutes and the drums grew silent, and the blinding red rays from the ruins snapped instantaneously out, leaving the village of doom lone and desolate in the wan beams of a new-risen moon.

===Chinese===

白衣的泥沼之灵半滑半浮在空中，正缓缓退向静静的水面和岛上的废墟，队形奇幻，暗示着某种古老而庄严的仪式之舞。她们挥舞的、半透明的臂膀，被那看不见的芦笛可憎的笛吹牵引着，以鬼异的节奏招引着一队踉跄的工人；工人狗一般跟着，盲目、无脑、深一脚浅一脚，仿佛被一个笨拙却不可抗拒的魔灵之意志拖着走。水仙们临近泥沼、航向不变时，又一行跌撞的掉队者醉汉般走出城堡，从我窗下远处的什么门里歪歪斜斜地出来，摸索着穿过院子、穿过那一小段村路，汇入平野上深一脚浅一脚的工人行列。尽管隔着那么远，我一眼认出他们是从北方带来的仆人，因为我认出了厨子那臃肿笨拙的身形——那副滑稽相如今变得说不出的悲惨。笛声吹得怕人，岛那边废墟的方向又传来鼓声。随后，水仙们悄然又优雅地到了水边，一个接一个融进古老的泥沼；跟着的队伍却速度不减，扑通扑通笨拙地跟着蹚进去，在一小涡不洁的气泡中没了影——猩红的光里，我勉强才看得见那点气泡。当最后一个可怜的掉队者、那个胖厨子，也沉沉没进那口阴沉的水池不见时，笛声和鼓声一齐哑了，废墟里那耀眼的赤红光束霎时熄灭，只留下那注定毁灭的村子，孤零零的，在新升残月苍白的清辉里。

===Original===

My condition was now one of indescribable chaos. Not knowing whether I was mad or sane, sleeping or waking, I was saved only by a merciful numbness. I believe I did ridiculous things such as offering prayers to Artemis, Latona, Demeter, Persephone, and Plouton. All that I recalled of a classic youth came to my lips as the horrors of the situation roused my deepest superstitions. I felt that I had witnessed the death of a whole village, and knew I was alone in the castle with Denys Barry, whose boldness had brought down a doom. As I thought of him new terrors convulsed me, and I fell to the floor; not fainting, but physically helpless. Then I felt the icy blast from the east window where the moon had risen, and began to hear the shrieks in the castle far below me. Soon those shrieks had attained a magnitude and quality which can not be written of, and which make me faint as I think of them. All I can say is that they came from something I had known as a friend.

---

At some time during this shocking period the cold wind and the screaming must have roused me, for my next impression is of racing madly through inky rooms and corridors and out across the courtyard into the hideous night. They found me at dawn wandering mindless near Ballylough, but what unhinged me utterly was not any of the horrors I had seen or heard before. What I muttered about as I came slowly out of the shadows was a pair of fantastic incidents which occurred in my flight; incidents of no significance, yet which haunt me unceasingly when I am alone in certain marshy places or in the moonlight.

As I fled from that accursed castle along the bog’s edge I heard a new sound; common, yet unlike any I had heard before at Kilderry. The stagnant waters, lately quite devoid of animal life, now teemed with a horde of slimy enormous frogs which piped shrilly and incessantly in tones strangely out of keeping with their size. They glistened bloated and green in the moonbeams, and seemed to gaze up at the fount of light. I followed the gaze of one very fat and ugly frog, and saw the second of the things which drove my senses away.

===Chinese===

我此刻的境地，是一片说不出的混乱。不知自己是疯是醒、是睡是梦，全靠一阵慈悲的麻木撑着。我相信自己干了些可笑的事，比如向阿耳忒弥斯、拉托娜、得墨忒耳、珀耳塞福涅和普路同祷告。年少时读过的古典，全涌到了嘴边，处境的恐怖把我最深处的迷信都惊醒了。我感到自己目击了一整座村庄的死，知道城堡里只剩我和德尼斯·巴里，是他的胆大招来了这场毁灭。一想到他，新的恐怖便抽搐过我全身，我跌倒在地；不是晕厥，是身子不听使唤了。随后我觉出东窗——月亮已从那里升起——灌进来的冰冷的寒风，开始听见城堡深处、我脚下远远的尖叫。很快那尖叫达到了一种无法形诸笔墨的强度和性质，如今一想起来还要发晕。我只能说，那尖叫出自一个我曾当作朋友的东西。

---

在这骇人的时辰里的某一刻，冷风和嘶喊想必把我激了起来，因为我的下一个知觉，便是疯了一样穿过墨黑的房间和走廊、冲过院子、奔进那可怕的夜里。天亮时人们在巴利洛附近找到了我，神志全无地游荡着；可真正把我彻底击垮的，并不是先前我见过听过的一切恐怖。我从阴影里慢慢走出来时喃喃念叨的，是逃亡路上发生的两桩怪事；事情本身无足轻重，可每当我独自在某些沼泽之地或月光下，它们便无休无止地缠上来。

我沿着泥沼边逃离那受诅的城堡时，听见一种新的声音；寻常，却不同于我在基尔德里听过的一切。那一潭死水，前不久还全无生气，如今挤满了黏滑的巨蛙，尖声不停地吹着，音调同它们的个头怪不相称。它们在月光里肿胀地发着绿光，仿佛都在仰望着那光的源头。我顺着一只极肥极丑的青蛙的目光望去，便看见了第二件把我的神智赶走的东西。

===Original===

Stretching directly from the strange olden ruin on the far islet to the waning moon, my eyes seemed to trace a beam of faint quivering radiance having no reflection in the waters of the bog. And upward along that pallid path my fevered fancy pictured a thin shadow slowly writhing; a vague contorted shadow struggling as if drawn by unseen demons. Crazed as I was, I saw in that awful shadow a monstrous resemblance﻿—a nauseous, unbelievable caricature﻿—a blasphemous effigy of him who had been Denys Barry.

===Chinese===

从远岛那座古怪的远古废墟直到残月，我的眼睛仿佛描出一线微微颤动的清辉，在泥沼的水面上却没有倒影。沿着那条苍白的路向上，我发热的幻想里映出一道瘦长的影子在缓缓扭动；一个模糊的、拧绞着的影子，挣扎着，仿佛被看不见的魔鬼拖拽。尽管我已疯了，我还是在那可怕的影子里认出了一种骇人的相似——一幅令人作呕的、难以置信的漫画——一幅渎神的、德尼斯·巴里其人的模拟像。

## The Music of Erich Zann / 埃里希·赞恩的音乐
===Original===

I have examined maps of the city with the greatest care, yet have never again found the Rue d’Auseil. These maps have not been modern maps alone, for I know that names change. I have, on the contrary, delved deeply into all the antiquities of the place; and have personally explored every region, of whatever name, which could possibly answer to the street I knew as the Rue d’Auseil. But despite all I have done, it remains an humiliating fact that I cannot find the house, the street, or even the locality, where, during the last months of my impoverished life as a student of metaphysics at the university, I heard the music of Erich Zann.

That my memory is broken, I do not wonder; for my health, physical and mental, was gravely disturbed throughout the period of my residence in the Rue d’Auseil, and I recall that I took none of my few acquaintances there. But that I cannot find the place again is both singular and perplexing; for it was within a half-hour’s walk of the university and was distinguished by peculiarities which could hardly be forgotten by anyone who had been there. I have never met a person who has seen the Rue d’Auseil.

The Rue d’Auseil lay across a dark river bordered by precipitous brick blear-windowed warehouses and spanned by a ponderous bridge of dark stone. It was always shadowy along that river, as if the smoke of neighboring factories shut out the sun perpetually. The river was also odorous with evil stenches which I have never smelled elsewhere, and which may some day help me to find it, since I should recognise them at once. Beyond the bridge were narrow cobbled streets with rails; and then came the ascent, at first gradual, but incredibly steep as the Rue d’Auseil was reached.

===Chinese===

我极尽仔细地查过这座城市的地图，却再也没有找到过奥塞尔街（Rue d'Auseil）。我查的并不只是现代地图，因为我知道街名会改。恰恰相反，我把这地方的古旧文献翻了个底朝天；又亲自踏勘了每一个街区，不管叫什么名字，只要可能对应我记忆中那条奥塞尔街，我都去了。可尽管做了这么多，一个令人难堪的事实依然是：我找不到那栋房子、那条街、甚至那片街区——我在大学读玄学、穷愁潦倒的时日的最后几个月里，就是在那里听见埃里希·赞恩的音乐的。

我的记忆残缺，我并不奇怪；因为住在奥塞尔街的那段日子里，我的身体和心神都受了严重的搅扰，我记得我一个熟人也没往那里带过。可我竟再也找不到那地方，就又古怪又叫人困惑；因为它离大学不过半小时步程，而且有些特色，凡是去过的人都不容易忘掉。我从未遇见一个见过奥塞尔街的人。

奥塞尔街横在一条黑河对岸，河两岸是砖砌陡立、窗色昏昧的货栈，河上一道笨重的黑石桥。那条河边永远是昏暗的，仿佛四邻工厂的烟永远遮着太阳。河水还带着我在别处从未闻过的恶臭，说不定哪天倒能帮我找到它，因为我一闻便认得。桥那头是有铁轨的窄石板街；再往上就是坡，起初还缓，到奥塞尔街口，陡得叫人不敢相信。

===Original===

I have never seen another street as narrow and steep as the Rue d’Auseil. It was almost a cliff, closed to all vehicles, consisting in several places of flights of steps, and ending at the top in a lofty ivied wall. Its paving was irregular, sometimes stone slabs, sometimes cobblestones, and sometimes bare earth with struggling greenish-grey vegetation. The houses were tall, peaked-roofed, incredibly old, and crazily leaning backward, forward, and sidewise. Occasionally an opposite pair, both leaning forward, almost met across the street like an arch; and certainly they kept most of the light from the ground below. There were a few overhead bridges from house to house across the street.

The inhabitants of that street impressed me peculiarly. At first I thought it was because they were all silent and reticent; but later decided it was because they were all very old. I do not know how I came to live on such a street, but I was not myself when I moved there. I had been living in many poor places, always evicted for want of money; until at last I came upon that tottering house in the Rue d’Auseil kept by the paralytic Blandot. It was the third house from the top of the street, and by far the tallest of them all.

---

My room was on the fifth story; the only inhabited room there, since the house was almost empty. On the night I arrived I heard strange music from the peaked garret overhead, and the next day asked old Blandot about it. He told me it was an old German viol-player, a strange dumb man who signed his name as Erich Zann, and who played evenings in a cheap theatre orchestra; adding that Zann’s desire to play in the night after his return from the theatre was the reason he had chosen this lofty and isolated garret room, whose single gable window was the only point on the street from which one could look over the terminating wall at the declivity and panorama beyond.

Thereafter I heard Zann every night, and although he kept me awake, I was haunted by the weirdness of his music. Knowing little of the art myself, I was yet certain that none of his harmonies had any relation to music I had heard before; and concluded that he was a composer of highly original genius. The longer I listened, the more I was fascinated, until after a week I resolved to make the old man’s acquaintance.

===Chinese===

我从未见过第二条街像奥塞尔街这样又窄又陡。它几乎是一道崖，一切车辆不通，好几处是一级级台阶，到顶是一面爬满常春藤的高墙。铺路极不齐整，有时是石板，有时是卵石，有时干脆是裸土，挣扎着一点灰绿的草。房子高高的，尖顶，老得没法说，前倾后仰、东倒西歪地斜着。偶尔对门两栋都朝前倾，几乎在街心上头合成一道拱；地上的光自然也被它们遮去了大半。有几道天桥凌空跨过街，从这家的楼通到那家的楼。

那条街的居民给我的印象尤其深。起初我以为是因为他们全都沉默寡言；后来断定，是因为他们全都老极了。我不知道自己怎么会住到这样一条街上去，搬去的时候我自己就不对劲。我在许多寒碜地方辗转，回回因为付不起钱被撵走；末了撞进奥塞尔街那所摇摇欲坠的房子，房东是瘫痪的布朗多（Blandot）。那是从街顶数第三栋，也是所有房子里最高的一栋。

---

我的房间在五层；整个一层楼只有这一间住人，因为房子几乎是空的。到的当晚，我听见头顶尖顶的阁楼里传出古怪的音乐，第二天便问老布朗多。他告诉我，那是个年老的德国拉提琴的，一个古怪的哑巴，署名埃里希·赞恩（Erich Zann），晚上在一家廉价戏院的乐队里演奏；他还说，赞恩从戏院回来后还要在夜里演奏，正是因为这个，他才挑了这间又高又孤的阁楼——那扇山墙独窗，是整条街上唯一一处能越过街顶那面墙、望见墙外坡地和更远处全景的地方。

此后我夜夜听见赞恩，他吵得我睡不着，可他音乐里那种怪异缠住了我。我自己于音乐所知甚少，却敢断定他的和声同我从前听过的一切音乐毫无关系；于是认定他是个独创性极高的天才作曲家。听得越久，我越入迷，一星期后，我决意结识这位老人。

===Original===

One night, as he was returning from his work, I intercepted Zann in the hallway and told him that I would like to know him and be with him when he played. He was a small, lean, bent person, with shabby clothes, blue eyes, grotesque, satyr-like face, and nearly bald head; and at my first words seemed both angered and frightened. My obvious friendliness, however, finally melted him; and he grudgingly motioned to me to follow him up the dark, creaking, and rickety attic stairs. His room, one of only two in the steeply pitched garret, was on the west side, toward the high wall that formed the upper end of the street. Its size was very great, and seemed the greater because of its extraordinary bareness and neglect. Of furniture there was only a narrow iron bedstead, a dingy washstand, a small table, a large bookcase, an iron music-rack, and three old-fashioned chairs. Sheets of music were piled in disorder about the floor. The walls were of bare boards, and had probably never known plaster; whilst the abundance of dust and cobwebs made the place seem more deserted than inhabited. Evidently Erich Zann’s world of beauty lay in some far cosmos of the imagination.

Motioning me to sit down, the dumb man closed the door, turned the large wooden bolt, and lighted a candle to augment the one he had brought with him. He now removed his viol from its moth-eaten covering, and taking it, seated himself in the least uncomfortable of the chairs. He did not employ the music-rack, but offering no choice and playing from memory, enchanted me for over an hour with strains I had never heard before; strains which must have been of his own devising. To describe their exact nature is impossible for one unversed in music. They were a kind of fugue, with recurrent passages of the most captivating quality, but to me were notable for the absence of any of the weird notes I had overheard from my room below on other occasions.

===Chinese===

一天夜里他从戏院回来，我在过道里截住赞恩，说我想认识他，想在他演奏时陪着他。他是个干瘦佝偻的小个子，衣衫破旧，蓝眼睛，一张古怪的、羊怪似的脸，头顶几乎全秃；听我头一句话，似乎又怒又怕。可我一片显然的善意终于把他软化；他不情愿地招手让我跟上，爬上黑暗、吱嘎作响、摇摇晃晃的阁楼楼梯。他的房间在陡峭阁楼仅有的两间里，朝西，面对着构成街上端的那面高墙。屋子极大，而且因为空得异乎寻常、无人料理，显得更大。家具只有一张窄铁床、一个发乌的洗脸架、一张小桌、一个大书架、一个铁谱架和三把旧式椅子。乐谱一叠叠乱堆在地上。墙壁是裸板，大概从没上过灰泥；尘土和蛛网密布，使这地方与其说有人住，不如说被废弃了。显然，埃里希·赞恩的美之世界，在想象力的某个遥远宇宙里。

哑巴招手让我坐下，关了门，上了大木闩，点起一支蜡烛，给他带来的那支添个伴。他从虫蛀的套子里取出提琴，抱着琴在几把椅子里挑了把最不硌人的坐下。他不用谱架，也不由我点曲，凭记忆演奏，用一个多小时迷住了我，全是我从未听过的调子；那些调子必是出于他自己的创制。要描画它们确切的性质，对一个不通音乐的人是不可能的。它们是一种赋格，循环往复的段落有最摄人的美质；但在我听来，最特别的是缺了我从前在楼下房间里偷听到的那些怪音。

===Original===

Those haunting notes I had remembered, and had often hummed and whistled inaccurately to myself, so when the player at length laid down his bow I asked him if he would render some of them. As I began my request the wrinkled satyr-like face lost the bored placidity it had possessed during the playing, and seemed to show the same curious mixture of anger and fright which I had noticed when first I accosted the old man. For a moment I was inclined to use persuasion, regarding rather lightly the whims of senility; and even tried to awaken my host’s weirder mood by whistling a few of the strains to which I had listened the night before. But I did not pursue this course for more than a moment; for when the dumb musician recognised the whistled air his face grew suddenly distorted with an expression wholly beyond analysis, and his long, cold, bony right hand reached out to stop my mouth and silence the crude imitation. As he did this he further demonstrated his eccentricity by casting a startled glance toward the lone curtained window, as if fearful of some intruder﻿—a glance doubly absurd, since the garret stood high and inaccessible above all the adjacent roofs, this window being the only point on the steep street, as the concierge had told me, from which one could see over the wall at the summit.

The old man’s glance brought Blandot’s remark to my mind, and with a certain capriciousness I felt a wish to look out over the wide and dizzying panorama of moonlit roofs and city lights beyond the hilltop, which of all the dwellers in the Rue d’Auseil only this crabbed musician could see. I moved toward the window and would have drawn aside the nondescript curtains, when with a frightened rage even greater than before the dumb lodger was upon me again; this time motioning with his head toward the door as he nervously strove to drag me thither with both hands. Now thoroughly disgusted with my host, I ordered him to release me, and told him I would go at once. His clutch relaxed, and as he saw my disgust and offence his own anger seemed to subside. He tightened his relaxing grip, but this time in a friendly manner, forcing me into a chair; then with an appearance of wistfulness crossing to the littered table, where he wrote many words with a pencil in the laboured French of a foreigner.

===Chinese===

那些缠人的调子我记得，还常常自己不成调地哼、吹；所以等演奏者终于放下弓，我便问他肯不肯拉几段那些。我一开口，那张皱巴巴的羊怪脸便失去了演奏时的那副倦怠的平静，仿佛又显出我初次搭话时注意到的那种古怪的怒与惧的混合。有一刻我想用劝的，把老年的执拗不当作一回事；甚至试着吹几声头晚听过的调子，想引出主人那更怪的心境。可这条路我走了不到一分钟；因为哑巴乐师一认出吹出的调子，他的脸骤然扭歪成一种全然无从分析的表情，那又长又冷的骨感右手伸过来捂住我的嘴，止住那拙劣的模仿。他一边这样做，一边又显出他的乖僻，惊惶地朝那扇挂着帘的独窗瞥了一眼，仿佛怕有什么闯入者——这一瞥加倍荒唐，因为阁楼高踞于四邻一切屋顶之上，人迹难至；这扇窗，正如看门人告诉过我的，是这条陡街上唯一能越过街顶的墙望出去的地方。

老人的目光让我想起布朗多的话；带着一种突发的任性，我起意想看一看墙外那片宽阔炫目的全景——月光下的屋顶、山巅之外的城市灯火——奥塞尔街的住户里，只有这个乖戾的乐师看得见。我走向窗口，正要拉开那几块不伦不类的帘子，哑巴房客带着比刚才更甚的惊怒又扑到我身上；这回他用头朝门示意，两手紧张地拖我过去。我对这位主人彻底厌恶了，喝令他放开，说我马上就走。他松了手；见我的嫌恶和愠怒，他自己的怒气似乎也消了。他重新抓着我，却这次是友好的，把我按进椅子；随后面露怅惘地走到堆满纸片的桌边，用外国人的法语，费劲地拿铅笔写下一行行字。

===Original===

The note which he finally handed me was an appeal for tolerance and forgiveness. Zann said that he was old, lonely, and afflicted with strange fears and nervous disorders connected with his music and with other things. He had enjoyed my listening to his music, and wished I would come again and not mind his eccentricities. But he could not play to another his weird harmonies, and could not bear hearing them from another; nor could he bear having anything in his room touched by another. He had not known until our hallway conversation that I could overhear his playing in my room, and now asked me if I would arrange with Blandot to take a lower room where I could not hear him in the night. He would, he wrote, defray the difference in rent.

As I sat deciphering the execrable French I felt more lenient toward the old man. He was a victim of physical and nervous suffering, as was I; and my metaphysical studies had taught me kindness. In the silence there came a slight sound from the window﻿—the shutter must have rattled in the night-wind, and for some reason I started almost as violently as did Erich Zann. So when I had finished reading I shook my host by the hand, and departed as a friend.

The next day Blandot gave me a more expensive room on the third floor, between the apartments of an aged moneylender and the room of a respectable upholsterer. There was no one on the fourth floor.

---

It was not long before I found that Zann’s eagerness for my company was not as great as it had seemed while he was persuading me to move down from the fifth story. He did not ask me to call on him, and when I did call he appeared uneasy and played listlessly. This was always at night﻿—in the day he slept and would admit no one. My liking for him did not grow, though the attic room and the weird music seemed to hold an odd fascination for me. I had a curious desire to look out of that window, over the wall and down the unseen slope at the glittering roofs and spires which must lie outspread there. Once I went up to the garret during theatre hours, when Zann was away, but the door was locked.

===Chinese===

他终于递给我的字条，是一份请求宽容与原谅的申诉。赞恩写道，他老了，孤独，为种种古怪的恐惧和神经的失调所苦，与他的音乐有关，也同别的事情有关。他很高兴我听他的音乐，愿我常来，别把他的怪僻放在心上。可他不能对另一个人演奏他那些怪异的和声，也不能忍受听别人奏出它们；他同样不能忍受自己房里的东西被旁人碰。直到过道里那次交谈，他才知道我在自己房间里听得见他的演奏；他问我肯不肯同布朗多商量，搬去一间低些的、夜里听不见他的屋子。他愿意，他写道，补上房租的差价。

我坐在那里解读这糟糕的法语，对老人宽容了几分。他是个肉体与神经痛苦的受害者，正如我一样；我的玄学研究教给了我仁慈。寂静中，窗口传来一声轻响——想必是窗板在夜风里磕了一下——不知为什么，我惊得几乎同埃里希·赞恩一样厉害。读完字条，我便同主人握了握手，作为朋友告辞。

第二天，布朗多给我换了三楼一间贵些的房间，一边住着个年老的放债人，一边是个正派的软垫匠。四层没有人住。

---

没过多久我便发现，赞恩巴望我做伴的热切，并不像他劝我搬下五楼时显得的那样。他不请我去找他；我去找他时，他显得不安，演奏也无精打采。这总在夜里——白天他睡觉，谁也不见。我对他的好感并没有增长，尽管那间阁楼和那怪异的音乐对我似乎有种古怪的魔力。我有一种古怪的欲望，想从那扇窗望出去，越过墙，朝那看不见的坡地下望——那底下必定铺展着闪闪的屋顶和尖塔。有一回，趁戏院开演、赞恩不在，我上到阁楼，门却锁着。

===Original===

What I did succeed in doing was to overhear the nocturnal playing of the dumb old man. At first I would tiptoe up to my old fifth floor, then I grew bold enough to climb the last creaking staircase to the peaked garret. There in the narrow hall, outside the bolted door with the covered keyhole, I often heard sounds which filled me with an indefinable dread﻿—the dread of vague wonder and brooding mystery. It was not that the sounds were hideous, for they were not; but that they held vibrations suggesting nothing on this globe of earth, and that at certain intervals they assumed a symphonic quality which I could hardly conceive as produced by one player. Certainly, Erich Zann was a genius of wild power. As the weeks passed, the playing grew wilder, whilst the old musician acquired an increasing haggardness and furtiveness pitiful to behold. He now refused to admit me at any time, and shunned me whenever we met on the stairs.

Then one night as I listened at the door I heard the shrieking viol swell into a chaotic babel of sound; a pandemonium which would have led me to doubt my own shaking sanity had there not come from behind that barred portal a piteous proof that the horror was real﻿—the awful, inarticulate cry which only a mute can utter, and which rises only in moments of the most terrible fear or anguish. I knocked repeatedly at the door, but received no response. Afterward I waited in the black hallway, shivering with cold and fear, till I heard the poor musician’s feeble effort to rise from the floor by the aid of a chair. Believing him just conscious after a fainting fit, I renewed my rapping, at the same time calling out my name reassuringly. I heard Zann stumble to the window and close both shutter and sash, then stumble to the door, which he falteringly unfastened to admit me. This time his delight at having me present was real; for his distorted face gleamed with relief while he clutched at my coat as a child clutches at its mother’s skirts.

===Chinese===

我真正做到的，是偷听这哑巴老人的夜间演奏。起初我只敢踮脚上到原先的五楼；后来胆大了，敢爬最后一段吱嘎作响的楼梯，直到尖顶阁楼。在窄窄的过道里，在那扇闩死、锁眼蒙着的门外，我常听见一些声音，它们使我充满一种无可名状的畏——对朦胧奇迹和幽幽之谜的畏。倒不是那声音有多可憎，它们并不；而是它们携着的振动，暗示着这个地球上不存在的东西；而且在某些间歇，它们呈现出一种交响的性质，我几乎无法相信出自一个演奏者。无疑，埃里希·赞恩是个狂野之力量的天才。一星期一星期过去，演奏越来越狂，老乐师则添了一种与日俱增的憔悴和鬼祟，看得人心里发酸。他现在任何时刻都拒绝见我，楼梯上遇见也躲。

随后一天夜里，我正在门外听，那尖叫的提琴陡然涨成一片混沌的喧声；一片魔窟般的乱响——若不是那扇上了闩的门后传来一声可怜的明证，证明那恐怖是真的，这场大乱几乎要叫我相信自己疯了——那可怕的不成言语的喊，只有哑巴才发得出，只在最可怕的恐惧或剧痛的时刻才会升起。我一次次敲门，没有回应。后来我在黑暗的过道里等，冷得、怕得发抖，直到听见可怜的乐师撑着椅子、挣扎着从地上起身的微弱动静。想着他晕厥之后刚刚缓过神，我又敲起门来，一边报着自己的名字安他的心。我听见赞恩跌撞着走到窗前，合上窗板和窗扇，又跌撞着到门边，颤颤地开了闩放我进去。这一回，有我在场，他的高兴是真的；他扭曲的脸放出宽慰的光，抓住我的外套，像个孩子抓住母亲的裙子。

===Original===

Shaking pathetically, the old man forced me into a chair whilst he sank into another, beside which his viol and bow lay carelessly on the floor. He sat for some time inactive, nodding oddly, but having a paradoxical suggestion of intense and frightened listening. Subsequently he seemed to be satisfied, and crossing to a chair by the table wrote a brief note, handed it to me, and returned to the table, where he began to write rapidly and incessantly. The note implored me in the name of mercy, and for the sake of my own curiosity, to wait where I was while he prepared a full account in German of all the marvels and terrors which beset him. I waited, and the dumb man’s pencil flew.

It was perhaps an hour later, while I still waited and while the old musician’s feverishly written sheets still continued to pile up, that I saw Zann start as from the hint of a horrible shock. Unmistakably he was looking at the curtained window and listening shudderingly. Then I half fancied I heard a sound myself; though it was not a horrible sound, but rather an exquisitely low and infinitely distant musical note, suggesting a player in one of the neighboring houses, or in some abode beyond the lofty wall over which I had never been able to look. Upon Zann the effect was terrible, for, dropping his pencil, suddenly he rose, seized his viol, and commenced to rend the night with the wildest playing I had ever heard from his bow save when listening at the barred door.

---

It would be useless to describe the playing of Erich Zann on that dreadful night. It was more horrible than anything I had ever overheard, because I could now see the expression of his face, and could realise that this time the motive was stark fear. He was trying to make a noise; to ward something off or drown something out﻿—what, I could not imagine, awesome though I felt it must be. The playing grew fantastic, delirious, and hysterical, yet kept to the last the qualities of supreme genius which I knew this strange old man possessed. I recognised the air﻿—it was a wild Hungarian dance popular in the theatres, and I reflected for a moment that this was the first time I had ever heard Zann play the work of another composer.

===Chinese===

老人可怜地抖着，把我按进椅子，自己跌进另一把，他的琴和弓就随随便便撂在旁边地上。他呆坐了一阵，古怪地点着头，却又带着一种矛盾至极的、紧张而惊惶的倾听的暗示。随后他似乎放了心，挪到桌边一把椅子上，写下一张简短的字条递给我，又回到桌前，开始不停地疾书。字条以慈悲之名、以我自己的好奇心之名恳求我，在原地等他，等他用德文把围困他的一切奇迹与恐怖写一份完整的交代。我等着；哑巴的铅笔飞着。

大约一个钟头后，我还在等，老乐师狂热的字纸还在一页页加高，我看见赞恩猛地一惊，像挨了可怕的闷雷。分明不误，他正盯着挂帘的窗，战栗地听。随后我恍惚也听见了一个声音；那不是可怕的声音，倒是一缕精微之极、无限遥远的乐音，仿佛来自隔壁哪一栋房子，或高墙之外——墙外的景象我从来无缘得见——的某个居所。这乐音在赞恩身上激出的效果是可怕的：他丢下铅笔，霍地站起，抓起琴，开始撕裂这个夜——用我从他的弓下听过的最狂野的演奏，除了在那扇上闩的门后听过的之外。

---

要描画那可怕的一夜埃里希·赞恩的演奏，是徒劳的。它比我偷听过的一切都更骇人，因为如今我看得见他的脸，看得出这一回他的动机是赤裸裸的恐惧。他在设法弄出声响；要挡开什么，或压倒什么——什么，我想象不出，尽管我感到它必定骇人。演奏变得奇幻、谵狂、歇斯底里，却到底保持着至高天才的品质——我知道这个怪老人拥有它。我认出了那调子——是一支戏院里流行的狂野的匈牙利舞曲；我一时想到，这是我头一回听见赞恩演奏另一个作曲家的作品。

===Original===

Louder and louder, wilder and wilder, mounted the shrieking and whining of that desperate viol. The player was dripping with an uncanny perspiration and twisted like a monkey, always looking frantically at the curtained window. In his frenzied strains I could almost see shadowy satyrs and Bacchanals dancing and whirling insanely through seething abysses of clouds and smoke and lightning. And then I thought I heard a shriller, steadier note that was not from the viol; a calm, deliberate, purposeful, mocking note from far away in the west.

At this juncture the shutter began to rattle in a howling night-wind which had sprung up outside as if in answer to the mad playing within. Zann’s screaming viol now outdid itself, emitting sounds I had never thought a viol could emit. The shutter rattled more loudly, unfastened, and commenced slamming against the window. Then the glass broke shiveringly under the persistent impacts, and the chill wind rushed in, making the candles sputter and rustling the sheets of paper on the table where Zann had begun to write out his horrible secret. I looked at Zann, and saw that he was past conscious observation. His blue eyes were bulging, glassy, and sightless, and the frantic playing had become a blind, mechanical, unrecognisable orgy that no pen could even suggest.

===Chinese===

那绝望的提琴越叫越响，越叫越狂。演奏者淌着鬼气涔涔的汗，扭动得像只猴子，眼睛始终狂乱地瞟着挂帘的窗。在他狂乱的弦声里，我几乎看得见憧憧的羊怪和酒神的信女，在云、烟与电光沸腾的深渊里疯狂地旋舞。随后，我想我听见了一个更尖、更稳的音，不是出自提琴；一缕平静的、从容的、蓄意的、嘲弄的音，来自遥远的西边。

正在这时，窗外骤起呼啸的夜风，窗板开始格格地响，仿佛应和着屋里的疯狂演奏。赞恩尖叫的提琴此刻超出了它自己，发出的声音我从未想过一把提琴发得出。窗板响得更凶，脱开了，开始一下下砸在窗上。随后玻璃在持续不断的撞击下碎裂，寒风灌进来，吹得烛火噼啪，掀得赞恩开始誊写他那可怕的秘密的桌上字纸乱响。我看向赞恩，看出他已经顾不上有知觉的观察了。蓝眼睛暴突、失神、无光；狂乱的演奏变成一场盲目的、机械的、无可辨认的纵酒，任何一支笔都无从描画。

===Original===

A sudden gust, stronger than the others, caught up the manuscript and bore it toward the window. I followed the flying sheets in desperation, but they were gone before I reached the demolished panes. Then I remembered my old wish to gaze from this window, the only window in the Rue d’Auseil from which one might see the slope beyond the wall, and the city outspread beneath. It was very dark, but the city’s lights always burned, and I expected to see them there amidst the rain and wind. Yet when I looked from that highest of all gable windows, looked while the candles sputtered and the insane viol howled with the night-wind, I saw no city spread below, and no friendly lights gleaming from remembered streets, but only the blackness of space illimitable; unimagined space alive with motion and music, and having no semblance to anything on earth. And as I stood there looking in terror, the wind blew out both the candles in that ancient peaked garret, leaving me in savage and impenetrable darkness with chaos and pandemonium before me, and the demon madness of that night-baying viol behind me.

I staggered back in the dark, without the means of striking a light, crashing against the table, overturning a chair, and finally groping my way to the place where the blackness screamed with shocking music. To save myself and Erich Zann I could at least try, whatever the powers opposed to me. Once I thought some chill thing brushed me, and I screamed, but my scream could not be heard above that hideous viol. Suddenly out of the blackness the madly sawing bow struck me, and I knew I was close to the player. I felt ahead, touched the back of Zann’s chair, and then found and shook his shoulder in an effort to bring him to his senses.

===Chinese===

一阵比先前都强的狂风卷起手稿，朝窗口带去。我绝望地追着那些飞舞的字纸，可不等我扑到砸烂的窗格，它们已经没了。随后我想起自己那个旧愿——从这扇窗望出去，奥塞尔街唯一的、能望见墙外坡地和铺展在下面的城市的窗。天很黑，可城市的灯火永远亮着，我指望在风雨里望见它们。然而当我从那最高的山墙独窗望出去——烛火噼啪、癫狂的提琴同夜风一起嚎着的时候望出去——我没有看见下面铺展的城市，没有记忆中的街道透出的友好灯火，只有无垠太空的黑；一片无从想象的太空，游动着运动与音乐，同地上任何东西都没有相似之处。我惊恐地站在那里，风把那古老尖顶阁楼里的两支蜡烛全吹熄了，把我抛进一种蛮荒的、透不进的黑暗：眼前是混沌与魔窟，背后是那把向夜狂吠的提琴的魔鬼之狂。

我在黑暗里踉跄后退，没有火可点，撞上桌子，掀翻一把椅子，末了摸索着挪到黑暗中那震惊的音乐尖叫着的地方。为了救我自己，也救埃里希·赞恩，哪怕同我作对的是什么力量，我至少可以一试。有一刻我觉得什么冰凉的东西擦过我，我叫了出来；可我的叫声在那把可憎的提琴之上，谁也听不见。突然，黑暗里那疯狂拉锯的弓打在我身上，我知道我挨近演奏者了。我往前摸，摸到赞恩椅子的靠背，随即找到他的肩，摇着，想把他摇醒。

===Original===

He did not respond, and still the viol shrieked on without slackening. I moved my hand to his head, whose mechanical nodding I was able to stop, and shouted in his ear that we must both flee from the unknown things of the night. But he neither answered me nor abated the frenzy of his unutterable music, while all through the garret strange currents of wind seemed to dance in the darkness and babel. When my hand touched his ear I shuddered, though I knew not why﻿—knew not why till I felt of the still face; the ice-cold, stiffened, unbreathing face whose glassy eyes bulged uselessly into the void. And then, by some miracle finding the door and the large wooden bolt, I plunged wildly away from that glassy-eyed thing in the dark, and from the ghoulish howling of that accursed viol whose fury increased even as I plunged.

Leaping, floating, flying down those endless stairs through the dark house; racing mindlessly out into the narrow, steep, and ancient street of steps and tottering houses; clattering down steps and over cobbles to the lower streets and the putrid canyon-walled river; panting across the great dark bridge to the broader, healthier streets and boulevards we know; all these are terrible impressions that linger with me. And I recall that there was no wind, and that the moon was out, and that all the lights of the city twinkled.

---

Despite my most careful searches and investigations, I have never since been able to find the Rue d’Auseil. But I am not wholly sorry; either for this or for the loss in undreamable abysses of the closely written sheets which alone could have explained the music of Erich Zann.

===Chinese===

他没有反应，提琴仍在尖叫，毫不松劲。我把手挪到他的头——那机械的点动我止住了——冲他耳朵喊，说我们俩都得逃，逃开这夜里的无名之物。可他既不答我，也不稍减他那说不出的音乐的狂乱；而整个阁楼里，一阵阵怪风仿佛在黑暗与喧声中起舞。我的手触到他的耳朵时，我打了个寒噤，虽然不知为什么——直到我摸到那张不动了的脸；那张冰冷的、僵直的、不呼吸的脸，那双玻璃般的眼睛徒然暴突着望向虚空。随后，也不知是哪来的奇迹，我找到了门和大木闩，从黑暗里那个玻璃眼的东西旁边、从那把受诅提琴食尸鬼似的嚎叫里狂乱地撞了出来——我逃得越急，它的狂怒涨得越高。

跳着、浮着、飞着，下那无穷的楼梯，穿过黑暗的房子；没头没脑地狂奔，冲进那条窄的、陡的、古老的街，满街台阶和摇摇欲坠的房子；磕磕绊绊下了台阶、过了卵石路，奔向低处的街和那条污秽的、峡壁般的河；喘着气跑过漆黑的大桥，回到我们熟悉的、更宽更健康的街和大道——这一切，都是至今缠着我的可怕印象。我还记得，那一夜没有风，月亮出来了，城市的灯火全都亮着。

---

尽管我一次次最仔细的搜寻和调查，此后我再也没有找到奥塞尔街。但我并不十分惋惜——不为这个，也不为那密密写满的字纸失落于无从梦想的深渊；唯有它们，本可以解释埃里希·赞恩的音乐。

## The Other Gods / 另一些神
===Original===

Atop the tallest of earth’s peaks dwell the gods of earth, and suffer no man to tell that he hath looked upon them. Lesser peaks they once inhabited; but ever the men from the plains would scale the slopes of rock and snow, driving the gods to higher and higher mountains till now only the last remains. When they left their older peaks they took with them all signs of themselves, save once, it is said, when they left a carven image on the face of the mountain which they called Ngranek.

But now they have betaken themselves to unknown Kadath in the cold waste where no man treads, and are grown stern, having no higher peak whereto to flee at the coming of men. They are grown stern, and where once they suffered men to displace them, they now forbid men to come; or coming, to depart. It is well for men that they know not of Kadath in the cold waste, else they would seek injudiciously to scale it.

Sometimes when earth’s gods are homesick they visit in the still night the peaks where once they dwelt, and weep softly as they try to play in the olden way on remembered slopes. Men have felt the tears of the gods on white-capped Thurai, though they have thought it rain; and have heard the sighs of the gods in the plaintive dawn-winds of Lerion. In cloud-ships the gods are wont to travel, and wise cotters have legends that keep them from certain high peaks at night when it is cloudy, for the gods are not lenient as of old.

In Ulthar, which lies beyond the river Skai, once dwelt an old man avid to behold the gods of earth; a man deeply learned in the seven cryptical books of earth; and familiar with the Pnakotic Manuscripts of distant and frozen Lomar. His name was Barzai the Wise, and the villagers tell of how he went up a mountain on the night of the strange eclipse.

===Chinese===

大地最高峰的顶上，住着大地的众神；他们不许任何人说出自己曾见过他们。较低的山峰他们从前也住过；可平原上的人总是攀上岩坡雪坡，把众神往更高的山上驱赶，赶到如今，只剩最后一座了。离开旧峰时，他们把自身的一切痕迹都带走了；只除一回——据说——他们在一座山的山面上留下一幅刻出的影像，那山他们唤作恩格拉内克（Ngranek）。

可如今他们迁到了无人踏足的寒冷荒原上、无人知晓的卡达斯（Kadath），并且变得严厉了；人再来时，再没有更高的峰可供他们逃了。他们变得严厉；从前他们容人把自己挤走，如今他们禁止人来——来了，也禁止回去。人不知道寒冷荒原上的卡达斯，这是好的；不然他们会不知深浅地要去攀它。

有时，大地的众神想家了，便在寂静的夜里重访旧居的山峰，在记忆中的山坡上试着照旧时的方式嬉戏，轻轻地哭。白色戴雪的图莱（Thurai）峰上，人感受过众神的眼泪，只当那是雨；勒里翁（Lerion）黎明哀婉的风里，人听见过众神的叹息。众神惯乘云之船旅行；聪慧的庄稼人中间流传着一些传说，教他们在多云的夜里避开某几座高峰，因为众神已不像旧时那样宽仁了。

在斯凯河对岸的乌撒，曾住着一位渴望亲见大地众神的老人；他深研大地的七卷秘典，熟稔遥远冰封的洛马尔携来的纳克特手稿（Pnakotic Manuscripts）。他名叫智者巴尔扎伊（Barzai）；村民们至今讲着，在那奇异月食的夜晚，他怎样登上一座山。

===Original===

Barzai knew so much of the gods that he could tell of their comings and goings, and guessed so many of their secrets that he was deemed half a god himself. It was he who wisely advised the burgesses of Ulthar when they passed their remarkable law against the slaying of cats, and who first told the young priest Atal where it is that black cats go at midnight on St. John’s Eve. Barzai was learned in the lore of earth’s gods, and had gained a desire to look upon their faces. He believed that his great secret knowledge of gods could shield him from their wrath, so resolved to go up to the summit of high and rocky Hatheg-Kla on a night when he knew the gods would be there.

Hatheg-Kla is far in the stony desert beyond Hatheg, for which it is named, and rises like a rock statue in a silent temple. Around its peak the mists play always mournfully, for mists are the memories of the gods, and the gods loved Hatheg-Kla when they dwelt upon it in the old days. Often the gods of earth visit Hatheg-Kla in their ships of cloud, casting pale vapours over the slopes as they dance reminiscently on the summit under a clear moon. The villagers of Hatheg say it is ill to climb Hatheg-Kla at any time, and deadly to climb it by night when pale vapours hide the summit and the moon; but Barzai heeded them not when he came from neighboring Ulthar with the young priest Atal, who was his disciple. Atal was only the son of an innkeeper, and was sometimes afraid; but Barzai’s father had been a landgrave who dwelt in an ancient castle, so he had no common superstition in his blood, and only laughed at the fearful cotters.

Barzai and Atal went out of Hatheg into the stony desert despite the prayers of peasants, and talked of earth’s gods by their campfires at night. Many days they travelled, and from afar saw lofty Hatheg-Kla with his aureole of mournful mist. On the thirteenth day they reached the mountain’s lonely base, and Atal spoke of his fears. But Barzai was old and learned and had no fears, so led the way boldly up the slope that no man had scaled since the time of Sansu, who is written of with fright in the mouldy Pnakotic Manuscripts.

===Chinese===

巴尔扎伊于众神之事知道得那么多，众神的来去他说得出，众神的秘密他猜出了那么多，以致人把他自己也当作半个神。乌撒的父老们通过那条出色的禁杀猫的法令时，出谋划策的正是他；第一个告诉年轻的祭司阿塔尔（Atal）——黑色圣约翰之夜的猫在午夜去往何处的人，也是他。巴尔扎伊精研大地众神的学问，渐渐生出一种欲望：要看他们的脸。他相信，自己关于众神的博大秘知可以护住他，不受他们的震怒；于是决意在一个月夜里登上高峻多岩的哈提格-克拉（Hatheg-Kla）峰顶——他知道，那一夜众神必在那里。

哈提格-克拉远在哈提格村外的石头荒原深处，村名便成了它的名字；它像寂静神殿里一尊岩石雕像般拔起。峰顶四周，雾霭永远哀哀地游移，因为雾是众神的记忆，而众神住在它上面的旧日里爱过它。大地的众神常乘云船来访哈提格-克拉，在晴月之下于峰顶怀想地起舞时，往山坡上铺开苍白的蒸气。哈提格村的人说，任何时候登哈提格-克拉都不吉，夜里登更是死罪——当苍白的蒸气藏住峰顶和月亮的时候；可巴尔扎伊从邻村乌撒带着弟子、年轻的祭司阿塔尔来时，全不理会。阿塔尔不过是个客栈老板的儿子，有时会怕；巴尔扎伊的父亲却是一位住在古堡里的方伯，所以他血液里没有庸众的迷信，只笑话那些胆小的庄稼人。

巴尔扎伊和阿塔尔不顾农民的祷告，走出哈提格进了石头荒原，夜里围着营火谈论大地的众神。走了许多天，远远望见高峻的哈提格-克拉，戴着一环哀伤的雾冕。第十三天，他们到了山孤独的脚下，阿塔尔说出了他的怕。可巴尔扎伊又老又博学，无所畏惧，便领头大胆上坡——自桑苏（Sansu）以来，还没有人登上过这山；桑苏其人，发霉的纳克特手稿里带着惊怖记着。

===Original===

The way was rocky, and made perilous by chasms, cliffs, and falling stones. Later it grew cold and snowy; and Barzai and Atal often slipped and fell as they hewed and plodded upward with staves and axes. Finally the air grew thin, and the sky changed colour, and the climbers found it hard to breathe; but still they toiled up and up, marvelling at the strangeness of the scene and thrilling at the thought of what would happen on the summit when the moon was out and the pale vapours spread around. For three days they climbed higher, and higher toward the roof of the world; then they camped to wait for the clouding of the moon.

For four nights no clouds came, and the moon shone down cold through the thin mournful mists around the silent pinnacle. Then on the fifth night, which was the night of the full moon, Barzai saw some dense clouds far to the north, and stayed up with Atal to watch them draw near. Thick and majestic they sailed, slowly and deliberately onward; ranging themselves round the peak high above the watchers, and hiding the moon and the summit from view. For a long hour the watchers gazed, whilst the vapours swirled and the screen of clouds grew thicker and more restless. Barzai was wise in the lore of earth’s gods, and listened hard for certain sounds, but Atal felt the chill of the vapours and the awe of the night, and feared much. And when Barzai began to climb higher and beckon eagerly, it was long before Atal would follow.

So thick were the vapours that the way was hard, and though Atal followed on at last, he could scarce see the grey shape of Barzai on the dim slope above in the clouded moonlight. Barzai forged very far ahead, and seemed despite his age to climb more easily than Atal; fearing not the steepness that began to grow too great for any save a strong and dauntless man, nor pausing at wide black chasms that Atal could scarce leap. And so they went up wildly over rocks and gulfs, slipping and stumbling, and sometimes awed at the vastness and horrible silence of bleak ice pinnacles and mute granite steeps.

===Chinese===

路多岩石，裂谷、峭壁、滚石使它凶险。再往上，天冷了，落雪了；巴尔扎伊和阿塔尔拄杖挥斧，一路砍一路跋涉，常常滑倒、跌跤。到后来空气稀薄，天变了颜色，攀登的人呼吸艰难；可他们仍旧一步步向上劳作，一面惊叹眼前的奇景，一面想到月出雾漫时峰顶上将发生的事，心头震颤。整整三天，他们越登越高，向世界的屋顶登去；随后扎营，等月亮被云遮住。

四夜无云，冷冷的月光穿过寂静峰顶四周稀薄哀伤的雾。第五夜是望月之夜，巴尔扎伊望见北边远处聚起浓云，便同阿塔尔守着不睡，看它们过来。云又浓又威严地航行，缓慢而从容地推进；在两位守望者高上方绕着峰顶列开阵，把月亮和峰顶一齐遮没了。整整一个钟头，守望者凝望着，蒸气回旋，云的幕越积越厚、越不安分。巴尔扎伊于大地众神之学是智者，侧耳苦听某些声响；阿塔尔却感到蒸气的寒和夜的威，怕得厉害。等巴尔扎伊开始往上爬、热切地招手时，过了好久，阿塔尔才肯跟上。

蒸气浓得叫人看不清路；阿塔尔虽然终于跟了上去，在云遮的月光里，几乎望不见巴尔扎伊在昏暗山坡上的灰色身影。巴尔扎伊远远抢在前头，不顾年迈，爬得竟比阿塔尔轻捷；陡得只有强壮无畏的人才承受得住的坡，他不怕；阿塔尔勉强才跳得过的宽宽黑裂谷，他也不停步。他们就这样狂野地翻上岩石与深渊，滑着，绊着，有时被荒凉的冰尖峰和无声的花岗岩绝壁那浩大与可怖的寂静慑住。

===Original===

Very suddenly Barzai went out of Atal’s sight, scaling a hideous cliff that seemed to bulge outward and block the path for any climber not inspired of earth’s gods. Atal was far below, and planning what he should do when he reached the place, when curiously he noticed that the light had grown strong, as if the cloudless peak and moonlit meeting-place of the gods were very near. And as he scrambled on toward the bulging cliff and litten sky he felt fears more shocking than any he had known before. Then through the high mists he heard the voice of unseen Barzai shouting wildly in delight:

“I have heard the gods! I have heard earth’s gods singing in revelry on Hatheg-Kla! The voices of earth’s gods are known to Barzai the Prophet! The mists are thin and the moon is bright, and I shall see the gods dancing wildly on Hatheg-Kla that they loved in youth. The wisdom of Barzai hath made him greater than earth’s gods, and against his will their spells and barriers are as naught; Barzai will behold the gods, the proud gods, the secret gods, the gods of earth who spurn the sight of man!”

Atal could not hear the voices Barzai heard, but he was now close to the bulging cliff and scanning it for footholds. Then he heard Barzai’s voice grow shriller and louder:

“The mist is very thin, and the moon casts shadows on the slope; the voice of earth’s gods art high and wild, and they fear the coming of Barzai the Wise, who is greater than they.﻿ ﻿… The moon’s light flickers, as earth’s gods dance against it; I shall see the dancing forms of the gods that leap and howl in the moonlight.﻿ ﻿… The light is dimmer and the gods are afraid.﻿ ﻿…”

Whilst Barzai was shouting these things Atal felt a spectral change in all the air, as if the laws of earth were bowing to greater laws; for though the way was steeper than ever, the upward path was now grown fearsomely easy, and the bulging cliff proved scarce an obstacle when he reached it and slid perilously up its convex face. The light of the moon had strangely failed, and as Atal plunged upward through the mists he heard Barzai the Wise shrieking in the shadows:

===Chinese===

非常突然地，巴尔扎伊出了阿塔尔的视野：他正攀登一面可怕的崖壁，崖壁向外鼓凸，仿佛把路堵死，凡非大地众神所感发的人，一概休想上去。阿塔尔远远落在下面，正盘算着到了那里该怎么办，忽然奇怪地注意到，光变得强了，仿佛无云的峰顶和月光下众神聚会的场所，已经近在咫尺。他朝鼓凸的崖壁和被照亮的天空爬去，感到一种比从前经历过的任何恐惧都更震骇的恐惧。随后，透过高处的雾，他听见看不见的巴尔扎伊的声音，狂喜地大喊：

「我听见众神了！我听见大地的众神在哈提格-克拉上狂欢歌唱了！大地众神的声音，先知巴尔扎伊认得！雾稀了，月亮亮了，我要看见众神在哈提格-克拉上狂野地舞蹈了——他们年轻时爱这山。巴尔扎伊的智慧使他高于大地的众神；违背他的意志，他们的咒与障都等于无；巴尔扎伊必将看见众神，骄傲的众神，秘密的众神，那些厌见凡人的大地众神！」

巴尔扎伊听见的声音，阿塔尔听不见；可他已挨近那鼓凸的崖壁，正寻着落脚点。随后他听见巴尔扎伊的声音越来越尖、越来越高：

「雾很薄了，月亮在坡上投下影子；大地众神的声音高亢而狂野，他们惧怕智者巴尔扎伊来，他比他们大。……月光摇曳，是大地的众神在月前舞蹈；我要看见众神跳跃嚎叫的舞姿了。……光暗下去了，众神害怕了。……」

巴尔扎伊喊着这些的时候，阿塔尔感到整个空气起了幽灵般的变化，仿佛大地的法则正向更大的法则躬身；因为路虽比先前更陡，向上的路此刻却变得轻易得可怕；等他到了那鼓凸的崖壁，顺它外凸的面惊险地滑上去，它几乎算不得障碍了。月光古怪地熄弱了；阿塔尔穿雾向上猛进时，听见智者巴尔扎伊在阴影里尖喊：

===Original===

“The moon is dark, and the gods dance in the night; there is terror in the sky, for upon the moon hath sunk an eclipse foretold in no books of men or of earth’s gods.﻿ ﻿… There is unknown magic on Hatheg-Kla, for the screams of the frightened gods have turned to laughter, and the slopes of ice shoot up endlessly into the black heavens whither I am plunging.﻿ ﻿… Hei! Hei! At last! In the dim light I behold the gods of earth!”

And now Atal, slipping dizzily up over inconceivable steeps, heard in the dark a loathsome laughing, mixed with such a cry as no man else ever heard save in the Phlegethon of unrelatable nightmares; a cry wherein reverberated the horror and anguish of a haunted lifetime packed into one atrocious moment:

“The Other gods! The Other gods! The gods of the outer hells that guard the feeble gods of earth.﻿ ﻿… Look away.﻿ ﻿… Go back.﻿ ﻿… Do not see! Do not see! The vengeance of the infinite abysses.﻿ ﻿… That cursed, that damnable pit.﻿ ﻿… Merciful gods of earth, I am falling into the sky!”

And as Atal shut his eyes and stopped his eyes and stopped his ears and tried to jump downward against the frightful pull from unknown heights, there resounded on Hatheg-Kla that terrible peal of thunder which awaked the good cotters of the plains and the honest burgesses of Hatheg, Nir and Ulthar, and caused them to behold through the clouds that strange eclipse of the moon that no book ever predicted. And when the moon came out at last Atal was safe on the lower snows of the mountain without sight of earth’s gods, or of the Other gods.

Now it is told in the mouldy Pnakotic Manuscripts that Sansu found naught but wordless ice and rock when he did climb Hatheg-Kla in the youth of the world. Yet when the men of Ulthar and Nir and Hatheg crushed their fears and scaled that haunted steep by day in search of Barzai the Wise, they found graven in the naked stone of the summit a curious and Cyclopean symbol fifty cubits wide, as if the rock had been riven by some titanic chisel. And the symbol was like to one that learned men have discerned in those frightful parts of the Pnakotic Manuscripts which were too ancient to be read. This they found.

===Chinese===

「月亮黑了，众神在夜里舞蹈；天上有恐怖，月亮沉入了食——人的书和大地众神的书都没有预言过的食。……哈提格-克拉上有未知的魔法，受惊众神的尖叫变成了大笑，冰的坡面无穷无尽地向黑色天穹射上去，我正坠向那里。……嘿！嘿！终于！在微光里，我看见大地的众神了！」

此刻，阿塔尔晕眩地从不可想象的陡坡上滑升，在黑暗里听见一阵可憎的大笑，混着一声除了在无从言说的噩梦的弗莱格松火河里、谁也不曾听过的喊；那喊里回荡着闹鬼的一生压缩进一个狞恶瞬间的恐怖与剧痛：

「另一些神！另一些神！外层地狱的众神，看守着大地孱弱众神的那些。……别看。……回去。……不要看见！不要看见！无底深渊的复仇。……那受咒的、该死的坑。……大地的众神发发慈悲，我在往天上掉！」

阿塔尔闭上眼、捂住耳，想朝下跳，逆着那来自未知的高处的可怕的拽力——就在这时，哈提格-克拉上响起那声可怕的雷霆，惊醒了平原上善良的庄稼人和哈提格、尼尔、乌撒诚实的父老，叫他们透过云望见了那次奇异的月食，任何书都不曾预告过的月食。月亮终于出来时，阿塔尔已平安落回山下部的雪地里，没有看见大地的众神，也没有看见另一些神。

如今，发霉的纳克特手稿里讲：世界的年轻时代，桑苏登上哈提格-克拉，只找到无言的冰和岩石。可当乌撒、尼尔和哈提格的人压下恐惧，白天攀登那闹鬼的陡峰去寻找智者巴尔扎伊时，他们在峰顶裸露的岩石上发现一个古怪的蛮石巨构般的符号，宽五十肘，仿佛岩石曾被一柄泰坦的凿子劈开。那符号，同博学的人在纳克特手稿里辨认出的一个相似——在那些古老得无法卒读的骇人篇章里。他们找到的，就是这个。

===Original===

Barzai the Wise they never found, nor could the holy priest Atal ever be persuaded to pray for his soul’s repose. Moreover, to this day the people of Ulthar and Nir and Hatheg fear eclipses, and pray by night when pale vapours hide the mountaintop and the moon. And above the mists on Hatheg-Kla, earth’s gods sometimes dance reminiscently; for they know they are safe, and love to come from unknown Kadath in ships of cloud and play in the olden way, as they did when earth was new and men not given to the climbing of inaccessible places.

===Chinese===

智者巴尔扎伊，他们始终没有找到；神圣的祭司阿塔尔，也永远不能被劝动为他的灵魂安息祈祷。而且直到今天，乌撒、尼尔和哈提格的人都怕月食；当苍白的蒸气藏住山顶和月亮时，他们夜里要祈祷。在哈提格-克拉的雾之上，大地的众神有时还来怀想地起舞；因为他们知道自己安全了，爱从无人知晓的卡达斯乘云船来，照旧时的方式嬉戏——像大地还新、人还不会去攀登不可企及之地的年代那样。

## The Outsider / 异乡人
===Original===

“That night the Baron dreamt of many a woe;

And all his warrior-guests, with shade and form

Of witch, and demon, and large coffin-worm,

Were long be-nightmared.”

> Keats

Unhappy is he to whom the memories of childhood bring only fear and sadness. Wretched is he who looks back upon lone hours in vast and dismal chambers with brown hangings and maddening rows of antique books, or upon awed watches in twilight groves of grotesque, gigantic, and vine-encumbered trees that silently wave twisted branches far aloft. Such a lot the gods gave to me﻿—to me, the dazed, the disappointed; the barren, the broken. And yet I am strangely content, and cling desperately to those sere memories, when my mind momentarily threatens to reach beyond to *the other*.

I know not where I was born, save that the castle was infinitely old and infinitely horrible; full of dark passages and having high ceilings where the eye could find only cobwebs and shadows. The stones in the crumbling corridors seemed always hideously damp, and there was an accursed smell everywhere, as of the piled-up corpses of dead generations. It was never light, so that I used sometimes to light candles and gaze steadily at them for relief; nor was there any sun outdoors, since the terrible trees grew high above the topmost accessible tower. There was one black tower which reached above the trees into the unknown outer sky, but that was partly ruined and could not be ascended save by a well-nigh impossible climb up the sheer wall, stone by stone.

===Chinese===

“那一夜，男爵梦见了许多灾祸；

他所有的武士宾客，连同

女巫、恶魔和大棺材虫的形影，

久久被梦魇纠缠。”

——济慈

童年回忆只带来恐惧与悲哀的人，是不幸的。回望那些孤寂时辰——在挂着褐色帷幔、排着叫人发狂的古书的长而阴惨的大厅里，或是在暮色中那些怪诞、巨大、缠满藤蔓的树林里敬畏守夜，看扭曲的枝柯在极高处无声摇曳——这样的人，是可怜的。诸神把这样的命运给了我——给我，这恍惚的、幻灭的；贫瘠的、破碎的。然而我出奇地知足，死死抱住那些枯萎的记忆，每当我的心神一时威胁着要越过它们、伸向彼界。

我不知自己生在哪里，只知那城堡无限古老、无限可怕；满是黑暗的走廊，天花板高得眼睛只能寻见蛛网与暗影。崩坏走廊里的石头似乎永远湿得狰狞，四下里有一股受了诅咒的气味，像堆积的历代死尸。那里从不见光，我有时便点上蜡烛，盯着它们看，以求宽慰；外面也没有太阳，因为那些可怕的树长在最高可达的塔顶之上。有一座黑塔高出于树，探进未知的外部天空，但它半已倾颓，除非沿着绝壁一石一石地作那几乎不可能的攀登，无法上去。

===Original===

I must have lived years in this place, but I cannot measure the time. Beings must have cared for my needs, yet I can not recall any person except myself; or anything alive but the noiseless rats and bats and spiders. I think that whoever nursed me must have been shockingly aged, since my first conception of a living person was that of something mockingly like myself, yet distorted, shriveled, and decaying like the castle. To me there was nothing grotesque in the bones and skeletons that strewed some of the stone crypts deep down among the foundations. I fantastically associated these things with everyday events, and thought them more natural than the colored pictures of living beings which I found in many of the moldy books. From such books I learned all that I know. No teacher urged or guided me, and I do not recall hearing any human voice in all those years﻿—not even my own; for although I had read of speech, I had never thought to try to speak aloud. My aspect was a matter equally unthought of, for there were no mirrors in the castle, and I merely regarded myself by instinct as akin to the youthful figures I saw drawn and painted in the books. I felt conscious of youth because I remembered so little.

Outside, across the putrid moat and under the dark mute trees, I would often lie and dream for hours about what I read in the books; and would longingly picture myself amidst gay crowds in the sunny world beyond the endless forest. Once I tried to escape from the forest, but as I went farther from the castle the shade grew denser and the air more filled with brooding fear; so that I ran frantically back lest I lose my way in a labyrinth of nighted silence.

So through endless twilights I dreamed and waited, though I knew not what I waited for. Then in the shadowy solitude my longing for light grew so frantic that I could rest no more, and I lifted entreating hands to the single black ruined tower that reached above the forest into the unknown outer sky. And at last I resolved to scale that tower, fall though I might; since it were better to glimpse the sky and perish, than to live without ever beholding day.

---

===Chinese===

我必定在这地方住了许多年，却无法计量时光。必曾有生灵照料过我的需要，可除了我自己，我想不起任何人；也想不起任何活物，除了不出声的老鼠、蝙蝠和蜘蛛。我想，哺育我的人必定老得骇人，因为我对一个活人的头一个概念，就是一样嘲弄地像我、却扭曲、干瘪、同城堡一起腐朽的东西。对我来说，散落在地基深处那些石头地窖里的白骨与骷髅毫无怪诞可言。我异想天开地把这些东西同日常事件联系在一起，觉得它们比许多发霉的书里那些彩色的人物图画更自然。我所知的一切，都来自这样的书。没有教师督促或指引我，那些年里我不记得听见过任何人声——连我自己的也没有；因为虽然读到过言语，我却从没想过要试着出声说话。我的形貌同样不曾被想过，因为城堡里没有镜子，我只是凭本能把自己看作同书里画着的年轻人物相似。我自觉年轻，因为我记得的这样少。

在外面，隔着腐臭的护城河，在黑暗喑哑的树下，我常常一躺几个小时，梦想书里读到的东西；渴望地想象自己置身于无尽森林之外那个阳光世界里欢乐的人群中。有一回我试图逃出森林，可离城堡愈远，树荫愈密，空气里愈充满盘踞的恐惧；我发疯似的跑了回来，生怕在夜一般寂静的迷宫里迷了路。

就这样，在无尽的暮色里我梦想着、等待着，虽然不知道等的是什么。后来，在阴影的孤寂里，我对光的渴望狂乱得再也无法安歇，便朝那座高出森林、探进未知的外部天空的、唯一黑色残塔，举起哀求的双手。终于我决意攀上那座塔，哪怕摔下来；因为瞥一眼天空然后毁灭，也胜过活着却从不曾见过白昼。

===Original===

In the dank twilight I climbed the worn and aged stone stairs till I reached the level where they ceased, and thereafter clung perilously to small footholds leading upward. Ghastly and terrible was that dead, stairless cylinder of rock; black, ruined, and deserted, and sinister with startled bats whose wings made no noise. But more ghastly and terrible still was the slowness of my progress; for climb as I might, the darkness overhead grew no thinner, and a new chill as of haunted and venerable mold assailed me. I shivered as I wondered why I did not reach the light, and would have looked down had I dared. I fancied that night had come suddenly upon me, and vainly groped with one free hand for a window embrasure, that I might peer out and above, and try to judge the height I had attained.

All at once, after an infinity of awesome, sightless crawling up that concave and desperate precipice, I felt my head touch a solid thing, and I knew I must have gained the roof, or at least some kind of floor. In the darkness I raised my free hand and tested the barrier, finding it stone and immovable. Then came a deadly circuit of the tower, clinging to whatever holds the slimy wall could give; till finally my testing hand found the barrier yielding, and I turned upward again, pushing the slab or door with my head as I used both hands in my fearful ascent. There was no light revealed above, and as my hands went higher I knew that my climb was for the nonce ended; since the slab was the trapdoor of an aperture leading to a level stone surface of greater circumference than the lower tower, no doubt the floor of some lofty and capacious observation chamber. I crawled through carefully, and tried to prevent the heavy slab from falling back into place; but failed in the latter attempt. As I lay exhausted on the stone floor I heard the eery echoes of its fall, but hoped when necessary to pry it up again.

===Chinese===

在阴湿的暮色里，我爬上磨损的古石阶，直到石阶尽头的那一层，随后冒险攀住小小的落脚处继续向上。那死了的、没有阶梯的岩石圆筒阴森可怕：黑色，倾颓，荒弃，还有受惊的蝙蝠作祟，它们的翅膀没有一点声音。可更阴森更可怕的，是我的进展之慢；因为无论怎样爬，头顶的黑暗不见稀薄，一种新的寒气——像闹鬼的、古老的霉——袭击着我。我打着颤，纳闷自己为什么还到不了光，若敢的话真想低头看一眼。我恍惚觉得黑夜突然降临到我头上，便用空着的一只手徒然摸索窗洞，想探头向外、向上望，估一估已达的高度。

突然，在那凹壁的绝壁上爬过了可怕而无目的一世之后，我的头碰上了一件坚实的东西，我知道自己必定到顶了，或至少到了某种地板。黑暗里我举起空着的手，试探那屏障，发现是石头，纹丝不动。随后是绕塔一周的致命巡行，攀着滑腻的墙所能给的任何把手；直到最后，我试探的手发现屏障可以活动，我便重新向上，一边用头顶那块石板或门，一边双手并用，在恐惧中攀升。上方没有露出光来；双手再向上探时，我知道这一程攀登暂且到了头；因为那石板是一扇活板门，通向一个洞口，洞外是一圈比下面塔身更大的水平石面——无疑是什么高敞的观景室的地板。我小心地爬了出去，想挡住那块沉重的石板不让它落回原位；却没能做到。我精疲力竭地躺在石地板上时，听见它落下的森然回声，但指望必要时再把它撬开。

===Original===

Believing I was now at a prodigious height, far above the accursed branches of the wood, I dragged myself up from the floor and fumbled about for windows, that I might look for the first time upon the sky, and the moon and stars of which I had read. But on every hand I was disappointed; since all that I found were vast shelves of marble, bearing odious oblong boxes of disturbing size. More and more I reflected, and wondered what hoary secrets might abide in this high apartment so many eons cut off from the castle below. Then unexpectedly my hands came upon a doorway, where hung a portal of stone, rough with strange chiseling. Trying it, I found it locked; but with a supreme burst of strength I overcame all obstacles and dragged it open inward. As I did so there came to me the purest ecstasy I have ever known; for shining tranquilly through an ornate grating of iron, and down a short stone passageway of steps that ascended from the newly found doorway, was the radiant full moon, which I had never before seen save in dreams and in vague visions I dared not call memories.

Fancying now that I had attained the very pinnacle of the castle, I commenced to rush up the few steps beyond the door; but the sudden veiling of the moon by a cloud caused me to stumble, and I felt my way more slowly in the dark. It was still very dark when I reached the grating﻿—which I tried carefully and found unlocked, but which I did not open for fear of falling from the amazing height to which I had climbed. Then the moon came out.

Most demoniacal of all shocks is that of the abysmally unexpected and grotesquely unbelievable. Nothing I had before undergone could compare in terror with what I now saw; with the bizarre marvels that sight implied.
