The sight itself was as simple as it was stupefying, for it was merely this: instead of a dizzying prospect of treetops seen from a lofty eminence, there stretched around me on a level through the grating nothing less than *the solid ground*, decked and diversified by marble slabs and columns, and overshadowed by an ancient stone church, whose ruined spire gleamed spectrally in the moonlight.

===Chinese===

相信此刻自己已在骇人的高度，远在树林那些受诅咒的枝柯之上，我从地板上撑起身，四下摸索窗户，好第一次望一望天空，望一望我读到过的月亮和星星。可四面八方我都失望了；因为我找到的，只是一排排巨大的大理石架，架上摆着一格格尺寸得叫人心神不安的长方匣子。我愈想愈多，纳闷这间同下面的城堡隔绝了亿万年的高室里，究竟住着什么太古的秘密。随后，出乎意料地，我的手碰上了一道门口，挂着一扇石门，凿痕粗糙古怪。一推，锁着；但我鼓足平生之力一爆发，压倒了一切阻碍，把门向内拉开了。就在此时，来了我此生知道的最纯粹的狂喜：透过一格精工的铁栅，透过新发现的门内一段向上的短短石级通道，静静照进来一轮光华的满月——除了在梦里、在我不敢称为记忆的恍惚幻象里，我从不曾见过它。

这时我以为自己已达城堡的绝顶，便抢上门外那几级台阶；可月亮突然被云遮住，我绊了一下，在黑暗里放慢脚步摸索前行。到达栅栏时天仍很黑——我小心一试，它没有锁，但我没有推开，怕从爬上的惊人之高处跌下去。随后月亮出来了。

一切打击中最恶魔似的，是那深渊般出乎意料、怪诞得难以置信的一击。我从前经历过的一切，在恐怖上都无法同我此刻看见的相比；无法同这“看见”所暗示的奇观相比。看见的东西本身简单得叫人发懵，因为它不过是：透过栅栏，在我四周平摊开去的，不是从高处俯瞰的一片令人眩晕的树冠，而恰恰是坚实的地面，点缀着大理石的石板和石柱，一座古老石教堂的暗影笼在上面，它倾颓的尖顶在月光里泛着鬼影似的光。

===Original===

Half unconscious, I opened the grating and staggered out upon the white gravel path that stretched away in two directions. My mind, stunned and chaotic as it was, still held the frantic craving for light; and not even the fantastic wonder which had happened could stay my course. I neither knew nor cared whether my experience was insanity, dreaming, or magic; but was determined to gaze on brilliance and gayety at any cost. I knew not who I was or what I was, or what my surroundings might be; though as I continued to stumble along I became conscious of a kind of fearsome latent memory that made my progress not wholly fortuitous. I passed under an arch out of that region of slabs and columns, and wandered through the open country; sometimes following the visible road, but sometimes leaving it curiously to tread across meadows where only occasional ruins bespoke the ancient presence of a forgotten road. Once I swam across a swift river where crumbling, mossy masonry told of a bridge long vanished.

Over two hours must have passed before I reached what seemed to be my goal, a venerable ivied castle in a thickly wooded park; maddeningly familiar, yet full of perplexing strangeness to me. I saw that the moat was filled in, and that some of the well-known towers were demolished; whilst new wings existed to confuse the beholder. But what I observed with chief interest and delight were the open windows﻿—gorgeously ablaze with light and sending forth sound of the gayest revelry. Advancing to one of these I looked in and saw an oddly dressed company, indeed; making merry, and speaking brightly to one another. I had never, seemingly, heard human speech before; and could guess only vaguely what was said. Some of the faces seemed to hold expressions that brought up incredibly remote recollections; others were utterly alien.

---

===Chinese===

半失去知觉地，我推开栅栏，踉跄着走上那条向两头延伸的白色砾石小径。我的心神虽然震昏而混乱，仍怀着对光的那种狂乱的饥渴；哪怕已经发生的奇中之奇，也拦不住我。我的经历是疯狂、是梦还是魔法，我既不知道也不在意；只打定主意，不惜任何代价去看一眼光华与欢乐。我不知道自己是谁、是什么，我的周围又可能是什么；可随着继续跌跌撞撞地走，我意识到一种可怕的潜在记忆，使我的行进不全是瞎撞。我从一道拱门下走出那片石板石柱之地，在旷野里游荡；有时顺着看得见的大路，有时又古怪地撇下它，踏上草地——那里只有偶尔的残迹，表明一条被遗忘的古道曾经存在。有一回我泅过一条湍急的河，崩碎的长满苔藓的砖石，说明一座桥早已消失。

必定过了两个多小时，我才到达似乎是目的地的地方：一座密林园子里的、爬满常春藤的古老城堡；熟识得叫人发疯，对我却又满是费解的陌生。我看见护城河已经填平，几座熟知的塔已经拆毁；又添了新的侧翼，叫观者迷惑。但我怀着最大的兴趣和欢喜注意到的，是那些敞开的窗——灯火辉煌，透出最欢快的宴乐之声。我走向其中一扇，向里望去，看见确乎是一群装束古怪的宾客：正作乐着，彼此快活地谈笑。我似乎从不曾听过人言；只能含糊地猜他们说些什么。有些面孔上的表情，唤起遥远得难以置信的回忆；另一些则全然陌生。

===Original===

I now stepped through the low window into the brilliantly lighted room, stepping as I did so from my single bright moment of hope to my blackest convulsion of despair and realization. The nightmare was quick to come, for as I entered, there occurred immediately one of the most terrifying demonstrations I had ever conceived. Scarcely had I crossed the sill when there descended upon the whole company a sudden and unheralded fear of hideous intensity, distorting every face and evoking the most horrible screams from nearly every throat. Flight was universal, and in the clamor and panic several fell in a swoon and were dragged away by their madly fleeing companions. Many covered their eyes with their hands, and plunged blindly and awkwardly in their race to escape, overturning furniture and stumbling against the walls before they managed to reach one of the many doors.

The cries were shocking; and as I stood in the brilliant apartment alone and dazed, listening to their vanishing echoes, I trembled at the thought of what might be lurking near me unseen. At a casual inspection the room seemed deserted, but when I moved toward one of the alcoves I thought I detected a presence there﻿—a hint of motion beyond the golden-arched doorway leading to another and somewhat similar room. As I approached the arch I began to perceive the presence more clearly; and then, with the first and last sound I ever uttered﻿—a ghastly ululation that revolted me almost as poignantly as its noxious cause﻿—I beheld in full, frightful vividness the inconceivable, indescribable, and unmentionable monstrosity which had by its simple appearance changed a merry company to a herd of delirious fugitives.

I can not even hint what it was like, for it was a compound of all that is unclean, uncanny, unwelcome, abnormal, and detestable. It was the ghoulish shade of decay, antiquity, and desolation; the putrid, dripping eidolon of unwholesome revelation; the awful baring of that which the merciful earth should always hide. God knows it was not of this world﻿—or no longer of this world﻿—yet to my horror I saw in its eaten-away and bone-revealing outlines a leering, abhorrent travesty on the human shape; and in its moldy, disintegrating apparel an unspeakable quality that chilled me even more.

===Chinese===

此刻我跨过低窗，走进灯火通明的房间；这一跨，也就从我唯一一段光明的希望，跨进了我最黑的绝望与了悟的痉挛。梦魇立刻来了：我刚一进门，就发生了我所能设想的可怕至极的演示之一。我几乎还没跨过窗台，一阵突如其来的、毫无预兆的、狞恶已极的恐惧便降临到满堂宾客身上，扭曲了每一张脸，从几乎每一副喉咙里勾出最恐怖的尖叫。逃奔是普遍的；在喧嚷与恐慌里，有几个人晕倒在地，被疯狂奔逃的同伴拖走。许多人用手捂住眼睛，在夺路的赛跑里瞎冲乱撞，撞翻家具，跌在墙上，好不容易才摸到那一扇扇门里的一扇。

那一片哭喊惊心动魄；当我独自站在明亮的大厅里，发着懵，听那喊声的回音消逝，我一想到可能有什么看不见的东西正潜伏在我近旁，便浑身发抖。粗粗一看，房间似乎空了；可当我朝一处凹室走去时，我觉得那里有某种存在——在那道通向另一间相似房间的金拱门后，有一点动静的暗示。走近拱门时，我开始更清楚地觉出那个存在；随后，随着我平生发出的第一声、也是最后一声声响——一声森然的嚎叫，它几乎同它那有毒的起因一样刺得我作呕——我完完整整、惊心怵目地看见了那不可想象、无法描述、不可名状的怪物，它仅凭一现，就把一堂欢宴变成了一群谵狂的逃亡者。

我连暗示它像什么都不能，因为它是一切不洁、不祥、不受欢迎、反常、可憎之物的复合体。它是朽烂、太古与荒凉的那食尸鬼似的阴影；是恶臭的、滴沥的、不洁启示的幻象；是仁慈的大地永远该掩藏之物的可怕裸露。上帝知道它不属于这个世界——或者不再属于这个世界——然而我恐怖地看见，在它那被蛀空、露出白骨的轮廓里，是一副对人形的狞笑的、可憎的滑稽模仿；它那发霉的、解体的衣饰里，有一种说不出的东西，把我激得更冷。

===Original===

I was almost paralyzed, but not too much so to make a feeble effort toward flight; a backward stumble which failed to break the spell in which the nameless, voiceless monster held me. My eyes, bewitched by the glassy orbs which stared loathsomely into them, refused to close; though they were mercifully blurred, and showed the terrible object but indistinctly after the first shock. I tried to raise my hand to shut out the sight, yet so stunned were my nerves that my arm could not fully obey my will. The attempt, however, was enough to disturb my balance; so that I had to stagger forward several steps to avoid falling. As I did so I became suddenly and agonizingly aware of the *nearness* of the carrion thing, whose hideous hollow breathing I half fancied I could hear. Nearly mad, I found myself yet able to throw out a hand to ward off the fetid apparition which pressed so close; when in one cataclysmic second of cosmic nightmarishness and hellish accident *my fingers touched the rotting outstretched paw of the monster beneath the golden arch*.

I did not shriek, but all the fiendish ghouls that ride the night-wind shrieked for me as in that same second there crashed down upon my mind a single and fleeting avalanche of soul-annihilating memory. I knew in that second all that had been; I remembered beyond the frightful castle and the trees, and recognized the altered edifice in which I now stood; I recognized, most terrible of all, the unholy abomination that stood leering before me as I withdrew my sullied fingers from its own.

===Chinese===

我几乎瘫了，但还没有瘫到不能作一次软弱的逃奔；向后一个踉跄，却没能破除那无名无声的怪物攫住我的魔咒。我的眼睛被那对玻璃似的、可惜地瞪进来的眼球魅住，闭不上；幸好它们已经模糊，初惊之后只把那可怕的对象照得影影绰绰。我想抬手遮住那景象，可我的神经震得手臂不能全然听命。这一动却足够搅乱我的平衡；为了不倒，我只好向前趔趄了几步。就在此时，我突然、痛苦之至地意识到那腐尸之物近在咫尺，它那可怕的、空洞的呼吸，我恍惚觉得听见了半声。我几近疯狂，却发现自己还能伸出一只手，去挡开那逼得这样近的恶臭幻影；就在宇宙梦魇与地狱事故合并的那灾变的一秒里，我的手指，碰上了金色拱门下那怪物伸出的、腐烂的爪子。

我没有尖叫；但当记忆的单发而飞逝的雪崩在同一秒里轰然砸上我的心头时，所有骑夜风的恶魔食尸鬼都替我尖叫了。那一秒里我知道了曾经的一切；我记起了那可怕的古堡和树林之外的事，认出了我此刻所站的这座改了模样的建筑；最可怕的是，当我把玷污的手指从它自己的爪子里抽回时，我认出了那狞笑着立在我面前的、不圣洁的憎物。

===Original===

But in the cosmos there is balm as well as bitterness, and that balm is nepenthe. In the supreme horror of that second I forgot what had horrified me, and the burst of black memory vanished in a chaos of echoing images. In a dream I fled from that haunted and accursed pile, and ran swiftly and silently in the moonlight. When I returned to the churchyard place of marble and went down the steps I found the stone trapdoor immovable; but I was not sorry, for I had hated the antique castle and the trees. Now I ride with the mocking and friendly ghouls on the night-wind, and play by day amongst the catacombs of Nephren-Ka in the sealed and unknown valley of Hadoth by the Nile. I know that light is not for me, save that of the moon over the rock tombs of Neb, nor any gayety save the unnamed feasts of Nitokris beneath the Great Pyramid; yet in my new wildness and freedom I almost welcome the bitterness of alienage.

For although nepenthe has calmed me, I know always that I am an outsider; a stranger in this century and among those who are still men. This I have known ever since I stretched out my fingers to the abomination within that great gilded frame; stretched out my fingers and touched *a cold and unyielding surface of polished glass*.

===Chinese===

可宇宙里既有苦也有膏，那膏就是忘忧药。在那至高恐怖的一秒里，我忘掉了使我恐怖的东西，黑色记忆的爆发消散在一片回声似的形象混乱里。我在梦里逃出那闹鬼受咒的建筑，在月光下迅捷无声地奔跑。回到那片大理石的教堂墓地、走下台阶时，我发现石头的活板门已推不动了；我并不难过，因为我早已恨透那座古堡和那些树。如今我同那些嘲弄而友善的食尸鬼一起骑在夜风上，白日就在尼弗伦卡（Nephren-Ka）的地下墓穴里嬉戏——那墓穴在尼罗河边哈多斯（Hadoth）那封闭而无名的山谷里。我知道光不属于我，除了内布（Neb）岩墓上的月光；欢乐也不属于我，除了大金字塔下尼托克丽丝（Nitokris）的无名盛宴；然而在这新的狂野与自由里，我几乎欣然接受这放逐的苦味。

因为虽然忘忧药镇住了我，我却永远知道，我是一个异乡人；在这个世纪里、在这些仍是人的人们中间，是一个陌生人。自从我把手指伸向那镀金大框里的憎物，我就一直知道这一点；我伸出手去，触到的，是一面冰冷而不屈的、擦亮的玻璃。

## The Picture in the House / 屋中画
===Original===

Searchers after horror haunt strange, far places. For them are the catacombs of Ptolemais, and the carven mausolea of the nightmare countries. They climb to the moonlit towers of ruined Rhine castles, and falter down black cobwebbed steps beneath the scattered stones of forgotten cities in Asia. The haunted wood and the desolate mountain are their shrines, and they linger around the sinister monoliths on uninhabited islands. But the true epicure in the terrible, to whom a new thrill of unutterable ghastliness is the chief end and justification of existence, esteems most of all the ancient, lonely farmhouses of backwoods New England; for there the dark elements of strength, solitude, grotesqueness and ignorance combine to form the perfection of the hideous.

Most horrible of all sights are the little unpainted wooden houses remote from traveled ways, usually squatted upon some damp, grassy slope or leaning against some gigantic outcropping rock. Two hundred years and more they have leaned or squatted there, while the vines have crawled and the trees have swelled and spread. They are almost hidden now in lawless luxuriances of green and guardian shrouds of shadow; but the small-paned windows still stare shockingly, as if blinking through a lethal stupor which wards off madness by dulling the memory of unutterable things.

In such houses have dwelt generations of strange people, whose like the world has never seen. Seized with a gloomy and fanatical belief which exiled them from their kind, their ancestors sought the wilderness for freedom. There the scions of a conquering race indeed flourished, free from the restrictions of their fellows, but cowered in an appalling slavery to the dismal phantasms of their own minds.

===Chinese===

追寻恐怖的人，出没于古怪遥远的地方。托勒迈的地下墓穴、噩梦国度里凿出的陵寝，是为他们备下的。他们攀上莱茵河畔废堡的月光塔楼，也在亚洲被遗忘的城市、散乱的石块底下，顺着结满蛛网的黑色台阶踉跄而下。闹鬼的树林和荒凉的山，是他们的神龛；他们还在无人岛的狰狞独石旁流连。可是，真正嗜可怕如美食的人——那把难以言传的阴森的新战栗当作生存的主要目的与正当理由的人——最看重的，却是新英格兰穷乡僻壤里古老孤零的农舍；因为在那里，黑暗、幽独、古怪与愚昧诸元素合成了可怖的完美。

一切景象里最可怕的，是那些远离通行大道、不上漆的小木屋，多半蹲踞在潮湿多草的山坡上，或倚着一块冒出的巨岩。两百年还多，它们就那样倚着蹲着，藤蔓爬满，树木胀大铺开。如今它们几乎全藏进了放肆的葱茏和守护的浓荫里；可那小格子的窗子仍旧骇人地瞪着，仿佛在一种致死的昏沉里眨眼——那昏沉麻木着对不可言传之物的记忆，挡住了疯狂。

这样的人家里，住过一代代怪人，世上再没有他们的同类。他们的祖先怀着一种阴郁狂热的信仰，为同类所逐，到荒野里寻自由。一个征服种族的苗裔，在那里确实茂盛了，摆脱了族类的拘束，却又战栗着，沦为他们自己心里阴郁幻影的骇人奴隶。

===Original===

Divorced from the enlightenment of civilization, the strength of these Puritans turned into singular channels; and in their isolation, morbid self-repression, and struggle for life with relentless Nature, there came to them dark furtive traits from the prehistoric depths of their cold Northern heritage. By necessity practical and by philosophy stern, these folk were not beautiful in their sins. Erring as all mortals must, they were forced by their rigid code to seek concealment above all else; so that they came to use less and less taste in what they concealed. Only the silent, sleepy, staring houses in the backwoods can tell all that has lain hidden since the early days; and they are not communicative, being loath to shake off the drowsiness which helps them forget. Sometimes one feels that it would be merciful to tear down these houses, for they must often dream.

It was to a time-battered edifice of this description that I was driven one afternoon in November, 1896, by a rain of such chilling copiousness that any shelter was preferable to exposure. I had been traveling for some time amongst the people of the Miskatonic Valley in quest of certain genealogical data; and from the remote, devious, and problematical nature of my course, had deemed it convenient to employ a bicycle despite the lateness of the season. Now I found myself upon an apparently abandoned road which I had chosen as the shortest cut to Arkham; overtaken by the storm at a point far from any town, and confronted with no refuge save the antique and repellent wooden building which blinked with bleared windows from between two huge leafless oaks near the foot of a rocky hill.

Distant though it was from the remnant of a road, this house none the less impressed me unfavorably the very moment I espied it. Honest, wholesome structures do not stare at travelers so slyly and hauntingly, and in my genealogical researches I had encountered legends of a century before which biased me against places of this kind. Yet the force of the elements was such as to overcome my scruples, and I did not hesitate to wheel my machine up the weedy rise to the closed door which seemed at once so suggestive and secretive.

---

===Chinese===

割断了文明的启蒙，这些清教徒的力量便转进了奇特的河道；在孤绝中，在病态的自抑中，在同无情自然争夺生存中，他们寒冷的北方血统那史前的深处，泛起了黑暗而鬼祟的品性。这些人迫于实际、出于严厉的信条，连作恶都不好看。他们同一切凡人一样犯错，却教那死板的规矩逼着把遮掩看得重于一切；于是，遮掩的东西渐渐越来越不顾体面了。只有穷乡僻壤里这些沉默、昏睡、瞪眼的房子，说得出自早年起藏下的一切；可它们不健谈，不愿抖落那帮它们忘却的瞌睡。有时人会觉得，把这些房子拆倒倒是慈悲，因为它们一定常常做梦。

一八九六年十一月的某个下午，我就是被这样一场冷雨赶进了一座被时间打垮的屋宇，那雨又冷又密，任何遮蔽都比淋着强。我已在米斯卡塔尼克河谷一带的人群中游历了些时日，寻访某些宗谱资料；因我路线偏僻、迂回、没个准，虽已深秋，骑一辆自行车倒还算便利。此刻我发现自己行在一条显然废弃的路上——我选它作去阿卡姆的近路——在离任何镇子都远的所在被暴雨赶上，眼前唯一的躲避，只有那座古老而可憎的木屋：它在多石的山脚附近、两棵巨大的光秃橡树之间，用昏昧的窗子朝我眨眼。

那房子虽然离路的残段还有一段，可我一望见它就没来由地生出反感。正派健全的建筑不会这样鬼祟而缠人地瞪视过路客；再说，宗谱研究中我碰到过一世纪前的传说，叫我对这类地方先存了偏见。然而风雨的势力终究压过了我的顾忌，我把车推上长草的坡，到那扇一望而知既有所暗示又讳莫如深的门前，没有犹豫。

---

===Original===

I had somehow taken it for granted that the house was abandoned, yet as I approached it I was not so sure; for though the walks were indeed overgrown with weeds, they seemed to retain their nature a little too well to argue complete desertion. Therefore, instead of trying the door I knocked, feeling as I did so a trepidation I could scarcely explain.

As I waited on the rough, mossy rock which served as a doorstep, I glanced at the neighboring windows and the panes of the fanlight above me, and noticed that although old, rattling, and almost opaque with dirt, they were not broken. The building, then, must still be inhabited, despite its isolation and general neglect.

However, my rapping evoked no response, so after repeating the summons I tried the rusty latch and found the door unfastened. Inside was a little vestibule with walls from which the plaster was falling, and through the doorway came a faint but peculiarly hateful odor. I entered, carrying my bicycle, and closed the door behind me. Ahead rose a narrow staircase, flanked by a small door probably leading to the cellar, while to the left and right were closed doors leading to rooms on the ground floor.

Leaning my cycle against the wall I opened the door at the left, and crossed into a small low-ceiled chamber but dimly lighted by its two dusty windows and furnished in the barest and most primitive possible way. It appeared to be a kind of sitting-room, for it had a table and several chairs, and an immense fireplace above which ticked an antique clock on a mantel. Books and papers were very few, and in the prevailing gloom I could not readily discern the titles. What interested me was the uniform air of archaism as displayed in every visible detail. Most of the houses in this region I had found rich in relics of the past, but here the antiquity was curiously complete; for in all the room I could not discover a single article of definitely post-Revolutionary date. Had the furnishings been less humble, the place would have been a collector’s paradise.

As I surveyed this quaint apartment, I felt an increase in that aversion first excited by the bleak exterior of the house. Just what it was that I feared or loathed, I could by no means define; but something in the whole atmosphere seemed redolent of unhallowed age, of unpleasant crudeness, and of secrets which should be forgotten.

===Chinese===

我不知怎么就认定这房子没人住了；可走近时又拿不准了；因为小径上固然荒草没径，路径却似乎保存原形保存得太好，不像是彻底废弃的样子。于是我并去推门，只敲了敲门，一边敲，一边怀着一种几乎说不清的忐忑。

我等在那块充作门阶的粗糙生苔的石头上，扫了一眼旁边的窗和头顶气窗的玻璃，注意到它们虽老旧、松动、被污垢糊得半不透光，却没有破。那么这房子必然还有人住，尽管孤僻失修。

可是我敲了一阵无人应，再敲了一遍之后，我试了试锈住的门闩，发现门没有锁。里面是个小小的门厅，墙上的灰皮纷纷剥落；门洞里透出一股微弱却特别可憎的气味。我把自行车扛进去，回手关上门。迎面一道窄楼梯，旁边一扇小门，大约通地窖；左右各是一扇关着的门，通底层的房间。

我把车靠在墙上，打开左手那扇门，走进一间低顶的小屋，仅靠两扇蒙尘的窗透进昏光，陈设简陋原始到无以复加。它像是间起居室，有一张桌子、几把椅子，还有一座大壁炉，炉台上滴答着一座老钟。书报寥寥，昏暗里标题也看不清。叫我感兴趣的是每个可见细节里那统一的古旧气息。这一带多数人家我都发现过丰富的旧物，这里却是出奇地完整；整个房间里，我找不出一件确凿出于独立战争以后的物件。倘若陈设不那么寒碜，这地方简直是收藏家的天堂。

我打量着这间古怪的屋子，初见房子荒凉外观时激起的那种反感又深了一层。我究竟怕什么、厌什么，全然说不上来；只是整个气氛里的什么东西，仿佛透着不洁的年头、令人不快的粗鄙、和些应该被忘掉的秘密。

===Original===

I felt disinclined to sit down, and wandered about, examining the various articles which I had noticed. The first object of my curiosity was a book of medium size lying upon the table and presenting such an antediluvian aspect that I marveled at beholding it outside a museum or library. It was bound in leather with metal fittings, and was in an excellent state of preservation; being altogether an unusual sort of volume to encounter in an abode so lowly. When I opened it to the title page my wonder grew even greater, for it proved to be nothing less rare than Pigafetta’s account of the Congo region, written in Latin from the notes of the sailor Lopez and printed at Frankfort in 1598. I had often heard of this work, with its curious illustrations by the brothers De Bry, hence for a moment forgot my uneasiness in my desire to turn the pages before me. The engravings were indeed interesting, drawn wholly from imagination and careless descriptions, and represented negroes with white skins and Caucasian features; nor would I soon have closed the book had not an exceedingly trivial circumstance upset my tired nerves and revived my sensation of disquiet.

What annoyed me was merely the persistent way in which the volume tended to fall open to itself at Plate XII, which represented in gruesome detail a butcher’s shop of the cannibal Anziques. I experienced some shame at my susceptibility to so slight a thing, but the drawing nevertheless disturbed me, especially in connection with some adjacent passages descriptive of Anzique gastronomy.

I had turned to a neighboring shelf and was examining its meagre literary contents﻿—an eighteenth century Bible, a *Pilgrim’s Progress* of like period, illustrated with grotesque woodcuts and printed by the almanac-maker Isaiah Thomas, the rotting bulk of Cotton Mather’s *Magnalia Christi Americana*, and a few other books of evidently equal age﻿—when my attention was aroused by the unmistakable sound of walking in the room overhead.

===Chinese===

我不愿坐下，便踱来踱去，检视引起我注意的各种物件。头一样勾起我好奇的，是摊在桌上的一本中等开本的书，样子古老得如洪水之前，出了博物馆或图书馆居然还能见到，真叫我惊异。它皮面带金属配件，保存得极好；在这样一个寒陋的住处撞见，实在不同寻常。我翻到扉页，惊异更甚：它竟是皮加费塔的刚果地区纪行——据水手洛佩斯的笔记用拉丁文写成，一五九八年法兰克福印行——珍本中的珍本。这书我久闻其名，连同德·布里兄弟那些古怪的插图；一时之间，我竟在翻检书页的欲望里忘了不安。那些版画确有趣味，全凭想象和漫不经心的描述画成，把黑人画成了白皮肤、高加索人的相貌；若不是一桩极小的事故搅了我疲惫的神经、唤醒了我的不安，我一时半会儿还合不上这书。

搜我的不过是这卷书自己总往第十二图摊开的那股执拗劲儿——那幅图以狰狞的细部画着安济克食人生番的一个肉铺。为这么点小事就受影响，我有些惭愧；可那画到底搅得我不宁，尤其想到近旁几段描写安济克烹饪的文字。

我已转向旁边一个架子，检视架上寥寥的藏书——一部十八世纪的《圣经》，一部同期的《天路历程》，配着古怪的木刻，历书匠艾赛亚·托马斯印的；还有科顿·马瑟《美国基督伟业》的烂大部头，外加几部显然同样年头的书——这时，头顶房间里传来的确凿无疑的脚步声，唤起了我的注意。

===Original===

At first astonished and startled, considering the lack of response to my recent knocking at the door, I immediately afterward concluded that the walker had just awaked from a sound sleep; and listened with less surprise as the footsteps sounded on the creaking stairs. The tread was heavy, yet seemed to contain a curious quality of cautiousness; a quality which I disliked the more because the tread was heavy.

When I had entered the room I had shut the door behind me. Now, after a moment of silence during which the walker may have been inspecting my bicycle in the hall, I heard a fumbling at the latch and saw the paneled portal swing open again.

---

In the doorway stood a person of such singular appearance that I should have exclaimed aloud but for the restraints of good breeding. Old, white-bearded, and ragged, my host possessed a countenance and physique which inspired equal wonder and respect. His height could not have been less than six feet, and despite a general air of age and poverty he was stout and powerful in proportion.

His face, almost hidden by a long beard which grew high on the cheeks, seemed abnormally ruddy and less wrinkled than one might expect; while over a high forehead fell a shock of white hair little thinned by the years. His blue eyes, though a trifle bloodshot, seemed inexplicably keen and burning. But for his horrible unkemptness, the man would have been as distinguished-looking as he was impressive. This unkemptness, however, made him offensive despite his face and figure. Of what his clothing consisted I could hardly tell, for it seemed to me no more than a mass of tatters surmounting a pair of high, heavy boots; and his lack of cleanliness surpassed description.

The appearance of this man, and the instinctive fear he inspired, prepared me for something like enmity; so that I almost shuddered through surprise and a sense of uncanny incongruity when he motioned me to a chair and addressed me in a thin, weak voice full of fawning respect and ingratiating hospitality. His speech was very curious, an extreme form of Yankee dialect I had thought long extinct; and I studied it closely as he sat down opposite me for conversation.

===Chinese===

我先是惊愕——方才敲门无人应——随即断定，走动的人准是刚从酣睡中醒来；于是脚步声踏上吱嘎作响的楼梯时，我便听得没那么惊讶了。那脚步沉重，却似乎带着一种古怪的谨慎；这品质叫我愈发不喜欢，因为脚步本身是沉重的。

我进屋时随手关了门。此刻，一阵沉默之后——走动的人也许正在门厅里打量我的自行车——我听见门闩上一阵摸索，看见那镶板的门又荡开了。

---

门口立着一个人，相貌那样奇特，若非教养管着，我几乎要叫出声。我的主人老迈、白须、衣衫褴褛，却有着一副叫人又惊又敬的面容和身架。他身量绝不下六英尺，尽管一身的苍老与贫寒，体魄却按比例地壮硕有力。

他的脸几乎埋在一部从颧骨上生起的长须里，红得出奇，皱纹也比预想的少；高高的额头上披着一头白发，岁月竟没削去多少。蓝眼睛虽略有血丝，却不知怎的锐利灼灼。若非那骇人的邋遢，这人本可以仪表堂堂，同他的威严相称。正是这邋遢，坏了他那副脸和身架，使他惹人厌。他的衣着由什么构成，我几乎说不上来，在我看来不过是一堆破布，架在一双高统重靴上；他的不洁，则超出了描画的范围。

这人的模样和他本能激起的恐惧，叫我做好了迎接敌意的准备；所以当他招手请我坐、用一种细弱的声音对我说话时——那声音满是巴结的恭敬和讨好的殷勤——我几乎因惊异和一种鬼气的不协调而打了个寒噤。他的话很古怪，是我以为早已绝迹的新英格兰土话的极端形态；他在我对面坐下攀谈时，我细细地听。

===Original===

“Ketched in the rain, be ye?” he greeted, “glad ye was nigh the haouse en’ hed the sense ta come right in. I calc’late I was asleep, else I’d a heerd ye﻿—I ain’t as young as I uster be, an’ I need a paowerful sight o’ naps naowadays. Trav’lin’ fur? I hain’t seed many folks ’long this rud sence they tuk off the Arkham stage.”

I replied that I was going to Arkham, and apologized for my rude entry into his domicile, whereupon he continued:

“Glad ta see ye, young Sir﻿—new faces is scurce arount here, an’ I hain’t got much ta cheer me up these days. Guess yew hail from Bosting, don’t ye? I never ben thar, but I kin tell a taown man when I see ’im﻿—we hed one fer deestrick schoolmaster in ’eighty-four, but he quit suddent an’ no one never heerd on ’im sence﻿—”

Here the old man lapsed into a kind of chuckle, and made no explanation when I questioned him. He seemed to be in an aboundingly good humor, yet to possess those eccentricities which one might guess from his grooming. For some time he rambled on with an almost feverish geniality, when it struck me to ask him how he came by so rare a book as Pigafetta’s *Regnum Congo*. The effect of this volume had not left me, and I felt a certain hesitancy in speaking of it; but curiosity overmastered all the vague fears which had steadily accumulated since my first glimpse of the house. To my relief, the question did not seem an awkward one; for the old man answered freely and volubly.

“Oh, thet Afriky book? Cap’n Ebenezer Holt traded me thet in ’sixty-eight﻿—him as was kilt in the war.”

Something about the name of Ebenezer Holt caused me to look up sharply. I had encountered it in my genealogical work, but not in any record since the Revolution. I wondered if my host could help me in the task at which I was laboring, and resolved to ask him about it later on. He continued:

“Ebenezer was on a Salem merchantman fer years, an’ picked up a sight o’ queer stuff in every port. He got this in London, I guess﻿—he uster like ter buy things at the shops. I was up ta his haouse onet, on the hill, tradin’ hosses, when I see this book. I relished the picters, so he give it in on a swap. ’Tis a queer book﻿—here, leave me git on my spectacles﻿—”

===Chinese===

「叫雨截住了，是吧？」他招呼道，「亏得你挨着这房，还晓得赶紧进来。俺估摸俺睡着了，不然咋会听不见你——俺不比从前年轻了，眼下离不了瞌睡。出门远走？打他们撤了阿卡姆的驿车，这条道上俺没大见过人。」

我答说我要去阿卡姆，并为唐突进屋道了歉；他接下去说：

「见到你高兴，年轻的老爷——这块儿新面孔稀罕，俺这些日子也没啥开心事。你打波士顿来，俺猜？俺没去过，可俺一眼认得出城里人——八四年俺们这儿有过一个，当学区教员，可他走得突然，往后谁也没再听说——」

说到这里老人发出一阵嘿嘿的笑，我追问时他也不解释。他似乎兴致极好，又带着那副从他仪容上猜得出的怪僻。他几乎热狂地和气地闲扯了一阵，我忽然想起，该问问他这本皮加费塔的《刚果王国》这样罕的书是怎么到手的。这卷书的印象一直没离我而去，提起它我还有几分踌躇；可好奇心压倒了一切模糊的恐惧——那些恐惧，从我一见这房子就在不断积聚。让我宽心的是，这问题似乎并不尴尬；老人答得痛快而滔滔。

「哦，那本阿非利加的书？埃比尼泽·霍尔特船长六八年跟俺换的——就是打仗死掉的那个。」

埃比尼泽·霍尔特这个名字叫我猛地抬头。我在宗谱工作里碰到过它，可都在独立战争以前的记录里。我心想这位主人兴许能帮上我手头的忙，决意回头问他。他接着说：

「埃比尼泽在塞勒姆的商船上干了多年，哪个码头都捡了些稀奇玩意儿。这本是他在伦敦弄的，俺猜——他顶爱在铺子里买东西。俺有一回上他山上的家里去换马，看见了这书。俺稀罕这里头的画，他就换给俺了。这书古怪——来，叫俺戴上眼镜——」

===Original===

The old man fumbled among his rags, producing a pair of dirty and amazingly antique glasses with small octagonal lenses and steel bows. Donning these, he reached for the volume on the table and turned the pages lovingly.

---

“Ebenezer cud read a leetle o’ this﻿—’tis Latin﻿—but I can’t. I hed two er three schoolmasters read me a bit, an’ Passon Clark, him they say got draownded in the pond﻿—kin yew make anything outen it?”

I told him that I could, and translated for his benefit a paragraph near the beginning. If I erred, he was not scholar enough to correct me; for he seemed childishly pleased at my English version. His proximity was becoming rather obnoxious, yet I saw no way to escape without offending him. I was amused at the childish fondness of this ignorant old man for the pictures in a book he could not read, and wondered how much better he could read the few books in English which adorned the room. This revelation of simplicity removed much of the ill-defined apprehension I had felt, and I smiled as my host rambled on:

“Queer haow picters kin set a body thinkin’. Take this un here near the front. Hev yew ever seed trees like thet, with big leaves a-floppin’ over an’ daown? And them men﻿—them can’t be niggers﻿—they dew beat all! Kinder like Injuns, I guess, even ef they be in Afriky. Some o’ these here critters looks like monkeys, or half monkeys an’ half men, but I never heerd o’ nothin’ like this un.” Here he pointed to a fabulous creature of the artist, which one might describe as a sort of dragon with the head of an alligator.

“But naow I’ll show ye the best un﻿—over here nigh the middle﻿—” The old man’s speech grew a trifle thicker and his eyes assumed a brighter glow; but his fumbling hands, though seemingly clumsier than before, were entirely adequate to their mission. The book fell open, almost of its own accord and as if from frequent consultation at this place, to the repellent twelfth plate showing a butcher’s shop amongst the Anzique cannibals. My sense of restlessness returned, though I did not exhibit it. The especially bizarre thing was that the artist had made his Africans look like white men﻿—the limbs and quarters hanging about the walls of the shop were ghastly, while the butcher with his axe was hideously incongruous. But my host seemed to relish the view as much as I disliked it.

===Chinese===

老人在破衣烂衫里摸索，摸出一副脏得可以的、老得惊人的眼镜，小小的八角镜片，钢架。他戴好，伸手去够桌上的书，爱惜地翻动书页。

---

「埃比尼泽能念一点这个——是拉丁文——俺不中。俺让两三个教员给俺念过一段，还有克拉克牧师——就是人家说掉进池塘里淹死的那个——你能从里头看出个啥吗？」

我告诉他我能，就为他的益处译了开头附近的一段。我若有错，他也没那份学问纠正我；因为他听了我的英文翻译，孩子似的欢喜。他挨得近了，越来越叫人难受，可我看不出怎样脱身才不得罪他。这无知的老头子对着一本他念不懂的书里的图画如此孩子气地痴爱，叫我暗暗好笑，也纳闷屋里那几本英文书，他能念得多好。这一份朴拙，驱散了我心中不少说不清的忧虑；主人絮叨下去时，我都笑了。

「画儿这东西能叫人琢磨，多怪。就说前头这张。你见过这样的树没——大叶子翻上翻下？还有那些人——那不能是黑人——真绝了！倒有点像印第安人，俺猜，哪怕他们是在阿非利加。这里头有几个家伙像猴，或者半猴半人，可这样的，俺从来没听说。」他指着画师幻想出的一头怪兽——那东西可以说是一条龙，长着鳄鱼的头。

「可现在俺给你看顶好的这张——这边靠中间的——」老人的口齿略略含混，眼睛亮起一层更亮的光；他摸索的手虽比先前更笨，办起事来却绰绰有余。书摊开了，几乎是自己摊开的，仿佛这一处常被翻看——正摊在那可憎的第十二图，安济克食人生番的肉铺。我的不安又回来了，只是没有露出来。尤其怪的是，画师把他那些非洲人画成了白人的模样——四壁挂着的肢体和零块骇人，持斧的屠夫更是狰狞得不伦不类。可我的主人赏看这画，正像我厌恶它。

===Original===

“What d’ye think o’ this﻿—ain’t never see the like hereabouts, eh? When I see this I telled Eb Holt, ‘Thar’s suthin’ ta stir ye up an’ make yer blood tickle!’ When I read in Scripter about slayin’﻿—like them Midianites was slew﻿—I kinder think things, but I ain’t got a picter of it. Here a body kin see all they is to it﻿—I s’pose ’tis sinful, but ain’t we all born an’ livin’ in sin?﻿—Thet feller bein’ chopped up gives me a tickle every time I look at ’im﻿—I hev ta keep lookin’ at ’im﻿—see whar the butcher cut off his feet? Thar’s his head on thet bench, with one arm side of it, an’ t’oter arm’s on the graound side o’ the meat block.”

As the man mumbled on in his shocking ecstasy the expression on his hairy, spectacled face became indescribable, but his voice sank rather than mounted. My own sensations can scarcely be recorded. All the terror I had dimly felt before rushed upon me actively and vividly, and I knew that I loathed the ancient and abhorrent creature so near me with an infinite intensity. His madness, or at least his partial perversion, seemed beyond dispute. He was almost whispering now, with a huskiness more terrible than a scream, and I trembled as I listened.

“As I says, ’tis queer haow picters sets ye thinkin’. D’ye know, young Sir, I’m right sot on this un here. Arter I got the book off Eb I uster look at it a lot, especial when I’d heerd Passon Clark rant o’ Sundays in his big wig. Onet I tried suthin’ funny﻿—here, young Sir, don’t git skeert﻿—all I done was ter look at the picter afore I kilt the sheep for market﻿—killin’ sheep was kinder more fun arter lookin’ at it﻿—”

The tone of the old man now sank very low, sometimes becoming so faint that his words were hardly audible. I listened to the rain, and to the rattling of the bleared, small-paned windows, and marked a rumbling of approaching thunder quite unusual for the season. Once a terrific flash and peal shook the frail house to its foundations, but the whisperer seemed not to notice it.

===Chinese===

「你觉得这张咋样——这一带谁也没见过这样的吧，嗯？俺头回见着就跟埃布·霍尔特说：『这玩意儿叫你精神，叫你血里发痒！』俺在《圣经》里念到杀伐——像米甸人被杀那些——俺也就那么琢磨琢磨，可俺没有画儿。这儿你可把名堂看全了——俺寻思这是罪，可俺们哪个不是生在罪里、活在罪里？——那个叫人剁了的家伙，俺每回瞧都要痒一阵——俺没法子，老得瞧他——瞧见屠夫剁下他脚的地方没？脑袋在那边板凳上，一条胳膊在旁边，另一条在地上，肉墩子边儿上。」

这人骇人地出神着咕哝下去，他那毛茸茸、架着眼镜的脸上的神情已无可描画，声音却是低下去而不是高上来。我自己的感觉几乎无从记录。先前隐隐感到的恐怖，此刻活生生地全扑到我身上；我知道，我以无限的强度憎厌着离我这么近的这个古老可憎的造物。他的疯癫，至少他半疯的乖戾，已无可置疑。此刻他几乎在耳语了，带着一种比尖叫更可怕的嘶哑；我听着，发着抖。

「就像俺说的，画儿叫人琢磨，多怪。你可知道，年轻的老爷，俺让这张迷住了。打埃布手里弄到这书以后，俺常看，礼拜天听了克拉克牧师戴着大假发讲道以后更是看。有一回俺试了件好玩儿的——来，年轻的老爷，别怕——俺没干啥，俺不过是在宰上市卖的羊以前，先看了看这张画——看了画再宰羊，可就更有味儿了——」

老人的嗓音此刻沉得极低，有时轻得几乎听不见字。我听着雨声，听着昏昧小格窗的格格响，还辨出一阵逼近的雷声——这个季节实属罕见。有一瞬，可怕的闪电和霹雳把这座单薄的房子撼到了根；可那耳语的人似乎浑然不觉。

===Original===

“Killin’ sheep was kinder more fun﻿—but d’ye know, ’twan’t quite *satisfyin’*. Queer haow a *cravin’* gits a holt on ye﻿—As ye love the Almighty, young man, don’t tell nobody, but I swar ter Gawd thet picter begun ta make me *hungry fer victuals I couldn’t raise nor buy*﻿—here, set still, what’s ailin’ ye?﻿—I didn’t do nothin’, only I wondered haow ’twud be ef I *did*﻿—They say meat makes blood an’ flesh, an’ gives ye new life, so I wondered ef ’twudn’t make a man live longer an’ longer ef ’twas *more the same*﻿—”

But the whisperer never continued. The interruption was not due to my fright, nor to the rapidly increasing storm amidst whose fury I was presently to open my eyes on a smoky solitude of blackened ruins. It was due to a very simple though somewhat unusual happening.

The open book lay flat between us, with the picture staring repulsively upward. As the old man whispered the words “*more the same*” a tiny spattering impact was heard, and something showed on the yellowed paper of the upturned volume. I thought of the rain and of a leaky roof, but rain is not red. On the butcher’s shop of the Anzique cannibals a small red spattering glistened picturesquely, lending vividness to the horror of the engraving. The old man saw it, and stopped whispering even before my expression of horror made it necessary; saw it and glanced quickly toward the floor of the room he had left an hour before. I followed his glance, and beheld just above us on the loose plaster of the ancient ceiling a large irregular spot of wet crimson which seemed to spread even as I viewed it. I did not shriek or move, but merely shut my eyes.

A moment later came the titanic thunderbolt of thunderbolts, striking the accursed house of unutterable secrets and bringing the oblivion which alone saved my mind.

===Chinese===

「宰羊是有味儿了——可你知道，总不大满足。馋劲儿怎么就攥住你，多怪——年轻人，看在全能的上帝份上，别跟人说：俺对老天爷起誓，那张画起头叫俺馋上了——馋那些俺自家养不出也买不起的吃食——来，坐稳，你咋啦？——俺啥也没干，俺就是琢磨，要是俺干了，会是啥样——人家说肉生血生肉，给你新生命，那俺就琢磨，要是更是一样的肉，是不是叫人活得越来越长——」

可耳语的人再没说下去。打断他的不是我的惊骇，也不是那场急速加骤的风暴——在它的狂怒里，我转眼便要在一地焦黑废墟的烟雾荒寂里睁开眼了。打断它的是一桩极简单、却也稍许不寻常的事。

摊开的书平平地躺在我们之间，那幅画可憎地朝上瞪着。老人耳语出「更是一样的肉」几个字的当口，一声细微的溅洒落下，翻开的泛黄纸页上现出了什么。我想到雨，想到漏的屋顶；可雨不是红的。安济克食人生番的肉铺上，一小片红色的溅洒如画地闪着，给版画的恐怖添了活气。老人看见了它，甚至不等我惊怖的表情提醒，耳语就停了；他看见了，飞快地朝他一个钟头前离开的那个房间的地面瞥去。我顺着他的目光，看见我们头顶、古老天花板的酥灰皮上，一大摊湿漉漉的深红正漫开来，我看着它，它仿佛还在漫。我没有叫，也没有动，只是闭上了眼睛。

片刻之后，来了雷霆中的雷霆，劈中这藏着不可言传之秘的受咒的房子，带来了那唯有它能给我的神志的湮没。

## The Quest of Iranon / 伊拉农的求索
===Original===

Into the granite city of Teloth wandered the youth, vine-crowned, his yellow hair glistening with myrrh and his purple robe torn with briers of the mountain Sidrak that lies across the antique bridge of stone. The men of Teloth are dark and stern, and dwell in square houses, and with frowns they asked the stranger whence he had come and what were his name and fortune. So the youth answered:

“I am Iranon, and come from Aira, a far city that I recall only dimly but seek to find again. I am a singer of songs that I learned in the far city, and my calling is to make beauty with the things remembered of childhood. My wealth is in little memories and dreams, and in hopes that I sing in gardens when the moon is tender and the west wind stirs the lotus-buds.”

When the men of Teloth heard these things they whispered to one another; for though in the granite city there is no laughter or song, the stern men sometimes look to the Karthian hills in the spring and think of the lutes of distant Oonai whereof travelers have told. And thinking thus, they bade the stranger stay and sing in the square before the Tower of Mlin, though they liked not the color of his tattered robe, nor the myrrh in his hair, nor his chaplet of vine-leaves, nor the youth in his golden voice. At evening Iranon sang, and while he sang an old man prayed and a blind man said he saw a nimbus over the singer’s head. But most of the men of Teloth yawned, and some laughed and some went away to sleep; for Iranon told nothing useful, singing only his memories, his dreams, and his hopes.

“I remember the twilight, the moon, and soft songs, and the window where I was rocked to sleep. And through the window was the street where the golden lights came, and where the shadows danced on houses of marble. I remember the square of moonlight on the floor, that was not like any other light, and the visions that danced in the moonbeams when my mother sang to me. And too, I remember the sun of morning bright above the many-colored hills in summer, and the sweetness of flowers borne on the south wind that made the trees sing.

===Chinese===

头戴葡萄藤冠的少年，走进了特洛斯这座花岗岩之城；他的金发抹着没药，闪闪发亮，紫色的袍子，被西德拉克山上的荆棘撕破了——那山横在古老的石桥对面。特洛斯人黝黑而严峻，住在方方正正的房子里；他们皱着眉问这外乡人从哪里来，叫什么名字，有什么营生。少年答道：

“我是伊拉农，来自艾拉，一座遥远的城，我记得它已模糊，却要寻它回来。我是个唱曲的人，曲子是在那遥远的城里学的；我的天职，是拿童年记得的东西来造美。我的财富，是小小的回忆与梦，还有希望——月亮温柔、西风搅动莲蕾的时节，我在园子里唱的就是它们。”

特洛斯人听了这些话，彼此窃窃私语；因为花岗岩的城里虽没有笑声和歌，严峻的人们到了春天，有时也会望向卡尔提亚的山丘，想起旅人们讲过的远方欧奈的琵琶。这样想着，他们便请外乡人留下，在姆林塔前的广场上唱一唱，虽然他们不喜欢他那件破袍子的颜色，不喜欢他头发里的没药，不喜欢他的葡萄叶冠，也不喜欢他那金嗓里的青春。傍晚伊拉农唱了；他唱着的时候，一个老人祈祷起来，一个盲人说自己看见歌者头顶有一轮光环。可特洛斯人大都打着呵欠，有的笑，有的自去睡觉；因为伊拉农讲不出什么有用的东西，只唱他的回忆、他的梦、他的希望。

“我记得暮色、月亮和轻柔的歌，还有那扇窗，我曾在窗边被摇着入睡。窗外是街，金色的灯火来到那里，影子在大理石的房子上跳舞。我记得地板上那方块月光，它不像任何别的光，还有母亲对我唱歌时，在月光里跳舞的幻象。我也记得夏日清晨明亮的太阳，高悬在多彩的群山之上，还有南风送来的花的甜香，它叫树木歌唱。

===Original===

“O Aira, city of marble and beryl, how many are thy beauties! How loved I the warm and fragrant groves across the hyaline Nithra, and the falls of the tiny Kra that flowed through the verdant valley! In those groves and in that vale the children wove wreaths for one another, and at dusk I dreamed strange dreams under the yath-trees on the mountain as I saw below me the lights of the city, and the curving Nithra reflecting a ribbon of stars.

“And in the city were palaces of veined and tinted marble, with golden domes and painted walls, and green gardens with cerulean pools and crystal fountains. Often I played in the gardens and waded in the pools, and lay and dreamed among the pale flowers under the trees. And sometimes at sunset I would climb the long hilly street to the citadel and the open place, and look down upon Aira, the magic city of marble and beryl, splendid in a robe of golden flame.

“Long have I missed thee, Aira, for I was but young when we went into exile; but my father was thy King and I shall come again to thee, for it is so decreed of Fate. All through seven lands have I sought thee, and some day shall I reign over thy groves and gardens, thy streets and palaces, and sing to men who shall know whereof I sing, and laugh not. For I am Iranon, who was a Prince in Aira.”

---

That night the men of Teloth lodged the stranger in a stable, and in the morning an archon came to him and told him to go to the shop of Athok the cobbler, and be apprenticed to him.

“But I am Iranon, a singer of songs,” he said, “and have no heart for the cobbler’s trade.”

“All in Teloth must toil,” replied the archon, “for that is the law.” Then said Iranon:

“Wherefore do ye toil; is it not that ye may live and be happy? And if ye toil only that ye may toil more, when shall happiness find you? Ye toil to live, but is not life made of beauty and song? And if ye suffer no singers among you, where shall be the fruits of your toil? Toil without song is like a weary journey without an end. Were not death more pleasing?” But the archon was sullen and did not understand, and rebuked the stranger.

===Chinese===

“哦，艾拉，大理石与绿玉之城，你的美有多少啊！我多么爱尼斯拉明净的河对岸那些温暖芬芳的树丛，爱小小的克拉的瀑布，它流过青翠的山谷！在那些树丛和那道山谷里，孩子们彼此编花环；黄昏时我在山上的亚斯树下做着奇异的梦，望见脚下的灯火，和映着一带星河的弯曲的尼斯拉。

“城里有纹理斑斓、染着色泽的大理石宫殿，金色的穹顶，彩绘的墙壁，还有绿园，园里有天青的水池和水晶的喷泉。我常在园中玩耍，蹚过池水，躺在树下的浅色花朵里做梦。有时日落时分，我沿着长长的上坡街爬上城堡和那片开阔地，俯瞰艾拉——大理石与绿玉的魔法之城，披着一袭金色火焰的华服，灿烂夺目。

“我想念你太久了，艾拉，因为我们流亡时我还年少；可我父亲是你的王，我还要回到你那里，命运是这样注定的。我找遍了七个国度，终有一日，我要在你的树丛和花园、你的街道和宫殿之上为王，向那些知道我唱的是什么、不再发笑的人们歌唱。因为我是伊拉农，在艾拉做过王子。”

当夜，特洛斯人安排外乡人睡在一间马厩里；早晨，一位执政官来对他说，叫他到鞋匠阿托克的铺子里去，拜师学徒。

“可我是伊拉农，一个唱曲的人，”他说，“我对鞋匠的营生没有心思。”

“特洛斯人人都得劳作，”执政官答，“因为这是法律。”伊拉农便说：

“你们为什么劳作？不就是为了活、为了快乐么？倘若你们劳作，只为更多地劳作，快乐几时才找得到你们？你们为活而劳作，可生命不就是美和歌造成的么？你们中间若容不得一个歌者，你们劳作的果实又在哪里？没有歌的劳作，像一场没有尽头的疲惫跋涉。这样还不如死了痛快？”执政官却阴沉着脸，不懂，斥责了外乡人。

===Original===

“Thou art a strange youth, and I like not thy face or thy voice. The words thou speakest are blasphemy, for the gods of Teloth have said that toil is good. Our gods have promised us a haven of life beyond death, where there shall be rest without end, and crystal coldness amidst which none shall vex his mind with thought or his eyes with beauty. Go thou then to Athok the cobbler or be gone out of the city by sunset. All here must serve, and song is folly.”

---

So Iranon went out of the stable and walked over the narrow stone streets between the gloomy square houses of granite, seeking something green, for all was of stone. On the faces of men were frowns, but by the stone embankment along the sluggish river Zuro sat a young boy with sad eyes gazing into the waters to spy green budding branches washed down from the hills by the freshets. And the boy said to him: “Art thou not indeed he of whom the archons tell, who seekest a far city in a fair land? I am Romnod, and born in the blood of Teloth, but am not old in the ways of the granite city, and yearn daily for the warm groves and the distant lands of beauty and song. *Beyond the Karthian hills lieth Oonai, the city of lutes and dancing, which men whisper of and say is both lovely and terrible.* Thither would I go were I old enough to find the way, and thither shouldst thou go and thou wouldst sing and have men listen to thee. Let us leave the city Teloth and fare together among the hills of spring. Thou shalt show me the ways of travel and I will attend thy songs at evening when the stars one by one bring dreams to the minds of dreamers. And peradventure it may be that Oonai the city of lutes and dancing is even the fair Aira thou seekest, for it is told that thou hast not known Aira since old days, and a name often changeth. Let us go to Oonai, O Iranon of the golden head, where men shall know our longings and welcome us as brothers, nor ever laugh or frown at what we say.” And Iranon answered:

===Chinese===

“你是个古怪的少年，我不喜欢你的脸，也不喜欢你的嗓音。你讲的话是渎神，因为特洛斯的神说过，劳作是好的。我们的神许给我们一个死后的生之港湾，那里有永无休止的安息，有水晶的清凉，谁也不必用思想搅扰他的心，用美搅扰他的眼。那么，你去鞋匠阿托克那里，要不就日落前出城去。这里人人都得服役，歌是蠢事。”

于是伊拉农走出马厩，在花岗岩的暗色方屋之间那些狭窄的石街上走着，寻找一点绿色的东西，因为这里样样都是石头。人们脸上都是皱眉；可沿着滞缓的祖罗河的石砌堤岸，坐着一个眼睛忧伤的男孩，正望着河水，想瞅一眼被春洪从山里冲下来的青翠发芽的枝条。男孩对他说：“你果真是执政官们讲的那个人么，在一片美好的土地上寻一座遥远的城？我叫罗姆诺德，生在特洛斯的血里，可我还没沾染花岗岩之城的习气，天天想念温暖的树丛，和远方那有美有歌的地方。卡尔提亚山丘的那一边是欧奈，琵琶与舞蹈之城，人们悄悄地说它，说它又可爱又可怕。要是我够大、认得路，我就到那里去；你也该去，你可以唱，人们会听你。我们离开特洛斯城吧，一起到春天的山里去。你教我赶路的本事，到了晚上，星星一颗颗把梦送进做梦人的心里时，我听你唱。说不定，琵琶与舞蹈之城欧奈，正是你寻找的美丽的艾拉呢；人家说你从旧日起就不认得艾拉了，而名字是常常改的。我们去欧奈吧，哦，金发的伊拉农，那里的人会懂得我们的渴望，把我们当兄弟欢迎，再不笑我们，也不对我们皱眉。”伊拉农答道：

===Original===

“Be it so, small one; if any in this stone place yearn for beauty he must seek the mountains and beyond, and I would not leave thee to pine by the sluggish Zuro. But think not that delight and understanding dwell just across the Karthian hills, or in any spot thou canst find in a day’s, or a year’s, or a lustrum’s journey. Behold, when I was small like thee I dwelt in the valley of Narthos by the frigid Xari, where none would listen to my dreams; and I told myself that when older I would go to Sinara on the southern slope, and sing to smiling dromedarymen in the market place. But when I went to Sinara I found the dromedarymen all drunken and ribald, and saw that their songs were not as mine; so I travelled in a barge down the Xari to onyx-walled Jaren. And the soldiers at Jaren laughed at me and drave me out, so that I wandered to other cities.

“I have seen Stethelos that is below the great cataract, and have gazed on the marsh where Sarnath once stood. I have been to Thraa, Ilarnek, and Kadatheron on the winding river Ai, and have dwelt long in Olathoe in the land of Lomar. But though I have had listeners sometimes, they have ever been few, and I know that welcome shall wait me only in Aira, the city of marble and beryl where my father once ruled as King. So for Aira shall we seek, though it were well to visit distant and lute-blessed Oonai across the Karthian hills, which may indeed be Aira, though I think not. Aira’s beauty is past imagining, and none can tell of it without rapture, whilst of Oonai the camel-drivers whisper leeringly.”

---

===Chinese===

“就这样吧，小家伙；这石头地方若有人渴望美，他就得去寻群山和山外。我不会把你丢在滞缓的祖罗河边憔悴。可别以为欢乐和了解就住在卡尔提亚山丘的那一边，或者住在一天、一年、五年的路程里找得到的地方。听着，我像你这么小的时候，住在严寒的克萨里河边的纳索斯山谷，那里没人肯听我的梦；我对自己说，长大了我就去南坡的西纳拉，到市场里向微笑的赶驼人唱歌。可我到了西纳拉，发现赶驼人个个酗酒、粗鄙，他们的歌同我的不一样；我便乘一艘驳船沿克萨里下行，到了玛瑙筑墙的贾伦。贾伦的士兵嘲笑我，把我赶了出来，我便流浪到别的城。

“我见过大瀑布下面的斯特塞洛斯，凝望过萨尔纳斯曾经矗立的沼泽。我去过曲折的艾河上的斯拉、伊拉内克和卡达瑟隆，在洛马尔之地的奥拉索埃住过很久。可虽然有时也有听我的人，从来寥寥，我知道，欢迎只会在艾拉等我——那大理石与绿玉之城，我父亲曾在那里为王。所以，我们要寻的是艾拉；不过，先去远方卡尔提亚山丘那琵琶加身的欧奈看看也好，它也许真是艾拉，虽然我想不是。艾拉的美是想不出的，谁讲起它都不能不心醉；而欧奈，赶骆驼的人讲起它，是挤眉弄眼的。”

===Original===

At the sunset Iranon and small Romnod went forth from Teloth, and for long wandered amidst the green hills and cool forests. The way was rough and obscure, and never did they seem nearer to Oonai the city of lutes and dancing; but in the dusk as the stars came out Iranon would sing of Aira and its beauties and Romnod would listen, so that they were both happy after a fashion. They ate plentifully of fruit and red berries, and marked not the passing of time, but many years must have slipped away. Small Romnod was now not so small, and spoke deeply instead of shrilly, though Iranon was always the same, and decked his golden hair with vines and fragrant resins found in the woods. So it came to pass one day that Romnod seemed older than Iranon, though he had been very small when Iranon had found him watching for green budding branches in Teloth beside the sluggish stone-banked Zura.

Then one night when the moon was full the travellers came to a mountain crest and looked down upon the myriad lights of Oonai. Peasants had told them they were near, and Iranon knew that this was not his native city of Aira. The lights of Oonai were not like those of Aira; for they were harsh and glaring, whilst the lights of Aira shine as softly and magically as shone the moonlight on the floor by the window where Iranon’s mother once rocked him to sleep with song. But Oonai was a city of lutes and dancing; so Iranon and Romnod went down the steep slope that they might find men to whom songs and dreams would bring pleasure. And when they were come into the town they found rose-wreathed revellers bound from house to house and leaning from windows and balconies, who listened to the songs of Iranon and tossed him flowers and applauded when he was done. Then for a moment did Iranon believe he had found those who thought and felt even as he, though the town was not an hundredth so fair as Aira.

===Chinese===

日落时分，伊拉农和小罗姆诺德出了特洛斯，在青翠的山丘和清凉的林间流浪了许久。路崎岖而晦暗，琵琶与舞蹈之城欧奈，似乎永远也不更近一步；可黄昏星出的时候，伊拉农便唱起艾拉和它的美，罗姆诺德便听着，两人就都有了各自的快活。他们饱吃野果和红浆果，不记时日，可许多年必定就这样滑过去了。小小的罗姆诺德如今不小了，说话的声音由尖细变得低沉；伊拉农却始终如一，用林中寻来的藤蔓和香树脂装饰他的金发。于是有一天，罗姆诺德看起来竟比伊拉农老了，虽然伊拉农初见他时——在特洛斯，在石岸滞缓的祖罗河边，他守望着青翠的发芽枝条——他还是个很小很小的孩子。

后来一个月圆之夜，旅人们登上一道山脊，望见了欧奈的万家灯火。农人们说快到了；伊拉农知道，这不是他故乡的艾拉。欧奈的灯火同艾拉的不一样：它们生硬刺眼，而艾拉的灯火，温柔而魔魅地亮着，像从前伊拉农的母亲唱着歌摇他入睡时，照在窗边地板上的月光。可欧奈是琵琶与舞蹈之城；于是伊拉农和罗姆诺德下了陡坡，好去找那些能从歌与梦里得到乐趣的人。进城之后，他们看见佩着玫瑰花的寻欢者成群结队，从一家串到一家，探身窗外和阳台，听伊拉农的歌，朝他抛花，唱完了便喝彩。于是有一刻，伊拉农相信自己找到了同他一样想、一样感的人，虽然这城不及艾拉美的一个零头。

===Original===

When dawn came Iranon looked about with dismay, for the domes of Oonai were not golden in the sun, but gray and dismal. And the men of Oonai were pale with revelling, and dull with wine, and unlike the radiant men of Aira. But because the people had thrown him blossoms and acclaimed his songs Iranon stayed on, and with him Romnod, who liked the revelry of the town and wore in his dark hair roses and myrtle. Often at night Iranon sang to the revellers, but he was always as before, crowned only with the vine of the mountains and remembering the marble streets of Aira and the hyaline Nithra. In the frescoed halls of the monarch did he sing, upon a crystal dais raised over a floor that was a mirror, and as he sang, he brought pictures to his hearers till the floor seemed to reflect old, beautiful and half-remembered things instead of the wine-reddened feasters who pelted him with roses. And the King bade him put away his tattered purple, and clothed him in satin and cloth-of-gold, with rings of green jade and bracelets of tinted ivory, and lodged him in a gilded and tapestried chamber on a bed of sweet carven wood with canopies and coverlets of flower-embroidered silk. Thus dwelt Iranon in Oonai, the city of lutes and dancing.

It is not known how long Iranon tarried in Oonai, but one day the King brought to the palace some wild whirling dancers from the Liranian desert, and dusky flute-players from Drinen in the East, and after that the revellers threw their roses not so much at Iranon as at the dancers and the flute-players. And day by day that Romnod who had been a small boy in granite Teloth grew coarser and redder with wine, till he dreamed less and less, and listened with less delight to the songs of Iranon. But though Iranon was sad he ceased not to sing, and at evening told again his dreams of Aira, the city of marble and beryl. Then one night the reddened and fattened Romnod snored heavily amidst the poppied silks of his banquet-couch and died writhing, whilst Iranon, pale and slender, sang to himself in a far corner. And when Iranon had wept over the grave of Romnod and strewn it with green budding branches, such as Romnod used to love, he put aside his silks and gauds and went forgotten out of Oonai the city of lutes and dancing clad only in the ragged purple in which he had come, and garlanded with fresh vines from the mountains.

===Chinese===

天亮了，伊拉农沮丧地四下张望：欧奈的穹顶在太阳底下不是金的，而是灰暗惨淡的。欧奈人寻欢得脸色苍白，饮酒饮得迟钝，同艾拉容光焕发的人们不一样。可因为众人抛过他花朵、夸过他的歌，伊拉农留了下来；同他一起的还有罗姆诺德，他喜欢城里的狂欢，黑发上插着玫瑰和桃金娘。夜里伊拉农常向寻欢者歌唱，可他依旧是从前的他，头上只戴着山间的葡萄藤，心里记着艾拉的大理石街道和明净的尼斯拉。他在君王的彩绘大厅里唱，站在一座架在镜面地板上的水晶台上；他唱着，把一幅幅图景送进听者的心里，直到那地板映出的，仿佛不再是拿玫瑰掷他的、酒红了脸的宴客，而是古老、美丽、记了一半的东西。国王叫他脱下破紫袍，给他穿上缎子和织金的衣裳，戴上绿玉的指环和染色的象牙镯子，安置他住进一间贴金挂毯的屋子，睡一张芳香的雕木床，床上有花绣丝绸的顶盖和衾被。伊拉农就这样住在欧奈，琵琶与舞蹈之城。

伊拉农在欧奈耽了多久，没有人知道；可有一天，国王带了几名利拉尼亚荒野来的疯狂的旋舞者、几个东方德里南来的黝黑的吹笛人进宫，从此寻欢者们的玫瑰，就不大掷向伊拉农，都掷向舞者和笛手了。日子一天天过去，曾在花岗岩特洛斯做过小男孩的罗姆诺德，酒愈喝愈粗、愈喝愈红，梦愈做愈少，听伊拉农的歌，也愈听愈无心绪。可伊拉农虽然悲伤，歌没有停；傍晚又讲起他的艾拉之梦，那大理石与绿玉之城。后来的一夜，喝红了养肥了的罗姆诺德，在他罂粟花纹的宴榻丝褥里鼾声大作，抽搐着死了；那时伊拉农正苍白而纤瘦，在远处一个角落里对自己唱着。伊拉农在罗姆诺德坟上哭过，撒满青翠的发芽枝条——罗姆诺德从前就爱这些——便收起他的丝绸和彩饰，被人忘却地走出了欧奈，琵琶与舞蹈之城；身上只穿着他来时那件破紫袍，头上戴着山间新采的藤冠。

===Original===

Into the sunset wandered Iranon, seeking still for his native land and for men who would understand and cherish his songs and dreams. In all the cities of Cydathria and in the lands beyond the Bnazic desert gay-faced children laughed at his olden songs and tattered robe of purple; but Iranon stayed ever young, and wore wreaths upon his golden head whilst he sang of Aira.

---

So came he one night to the squalid cot of an antique shepherd, bent and dirty, who kept flocks on a stony slope above a quicksand marsh. To this man Iranon spoke, as to so many others:

“Canst thou tell me where I may find Aira, the city of marble and beryl, where flows the hyaline Nithra and where the falls of the tiny Kra sing to verdant valleys and hills forested with yath-trees?” And the shepherd, hearing, looked long and strangely at Iranon, as if recalling something very far away in time, and noted each line of the stranger’s face, and his golden hair, and his crown of vine-leaves. But he was old, and replied:

“O stranger, I have indeed heard the name of Aira, and the other names thou hast spoken, but they come to me from afar down the waste of long years. I heard them in my youth from the lips of a playmate, a beggar’s boy given to strange dreams, who would weave long tales about the moon and the flowers and the west wind. We used to laugh at him, for we knew him from his birth though he thought himself a King’s son. He was comely, even as thou, but full of folly and strangeness; and he ran away when small to find those who would listen gladly to his songs and dreams. How often hath he sung to me of lands that never were, and things that never can be! Of Aira did he speak much; of Aira and the river Nithra, and the falls of the tiny Kra. There would he ever say he once dwelt as a Prince, though here we knew him from his birth. Nor was there ever a marble city of Aira, or those who could delight in strange songs, save in the dreams of mine old playmate Iranon who is gone.”

And in the twilight, as the stars came out one by one and the moon cast on the marsh a radiance like that which a child sees quivering on the floor as he is rocked to sleep at evening, there walked into the lethal quicksands a very old man in tattered purple, crowned with withered vine leaves and gazing ahead as if upon the golden domes of a fair city where dreams are understood.

===Chinese===

伊拉农走进落日里，仍旧寻着他的故乡，寻着能懂、能珍爱他的歌与梦的人。在基达斯利亚所有的城里，在布纳齐克沙漠外的土地上，快活脸的孩子们笑他古老的歌和褴褛的紫袍；可伊拉农永远年轻，金发上戴着花环，一路唱着艾拉。

后来的一夜，他来到一个古老牧人的肮脏小屋前；牧人伛偻污浊，在流沙沼泽上方一道多石的山坡上放着羊。伊拉农对他说话，同对许多人说的一样：

“你能告诉我哪里能找到艾拉么，大理石与绿玉之城？明净的尼斯拉在那里流，小小的克拉的瀑布在那里向青翠的山谷和长满亚斯树的山丘歌唱。”牧人听了，久久地、怪异地望着伊拉农，像在回想时间上非常遥远的一件事，端详着外乡人脸上的每一根线条，他的金发，他的葡萄叶冠。可他老了，答道：

“外乡人啊，我的确听过艾拉这名字，还有你说的那些名字，可它们隔着长长的岁月之荒，从远处来到我这里。我年轻时从一个玩伴嘴里听来的，一个爱做怪梦的乞丐男孩，他会编长长的故事，讲月亮，讲花，讲西风。我们常笑他，因为我们从他生下就认得他，他却自以为是国王的儿子。他生得好看，就像你一样，可满心是痴气和怪念头；他还小的时候就跑掉了，去找那些乐意听他歌与梦的人。他多少次对我唱那些从来不曾有过的地方、从来不能有的事物啊！他讲艾拉讲得最多；讲艾拉，讲尼斯拉河，讲小小的克拉的瀑布。他总说他在那里做过王子，可我们这里是从他生下就认得他的。从来就没有什么大理石的城艾拉，也没有什么能欣赏怪歌的人，除了我那老玩伴伊拉农的梦——他已经不在了。”

暮色里，星星一颗颗出来了，月亮把一片光辉投在沼泽上，就像孩子傍晚被摇着入睡时，看见地板上颤动的那种光辉；这时，一个穿着破紫袍的老人，戴着枯萎的葡萄叶冠，走进那致命的流沙，眼睛望着前方，仿佛望着一座美丽的城池的金色穹顶——在那里，梦是有人懂的。

===Original===

That night something of youth and beauty died in the elder world.

===Chinese===

那一夜，上古世界里的什么青春与美，死去了。

## The Rats in the Walls / 墙中之鼠
===Original===

On July 16, 1923, I moved into Exham Priory after the last workman had finished his labors. The restoration had been a stupendous task, for little had remained of the deserted pile but a shell-like ruin; yet because it had been the seat of my ancestors I let no expense deter me. The place had not been inhabited since the reign of James the First, when a tragedy of intensely hideous, though largely unexplained, nature had struck down the master, five of his children, and several servants; and driven forth under a cloud of suspicion and terror the third son, my lineal progenitor and the only survivor of the abhorred line.

With this sole heir denounced as a murderer, the estate had reverted to the crown, nor had the accused man made any attempt to exculpate himself or regain his property. Shaken by some horror greater than that of conscience or the law, and expressing only a frantic wish to exclude the ancient edifice from his sight and memory, Walter de la Poer, eleventh Baron Exham, fled to Virginia and there founded the family which by the next century had become known as Delapore.

Exham Priory had remained untenanted, though later allotted to the estates of the Norrys family and much studied because of its peculiarly composite architecture; an architecture involving Gothic towers resting on a Saxon or Romanesque substructure, whose foundation in turn was of a still earlier order or blend of orders﻿—Roman, and even Druidic or native Cymric if legends speak truly. This foundation was a very singular thing, being merged on one side with the solid limestone of the precipice from whose brink the priory overlooked a desolate valley three miles west of the village of Anchester.

Architects and antiquarians loved to examine this strange relic of forgotten centuries, but the country folk hated it. They had hated it hundreds of years before, when my ancestors lived there, and they hated it now, with the moss and mould of abandonment on it. I had not been a day in Anchester before I knew I came of an accursed house. And this week workmen have blown up Exham Priory, and are busy obliterating the traces of its foundations.

---

===Chinese===

一九二三年七月十六日，最后一个工匠收工之后，我搬进了埃克瑟姆修道院（Exham Priory）。修复是一项浩大的工程，因为这座荒废的建筑除了空壳般的残骸几乎什么也没剩下；但它是我祖先的宅邸，我没有让任何开销拦住我。这地方自詹姆士一世一朝就无人居住——那朝发生过一场无比狰狞、却又大体无从解释的悲剧，夺去了主人、他的五个孩子和几名仆人的性命；三子，我的直系先祖、这一门受憎厌的血裔中唯一的幸存者，则在嫌疑与恐怖的阴云下被逐出了家门。

这位独一的继承人被指为凶手，产业归了王室；被告也没有任何洗清自己、收回产业的举动。沃尔特·德·拉·波尔（Walter de la Poer），第十一代埃克瑟姆男爵，被某种比良心和法律更可怕的恐怖摇撼着，只表达了一个狂乱的愿望：让那座古老建筑从他的眼前、从他的记忆里消失。他逃到弗吉尼亚，在那里建立了这个家系，到下个世纪，它以德拉波尔（Delapore）之名为人所知。

埃克瑟姆修道院一直空着，后来划入诺里斯（Norrys）家的产业；因其格外混合的建筑式样而备受研究——哥特式的塔楼，坐落在撒克逊或罗马式的底层结构上，那地基又出于更早的一种或数种式样：罗马的，倘若传说不虚，甚至还有德鲁伊的或本土凯尔特的。这地基是一件非常奇异的东西：一侧同石灰岩峭壁的整石融为一体；修道院就从崖缘俯瞰一道荒凉的山谷，在安彻斯特村（Anchester）以西三英里。

建筑师和古物学家爱考察这座被遗忘世纪的古怪遗迹，乡民却恨它。几百年前我的祖先住在那里时他们就恨它；如今它披着荒废的苔藓和霉，他们还恨它。到安彻斯特不出一天我就明白了：我出身于一个受诅咒的门第。就在这个星期，工人们炸掉了埃克瑟姆修道院，正忙着抹去它地基的痕迹。

---

===Original===

The bare statistics of my ancestry I had always known, together with the fact that my first American forbear had come to the colonies under a strange cloud. Of details, however, I had been kept wholly ignorant through the policy of reticence always maintained by the Delapores. Unlike our planter neighbors, we seldom boasted of crusading ancestors or other medieval and Renaissance heroes; nor was any kind of tradition handed down except what may have been recorded in the sealed envelope left before the Civil War by every squire to his eldest son for posthumous opening. The glories we cherished were those achieved since the migration; the glories of a proud and honorable, if somewhat reserved and unsocial Virginia line.

During the war our fortunes were extinguished and our whole existence changed by the burning of Carfax, our home on the banks of the James. My grandfather, advanced in years, had perished in that incendiary outrage, and with him the envelope that bound us all to the past. I can recall that fire today as I saw it then at the age of seven, with the Federal soldiers shouting, the women screaming, and the negroes howling and praying. My father was in the army, defending Richmond, and after many formalities my mother and I were passed through the lines to join him.

When the war ended we all moved north, whence my mother had come; and I grew to manhood, middle age, and ultimate wealth as a stolid Yankee. Neither my father nor I ever knew what our hereditary envelope had contained, and as I merged into the greyness of Massachusetts business life I lost all interest in the mysteries which evidently lurked far back in my family tree. Had I suspected their nature, how gladly would I have left Exham Priory to its moss, bats, and cobwebs!

===Chinese===

我家世系那些干巴巴的数字我一向知道，连同我的第一位美国先人是顶着古怪的阴云来到殖民地这一事实。可细节呢，德拉波尔家一贯的缄默政策让我全然不知。同我们种园地的邻居不一样，我们很少夸耀参加十字军的祖先或别的中世纪、文艺复兴的英雄；传下来的传统也没有，只有内战前每位庄主留给长子、嘱咐死后拆封的信封里可能记下的那点什么。我们珍视的光荣，都是迁徙以后挣来的：一个骄傲而体面的弗吉尼亚门第的光荣——虽说有点拘谨，不喜交际。

战争期间，我们的家运熄灭了，全家的存在都因詹姆斯河畔的家宅卡法克斯（Carfax）被焚而改变。我祖父已届高龄，死于那场纵火的暴行，同他一起化为灰烬的，还有那只把我们全体同过去拴在一起的信封。那场火我至今记得，像七岁的我当时看见的那样：北军士兵呼喝，女人们尖叫，黑人们嚎哭祷告。我父亲在军中保卫里士满；几番手续之后，我母亲和我获准穿过防线去同他会合。

战争结束，我们全家迁往北方，我母亲的来处；我长大成人、步入中年、积起终身的财富，成了一个古板的北方佬。我父亲和我，谁也不曾知道我们世代相传的那只信封里装着什么；而我融进马萨诸塞灰色的商业生活之后，对我家谱深处显然潜伏的种种谜，也失去了全部兴趣。倘若我疑心过它们的性质，我会多么乐意让埃克瑟姆修道院留给它的苔藓、蝙蝠和蛛网！

===Original===

My father died in 1904, but without any message to leave to me, or to my only child, Alfred, a motherless boy of ten. It was this boy who reversed the order of family information, for although I could give him only jesting conjectures about the past, he wrote me of some very interesting ancestral legends when the late war took him to England in 1917 as an aviation officer. Apparently the Delapores had a colorful and perhaps sinister history, for a friend of my son’s, Capt. Edward Norrys of the Royal Flying Corps, dwelt near the family seat at Anchester and related some peasant superstitions which few novelists could equal for wildness and incredibility. Norrys himself, of course, did not take them seriously; but they amused my son and made good material for his letters to me. It was this legendry which definitely turned my attention to my transatlantic heritage, and made me resolve to purchase and restore the family seat which Norrys showed to Alfred in its picturesque desertion, and offered to get for him at a surprisingly reasonable figure, since his own uncle was the present owner.

I bought Exham Priory in 1918, but was almost immediately distracted from my plans of restoration by the return of my son as a maimed invalid. During the two years that he lived I thought of nothing but his care, having even placed my business under the direction of partners.

In 1921, as I found myself bereaved and aimless, a retired manufacturer no longer young, I resolved to divert my remaining years with my new possession. Visiting Anchester in December, I was entertained by Capt. Norrys, a plump, amiable young man who had thought much of my son, and secured his assistance in gathering plans and anecdotes to guide in the coming restoration. Exham Priory itself I saw without emotion, a jumble of tottering medieval ruins covered with lichens and honeycombed with rooks’ nests, perched perilously upon a precipice, and denuded of floors or other interior features save the stone walls of the separate towers.

===Chinese===

一九〇四年我父亲去世，没有留下一句话给我，也没有给我唯一的孩子——十岁丧母的男孩阿尔弗雷德（Alfred）。正是这个孩子，把家族信息的流向倒了过来：过去我只能对他打趣地猜测，而一九一七年大战把他作为航空军官带到英国时，他写信给我讲了些非常有意思的祖先传说。显然，德拉波尔家有一段多彩的、兴许阴惨的历史，因为我儿子的朋友、皇家飞行队的爱德华·诺里斯上尉（Capt. Edward Norrys），就住在安彻斯特的祖宅近旁，讲过一些农民的迷信，其狂野和离奇，很少有小说家及得上。诺里斯本人当然不把它们当真；可它们逗乐了我儿子，也成了他写给我的信的好材料。正是这些传说把我的注意力断然引向我大西洋彼岸的祖产，使我决意买下并修复那座祖宅——诺里斯带阿尔弗雷德看过它风景如画的荒废，还提出可以一个出奇公道的价钱替他弄到手，因为现在的房主正是他自己的伯父。

一九一八年我买下了埃克瑟姆修道院，可几乎立刻被儿子的归来岔开了修复的计划——他成了残废。他活着的两年里，我心里只有照护他一件事，连生意都交给了合伙人打理。

一九二一年，我发现自己孑然一身、无所事事，一个不再年轻的退了休的制造业者，便决意用余生消磨在这件新产业上。十二月我造访安彻斯特，受到诺里斯上尉的款待——一个胖乎乎、和气的年轻人，很惦念我儿子——并在他的协助下收集了图纸和掌故，为即将开始的修复作指引。埃克瑟姆修道院本身，我看得毫无波澜：一堆摇摇欲坠的中世纪废墟，覆满地衣，白嘴鸦的巢把它蛀成蜂窝，岌岌可危地骑在一道峭壁上；楼板和内部的一切都已不存，只剩下几座塔楼的石墙。

===Original===

As I gradually recovered the image of the edifice as it had been when my ancestors left it over three centuries before, I began to hire workmen for the reconstruction. In every case I was forced to go outside the immediate locality, for the Anchester villagers had an almost unbelievable fear and hatred of the place. This sentiment was so great that it was sometimes communicated to the outside laborers, causing numerous desertions; whilst its scope appeared to include both the priory and its ancient family.

My son had told me that he was somewhat avoided during his visits because he was a de la Poer, and I now found myself subtly ostracised for a like reason until I convinced the peasants how little I knew of my heritage. Even then they sullenly disliked me, so that I had to collect most of the village traditions through the mediation of Norrys. What the people could not forgive, perhaps, was that I had come to restore a symbol so abhorrent to them; for, rationally or not, they viewed Exham Priory as nothing less than a haunt of fiends and werewolves.

---

Piecing together the tales which Norrys collected for me, and supplementing them with the accounts of several savants who had studied the ruins, I deduced that Exham Priory stood on the site of a prehistoric temple; a Druidical or ante-Druidical thing which must have been contemporary with Stonehenge. That indescribable rites had been celebrated there, few doubted, and there were unpleasant tales of the transference of these rites into the Cybele-worship which the Romans had introduced.

===Chinese===

随着祖先三个多世纪前离开时的面貌在我脑子里渐渐复原，我开始雇工重建。每一回我都不得不去本地以外招人，因为安彻斯特村人对这地方的恐惧和憎恨几乎叫人不能相信。这情绪重到有时会传染给外来的工人，造成成群的逃跑；而它笼罩的范围，似乎把修道院和它古老的家族一并包了进去。

我儿子说过，他来访时多少被人躲着，因为他姓德·拉·波尔；如今我也为同样的缘故被微妙地孤立，直到我说服了农民们：我对自己的祖产知道得多么少。即便到那时，他们还是闷闷地不喜欢我，村里大部分传说，我只得通过诺里斯居中收集。人们不能饶恕的，或许是我来恢复一个他们如此憎厌的象征；因为不论有没有道理，他们把埃克瑟姆修道院看成不折不扣的魔鬼和狼人的巢穴。

---

把诺里斯替我收集的故事缀起来，再补上几个研究过废墟的学者的记述，我推想：埃克瑟姆修道院立在一座史前神庙的旧址上；一件德鲁伊的、或前德鲁伊的东西，必是与巨石阵同时的。那里庆祝过无从形容的仪式，少有人怀疑；还有不祥的传闻，说这些仪式转入了罗马人引进的库柏勒崇拜。

===Original===

Inscriptions still visible in the sub-cellar bore such unmistakable letters as “**Div﻿ ﻿… Ops﻿ ﻿… Magna. Mat﻿ ﻿…**” sign of the Magna Mater whose dark worship was once vainly forbidden to Roman citizens. Anchester had been the camp of the third Augustan legion, as many remains attest, and it was said that the temple of Cybele was splendid and thronged with worshippers who performed nameless ceremonies at the bidding of a Phrygian priest. Tales added that the fall of the old religion did not end the orgies at the temple, but that the priests lived on in the new faith without real change. Likewise was it said that the rites did not vanish with the Roman power, and that certain among the Saxons added to what remained of the temple, and gave it the essential outline it subsequently preserved, making it the center of a cult feared through half the heptarchy. About 1000 AD the place is mentioned in a chronicle as being a substantial stone priory housing a strange and powerful monastic order and surrounded by extensive gardens which needed no walls to exclude a frightened populace. It was never destroyed by the Danes, though after the Norman Conquest it must have declined tremendously; since there was no impediment when Henry the Third granted the site to my ancestor, Gilbert de la Poer, First Baron Exham, in 1261.

Of my family before this date there is no evil report, but something strange must have happened then. In one chronicle there is a reference to a de la Poer as “cursed of God” in 1307, whilst village legendry had nothing but evil and frantic fear to tell of the castle that went up on the foundations of the old temple and priory. The fireside tales were of the most grisly description, all the ghastlier because of their frightened reticence and cloudy evasiveness. They represented my ancestors as a race of hereditary daemons beside whom Gilles de Retz and the Marquis de Sade would seem the veriest tyros, and hinted whisperingly at their responsibility for the occasional disappearances of villagers through several generations.

===Chinese===

地下深窖里仍可辨认的铭文，带着「Div…Ops…Magna. Mat…」这样确凿的字样——大母神的记号，她那黑暗的崇拜，罗马公民曾被禁止信奉而徒然。安彻斯特曾是奥古斯都第三军团的驻地，许多遗迹可证；据说库柏勒的神庙气象宏大，礼拜者济济一堂，在一个弗里吉亚祭司的号令下行着无名的仪式。传说又添说：旧教的衰落并没有结束神庙里的纵酒，祭司们在新信仰里照样活着，实质未改。同样据说，仪式也没有随罗马的权势一同消亡，撒克逊人中有一些给神庙的残余添了工，给了它后来一直保存的基本轮廓，使它成为一个教团的中心，半个七国都闻风丧胆。约公元一〇〇〇年，一部编年史提到这地方是一座像样的石头隐修院，住着一个古怪而有势力的修会，四周环绕着广阔的园圃——无需围墙来隔绝惊恐的民众。它从未被丹麦人毁掉；诺曼征服之后想必大大衰落了，因为一二六一年亨利三世把这块地赐给我祖先吉尔伯特·德·拉·波尔（Gilbert de la Poer）、第一代埃克瑟姆男爵时，没有遇到任何障碍。

在这日子以前，我家没有什么恶评；可那时一定出了什么怪事。一部编年史里，一三〇七年有一条提到一个德·拉·波尔「受上帝诅咒」；而村中传说讲到那座建在古神庙和隐修院地基上的城堡时，只有邪恶和狂乱的恐惧。炉边的故事都最阴惨，又因为讲述者惊惶的讳莫如深和云遮雾罩的闪避而愈加骇人。它们把我祖先描绘成一个世袭的恶魔种族，吉尔·德·雷和萨德侯爵在他们旁边都像生手；还咬耳朵暗示，几代人里村里偶尔的失踪，责任都在他们。

===Original===

The worst characters, apparently, were the barons and their direct heirs; at least, most was whispered about these. If of healthier inclinations, it was said, an heir would early and mysteriously die to make way for another more typical scion. There seemed to be an inner cult in the family, presided over by the head of the house, and sometimes closed except to a few members. Temperament rather than ancestry was evidently the basis of this cult, for it was entered by several who married into the family. Lady Margaret Trevor from Cornwall, wife of Godfrey, the second son of the fifth baron, became a favorite bane of children all over the countryside, and the daemon heroine of a particularly horrible old ballad not yet extinct near the Welsh border. Preserved in balladry, too, though not illustrating the same point, is the hideous tale of Lady Mary de la Poer, who shortly after her marriage to the Earl of Shrewsfield was killed by him and his mother, both of the slayers being absolved and blessed by the priest to whom they confessed what they dared not repeat to the world.

These myths and ballads, typical as they were of crude superstition, repelled me greatly. Their persistence, and their application to so long a line of my ancestors, were especially annoying; whilst the imputations of monstrous habits proved unpleasantly reminiscent of the one known scandal of my immediate forbears﻿—the case of my cousin, young Randolph Delapore of Carfax, who went among the negroes and became a voodoo priest after he returned from the Mexican War.

I was much less disturbed by the vaguer tales of wails and howlings in the barren, windswept valley beneath the limestone cliff; of the graveyard stenches after the spring rains; of the floundering, squealing white thing on which Sir John Clave’s horse had trod one night in a lonely field; and of the servant who had gone mad at what he saw in the priory in the full light of day. These things were hackneyed spectral lore, and I was at that time a pronounced skeptic. The accounts of vanished peasants were less to be dismissed, though not especially significant in view of medieval custom. Prying curiosity meant death, and more than one severed head had been publicly shown on the bastions﻿—now effaced﻿—around Exham Priory.

===Chinese===

显然，最坏的角色是历代男爵和他们的直系继承人；至少，窃窃私语多半围着这些人。据说，倘若哪个继承人天性健全些，他就会早早地、神秘地死去，让位给另一个更典型的苗裔。这家里面似乎有个内层的教团，由家主主持，有时只对寥寥几名成员开放。这教团的基础显然是气质而非血统，因为嫁进家来的也有几个入了团。康沃尔来的玛格丽特·特雷弗，第五代男爵次子戈弗雷的妻子，成了全乡孩童的煞星，一支特别可怕的古老民谣里妖魔般的女主角——那歌谣在威尔士边境一带至今未绝。民谣里还保存着玛丽·德·拉·波尔夫人的骇人故事，虽然讲的不是同一回事：她嫁给施鲁斯菲尔德伯爵后不久，就被丈夫和婆婆杀死；两个凶手都得到了他们忏悔神父的赦罪和祝福——他们向他告解了不敢向世人复述的东西。

这些神话和民谣，虽是粗陋迷信的典型，却叫我大大反感。它们流传得那么久，又落到我这么长的一列祖先头上，尤其恼人；而那些怪异习性的指摘，又不愉快地叫人想起我直系先辈唯一一桩出了名的丑闻——我堂弟、卡法克斯年轻的伦道夫·德拉波尔的案子：他从墨西哥战争回来后，混到黑人中间，当上了伏都教的祭司。

叫我不安得少些的，是那些更含糊的传说：石灰岩崖下荒风飕飕的谷里的哭嚎，春雨后墓园似的恶臭，约翰·克莱夫爵士的马一天夜里在僻静田里踩上的那团扑腾尖叫的白东西，还有在大天白日里看见了修道院里的什么而疯掉的仆人。这些都属陈腐的幽灵故事；我那时是个响当当的怀疑派。失踪农民的记述倒不好轻易打发，不过照中世纪的习俗，也算不得特别蹊跷。打探的好奇心意味着死；埃克瑟姆修道院四周的碉楼——如今已铲平——上，不止一颗割下的人头公开展示过。

===Original===

A few of the tales were exceedingly picturesque, and made me wish I had learnt more of the comparative mythology in my youth. There was, for instance, the belief that a legion of bat-winged devils kept witches’ sabbath each night at the priory﻿—a legion whose sustenance might explain the disproportionate abundance of coarse vegetables harvested in the vast gardens. And, most vivid of all, there was the dramatic epic of the rats﻿—the scampering army of obscene vermin which had burst forth from the castle three months after the tragedy that doomed it to desertion﻿—the lean, filthy, ravenous army which had swept all before it and devoured fowl, cats, dogs, hogs, sheep, and even two hapless human beings before its fury was spent. Around that unforgettable rodent army a whole separate cycle of myths revolves, for it scattered among the village homes and brought curses and horrors in its train.

Such was the lore that assailed me as I pushed to completion, with an elderly obstinacy, the work of restoring my ancestral home. It must not be imagined for a moment that these tales formed my principal psychological environment. On the other hand, I was constantly praised and encouraged by Capt. Norrys and the antiquarians who surrounded and aided me. When the task was done, over two years after its commencement, I viewed the great rooms, wainscotted walls, vaulted ceilings, mullioned windows, and broad staircases with a pride which fully compensated for the prodigious expense of the restoration.

Every attribute of the Middle Ages was cunningly reproduced, and the new parts blended perfectly with the original walls and foundations. The seat of my fathers was complete, and I looked forward to redeeming at last the local fame of the line which ended in me. I would reside here permanently, and prove that a de la Poer (for I had adopted again the original spelling of the name) need not be a fiend. My comfort was perhaps augmented by the fact that, although Exham Priory was medievally fitted, its interior was in truth wholly new and free from old vermin and old ghosts alike.

---

===Chinese===

有几则传说极其生动，叫我但愿年轻时多学点比较神话学。比如有一说：一军团蝙蝠翅膀的魔鬼夜夜在修道院行巫安息日——这一大群的口粮，也许正好解释那广阔园圃里粗蔬反常的丰收。而最鲜活的，是关于老鼠的戏剧史诗——那支从城堡里涌出的、蹦跳的秽鼠大军，就在注定它荒废的悲剧发生三个月后冲了出来——一支精瘦、龌龊、饿疯的大军，横扫一切，吞吃了鸡、猫、狗、猪、羊，甚至两个倒霉的人，狂怒才告平息。围绕那支难忘的啮齿大军，整整一个独立的神话循环在旋转，因为它散进了村舍，一路带来诅咒和恐怖。

当我以老年人的执拗推进祖宅修复工程、直至完工时，向我袭来的，就是这一套传说。千万别以为这些故事构成了我主要的心理环境。恰恰相反，诺里斯上尉和帮助我的古物学家们一直在夸我、鼓励我。工程告成——开工两年之后——我看着那些巨大的厅堂、装板的墙、拱顶的天花、格子窗和宽阔的楼梯，怀着一种完全抵偿了修复那笔巨资的骄傲。

中世纪的每一样特质都被巧妙地复现，新修的部分同原有的墙基融成一体。我父辈的宅邸完备了；我指望终于挽回这一脉——终结于我这一脉——在本地的好名声。我要在这里长住，证明一个德·拉·波尔（我又采用了这姓氏原本的拼法）不必是恶魔。叫我宽心的还有一桩：埃克瑟姆修道院虽是中世纪的装束，内里其实全新，既没有老虫豸，也没有老鬼魂。

===Original===

As I have said, I moved in on July 16, 1923. My household consisted of seven servants and nine cats, of which latter species I am particularly fond. My eldest cat, “Nigger-Man,” was seven years old and had come with me from my home in Bolton, Massachusetts; the others I had accumulated whilst living with Capt. Norrys’ family during the restoration of the priory.

For five days our routine proceeded with the utmost placidity, my time being spent mostly in the codification of old family data. I had now obtained some very circumstantial accounts of the final tragedy and flight of Walter de la Poer, which I conceived to be the probable contents of the hereditary paper lost in the fire at Carfax. It appeared that my ancestor was accused with much reason of having killed all the other members of his household, except four servant confederates, in their sleep, about two weeks after a shocking discovery which changed his whole demeanor, but which, except by implication, he disclosed to no one save perhaps the servants who assisted him and afterward fled beyond reach.

This deliberate slaughter, which included a father, three brothers, and two sisters, was largely condoned by the villagers, and so slackly treated by the law that its perpetrator escaped honored, unharmed, and undisguised to Virginia; the general whispered sentiment being that he had purged the land of an immemorial curse. What discovery had prompted an act so terrible, I could scarcely even conjecture. Walter de la Poer must have known for years the sinister tales about his family, so that this material could have given him no fresh impulse. Had he, then, witnessed some appalling ancient rite, or stumbled upon some frightful and revealing symbol in the priory or its vicinity? He was reputed to have been a shy, gentle youth in England. In Virginia he seemed not so much hard or bitter as harassed and apprehensive. He was spoken of in the diary of another gentleman adventurer, Francis Harley of Bellview, as a man of unexampled justice, honor, and delicacy.

===Chinese===

如我所说，我于一九二三年七月十六日迁入。我的家口由七名仆人和九只猫组成，后一属我尤其钟爱。我最老的猫「小黑」（Nigger-Man）七岁了，是随我从马萨诸塞博尔顿的家一起来的；其余的是修复修道院期间我住在诺里斯上尉家时陆续攒下的。

头五天，一切按部就班，平静至极，我的时间多半用于整理旧家世的资料。这时我已拿到一些关于沃尔特·德·拉·波尔最后那场悲剧和出走的确凿记载，我猜想那正是卡法克斯大火里遗失的那份祖传文书的内容。原来我的先祖被指控——指控得大有道理——在一次骇人的发现之后约两个星期，趁全家熟睡杀了全家，只除了四名同谋的仆人；那次发现改变了他的整个举止，但除了暗示，他没有向任何人吐露过，或许只向协助他、事后逃得无影无踪的仆人们吐露过。

这场蓄意的杀戮，受害者包括一位父亲、三个兄弟和两个姐妹，却大得村人原谅，法律也敷衍了事，凶手体面、无伤、毫不遮掩地逃到了弗吉尼亚；众人交头接耳的意思是：他涤清了这块土地上太古的诅咒。什么发现促成了这样可怕的行为，我连猜都几乎猜不着。沃尔特·德·拉·波尔对其家族的阴森传说想必早有多年耳闻，这些材料给不了他新的刺激。那么，他是目击了某场骇人的古仪式，还是在修道院或其左近撞见了什么可怕而泄露天机的符号？在英国，他被认为是个腼腆温和的青年。在弗吉尼亚，与其说他变得硬心肠或怨毒，不如说他惶惶不可终日。另一位绅士冒险家、贝尔维尤的弗朗西斯·哈利的日记里说他，是一个正义、荣誉和体贴都无可比拟的人。

===Original===

On July 22 occurred the first incident which, though lightly dismissed at the time, takes on a preternatural significance in relation to later events. It was so simple as to be almost negligible, and could not possibly have been noticed under the circumstances; for it must be recalled that since I was in a building practically fresh and new except for the walls, and surrounded by a well-balanced staff of servitors, apprehension would have been absurd despite the locality.

What I afterward remembered is merely this﻿—that my old black cat, whose moods I know so well, was undoubtedly alert and anxious to an extent wholly out of keeping with his natural character. He roved from room to room, restless and disturbed, and sniffed constantly about the walls which formed part of the old Gothic structure. I realize how trite this sounds﻿—like the inevitable dog in the ghost story, which always growls before his master sees the sheeted figure﻿—yet I cannot consistently suppress it.

The following day a servant complained of restlessness among all the cats in the house. He came to me in my study, a lofty west room on the second story, with groined arches, black oak panelling, and a triple Gothic window overlooking the limestone cliff and desolate valley; and even as he spoke I saw the jetty form of Nigger-Man creeping along the west wall and scratching at the new panels which overlaid the ancient stone.

I told the man that there must be some singular odor or emanation from the old stonework, imperceptible to human senses, but affecting the delicate organs of cats even through the new woodwork. This I truly believed, and when the fellow suggested the presence of mice or rats, I mentioned that there had been no rats there for three hundred years, and that even the field mice of the surrounding country could hardly be found in these high walls, where they had never been known to stray. That afternoon I called on Capt. Norrys, and he assured me that it would be quite incredible for field mice to infest the priory in such a sudden and unprecedented fashion.

===Chinese===

七月二十二日，发生了头一桩事件——当时轻轻放过了，如今联系后事，却显出超自然的分量。它简单得几乎不值一提，何况在那样的处境下根本不会有人留意；须知，我住的是一座除墙体以外焕然如新的建筑，身边又是一班称职安稳的仆役，尽管地段如此，惊惶本属荒唐。

我后来记得的只是这样：我的老黑猫——它的脾性我了如指掌——那种警觉和焦躁，全然出了它天性的格。它一个房间一个房间地转，不安而紊乱，不停地在哥特老结构的墙根嗅来嗅去。我知道这话听着多么俗套——像鬼故事里那条少不了的狗，总在主人看见床单裹的人影之前先吠——可我没法按部就班地略去它。

第二天，一个仆人抱怨说满屋的猫都不安分。他到书房来找我——书房在二层，是一间高峻的西屋，棱拱的天顶，黑橡木镶板，一扇三联的哥特窗俯瞰着石灰岩峭壁和荒谷——正说着，我就看见小黑那乌黑的身形贴着西墙潜行，在新装的本板上抓挠，板下是古老的石头。

我对那人说，想必是老石墙里有什么特别的气味或散发，人的感官察觉不到，却透过新木作影响着猫的精细器官。这话我真信；当那伙计提议是老鼠捣乱时，我说这里三百年没有老鼠了，连四野的田鼠也难得进这些高墙，从来没听说它们走失到这儿过。当天下午我拜访诺里斯上尉，他向我保证，田鼠这样突然地、破例地侵入住修院，是难以置信的。

===Original===

That night, dispensing as usual with a valet, I retired in the west tower chamber which I had chosen as my own, reached from the study by a stone staircase and short gallery﻿—the former partly ancient, the latter entirely restored. This room was circular, very high, and without wainscotting, being hung with arras which I had myself chosen in London.

Seeing that Nigger-Man was with me, I shut the heavy Gothic door and retired by the light of the electric bulbs which so cleverly counterfeited candles, finally switching off the light and sinking on the carved and canopied four-poster, with the venerable cat in his accustomed place across my feet. I did not draw the curtains, but gazed out at the narrow north window which I faced. There was a suspicion of aurora in the sky, and the delicate traceries of the window were pleasantly silhouetted.

At some time I must have fallen quietly asleep, for I recall a distinct sense of leaving strange dreams, when the cat started violently from his placid position. I saw him in the faint auroral glow, head strained forward, forefeet on my ankles, and hind feet stretched behind. He was looking intensely at a point on the wall somewhat west of the window, a point which to my eye had nothing to mark it, but toward which all my attention was now directed.

And as I watched, I knew that Nigger-Man was not vainly excited. Whether the arras actually moved I cannot say. I think it did, very slightly. But what I can swear to is that behind it I heard a low, distinct scurrying as of rats or mice. In a moment the cat had jumped bodily on the screening tapestry, bringing the affected section to the floor with his weight, and exposing a damp, ancient wall of stone; patched here and there by the restorers, and devoid of any trace of rodent prowlers.

Nigger-Man raced up and down the floor by this part of the wall, clawing the fallen arras and seemingly trying at times to insert a paw between the wall and the oaken floor. He found nothing, and after a time returned wearily to his place across my feet. I had not moved, but I did not sleep again that night.
