===Chinese===

当夜，照例不用贴身仆人，我睡进西塔楼我选作卧室的房间，由书房经一道石楼梯和短短的画廊抵达——楼梯一半是古物，画廊则完全新修。房间是圆形的，非常高，没有墙板，挂着我在伦敦亲自挑选的花毡。

见小黑同我在一起，我关上厚重的哥特式房门，就着巧妙地仿成蜡烛的电灯泡的光上床，末了熄灯，陷进带雕顶篷的四柱床，那只可敬的猫照例睡在我脚头。我没有拉帘，望着面前的窄窄北窗。天上有一丝极光的迹象，窗棂精巧的纹样衬在天光上，悦目得很。

不知什么时候我一定已静静睡着，因为记得正从怪梦里脱身的清楚感觉，猫却猛地从它安详的位置惊起。我借着微弱的极光看见它，头紧张地前伸，前脚搭在我脚踝上，后脚朝后蹬直。它死死盯着墙上窗子偏西的一个点——在我眼里那一点毫无记认，可此刻我的全部注意都朝它去了。

我望着，便知道小黑的兴奋不是无端。花毡究竟动没动，我说不准。我想是动了，动得极轻。可我能起誓的是：毡后我听见了低低的、分明的疾奔声，像老鼠。转眼间猫已整个扑上遮挡的花毡，把那一段带翻在地，露出一面潮湿的古石墙——修复者在这里那里补过，全无啮齿动物出没的痕迹。

小黑顺着这段墙根来回疾窜，爪子抓着落地的花毡，似乎时时还想把一只爪子塞进墙和橡木地板的缝里。它什么也没找到，过一阵疲疲地回到我脚头老位置。我没有动，可那夜再没睡着。

===Original===

In the morning I questioned all the servants, and found that none of them had noticed anything unusual, save that the cook remembered the actions of a cat which had rested on her windowsill. This cat had howled at some unknown hour of the night, awaking the cook in time for her to see him dart purposefully out of the open door down the stairs. I drowsed away the noontime, and in the afternoon called again on Capt. Norrys, who became exceedingly interested in what I told him. The odd incidents﻿—so slight yet so curious﻿—appealed to his sense of the picturesque, and elicited from him a number of reminiscences of local ghostly lore. We were genuinely perplexed at the presence of rats, and Norrys lent me some traps and paris-green, which I had the servants place in strategic localities when I returned.

I retired early, being very sleepy, but was harassed by dreams of the most horrible sort. I seemed to be looking down from an immense height upon a twilit grotto, knee-deep with filth, where a white-bearded daemon swineherd drove about with his staff a flock of fungous, flabby beasts whose appearance filled me with unutterable loathing. Then, as the swineherd paused and nodded over his task, a mighty swarm of rats rained down on the stinking abyss and fell to devouring beasts and man alike.

From this terrific vision I was abruptly awaked by the motions of Nigger-Man, who had been sleeping as usual across my feet. This time I did not have to question the source of his snarls and hisses, and of the fear which made him sink his claws into my ankle, unconscious of their effect; for on every side of the chamber the walls were alive with nauseous sound﻿—the verminous slithering of ravenous, gigantic rats. There was now no aurora to show the state of the arras﻿—the fallen section of which had been replaced﻿—but I was not too frightened to switch on the light.

===Chinese===

早晨我问遍了仆人，没有人觉察任何异常，只有厨娘记得一只在她窗台上歇过的猫的举动。那猫在夜里不知什么时候嚎叫，叫醒了厨娘，正好看见它一头冲出敞开的门，窜下楼梯。中午我打了个盹，下午又去拜访诺里斯上尉，他对我讲的极其感兴趣。这些古怪的事件——那么轻，又那么蹊跷——正投他那爱奇观的脾胃，引出了他一大堆本地鬼传说的旧话。对老鼠的出现我们真摸不着头脑；诺里斯借了我几只捕鼠夹和巴黎绿，我回去后叫仆人安置在要紧的处所。

我早早睡了，困得很，却被最可怕的梦纠缠着。我仿佛从一个无极高处俯望一个暮光的地穴，没膝的秽物里，一个白须的魔鬼猪倌拿杖赶着一群生了霉、软塌塌的牲畜，那模样叫我生出说不出的憎恶。随后，猪倌停住，对着他的活计点头，一大群老鼠便降进这恶臭的深渊，动手把牲畜和猪倌一并吃掉。

我从这可怕的幻象里猛地被小黑的动作弄醒——它照例睡在我脚头。这一次，我不必再问它低吼和嘶叫的来由，不必再问它把爪子不自觉地掐进我脚踝的恐惧；因为房间四壁的墙里，到处都活着令人作呕的声音——饥饿的、巨鼠的、蠕虫般的窸窣疾奔。此刻没有极光照出花毡的状况——翻落的那段已经重新挂好——但我还没有怕到不敢开灯。

===Original===

As the bulbs leapt into radiance I saw a hideous shaking all over the tapestry, causing the somewhat peculiar designs to execute a singular dance of death. This motion disappeared almost at once, and the sound with it. Springing out of bed, I poked at the arras with the long handle of a warming-pan that rested near, and lifted one section to see what lay beneath. There was nothing but the patched stone wall, and even the cat had lost his tense realization of abnormal presences. When I examined the circular trap that had been placed in the room, I found all of the openings sprung, though no trace remained of what had been caught and had escaped.

Further sleep was out of the question, so, lighting a candle, I opened the door and went out in the gallery toward the stairs to my study, Nigger-Man following at my heels. Before we had reached the stone steps, however, the cat darted ahead of me and vanished down the ancient flight. As I descended the stairs myself, I became suddenly aware of sounds in the great room below; sounds of a nature which could not be mistaken.

The oak-paneled walls were alive with rats, scampering and milling, whilst Nigger-Man was racing about with the fury of a baffled hunter. Reaching the bottom, I switched on the light, which did not this time cause the noise to subside. The rats continued their riot, stampeding with such force and distinctness that I could finally assign to their motions a definite direction. These creatures, in numbers apparently inexhaustible, were engaged in one stupendous migration from inconceivable heights to some depth conceivably, or inconceivably, below.

I now heard steps in the corridor, and in another moment two servants pushed open the massive door. They were searching the house for some unknown source of disturbance which had thrown all the cats into a snarling panic and caused them to plunge precipitately down several flights of stairs and squat, yowling, before the closed door to the sub-cellar. I asked them if they had heard the rats, but they replied in the negative. And when I turned to call their attention to the sounds in the panels, I realized that the noise had ceased.

===Chinese===

灯泡一亮，我看见整幅花毡一阵可憎的抖动，使那些本就古怪的图样跳起了一场奇特的死亡之舞。抖动几乎立刻止了，声音也随之消失。我跳下床，拿起近旁一只长柄温锅，捅了捅花毡，掀起一段看底下有什么。只有补过的石墙；连猫也松开了它对异常存在的紧张察觉。我检查了屋里放置的圆形捕鼠夹，发现所有的门都弹开了，却毫无被捉住又逃脱者的痕迹。

再睡是不用想了；于是我点起蜡烛，开门走进画廊，朝书房的楼梯去，小黑跟着脚跟。还没到石阶，猫已窜到我前头，消失在古老的楼梯下了。我自己下楼时，忽然听见下面大厅里的声音；那声音的性质不会听错。

橡木镶板的墙里满是老鼠，奔突打转；小黑正带着失意的猎人的狂怒四处猛冲。到了底下，我打开灯，这一次声音并没有平息。老鼠继续它们的骚乱，奔踏得那样有力、那样分明，我终于能给它们的动向指定一个确切的方向。这些数目显然取之不尽的家伙，正从事一场浩大的迁徙——从不可想象的高处，迁往某个可以想象、或不可想象的深处。

这会儿走廊里响起脚步，转眼两个仆人推开沉重的门。他们正在全屋搜寻这莫名的骚源——它把所有的猫都抛进咆哮的恐慌，叫它们一头冲下好几段楼梯，蹲在地下深窖紧闭的门前嚎叫。我问他们听见老鼠没有，他们答说没有。等我转身叫他们注意镶板里的声音时，我发觉声音已经停了。

===Original===

With the two men, I went down to the door of the sub-cellar, but found the cats already dispersed. Later I resolved to explore the crypt below, but for the present I merely made a round of the traps. All were sprung, yet all were tenantless. Satisfying myself that no one had heard the rats save the felines and me, I sat in my study till morning, thinking profoundly, and recalling every scrap of legend I had unearthed concerning the building I inhabited.

---

I slept some in the forenoon, leaning back in the one comfortable library chair which my medieval plan of furnishing could not banish. Later I telephoned to Capt. Norrys, who came over and helped me explore the sub-cellar.

Absolutely nothing untoward was found, although we could not repress a thrill at the knowledge that this vault was built by Roman hands. Every low arch and massive pillar was Roman﻿—not the debased Romanesque of the bungling Saxons, but the severe and harmonious classicism of the age of the Caesars; indeed, the walls abounded with inscriptions familiar to the antiquarians who had repeatedly explored the place﻿—things like “**P. Getae. Prop﻿ ﻿… Temp﻿ ﻿… Dona﻿ ﻿…**” and “**L. Praec﻿ ﻿… Vs﻿ ﻿… Pontifi﻿ ﻿… Atys﻿ ﻿…**”

The reference to Atys made me shiver, for I had read Catullus and knew something of the hideous rites of the Eastern god, whose worship was so mixed with that of Cybele. Norrys and I, by the light of lanterns, tried to interpret the odd and nearly effaced designs on certain irregularly rectangular blocks of stone generally held to be altars, but could make nothing of them. We remembered that one pattern, a sort of rayed sun, was held by students to imply a non-Roman origin, suggesting that these altars had merely been adopted by the Roman priests from some older and perhaps aboriginal temple on the same site. On one of these blocks were some brown stains which made me wonder. The largest, in the center of the room, had certain features on the upper surface which indicated its connection with fire﻿—probably burnt offerings.

===Chinese===

同那两个人一起，我下到深窖门口，猫却已经散了。后来我决意探一探底下的地窟，眼下只先巡视了一圈捕鼠夹。夹子全都弹开，又全都空着。确认了除了猫和我没人听见过老鼠之后，我在书房里坐到天亮，深深想着，把掘出的关于我栖身这座建筑的传说，一条条回想。

---

上午我斜在中世纪陈设没能赶走的那把舒服的图书室座椅里睡了些时。随后我打电话给诺里斯上尉，他过来帮我探查深窖。

绝对没有发现任何异状，尽管我们无法压抑一阵战栗——因为知道这地窟出自罗马人之手。每一道矮拱、每一根巨柱都是罗马的——不是笨拙撒克逊人的堕落罗马风，而是凯撒时代严峻而和谐的古典；墙壁上确实布满铭文，反复探察此地的古物学家们都熟——比如「P. Getae. Prop…Temp…Dona…」和「L. Praec…Vs…Pontifi…Atys…」

提到阿提斯叫我打了个寒噤，因为我读过卡图卢斯，知道这位东方之神那些可怖仪式的一些，他的崇拜同库柏勒的混得那样深。我和诺里斯打着灯笼，试着辨认某些不规则长方石块——一般认作祭坛——上那些古怪而几乎磨灭的图样，但什么也认不出。我们记起，其中一种图样，一种放射的太阳，学者们认为它暗示非罗马的来源，说明这些祭坛只是罗马祭司从同址某座更古老、或许原住民的神庙里沿用来的。其中一块上有几点棕色的渍，叫我犯琢磨。最大的一块在屋子正中，上表面有些特征表明它同火有关——多半是燔祭。

===Original===

Such were the sights in that crypt before whose door the cats had howled, and where Norrys and I now determined to pass the night. Couches were brought down by the servants, who were told not to mind any nocturnal actions of the cats, and Nigger-Man was admitted as much for help as for companionship. We decided to keep the great oak door﻿—a modern replica with slits for ventilation﻿—tightly closed; and, with this attended to, we retired with lanterns still burning to await whatever might occur.

The vault was very deep in the foundations of the priory, and undoubtedly far down on the face of the beetling limestone cliff overlooking the waste valley. That it had been the goal of the scuffling and unexplainable rats I could not doubt, though why, I could not tell. As we lay there expectantly, I found my vigil occasionally mixed with half-formed dreams from which the uneasy motions of the cat across my feet would rouse me.

These dreams were not wholesome, but horribly like the one I had had the night before. I saw again the twilit grotto, and the swineherd with his unmentionable fungous beasts wallowing in filth, and as I looked at these things they seemed nearer and more distinct﻿—so distinct that I could almost observe their features. Then I did observe the flabby features of one of them﻿—and awaked with such a scream that Nigger-Man started up, whilst Capt. Norrys, who had not slept, laughed considerably. Norrys might have laughed more﻿—or perhaps less﻿—had he known what it was that made me scream. But I did not remember myself till later. Ultimate horror often paralyzes memory in a merciful way.

Norrys waked me when the phenomena began. Out of the same frightful dream I was called by his gentle shaking and his urging to listen to the cats. Indeed, there was much to listen to, for beyond the closed door at the head of the stone steps was a veritable nightmare of feline yelling and clawing, whilst Nigger-Man, unmindful of his kindred outside, was running excitedly around the bare stone walls, in which I heard the same babel of scurrying rats that had troubled me the night before.

===Chinese===

猫曾在那地窟门前嚎叫；如今我和诺里斯决定就在里面过夜。仆人搬下睡榻，吩咐他们别管猫在夜里的任何举动；小黑也被放了进来，一半为伴，一半为帮。我们决定把那扇大橡木门——一件带通风缝的现代复制品——紧紧关上；办妥之后，我们躺下，灯笼仍点着，等可能发生的任何事。

那地窖深在修道院地基里，无疑也深在俯瞰荒谷的、壁立的石灰岩崖面上。它是那阵窸窣而无法解释的鼠群的目的地，这一点我不怀疑，虽然为什么，我说不出。我们期待地躺着，我发觉守夜时时混进半成的梦，猫在我脚头的不安动静会把我惊醒。

这些梦不干净，同头晚那个像得可怕。我又看见暮光的地穴、猪倌和他那些说不出口的生霉的牲口在秽物里打滚；我望着，它们显得越来越近、越来越分明——分明得我几乎能看清它们的脸。随后我当真看清了其中一只那张软塌塌的脸——并且尖叫着醒来，惊得小黑跳起来，而彻夜未眠的诺里斯上尉笑了个够。倘若诺里斯知道是什么叫我尖叫，他也许笑得更多——或者更少。可我自己也是后来才记起来。极度的恐怖常会慈悲地瘫痪记忆。

异象开始时，诺里斯唤醒了我。我从同样可怕的梦里被他轻轻摇醒，听他催我听猫。确实大有可听：石阶顶上紧闭的门那一面，是一场名副其实的猫叫和抓挠的噩梦；而小黑全然不管门外的同类，正绕着光秃的石墙激动地奔逐——墙里，我又听见了头晚搅扰我的那阵疾奔老鼠的喧声。

===Original===

An acute terror now rose within me, for here were anomalies which nothing normal could well explain. These rats, if not the creatures of a madness which I shared with the cats alone, must be burrowing and sliding in Roman walls I had thought to be of solid limestone blocks﻿ ﻿… unless perhaps the action of water through more than seventeen centuries had eaten winding tunnels which rodent bodies had worn clear and ample﻿ ﻿… But even so, the spectral horror was no less; for if these were living vermin why did not Norrys hear their disgusting commotion? Why did he urge me to watch Nigger-Man and listen to the cats outside, and why did he guess wildly and vaguely at what could have aroused them?

By the time I had managed to tell him, as rationally as I could, what I thought I was hearing, my ears gave me the last fading impression of the scurrying; which had retreated still downward, far underneath this deepest of sub-cellars till it seemed as if the whole cliff below were riddled with questing rats. Norrys was not as skeptical as I had anticipated, but instead seemed profoundly moved. He motioned to me to notice that the cats at the door had ceased their clamor, as if giving up the rats for lost; whilst Nigger-Man had a burst of renewed restlessness, and was clawing frantically around the bottom of the large stone altar in the center of the room, which was nearer Norrys’ couch than mine.

My fear of the unknown was at this point very great. Something astounding had occurred, and I saw that Capt. Norrys, a younger, stouter, and presumably more naturally materialistic man, was affected fully as much as myself﻿—perhaps because of his lifelong and intimate, familiarity with local legend. We could for the moment do nothing but watch the old black cat as he pawed with decreasing fervor at the base of the altar, occasionally looking up and mewing to me in that persuasive manner which he used when he wished me to perform some favor for him.

Norrys now took a lantern close to the altar and examined the place where Nigger-Man was pawing; silently kneeling and scraping away the lichens of centuries which joined the massive pre-Roman block to the tesselated floor. He did not find anything, and was about to abandon his efforts when I noticed a trivial circumstance which made me shudder, even though it implied nothing more than I had already imagined.

===Chinese===

此刻我心里升起一阵尖锐的恐怖，因为这里的反常，没有任何正常的东西解释得了。这些老鼠，若不是我同猫共享的一种疯狂造出来的东西，就必定在我以为整块石灰岩的罗马墙里打洞、滑行……除非十七个多世纪里水的侵蚀蚀出了蜿蜒的隧道，啮齿的身体又把它们磨得通畅宽绰……可即便如此，那幽灵般的恐怖丝毫未减；因为这些若是活的老鼠，诺里斯为什么听不见它们那令人作呕的骚动？他为什么只一味叫我看着小黑、听着外面的猫，为什么对什么惊动了它们只能胡乱地、含糊地猜？

等我把自以为听见的东西，尽量理性地告诉他，我耳朵里捕捉到疾奔声最后的余息；它又向下退去了，远远退到这最深的地窖底下，直到仿佛整个崖体都被寻径的老鼠蛀遍。诺里斯没有我预想的那样怀疑，反而大受震动。他示意我看：门边的猫已经止了喧哗，仿佛对老鼠死了心；而小黑又爆发了一阵新的不安，正围着屋子中央那座大石祭坛的底座狂抓乱扒——那祭坛离诺里斯的睡榻比离我的近。

我对未知的恐惧此刻非常之大。有了不得了的事，而我看得出，诺里斯上尉——更年轻、更壮实、照理更天生唯物的人——受的震动不在我之下；或许是因为他终身亲近本地传说之故。此刻我们一筹莫展，只能看着那老黑猫，看它以渐减的热忱拍打祭坛底部，时时抬头朝我喳喳，用那种它要我帮它忙时的恳求样子。

诺里斯于是提一盏灯笼凑近祭坛，查看小黑扒抓的地方；默默跪下，刮去把前罗马大石块同嵌花地面连在一起的几个世纪的地衣。他一无所获，正要罢手，我注意到一件小事，叫我打了个寒噤——尽管它意味的无非是我已经想象过的。

===Original===

I told him of it, and we both looked at its almost imperceptible manifestation with the fixedness of fascinated discovery and acknowledgment. It was only this﻿—that the flame of the lantern set down near the altar was slightly but certainly flickering from a draught of air which it had not before received, and which came indubitably from the crevice between floor and altar where Norrys was scraping away the lichens.

---

We spent the rest of the night in the brilliantly-lighted study, nervously discussing what we should do next. The discovery that some vault deeper than the deepest known masonry of the Romans underlay this accursed pile; some vault unsuspected by the curious antiquarians of three centuries; would have been sufficient to excite us without any background of the sinister. As it was, the fascination became twofold; and we paused in doubt whether to abandon our search and quit the priory forever in superstitious caution, or to gratify our sense of adventure and brave whatever horrors might await us in the unknown depths.

By morning we had compromised, and decided to go to London to gather a group of archaeologists and scientific men fit to cope with the mystery. It should be mentioned that before leaving the sub-cellar we had vainly tried to move the central altar which we now recognized as the gate to a new pit of nameless fear. What secret would open the gate, wiser men than we would have to find.

During many days in London Capt. Norrys and I presented our facts, conjectures, and legendary anecdotes to five eminent authorities, all men who could be trusted to respect any family disclosures which future explorations might develop. We found most of them little disposed to scoff, but, instead, intensely interested and sincerely sympathetic. It is hardly necessary to name them all, but I may say that they included Sir William Brinton, whose excavations in the Troad excited most of the world in their day. As we all took the train for Anchester I felt myself poised on the brink of frightful revelations, a sensation symbolized by the air of mourning among the many Americans at the unexpected death of the President on the other side of the world.

---

===Chinese===

我告诉了他；我们两人盯着它那几乎无法察觉的显示，怀着有所发现的入迷和确认。只是这样：放在祭坛近旁的灯笼的火苗，轻微却确凿地闪动着，被一股气流——一股它先前不曾受到的、无疑来自地面与祭坛之间缝隙的气流，那缝隙正是诺里斯刮地衣的地方。

---

这夜余下的时间，我们在灯光明亮的书房里神经过敏地商量下一步。发现这座受诅的建筑底下，还有比已知最深的罗马砌工更深的地窖——三个世纪里好奇的古物学家们都未曾料到的地窖——单是这一点，没有那阴森的底色，也够叫我们兴奋了。如今这样，魅力成了双份；我们停住，进退两难：是放弃搜寻，出于迷信的谨慎永远离开修道院呢，还是满足冒险之心，去面对未知深处可能等着我们的一切恐怖。

到早晨我们折中了：决定去伦敦，集一组考古学家和科学人士，来对付这个谜。应当一提，离开深窖之前，我们试图挪动中央那座祭坛——如今我们认出它是通往一个新的、无名恐惧之坑的门——但没有成功。什么秘密能开这扇门，得由比我们更聪明的人来找。

在伦敦的许多天里，我和诺里斯上尉把事实、推测和掌故摆给五位显赫的权威——都是些可望尊重日后发掘可能揭出的任何家私的人。我们发现他们大多无意嘲笑，反而兴致极浓、真诚同情。不必一一列举姓名，只消说其中包括威廉·布林顿爵士，他在特洛亚德的发掘，当年轰动过半个世界。当我们全体坐上开往安彻斯特的火车，我自觉正站在可怕启示的崖沿——那感觉，同当天世界上许多美国人隔着半个地球为总统的猝死而哀悼的气氛，恰成象征。

---

===Original===

On the evening of August 7th we reached Exham Priory, where the servants assured me that nothing unusual had occurred. The cats, even old Nigger-Man, had been perfectly placid; and not a trap in the house had been sprung. We were to begin exploring on the following day, awaiting which I assigned well-appointed rooms to all my guests.

I myself retired in my own tower chamber, with Nigger-Man across my feet. Sleep came quickly, but hideous dreams assailed me. There was a vision of a Roman feast like that of Trimalchio, with a horror in a covered platter. Then came that damnable, recurrent thing about the swineherd and his filthy drove in the twilit grotto. Yet when I awoke it was full daylight, with normal sounds in the house below. The rats, living or spectral, had not troubled me; and Nigger-Man was still quietly asleep. On going down, I found that the same tranquillity had prevailed elsewhere; a condition which one of the assembled savants﻿—a fellow named Thornton, devoted to the psychic﻿—rather absurdly laid to the fact that I had now been shown the thing which certain forces had wished to show me.

All was now ready, and at 11 a.m. our entire group of seven men, bearing powerful electric searchlights and implements of excavation, went down to the sub-cellar and bolted the door behind us. Nigger-Man was with us, for the investigators found no occasion to despise his excitability, and were indeed anxious that he be present in case of obscure rodent manifestations. We noted the Roman inscriptions and unknown altar designs only briefly, for three of the savants had already seen them, and all knew their characteristics. Prime attention was paid to the momentous central altar, and within an hour Sir William Brinton had caused it to tilt backward, balanced by some unknown species of counterweight.

There now lay revealed such a horror as would have overwhelmed us had we not been prepared. Through a nearly square opening in the tiled floor, sprawling on a flight of stone steps so prodigiously worn that it was little more than an inclined plane at the center, was a ghastly array of human or semi-human bones. Those which retained their collocation as skeletons showed attitudes of panic fear, and over all were the marks of rodent gnawing. The skulls denoted nothing short of utter idiocy, cretinism, or primitive semi-apedom.

===Chinese===

八月七日傍晚，我们抵达埃克瑟姆修道院，仆人向我保证一切如常。猫，连老小黑在内，一直安安静静；屋里一只夹子也没有弹开。探测定于次日开始；等候期间，我给每位客人分派了舒适的房间。

我自己照旧睡在塔楼卧室，小黑卧在脚头。睡意来得快，可骇人的梦又来纠缠。有一回梦见一场特里马尔基奥式的罗马盛宴，带盖的大盘里盛着恐怖。随后又是那该死的、反复的猪倌和暮光地穴里他那龌龊的猪群。可醒来已是白天，楼下家里的声响如常。老鼠，活的也罢幽灵的也罢，没有搅我；小黑还静静睡着。下楼一看，各处同样平静；与会的学者之一，一个研究灵学、名叫桑顿的，把这归因于我已被某些力量要给我看的东西给看过了——这解释相当荒唐。

一切就绪。上午十一点，我们七人一组，带着强力的电探灯和发掘器械，下到深窖，闩上了身后的门。小黑随我们同去——研究者们没有谁看不起它的易激动，反而巴不得它在场，以防晦暗的啮齿迹象再现。罗马铭文和无名祭坛图样只草草看了一眼，三位学者已经见过，特色人人皆知。首要的注意给了中央那座关系重大的祭坛；不出一个钟头，威廉·布林顿爵士已设法叫它向后倾侧，由某种未知的配重平衡着。

于是显露出来的，是若非早有准备、我们必将被压倒的恐怖。嵌花地面一处近乎方形的开口里，一串石阶被磨得没了形状，中央几乎成了一道斜坡，上面狼藉着一堆人骨或半人的骸骨。保持骨架排列的那些，显出惊逃的姿势；所有骨上都有啮齿啃过的痕。那些头骨说明的，不折不扣是彻底的白痴、呆小症，或原始的半猿。

===Original===

Above the hellishly littered steps arched a descending passage seemingly chiseled from the solid rock, and conducting a current of air. This current was not a sudden and noxious rush as from a closed vault, but a cool breeze with something of freshness in it. We did not pause long, but shiveringly began to clear a passage down the steps. It was then that Sir William, examining the hewn walls, made the odd observation that the passage, according to the direction of the strokes, must have been chiseled *from beneath*.

---

I must be very deliberate now, and choose my words.

After ploughing down a few steps amidst the gnawed bones we saw that there was light ahead; not any mystic phosphorescence, but a filtered daylight which could not come except from unknown fissures in the cliff that overlooked the waste valley. That such fissures had escaped notice from outside was hardly remarkable, for not only is the valley wholly uninhabited, but the cliff is so high and beetling that only an aeronaut could study its face in detail. A few steps more, and our breaths were literally snatched from us by what we saw; so literally that Thornton, the psychic investigator, actually fainted in the arms of the dazed man who stood behind him. Norrys, his plump face utterly white and flabby, simply cried out inarticulately; whilst I think that what I did was to gasp or hiss, and cover my eyes.

The man behind me﻿—the only one of the party older than I﻿—croaked the hackneyed “My God!” in the most cracked voice I ever head. Of seven cultivated men, only Sir William Brinton retained his composure, a thing the more to his credit because he led the party and must have seen the sight first.

===Chinese===

在地狱般狼藉的台阶上方，一道向下的通道仿佛从整岩里凿出，透着一股气流。这气流不是密闭地窖里那种突发的毒风，而是一阵凉爽的、带着几分清新气息的微风。我们没有多停，打着抖开始清理台阶的通路。就在那时，威廉爵士检查凿痕累累的壁面，发表了那句古怪的议论：照凿痕的方向，这条通道必定是从底下凿上来的。

---

现在，我必须写得非常审慎，字字斟酌。

踩着啃过的白骨下了几级台阶，我们看见前面有光；不是什么神秘的磷光，而是一线滤过的日光，只可能来自俯瞰荒谷的峭壁上未知的裂罅。那些裂罅从外面没被注意到，并不奇怪：谷里全无人烟，崖又高又险，只有飞行家才能细看崖面。再走几步，我们的呼吸简直被眼前的景象夺走了；简直到这样的地步：灵学研究者桑顿真的晕倒在身后一个发怔的人怀里。诺里斯，胖脸彻底白了、软了，只发出不成声的喊叫；我想我做的，是倒抽一口冷气，然后捂住了眼睛。

我身后那个人——一行人里唯一比我年长的——用我听过的最破的嗓子，哑出那句俗套的「我的上帝！」七个有教养的人里，只有威廉·布林顿爵士保住了镇定，这尤其值得称道，因为他领队，必定头一个看见那景象。

===Original===

It was a twilit grotto of enormous height, stretching away farther than any eye could see; a subterraneous world of limitless mystery and horrible suggestion. There were buildings and other architectural remains﻿—in one terrified glance I saw a weird pattern of tumuli, a savage circle of monoliths, a low-domed Roman ruin, a sprawling Saxon pile, and an early English edifice of wood﻿—but all these were dwarfed by the ghoulish spectacle presented by the general surface of the ground. For yards about the steps extended an insane tangle of human bones, or bones at least as human as those on the steps. Like a foamy sea they stretched, some fallen apart, but others wholly or partly articulated as skeletons; these latter invariably in postures of daemoniac frenzy, either fighting off some menace or clutching other forms with cannibal intent.

When Dr. Trask, the anthropologist, stooped to classify the skulls, he found a degraded mixture which utterly baffled him. They were mostly lower than the Piltdown man in the scale of evolution, but in every case definitely human. Many were of higher grade, and a very few were the skulls of supremely and sensitively developed types. All the bones were gnawed, mostly by rats, but somewhat by others of the half-human drove. Mixed with them were many tiny bones of rats﻿—fallen members of the lethal army which closed the ancient epic.

I wonder that any man among us lived and kept his sanity through that hideous day of discovery. Not Hoffman or Huysmans could conceive a scene more wildly incredible, more frenetically repellent, or more Gothically grotesque than the twilit grotto through which we seven staggered; each stumbling on revelation after revelation, and trying to keep for the nonce from thinking of the events which must have taken place there three hundred, or a thousand, or two thousand, or ten thousand years ago. It was the antechamber of hell, and poor Thornton fainted again when Trask told him that some of the skeleton things must have descended as quadrupeds through the last twenty or more generations.

---

===Chinese===

那是一个暮光的地穴，高得吓人，伸向目力不及的远方；一个地下的世界，无边的神秘和可怖的暗示。有建筑和其他建筑遗迹——惊惶的一瞥里，我看见坟丘的诡异布局、独石围成的野蛮圆阵、一座低圆顶的罗马废墟、一片摊开的撒克逊建筑，还有一座早期英格兰的木屋——可这一切，都被地面整体呈现的食尸鬼景象比成了侏儒。台阶四周几码之内，摊着人骨的疯狂乱丛——或者至少同台阶上那些一样人的骨头。它们像起沫的海铺开去，有的散了架，有的整个或部分还连成骨架；后者一概摆着魔鬼般狂乱的姿势，不是在抵挡什么威胁，就是怀着吃人的意图攫住别的形体。

人类学家特拉斯克博士俯身去分类那些头骨，发现一种令他全然不知所措的退化混杂。它们大多低于皮尔当人的进化层级，却每一例都确凿是人。许多属于较高层级，极少数是至为发达、至为精细的类型之颅。骨头全被啃过，多半是老鼠，有些是那半人畜群里的其他成员。中间混着大量细小的鼠骨——那支终结了古老史诗的致命大军的阵亡者。

我们中间居然有人在那可怕的发现之日后活着保住神志，我至今奇怪。霍夫曼或于斯曼也设想不出比这暮光地穴更狂乱、更难信、更哥特地狰狞的场面；我们七个人踉跄行在其间，一个接一个地栽进启示，还勉强暂且不去想三百年、一千年、两千年前、一万年前这里必定发生过的事。那是地狱的前厅；可怜的桑顿又晕了一回，当特拉斯克告诉他，那些骨架之物里有几个，想必最后二十代乃至更多代都是四肢着地爬行下来的。

---

===Original===

Horror piled on horror as we began to interpret the architectural remains. The quadruped things﻿—with their occasional recruits from the biped class﻿—had been kept in stone pens, out of which they must have broken in their last delirium of hunger or rat-fear. There had been great herds of them, evidently fattened on the coarse vegetables whose remains could be found as a sort of poisonous ensilage at the bottom of huge stone bins older than Rome. I knew now why my ancestors had had such excessive gardens﻿—would to heaven I could forget! The purpose of the herds I did not have to ask.

Sir William, standing with his searchlight in the Roman ruin, translated aloud the most shocking ritual I have ever known; and told of the diet of the antediluvian cult which the priests of Cybele found and mingled with their own. Norrys, used as he was to the trenches, could not walk straight when he came out of the English building. It was a butcher shop and kitchen﻿—he had expected that﻿—but it was too much to see familiar English implements in such a place, and to read familiar English *graffiti* there, some as recent as 1610. I could not go in that building﻿—that building whose daemon activities were stopped only by the dagger of my ancestor Walter de la Poer.

What I did venture to enter was the low Saxon building, whose oaken door had fallen, and there I found a terrible row of ten stone cells with rusty bars. Three had tenants, all skeletons of high grade, and on the bony forefinger of one I found a seal ring with my own coat-of-arms. Sir William found a vault with far older cells below the Roman chapel, but these cells were empty. Below them was a low crypt with cases of formally arranged bones, some of them bearing terrible parallel inscriptions carved in Latin, Greek, and the tongue of Phrygia.

Meanwhile, Dr. Trask had opened one of the prehistoric tumuli, and brought to light skulls which were slightly more human than a gorilla’s, and which bore indescribable ideographic carvings. Through all this horror my cat stalked unperturbed. Once I saw him monstrously perched atop a mountain of bones, and wondered at the secrets that might lie behind his yellow eyes.

===Chinese===

当我们开始解读那些建筑遗迹，恐怖之上又摞恐怖。那些四足的东西——偶尔有从两足那边补充进来的——养在石栏里，想必是在最后的饥饿或鼠惧的谵狂里破栏而出的。它们的数量曾是大群，显然用粗蔬催肥——那残剩如今还以毒饲料的形态堆在比罗马还老的大石槽底。我现在明白了我的祖先为什么有那么过分的园圃——但愿上天叫我忘掉！畜群的用途，我不必问。

威廉爵士举着探灯站在罗马废墟里，高声译出了我所知的最骇人的祭仪；讲了大洪水前那个教团的食谱——库柏勒的祭司们发现它，又把它揉进了自己的。诺里斯，尽管惯了战壕，从那座英格兰建筑里出来时脚步都直不起来。那是一间肉铺兼厨房——他料到了——可是在那样的地方看见熟悉的英格兰家什，又在那里读到熟悉的英文涂鸦，有的近到一六一〇年，实在叫人受不了。我进不去那座建筑——那座建筑的魔鬼行止，只被我先祖沃尔特·德·拉·波尔的匕首制止。

我敢进去的，是那座低矮的撒克逊建筑，橡木门已倒；我在里面发现一排十个带锈栏的石囚室，可怕的行列。三间有住客，全是高级的骨架；其中一具的骨指上，我找到一枚印章戒指，刻着我自己的纹章。威廉爵士在罗马小堂底下又发现一座地窖，带更古老的囚室，但囚室是空的。再往下，是一间矮地宫，排着一柜一柜的骨殖，有的带着骇人的、拉丁、希腊和弗里吉亚语并刻的铭文。

其间，特拉斯克博士打开了一座史前坟丘，起出一些只比大猩猩多几分人样的头骨，带着无从形容的表意刻痕。这一切恐怖中间，我的猫昂然踱步，不为所动。有一回我看见它狰狞地蹲踞在一座白骨山的顶上，暗想它那双黄眼睛背后，可能藏着什么样的秘密。

===Original===

Having grasped to some slight degree the frightful revelations of this twilit area﻿—an area so hideously foreshadowed by my recurrent dream﻿—we turned to that apparently boundless depth of midnight cavern where no ray of light from the cliff could penetrate. We shall never know what sightless Stygian worlds yawn beyond the little distance we went, for it was decided that such secrets are not good for mankind. But there was plenty to engross us close at hand, for we had not gone far before the searchlights showed that accursed infinity of pits in which the rats had feasted, and whose sudden lack of replenishment had driven the ravenous rodent army first to turn on the living herds of starving things, and then to burst forth from the priory in that historic orgy of devastation which the peasants will never forget.

God! those carrion black pits of sawed, picked bones and opened skulls! Those nightmare chasms choked with the pithecanthropoid, Celtic, Roman, and English bones of countless unhallowed centuries! Some of them were full, and none can say how deep they had once been. Others were still bottomless to our searchlights, and peopled by unnamable fancies. What, I thought, of the hapless rats that stumbled into such traps amidst the blackness of their quests in this grisly Tartarus?

Once my foot slipped near a horribly yawning brink, and I had a moment of ecstatic fear. I must have been musing a long time, for I could not see any of the party but the plump Capt. Norrys. Then there came a sound from that inky, boundless, farther distance that I thought I knew; and I saw my old black cat dart past me like a winged Egyptian god, straight into the illimitable gulf of the unknown. But I was not far behind, for there was no doubt after another second. It was the eldritch scurrying of those fiend-born rats, always questing for new horrors, and determined to lead me on even unto those grinning caverns of earth’s center where Nyarlathotep, the mad faceless god, howls blindly in the darkness to the piping of two amorphous idiot flute-players.

My searchlight expired, but still I ran. I heard voices, and yowls, and echoes, but above all there gently rose that impious, insidious scurrying; gently rising, rising, as a stiff bloated corpse gently rises above an oily river that flows under endless onyx bridges to a black, putrid sea.

---

===Chinese===

对这个暮光之地可怖的启示稍稍有所把握——我那反复的梦早已阴森地预告过的启示——之后，我们转向那显然无边无底的午夜洞窟，崖上没有一线光透得进去。再往前我们走了一小段之外，那些无光的冥界张着怎样的巨口，我们永远不会知道了；因为已经议定，那样的秘密于人类无益。可近在手边的就尽够我们忙的：没走多远，探灯就照出那一望无际的受诅的坑——老鼠们曾在里面饱餐，而补给骤然一断，那支饿疯的啮齿大军便先转向活的、挨饿的畜群，随后冲出修道院，酿成农民们永不能忘的那场历史性的浩劫。

上帝啊！那些塞满锯断捡净的骨头、敲开的颅壳的藏尸黑坑！那些哽着无数不圣的世纪里猿人、凯尔特、罗马和英格兰骨殖的噩梦巨壑！有些是满的，谁也说不出它们曾经多深。另一些，在我们的探灯下仍然无底，游着无可名状的幻影。我想：那些倒霉的老鼠，在这个狰狞的塔耳塔洛斯里摸黑寻路，一头栽进这样的陷阱时，又当如何？

有一回我的脚在一道可怕地张开的坑沿滑了一下，我尝了一瞬迷狂的恐惧。我一定是出神了很久，因为一行人里我谁也看不见了，只看得见胖胖的诺里斯上尉。随后，从那墨黑的、无垠的更远处，传来一个我以为我认得的声音；我看见我的老黑猫像一位带翼的埃及神，从我身边射过去，径直射进那无底的未知。可我没有落后多远，因为再过一秒就毫无疑问了。那是那群魔鬼所生、永远寻着新恐怖的老鼠的疾奔，它们决意领我一直走下去，走到地球中心那些狞笑的洞窟——疯癫的、无面的神奈亚拉托提普正在那里，就着两个无定形的白痴吹笛人的笛声，在黑暗中盲嚎。

我的探灯熄了，可我还在跑。我听见人声、嚎叫和回声，但高于一切的，是那一缕不敬的、阴险的疾奔，轻轻地涨、轻轻地涨，像一具僵硬的浮尸轻轻浮起在一条油亮的河上——那河流过无尽的玛瑙桥，流向一个黑色的、腐臭的海。

---

===Original===

Something bumped into me﻿—something soft and plump. It must have been the rats; the viscous, gelatinous, ravenous army that feast on the dead and the living.﻿ ﻿… Why shouldn’t rats eat a de la Poer as a de la Poer eats forbidden things?﻿ ﻿… The war ate my boy, damn them all﻿ ﻿… and the Yanks ate Carfax with flames and burnt Grandsire Delapore and the secret﻿ ﻿… No, no, I tell you, I am *not* that daemon swineherd in the twilit grotto! It was not Edward Norrys’ fat face on that flabby, fungous thing! Who says I am a de la Poer? He lived, but my boy died!﻿ ﻿… Shall a Norrys hold the lands of a de la Poer?﻿ ﻿… It’s voodoo, I tell you﻿ ﻿… that spotted snake﻿ ﻿… Curse you, Thornton, I’ll teach you to faint at what my family do!﻿ ﻿… ’Sblood, thou stinkard, I’ll learn ye how to gust﻿ ﻿… wolde ye swynke me thilke wys?﻿ ﻿… *Magna Mater! Magna Mater!﻿ ﻿… Atys*﻿ ﻿… *Dia ad aghaidh ’s ad aodaun﻿ ﻿… agus bas dunach ort! Dhonas ’s dholas ort, agus leat-sa!﻿ ﻿…* *Ungl﻿ ﻿… nngl﻿ ﻿… rrrlh﻿ ﻿… ckckck.﻿ ﻿…*

That is what they say I said when they found me in the blackness after three hours; found me crouching in the blackness over the plump, half-eaten body of Captain Norrys, with my own cat leaping and tearing at my throat. Now they have blown up Exham Priory, taken my Nigger-Man away from me, and shut me into this barred room at Hanwell with fearful whispers about my heredity and experiences. Thornton is in the next room, but they prevent me from talking to him. They are trying, too, to suppress most of the facts concerning the priory. When I speak of poor Norrys they accuse me of a hideous thing, but they must know that I did not do it They must know it was the rats; the slithering, scurrying rats whose scampering will never let me sleep; the daemon rats that race behind the padding in this room and beckon me down to greater horrors than I have ever known; the rats they can never hear; the rats, the rats in the walls!

===Chinese===

有什么东西撞上了我——软的、胖的。那一定是老鼠；那支黏滑的、贪馋的、以死人活人为食的大军。……老鼠吃一个德·拉·波尔，又有什么不该？德·拉·波尔也吃禁物。……战争吃掉了我的儿子，他们全都该死……北方佬用火吃掉了卡法克斯，烧掉了老德拉波尔和那个秘密……不，不，我告诉你们，我不是那暮光地穴里的魔鬼猪倌！那张软塌塌、生着霉的脸上，并不是爱德华·诺里斯的胖脸！谁说我是德·拉·波尔？他活着，我的儿子却死了！……诺里斯家的人，配占德·拉·波尔家的地？……是伏都，我告诉你们……那条花蛇……该死的，桑顿，我家里做的事把你吓晕，我来教教你！……呸！你这臭货，俺教你尝尝滋味……你要俺那般卖力气么？……大母神！大母神！……阿提斯……Dia ad aghaidh 's ad aodaun… agus bas dunach ort! Dhonas 's dholas ort, agus leat-sa!……Ungl…nngl…rrrlh…ckckck。……

他们三小时后在黑暗里找到我时，说我说的就是这些；发现我蹲在黑暗里，伏在诺里斯上尉被吃掉一半的胖尸体上，而我自己的猫正扑在我的喉咙上撕咬。如今他们炸掉了埃克瑟姆修道院，把我的小黑从我身边带走，把我关进汉韦尔这间钉着栏的房间，怀着对我血统和经历的可怕的窃窃私语。桑顿在隔壁房间，他们不许我同他说话。他们也正设法压下关于修道院的大半事实。我一提起可怜的诺里斯，他们就指控我那件可怕的事；可他们必定知道那不是我干的。他们必定知道那是老鼠；那窸窸窣窣、奔奔突突的老鼠，它们的奔窜永远不让我睡；那魔鬼的老鼠，在这房间的衬垫后面赛跑，招我下去，去见识比我从经历过的更大的恐怖；那他们永远听不见的老鼠；墙里的老鼠，墙中之鼠！

## The Shadow Over Innsmouth / 印斯茅斯的阴霾
===Original===



===Chinese===

印斯茅斯的阴霾

### I / 一

### I /

### I /

### I /

### I / 
===Original===

During the winter of 1927﻿–﻿28 Federal government officials made a strange and secret investigation of certain conditions in the ancient Massachusetts seaport of Innsmouth. The public first learned of it in February, when a vast series of raids and arrests occurred, followed by the deliberate burning and dynamiting﻿—under suitable precautions﻿—of an enormous number of crumbling, worm-eaten, and supposedly empty houses along the abandoned waterfront. Uninquiring souls let this occurrence pass as one of the major clashes in a spasmodic war on liquor.

Keener news-followers, however, wondered at the prodigious number of arrests, the abnormally large force of men used in making them, and the secrecy surrounding the disposal of the prisoners. No trials, or even definite charges, were reported; nor were any of the captives seen thereafter in the regular jails of the nation. There were vague statements about disease and concentration camps, and later about dispersal in various naval and military prisons, but nothing positive ever developed.

Complaints from many liberal organizations were met with long confidential discussions, and representatives were taken on trips to certain camps and prisons. As a result, these societies became surprisingly passive and reticent. Newspaper men were harder to manage, but seemed largely to cooperate with the government in the end. Only one paper﻿—a tabloid always discounted because of its wild policy﻿—mentioned the deep-diving submarine that discharged torpedoes downward in the marine abyss just beyond Devil Reef. That item, gathered by chance in a haunt of sailors, seemed indeed rather farfetched; since the low, black reef lies a full mile and a half out from Innsmouth Harbor.

But at last I am going to defy the ban on speech about this thing. Results, I am certain, are so thorough that no public harm save a shock of repulsion could ever accrue from a hinting of what was found by those horrified raiders at Innsmouth. For my contact with this affair has been closer than that of any other layman, and I have carried away impressions which are yet to drive me to drastic measures.

===Chinese===

1927—28年冬，联邦政府官员对马萨诸塞州古老海港印斯茅斯的某些状况做了一次奇怪而秘密的调查。公众最早是在2月知道的：一连串大规模的突袭与逮捕之后，沿废弃的滨水区，一大批朽烂虫蛀、想来无人的房屋，在周密的防范下被有意地烧掉、炸掉。不爱刨根问底的人，只当它是禁酒之战里一时发作的一场大冲突，让它过去了。

消息灵通些的人却不免纳闷：逮捕的人数何以如此惊人，动手的人手何以如此庞大，囚犯的下落又何以如此保密。没有审判，连明确的罪名也没有听说；此后在全国的正规监狱里，也没人再见过这些被俘的人。有过些含糊其辞的说法，一时说疾病和集中营，后来又说分散到各个海军和陆军监狱，可始终没有下文。

许多自由派组织的抗议，换来的只是冗长的机密商谈；代表们还被领去看了某些营地和监狱。结果，这些社团出奇地变得沉默而不再过问。记者们更难对付，但最后似乎也大都同政府合作了。只有一家小报——素来因为立场狂放而不受重视——提到一艘深潜潜艇，在魔鬼礁外那海洋的深渊里朝下发射鱼雷。这条消息是在水手窝里偶然捡来的，听起来确实牵强；因为那道低黑的礁石，离印斯茅斯港足足有一英里半。

但如今我终于要违抗关于这件事的缄口令了。结果，我确信，已经做得彻底；即便对那些惊骇的突袭者在印斯茅斯的所见暗示一二，除了令人作呕的惊愕，也不可能再有什么公众的危害。因为同这件事的牵连，我比任何别的圈外人都深；我带走的那份印象，至今还在驱使我采取断然的手段。

===Original===

It was I who fled frantically out of Innsmouth in the early morning hours of July 16, 1927, and whose frightened appeals for government inquiry and action brought on the whole reported episode. I was willing enough to stay mute while the affair was fresh and uncertain; but now that it is an old story, with public interest and curiosity gone, I have an odd craving to whisper about those few frightful hours in that ill-rumored and evilly-shadowed seaport of death and blasphemous abnormality.

I never heard of Innsmouth till the day before I saw it for the first and﻿—so far﻿—last time. I was celebrating my coming of age by a tour of New England﻿—sightseeing, antiquarian, and genealogical﻿—and had planned to go directly from ancient Newburyport to Arkham, whence my mother’s family was derived. I had no car, but was traveling by train, trolley, and motor-coach, always seeking the cheapest possible route. In Newburyport they told me that the steam train was the thing to take to Arkham; and it was only at the station ticket-office, when I demurred at the high fare, that I learned about Innsmouth. The stout, shrewd-faced agent, whose speech showed him to be no local man, seemed sympathetic toward my efforts at economy, and made a suggestion that none of my other informants had offered.

“You *could* take that old bus, I suppose,” he said with a certain hesitation, “but it ain’t thought much of hereabouts. It goes through Innsmouth﻿—you may have heard about that﻿—and so the people don’t like it. Run by an Innsmouth fellow﻿—Joe Sargent﻿—but never gets any custom from here, or Arkham either, I guess. Leaves the Square﻿—front of Hammond’s Drug Store﻿—at 10 a.m. and 7 p.m. unless they’ve changed lately. Looks like a terrible rattletrap﻿—I’ve never been on it.”

That was the first I ever heard of shadowed Innsmouth. Any reference to a town not shown on common maps or listed in recent guidebooks would have interested me, and the agent’s old manner of allusion roused something like real curiosity. So I asked the agent to tell me something about it.

He was very deliberate, and spoke with an air of feeling slightly superior to what he said.

===Chinese===

1927年7月16日凌晨发疯似的逃出印斯茅斯的，正是我；那声声惊惶的、要求政府调查处理的呼吁，引出了报道出来的这整件事。事态新鲜、结局未卜的时候，我很愿意缄口；可如今它已是一桩旧闻，公众的兴趣与好奇都已散尽，我却生出一股古怪的渴望，想低声讲讲在那座恶名昭著、邪影幢幢的死亡之港——那渎神的畸变之港——里那可怕的几个小时。

在第一次、也是迄今为止最后一次见到印斯茅斯的前一天，我才听说过它。我正在旅行庆祝自己的成年——游历新英格兰，看风景，访古迹，查家谱——原计划从古城纽伯里波特直接去阿卡姆，我母亲的家族就出自那里。我没有汽车，坐的是火车、电车和长途汽车，专拣最省钱的路线走。在纽伯里波特，人家告诉我去阿卡姆该坐蒸汽火车；直到车站售票处里，我对高昂的票价面露难色时，才听说了印斯茅斯。那位胖胖的、一脸精明的售票员——口音一听就不是本地人——似乎很同情我省钱的打算，提出了一个别的指点人都没有提过的办法。

“你也可以坐那班老巴士，”他带着几分迟疑说，“不过这一带的人不大瞧得上它。它要穿过印斯茅斯——你也许听说过——所以大家都不喜欢。开车的是个印斯茅斯人，乔·萨金特——可我看从来揽不到这里的客人，阿卡姆那头也一样。从广场发车——哈蒙德药店门口——上午10点，晚上7点，除非近来改了点。瞧那车破得吓人——我从没坐过。”

这就是我头一回听说那阴影笼罩的印斯茅斯。任何一座在普通地图上找不见、在新出的导游书里没有的镇子，都会叫我感兴趣，售票员那种旧式的闪烁口吻，更勾起了近乎真正的好奇。我便请他讲讲这地方。

他不慌不忙，说话的神气，仿佛自认比所说的内容高出一头。

===Original===

“Innsmouth? Well, it’s a queer kind of town down at the mouth of the Manuxet. Used to be almost a city﻿—quite a port before the War of 1812﻿—but all gone to pieces in the last hundred years or so. No railroad now﻿—B. & M. never went through, and the branch line from Rowley was given up years ago.

“More empty houses than there are people, I guess, and no business to speak of except fishing and lobstering. Everybody trades mostly either here or in Arkham or Ipswich. Once they had quite a few mills, but nothing’s left now except one gold refinery running on the leanest kind of part time.

“That refinery, though, used to be a big thing, and Old Man Marsh, who owns it, must be richer’n Croesus. Queer old duck, though, and sticks mighty close in his home. He’s supposed to have developed some skin disease or deformity late in life that makes him keep out of sight. Grandson of Captain Obed Marsh, who founded the business. His mother seems to’ve been some kind of foreigner﻿—they say a South Sea islander﻿—so everybody raised Cain when he married an Ipswich girl fifty years ago. They always do that about Innsmouth people, and folks here and hereabouts always try to cover up any Innsmouth blood they have in ’em. But Marsh’s children and grandchildren look just like anybody else so far’s I can see. I’ve had ’em pointed out to me here﻿—though, come to think of it, the elder children don’t seem to be around lately. Never saw the old man.

“And why is everybody so down on Innsmouth? Well, young fellow, you mustn’t take too much stock in what people around here say. They’re hard to get started, but once they do get started they never let up. They’ve been telling things about Innsmouth﻿—whispering ’em, mostly﻿—for the last hundred years, I guess, and I gather they’re more scared than anything else. Some of the stories would make you laugh﻿—about old Captain Marsh driving bargains with the devil and bringing imps out of hell to live in Innsmouth, or about some kind of devil-worship and awful sacrifices in some place near the wharves that people stumbled on around 1845 or thereabouts﻿—but I come from Panton, Vermont, and that kind of story don’t go down with me.

===Chinese===

“印斯茅斯？嗯，是马努克塞特河口上一座古怪的镇子。从前差不多算座城——1812年战争前还是个满像样的港口——可近一百年左右全败落了。现在没有铁路——波士顿—缅因线一直没通，罗利的支线也早废弃了。

“空房子比人多，我看是；除了打鱼捉龙虾，也没有什么生意可讲。大家的买卖多半不是在这儿做，就是在阿卡姆或者伊普斯威奇。从前有过几座厂子，如今只剩一家炼金厂，三天打鱼两天晒网地开着。

“不过那家厂从前是份大产业，厂主老马什，想必富得赛过克罗伊斯。老家伙人挺怪，深居简出。据说上了年纪后得了什么皮肤病还是畸形，从此不肯见人。是奥贝德·马什船长的孙子，创这份家业的就是老船长。他母亲好像是个外国人——说是南洋群岛的——所以五十年前他娶了伊普斯威奇的姑娘，大家闹翻了天。对印斯茅斯人，他们从来都这样；这一带的人，凡自己血里有印斯茅斯的，总想法子遮掩。不过马什的儿孙，我瞧着同旁人没什么两样。在这儿有人指给我看过——哦，想起来了，大的那几个孩子近来好像不露面了。老头子我从来没见过。

“至于为什么人人都瞧不上印斯茅斯？这个，小伙子，这一带人的话你可别太当真。他们起头难，可一旦起了头就没个完。印斯茅斯的事他们讲了一百年了——多半是咬耳朵讲的——我听着，他们更多的还是害怕。有些故事能叫你发笑——说老马什船长同魔鬼做买卖，把小鬼从地狱里领到印斯茅斯住啦；说码头上什么地方的魔鬼崇拜和骇人的祭献，1845年前后叫人撞见啦——可我是佛蒙特州潘顿人，这类故事糊弄不了我。

===Original===

“You ought to hear, though, what some of the old-timers tell about the black reef off the coast﻿—Devil Reef, they call it. It’s well above water a good part of the time, and never much below it, but at that you could hardly call it an island. The story is that there’s a whole legion of devils seen sometimes on that reef﻿—sprawled about, or darting in and out of some kind of caves near the top. It’s a rugged, uneven thing, a good bit over a mile out, and toward the end of shipping days sailors used to make big detours just to avoid it.

“That is, sailors that didn’t hail from Innsmouth. One of the things they had against old Captain Marsh was that he was supposed to land on it sometimes at night when the tide was right. Maybe he did, for I dare say the rock formation was interesting, and it’s just barely possible he was looking for pirate loot and maybe finding it; but there was talk of his dealing with demons there. Fact is, I guess on the whole it was really the captain that gave the bad reputation to the reef.

“That was before the big epidemic of 1846, when over half the folks in Innsmouth was carried off. They never did quite figure out what the trouble was, but it was probably some foreign kind of disease brought from China or somewhere by the shipping. It surely was bad enough﻿—there was riots over it, and all sorts of ghastly doings that I don’t believe ever got outside of town﻿—and it left the place in awful shape. Never came back﻿—there can’t be more’n 300 or 400 people living there now.

“But the real thing behind the way folks feel is simply race prejudice﻿—and I don’t say I’m blaming those that hold it. I hate those Innsmouth folks myself, and I wouldn’t care to go to their town. I s’pose you know﻿—though I can see you’re a Westerner by your talk﻿—what a lot our New England ships used to have to do with queer ports in Africa, Asia, the South Seas, and everywhere else, and what queer kinds of people they sometimes brought back with ’em. You’ve probably heard about the Salem man that came home with a Chinese wife, and maybe you know there’s still a bunch of Fiji Islanders somewhere around Cape Cod.

===Chinese===

“不过你真该听听有些老家伙讲海边那道黑礁——他们叫它魔鬼礁。它有大半天工夫露在水面老高，落潮也沉不了多少，可就算这样你也很难叫它一座岛。故事说，那礁石上有时看得见整整一军团的魔鬼——东倒西歪摊着，或者在近顶上的一些洞窟里钻进钻出。那是个嶙峋不平的东西，离岸足足一英里开外，航运年代快结束的时候，水手们宁可绕大弯也要避开它。

“我是说，不是印斯茅斯籍的水手。老马什船长挨的一条罪名，就是说他有时趁夜潮合适，在那礁上登陆。也许他真上过，礁石的构造想必有意思，他也未尝不是在找海盗的窖藏，兴许还真找着了；可传说讲的是他在那上头同恶魔做交易。说实在的，我看这礁的坏名声，多半还真是船长给挣下的。

“那还是1846年大疫之前的事。那场瘟疫，印斯茅斯一半多的人都被带走了。到底毛病是什么，他们始终没弄清，多半是船从中国还是什么地方带来的洋病。那场病确实够呛——为它出过乱子，还有种种见不得人的事，我想从没传出过镇子——把整个地方糟蹋得不成样子。元气再没回来——如今住在那儿的，超不过三四百人。

“可大家这种心思背后的真东西，说白了是种族偏见——我不说我怪抱偏见的人。我自己就讨厌那些印斯茅斯人，也不乐意上他们镇子去。我料想你是知道的——听口音你是个西部人——咱们新英格兰的船从前同非洲、亚洲、南太平洋各处的怪港口有多少来往，有时又带回来些多么怪的人。那个塞勒姆人带中国老婆回家的事，你多半听说过；科德角什么角落里如今还住着一小群斐济岛人，这你可能也知道。

===Original===

“Well, there must be something like that back of the Innsmouth people. The place always was badly cut off from the rest of the country by marshes and creeks, and we can’t be sure about the ins and outs of the matter; but it’s pretty clear that old Captain Marsh must have brought home some odd specimens when he had all three of his ships in commission back in the twenties and thirties. There certainly is a strange kind of a streak in the Innsmouth folks today﻿—I don’t know how to explain it, but it sort of makes you crawl. You’ll notice a little in Sargent if you take his bus. Some of ’em have queer narrow heads with flat noses and bulgy, starey eyes that never seem to shut, and their skin ain’t quite right. Rough and scabby, and the sides of their necks are all shriveled or creased up. Get bald, too, very young. The older fellows look the worst﻿—fact is, I don’t believe I’ve ever seen a very old chap of that kind. Guess they must die of looking in the glass! Animals hate ’em﻿—they used to have lots of horse trouble before autos came in.

“Nobody can ever keep track of those people, and state school officials and census men have a devil of a time. You can bet that prying strangers ain’t welcome around Innsmouth. I’ve heard personally of more’n one business or government man that’s disappeared there, and there’s loose talk of one who went crazy and is out at Danvers now. They must have fixed up some awful scare for that fellow.

“That’s why I wouldn’t go at night if I was you. I’ve never been there and have no wish to go, but I guess a daytime trip couldn’t hurt you﻿—even though the people hereabouts will advise you not to make it. If you’re just sightseeing, and looking for old-time stuff, Innsmouth ought to be quite a place for you.”

And so I spent part of that evening at the Newburyport Public Library looking up data about Innsmouth. The Essex County histories on the library shelves had very little to say, except that the town was founded in 1643, noted for shipbuilding before the Revolution, a seat of great marine prosperity in the early 19th century, and later a minor factory center using the Manuxet as power. The epidemic and riots of 1846 were very sparsely treated, as if they formed a discredit to the country.

===Chinese===

“嗯，印斯茅斯人背后多半就有这么一档子事。那地方一向被沼泽和溪流同内地隔开，事情的原委谁也说不准；不过老马什船长在二三十年代三条船全都出海的当口，多半是带回家过些古怪的货色，这倒差不多是明白的。如今的印斯茅斯人身上确实有一股怪劲——我说不上怎么解释，反正有点叫你发毛。你坐萨金特的车就能看出一点。他们有些人脑袋又窄又怪，塌鼻子，鼓眼睛，眼睛水汪汪地瞪着，好像永远不闭，皮肤也不大对头。粗糙，结痂，脖子两侧全皱缩或者打了褶。还秃，小小年纪就秃。老的一辈模样最糟——说真的，我就没见过这号人里有什么很老的。想来是照镜子照死的！牲口恨他们——没汽车的年头，马见他们就闹的事出过不老少。

“这些人谁也数不清，州里的学监和人口普查员为他们伤透了脑筋。你放心，好事生人的外乡人在印斯茅斯不受欢迎。我个人就听说过不止一个公事人、政府人在那儿没了影儿；还有闲话说有一个疯了，如今关在丹弗斯。他们必定给那位安排了什么了不得的惊吓。

“所以要是我啊，夜里就不去。我自己没去过，也不想去了；不过白天走一趟，我想伤不着你——虽然这一带的人会劝你别去。要是你就为看看风景、找找老古董，印斯茅斯对你倒满够一瞧。”

于是那天晚上，我在纽伯里波特公共图书馆查印斯茅斯的资料，消磨了一部分时光。架上埃塞克斯县的各种志书讲得很少，只说这镇子建于1643年，革命前以造船著称，19世纪初是海上繁荣的重镇，后来靠马努克塞特河的水力，做过一阵小规模的工厂中心。1846年的瘟疫和动乱，写得一笔带过，仿佛是全县的一件丑事。

===Original===

References to decline were few, though the significance of the later record was unmistakable. After the Civil War all industrial life was confined to the Marsh Refining Company, and the marketing of gold ingots formed the only remaining bit of major commerce aside from the eternal fishing.

Most interesting of all was a glancing reference to the strange jewelry vaguely associated with Innsmouth. It had evidently impressed the whole countryside more than a little, for mention was made of specimens in the museum of Miskatonic University at Arkham, and in the display room of the Newburyport Historical Society. I resolved to see the local sample﻿—said to be a large, queerly-proportioned thing evidently meant for a tiara﻿—if it could possibly be arranged.

The librarian gave me a note of introduction to the curator of the Society, a Miss Anna Tilton, who lived nearby, and after a brief explanation that ancient gentlewoman was kind enough to pilot me into the closed building, since the hour was not outrageously late. The collection was a notable one indeed, but in my present mood I had eyes for nothing but the bizarre object which glistened in a corner cupboard under the electric lights.

It took no excessive sensitiveness to beauty to make me literally gasp at the strange, unearthly splendor of the alien, opulent fantasy that rested there on a purple velvet cushion. The longer I looked, the more the thing fascinated me; and in this fascination there was a curiously disturbing element hardly to be classified or accounted for. I decided that it was the queer otherworldly quality of the art which made me uneasy. It was as if the workmanship were that of another planet.

The patterns all hinted of remote secrets and unimaginable abysses in time and space, and the monotonously aquatic nature of the reliefs became almost sinister. Among these reliefs were fabulous monsters of abhorrent grotesqueness and malignity﻿—wholly primal and awesomely ancestral.

At times I fancied that every contour of these blasphemous fish-frogs was overflowing with the ultimate quintessence of unknown and inhuman evil.

In odd contrast to the tiara’s aspect was its brief and prosy history as related by Miss Tilton. It had been pawned for a ridiculous sum at a shop in State Street in 1873, by a drunken Innsmouth man shortly afterward killed in a brawl.

===Chinese===

衰落的记载寥寥，可后来那份记录的含义错认不了。内战之后，全部工业都收缩在马什炼金公司一家里，金锭的买卖，是除永恒不衰的渔业之外仅剩的一点大生意。

最有趣的，是顺带提到同印斯茅斯隐隐相关的那些古怪首饰。它显然给整个乡间留下了不小的印象，因为文中提到阿卡姆米斯卡塔尼克大学的博物馆和纽伯里波特历史学会的陈列室里都存着样品。本地这件，据说是一枚巨大、比例古怪的东西，显见是顶冕——只要安排得开，我决意去看一眼。

图书馆员给我开了张介绍便条，去会学会的管理员安娜·蒂尔顿小姐，她住在近处；略作说明后，这位老淑女见时辰还不算太晚，好心领我进了闭馆的楼。藏品确实可观，可在我此刻的心境里，我眼里只剩那件在角落柜里、电灯下闪光的古怪物事。

不必对美有多过敏的感受力，任何人也会对那件异域的、丰赡的奇物——它安放在一方紫色天鹅绒垫上——那陌生的、非尘世的辉光，当场倒抽一口气。我愈看愈被它迷住；这迷恋里又有一股说不清道不明的不安，难以归类，也无法解释。我断定，是那门艺术古怪的异界气质叫我心里发毛，那手工仿佛出自另一颗行星。

纹样无一不暗示时间与空间里遥远的秘密和不可想象的深渊，浮雕那一律的水性，几乎显出恶意。浮雕中有种种荒诞的怪物，狞恶得可憎，乖戾得可怖——全然原始，森然古老。

有时我恍惚觉得，这些渎神的人鱼蛙怪的每一道轮廓里，都溢着某种未知的、非人的至恶的精粹。

同这顶冕的形貌成古怪对照的，是蒂尔顿小姐讲的那段简短乏味的历史。1873年，一个印斯茅斯醉汉把它押在州街一家铺子里，换了笔少得可笑的钱，随后不久就在一场斗殴里送了命。

===Original===

Miss Tilton was inclined to believe that it formed part of some exotic pirate hoard discovered by old Captain Obed Marsh. This view was surely not weakened by the insistent offers of purchase at a high price which the Marshes began to make as soon as they knew of its presence, and which they repeated to this day despite the Society’s unvarying determination not to sell.

As the good lady showed me out of the building, she assured me that the rumors of devil-worship were partly justified by a peculiar secret cult which had gained force there and engulfed all the orthodox churches.

It was called, she said, “The Esoteric Order of Dagon,” and was undoubtedly a debased, quasi-pagan thing imported from the East a century before, at a time when Innsmouth fisheries seemed to be going barren. Its persistence among a simple people was quite natural in view of the sudden and permanent return of abundantly fine fishing, and it soon came to be the greatest influence on the town.

All this, to the pious Miss Tilton, formed an excellent reason for shunning the ancient town of decay and desolation; but to me it was merely a fresh incentive; and I could scarcely sleep in my small room at the “Y” as the night wore away.

===Chinese===

蒂尔顿小姐倾向于认为，它是老船长奥贝德·马什发现的某处异邦海盗窖藏的一部分。马什家的人一得知它在哪儿，就开始高价求购，至今不断，而学会始终坚持不卖——这股执拗劲，当然只会叫人更信她的看法。

这位好心的太太送我出楼时向我担保，魔鬼崇拜的传闻有几分是真的：那里兴起过一个古怪的秘教，把正宗教会尽数吞没了。

她说，这教叫“达贡秘教”（The Esoteric Order of Dagon），无疑是大约一世纪前从东方传来的一种堕落的、半异教的东西，其时印斯茅斯的渔场似乎正闹着荒。渔业突然又永久地重新丰收，这教在一片淳朴人家里扎下根来，原也十分自然；不久它便成了镇上最大的势力。

这一切，在虔诚的蒂尔顿小姐看来，正是躲避那座衰败荒凉的老城的绝好理由；对我却只是新添的一味诱饵。夜愈来愈深，我在青年会的小房间里几乎睡不着。

===Original===

Shortly before ten the next morning I stood with my one small valise in front of Hammond’s Drug Store in old Market Square waiting for the Innsmouth bus. In a few moments a small motor-coach of extreme decrepitude and dirty gray color rattled down State Street, made a turn, and drew up at the curb beside me. I felt immediately that it was the right one; a guess which the half-illegible sign on the windshield﻿—“*Arkham-Innsmouth-Newb’port*”﻿—soon verified.

There were only three passengers﻿—dark, unkempt men of sullen visage and somewhat youthful cast﻿—and when the vehicle stopped they clumsily shambled out and began walking up State Street in a silent, almost furtive fashion. The driver also alighted. This, I reflected, must be the Joe Sargent mentioned by the ticket-agent; and even before I had noticed any details there spread over me a wave of spontaneous aversion which could be neither checked nor explained.

He was a thin, stoop-shouldered man not much under six feet tall, dressed in shabby blue civilian clothes and wearing a frayed gray golf cap. His age was perhaps thirty-five, but the odd, deep creases in the sides of his neck made him seem older when one did not study his dull, expressionless face. He had a narrow head, bulging, watery blue eyes that seemed never to wink, a flat nose, a receding forehead and chin, and singularly undeveloped ears. As he walked toward the bus I observed his peculiarly shambling gait and saw that his feet were inordinately immense. The more I studied them the more I wondered how he could buy any shoes to fit them.

A certain greasiness about the fellow increased my dislike. He was evidently given to working or lounging around the fish docks, and carried with him much of their characteristic smell. Just what foreign blood was in him I could not even guess.

I was sorry when I saw that there would be no other passengers on the bus. Somehow I did not like the idea of riding alone with this driver. But as the leaving time obviously approached I conquered my qualms and followed the man aboard, extending him a dollar bill and murmuring the single word “Innsmouth.”

At length the decrepit vehicle started with a jerk, and rattled noisily past the old brick buildings of State Street amidst a cloud of vapor from the exhaust.

===Chinese===

第二天上午将到10点，我拎着我的一只小提箱，站在老市场广场哈蒙德药店门前，等去印斯茅斯的巴士。不多时，一辆破败到极点、灰不溜丢的小型长途车顺着州街咔啦咔啦驶来，转了个弯，在我身边的道牙前停住。我立刻觉得就是它；挡风玻璃上那半截认不清的字——“阿卡姆—印斯茅斯—纽伯里波特”——很快证实了这一猜。

车上只有三个乘客——皮肤黝黑、邋里邋遢的汉子，面色阴沉，年纪倒都不大——车一停，他们笨拙地拖着脚步下来，沿着州街走了，一声不吭，几乎鬼鬼祟祟。司机也下了车。我心想，这必是售票员提到的乔·萨金特了；还没容我细看，一股无缘无故的反感已经漫过我的全身，压不住，也说不清。

他瘦高个儿，将近六英尺，肩膀佝偻，穿一身寒酸的蓝便装，戴一顶磨秃了的灰色高尔夫帽。年纪大约三十五，可脖颈两侧那些古怪的深褶，叫人不去细看他那张呆滞无表情的脸时，只当他更老。他脑袋窄，一双鼓凸的、水汪汪的蓝眼睛仿佛永远不眨，塌鼻子，额头和下巴都往后缩，两只耳朵小得出奇地没长开。他朝巴士走来时，我看见他那副特别的拖着脚的步态，看见他的脚大得离谱。愈看愈纳闷：他上哪儿能买到合脚的鞋。

这家伙身上一股油腻，愈发叫我不喜欢。他显然惯于在鱼码头干活或者闲混，身上带着那地方特有的气味，去也去不掉。他血里混的是哪国的血，我连猜也猜不着。

看到车上不会再有别的乘客，我心里一沉。同这样一个司机单独赶路，我实在不喜欢。可发车的时间显然到了，我压下心里的别扭，跟着这人上了车，递过去一张一块钱的票子，咕哝了一个词：“印斯茅斯。”

那辆破车终于一颠一颠地起了步，喷着一团废气，轰隆隆驶过州街的老砖楼。

===Original===

The day was warm and sunny, but the landscape of sand, sedge-grass, and stunted shrubbery became more and more desolate as we proceeded. Out the window I could see the blue water and the sandy line of Plum Island, and we presently drew very near the beach as our narrow road veered off from the main highway to Rowley and Ipswich.

At last we lost sight of Plum Island and saw the vast expanse of the open Atlantic on our left. Our narrow course began to climb steeply, and I felt a singular sense of disquiet in looking at the lonely crest ahead where the rutted roadway met the sky. It was as if the bus were about to keep on its ascent leaving the sane earth altogether and merging with the unknown arcana of upper air and cryptical sky. The smell of the sea took on ominous implications, and the silent driver’s bent, rigid back and narrow head became more and more hateful. As I looked at him I saw that the back of his head was almost as hairless as his face, having only a few straggling yellow strands upon a gray scabrous surface.

Then we reached the crest and beheld the outspread valley beyond, where the Manuxet joins the sea just north of the long line of cliffs that culminate in Kingsport Head; all my attention was captured by the nearer panorama just below me. I had, I realized, come face to face with rumor-shadowed Innsmouth.

It was a town of wide extent and dense construction, yet one with a portentous dearth of visible life. The vast huddle of sagging gambrel roofs and peaked gables conveyed with offensive clearness the idea of wormy decay, and as we approached along the now descending road I could see that many roofs had wholly caved in. Stretching inland I saw the rusted, grass-grown line of the abandoned railway, with leaning telegraph-poles now devoid of wires.

Here and there the ruins of wharves jutted out from the shore to end in indeterminate rottenness, those farthest south seeming the most decayed. And far out at sea, despite a high tide, I glimpsed a long, black line scarcely rising above the water yet carrying a suggestion of odd latent malignancy. This, I knew, must be Devil Reef. As I looked, a subtle, curious sense of beckoning seemed superadded to the grim repulsion; and oddly enough, I found this overtone more disturbing than the primary impression.

===Chinese===

天气暖和晴朗，可车窗外沙丘、莎草和矮树丛构成的原野，愈走愈荒凉。凭窗望去，看得见蓝色的海水和普拉姆岛的沙线；我们那条窄路离开通往罗利和伊普斯威奇的大道后，不久就贴到了海滩近旁。

终于普拉姆岛看不见了，左边展开大西洋浩渺的一片。窄路开始陡陡地爬坡，望着前方那道孤零零的、车辙纵横的路直上天际的山脊，我心里生出一阵说不出的不安。仿佛这巴士要一路爬上去，把清醒的大地整个抛下，融进上层空气和诡异天空的未知秘境里。海的气味带上了不祥的含义；那沉默的司机佝偻僵硬的脊背和窄窄的头，也愈看愈可憎。我打量他，看见他后脑勺几乎同脸一样地没有头发，灰白的结痂头皮上只稀稀拉拉剩几缕黄毛。

随后我们上了山顶，望见山那边铺开的山谷：马努克塞特河就在长长一线尽处是金斯波特角的山崖以北入海；可我的注意力全被脚下近处的全景抓去了。我意识到，我已同传闻笼着阴影的印斯茅斯打了个照面。

那是一片幅员广阔、屋舍稠密的镇子，却透着一股骇人的、几乎不见人烟的死寂。成片歪斜的复折屋顶和尖山墙，把虫蛀的朽败这层意思，明明白白地糊在人脸上；顺着现在下坡的路驶近时，我看见许多屋顶已经整个塌陷。朝内陆望去，是废弃铁路锈迹斑斑、长满荒草的一线，电线杆歪着，早没了电线。

岸边处处突出着码头的残骸，尽头烂成一片混沌，最南头那些朽坏得最狠。而远远的海上，虽然正是涨潮，我瞥见一道长长的黑线，仅仅浮出水面，却带着一股说不出的、潜伏的恶意。我知道，这必是魔鬼礁。我望着它，一层微妙而古怪的召唤之感，竟加在那森然的憎厌之上；说也奇怪，我觉得这层意味比头一层印象更搅得人心神不定。

===Original===

As the bus reached a lower level I began to catch the steady note of a waterfall through the unnatural stillness. The leaning, unpainted houses grew thicker, lined both sides of the road, and displayed more urban tendencies than did those we were leaving behind. The panorama ahead had contracted to a street scene, and in spots I could see where a cobblestone pavement and stretches of brick sidewalk had formerly existed. All the houses were apparently deserted, and there were occasional gaps where tumbledown chimneys and cellar walls told of buildings that had collapsed. Pervading everything was the most nauseous fishy odor imaginable.

And I was not to reach my destination without one other very strong impression of poignantly disagreeable quality. The bus had come to a sort of open concourse or radial point with churches on two sides and the bedraggled remains of a circular green in the center, and I was looking at a large pillared hall on the right-hand junction ahead. The structure’s once white paint was now gray and peeling, and the black and gold sign on the pediment was so faded that I could only with difficulty make out the words “Esoteric Order of Dagon.”

The door of the church basement was open, revealing a rectangle of blackness inside. And as I looked, a certain object crossed or seemed to cross that dark rectangle; burning into my brain a momentary conception of nightmare which was all the more maddening because analysis could not show a single nightmarish quality in it.

It was a living object﻿—the first except the driver that I had seen since entering the compact part of the town﻿—and had I been in a steadier mood I would have found nothing whatever of terror in it. Clearly, as I realized a moment later, it was the pastor; clad in some peculiar vestments doubtless introduced since the Order of Dagon had modified the ritual of the local churches. The thing which had probably caught my first subconscious glance and supplied the touch of bizarre horror was the tall tiara he wore; an almost exact duplicate of the one Miss Tilton had shown me the previous evening. This, acting on my imagination, had supplied namelessly sinister qualities to the indeterminate face and robed, shambling form beneath it.

===Chinese===

巴士下到较低处时，透过这不自然的寂静，我开始听见一道瀑布平稳的声响。歪斜的、没刷漆的房子密起来，排列在路的两旁，比我们撇在身后的那些更像城里样了。前方的全景缩成一条街景，有几处还看得出从前铺过圆石路面、有过砖砌人行道的痕迹。房子显然全都空着，间或豁出一片空地，塌倒的烟囱和地窖墙讲着房屋倾覆的故事。笼罩一切的，是一股想象得出最叫人作呕的鱼腥气。

而我的目的地还不会让我省下另一桩印象——一桩刺人地不快的强印象。巴士来到一处开阔的路口，或者说是放射形的广场，两边是教堂，中央是一圈惨遭践踏的绿地的残迹；我正望着右手路口上那座有柱廊的大厅。那建筑曾经的白漆如今灰暗剥落，山墙上黑底金字的招牌褪得只剩吃力的几个词：“达贡秘教”。

教堂地下室的门开着，露出里面一方黑黢黢的长方块。正当我望着，一个什么东西从那黑方块里横过，或者仿佛横过；它往我脑子里烙下一个转瞬即逝的梦魇概念，那概念之所以格外熬人，是因为分析下来，它里面找不出半点梦魇的成分。

那是一个活物——进城以来除司机之外我见到的头一个——换我心情稳当些，我从它身上绝对看不出什么恐怖。显然，过一刻我便明白，那是教区的牧师；穿着某种古怪的祭衣，无疑是达贡教改造本地教会仪轨以后添置的。多半正是他戴的那顶高冕，抓住了我下意识的第一眼，补上了那一点怪诞的恐怖；它同蒂尔顿小姐前一晚给我看的那顶几乎一模一样。它在我的想象里作起祟来，给它底下那张分辨不清的脸和那裹着祭袍、拖着脚步的身形，平添了种种无名的阴毒。

===Original===

A very thin sprinkling of repellent-looking youngish people now became visible on the sidewalks﻿—lone individuals, and silent knots of two or three. The lower floors of the crumbling houses sometimes harbored small shops with dingy signs, and I noticed a parked truck or two as we rattled along. The sound of waterfalls became more and more distinct, and presently I saw a fairly deep river-gorge ahead, spanned by a wide, iron-railed highway bridge beyond which a large square opened out. Then we rolled into the large semicircular square across the river and drew up on the right-hand side in front of a tall, cupola-crowned building with remnants of yellow paint and with a half-effaced sign proclaiming it to be the Gilman House.

I was glad to get out of that bus, and at once proceeded to check my valise in the shabby hotel lobby. There was only one person in sight﻿—an elderly man without what I had come to call the “Innsmouth look”﻿—and I decided not to ask him any of the questions which bothered me; remembering that odd things had been noticed in this hotel. Instead, I strolled out on the square, from which the bus had already gone, and studied the scene minutely and appraisingly.

For some reason or other I chose to make my first inquiries at the chain grocery, whose personnel was not likely to be native to Innsmouth. I found a solitary boy of about seventeen in charge, and was pleased to note the brightness and affability which promised cheerful information. He seemed exceptionally eager to talk, and I soon gathered that he did not like the place, its fishy smell, or its furtive people. His family did not like him to work in Innsmouth, but the chain had transferred him there and he did not wish to give up his job.

There was, he said, no public library or chamber of commerce in Innsmouth, but I could probably find my way about. The street I had come down was Federal. West of that were the fine old residence streets﻿—Broad, Washington, Lafayette, and Adams﻿—and east of it were the shoreward slums.

===Chinese===

人行道上现在显出稀稀拉拉几伙面目可憎的年轻人——孤身一个的，两三个闷声不响扎堆的。朽坏房子的底层有时开着小店，挂着乌糟糟的招牌；车咔啦咔啦走过时，我看见路边停着一两辆卡车。瀑布声愈来愈清楚，不久我望见前方一道相当深的河谷，一道宽阔的铁栏公路桥横跨其上，桥那边展开一个大广场。我们随即驶过桥，滚进河那边半圆形的大广场，在右侧一幢顶着穹顶的高楼前停了车；楼上黄漆斑驳，半磨掉的招牌说它是吉尔曼旅馆。

能下车我叫松了口气，立刻到那寒酸的旅馆门厅里寄存了提箱。眼前只有一个人——一个没有我所称“印斯茅斯相貌”的老人——我决定什么烦人的问题也不问他；想起这家旅馆里被人注意到过怪事。我转而踱到广场上——巴士已经开走了——细细地、带估量地打量这场景。

不知怎么，我挑了连锁杂货店来问头一轮，店员想必不是印斯茅斯本地人。店里只有一个十七岁上下的男孩当班，他那一脸机灵和气，看来肯痛痛快快给消息，叫我心里高兴。他像是格外健谈，我很快听出：他不喜欢这地方，不喜欢鱼腥气，也不喜欢这里鬼祟的人。家里不愿他在印斯茅斯做工，可连锁店把他调了来，他也不想丢了饭碗。

他说，印斯茅斯没有公共图书馆，也没有商会，不过路我大概认得。我一路下来的那条街是联邦街。街西是几条漂亮的老住宅街——布罗德街、华盛顿街、拉斐特街、亚当斯街——街东是朝海的贫民窟。

===Original===

Certain spots were almost forbidden territory, as he had learned at considerable cost. One must not, for example, linger much around the Marsh refinery, or around any of the still used churches, or around the pillared Order of Dagon Hall at New Church Green. Those churches were very odd﻿—all violently disavowed by their respective denominations elsewhere, and apparently using the queerest kind of ceremonials and clerical vestments.

As for the Innsmouth people﻿—the youth hardly knew what to make of them. Their appearance﻿—especially those staring, unwinking eyes which one never saw shut﻿—was certainly shocking enough﻿—and their voices were disgusting. It was awful to hear them chanting in their churches at night, and especially during their main festivals or revivals, which fell twice a year on April 30 and October 31.

They were very fond of the water, and swam a great deal in both river and harbor. Swimming races out to Devil Reef were very common, and everyone in sight seemed well able to share in this arduous sport.

It would be of no use, my informant said, to ask the natives anything about the place. The only one who would talk was a very aged but normal-looking man who lived at the poorhouse on the north rim of the town and spent his time walking about or lounging around the fire station. This hoary character, Zadok Allen, was 96 years old and somewhat touched in the head, besides being the town drunkard. He was a strange, furtive creature who constantly looked over his shoulder as if afraid of something, and when sober could not be persuaded to talk at all with strangers. He was, however, unable to resist any offer of his favorite poison; and once drunk would furnish the most astonishing fragments of whispered reminiscence.

After all, though, little useful data could be gained from him; since his stories were all insane, incomplete hints of impossible marvels and horrors which could have no source save in his own distorted fancy. Nobody ever believed him, but the natives did not like him to drink and talk with any strangers; and it was not always safe to be seen questioning him. It was probably from him that some of the wildest popular whispers and delusions were derived.

===Chinese===

有几处地方几乎是禁区，这是他花了不小代价学来的。比如，不许在马什炼金厂旁边多流连，不许在还开着的那几座教堂旁边多流连，也不许在新教堂绿地那座有柱廊的达贡礼堂旁边多流连。那些教堂怪得很——各自的教派在外地全激烈地同它们划清界限，它们行的仪式和教士的祭衣，显然也是天底下最古怪的一路。

至于印斯茅斯人——小伙子简直不知道该怎么看他们。他们的长相——尤其那双直瞪瞪、永不闭合、谁也没见闭过的眼睛——当然够吓人的——他们的嗓音也叫人恶心。夜里听他们在教堂里诵唱已经够呛，赶上他们一年两度的大节或奋兴会——4月30日和10月31日——更是不得了。

他们极爱水，河里海里成天游。游到魔鬼礁的游泳比赛司空见惯，看得见的每个人似乎都拿得下这门辛苦的运动。

想从本地人嘴里问出这地方的事，我的这位消息源说，是白费劲。肯开口的只有一个：年纪非常老、模样却还正常的人，住在镇北边的贫民院里，成天不是溜达就是赖在消防站边上。这个老古董叫扎多克·艾伦，九十六岁，脑子有点糊涂，还是镇上的酒鬼。他是个鬼鬼祟祟的怪老头，说话时不断回头看，像怕什么；清醒时谁也别想劝他同生人讲一句话。可他架不住人家请他喝他钟爱的那口毒物；一灌醉，就会漏出最骇人的、咬耳朵的往事碎片。

不过说到底，从他身上也得不了多少有用的东西；因为他的故事全疯疯癫癫，尽是对不可能的奇迹与恐怖的残缺暗示，来源只能是他自己那拧歪的想象。从没有人信他，可本地人也不乐意他同生人喝酒谈话；叫人看见盘问他，不一定安全。民间那些最狂放的窃语和胡话，多半就是从他这儿来的。

===Original===

The Marshes, together with the other three gently bred families of the town﻿—the Waites, the Gilmans, and the Eliots﻿—were all very retiring. They lived in immense houses along Washington Street, and several were reputed to harbor in concealment certain kinsfolk whose personal aspect forbade public view, and whose deaths had been reported and recorded.

Warning me that most of the street signs were down, the youth drew for my benefit a rough but ample and painstaking sketch map of the town’s salient features. After a moment’s study I felt sure that it would be of great help, and pocketed it with profuse thanks.

Thus began my systematic though half-bewildered tour of Innsmouth’s narrow, shadow-blighted ways. Crossing the bridge and turning toward the roar of the lower falls, I passed close to the Marsh refinery, which seemed oddly free from the noise of industry. This building stood on the steep river bluff near a bridge and an open confluence of streets which I took to be the earliest civic center, displaced after the Revolution by the present Town Square.

Re-crossing the gorge on the Main Street bridge, I struck a region of utter desertion which somehow made me shudder. Collapsing huddles of gambrel roofs formed a jagged and fantastic skyline, above which rose the ghoulish, decapitated steeple of an ancient church.

Fish Street was as deserted as Main, though it differed in having many brick and stone warehouses still in excellent shape. Water Street was almost its duplicate, save that there were great seaward gaps where wharves had been. Not a living thing did I see, except for the scattered fishermen on the distant breakwater, and not a sound did I hear save the lapping of the harbor tides and the roar of the falls in the Manuxet.

I kept north along Main to Martin, then turning inland, crossing Federal Street safely north of the Green, and entering the decayed patrician neighborhood of northern Broad, Washington, Lafayette, and Adams Streets. Following Washington Street toward the river, I now faced a zone of former industry and commerce; noting the ruins of a factory ahead, and seeing others, with the traces of an old railway station and covered railway bridge beyond up the gorge on my right.

===Chinese===

马什家，连同镇上另外三家旧族——韦特家、吉尔曼家、埃利奥特家——都非常深居简出。他们住在华盛顿街上几幢大宅里，据传有几家还窝藏着某些见不得人的亲戚：他们的长相不许人看，死讯却早已上报登记。

小伙子提醒我，街牌大半都掉了，又替我画了一张粗略却周到细致的镇子要览图。略一过目，我断定它大有用处，连连道谢揣进了兜。

于是我开始对印斯茅斯那些窄而阴翳的街巷，作一场虽有系统却半带迷乱的巡行。过桥朝下瀑布的轰响走去，我从马什炼金厂近旁经过，那厂子奇怪地听不见一点工业的声响。厂房立在临河的陡崖上，靠着桥头一片开阔的街口；我猜这是最早的镇中心，革命后才被现在的镇广场取代的。

再从主街桥过河谷，我撞进一片全然荒弃的地带，不知怎么竟叫我打了个寒噤。成堆倾颓的复折屋顶锯齿般、幻梦般割出一条天际线，线上升起一座古老教堂那没头的、食尸鬼似的尖塔。

鱼街同主街一样不见人影，只是还立着许多完好的砖石货栈，算是不同。水街几乎是它的翻版，只是朝海一面豁出一个个大缺口，码头就曾在那里。我看不到一个活物，只有远处防波堤上散着的几个渔人；听不到一点声音，只有港里潮水的舔拍和马努克塞特河上瀑布的轰响。

我沿主街北行到马丁街，折向内陆，从绿地北边安全穿过联邦街，走进布罗德、华盛顿、拉斐特、亚当斯各街北段那没落的世家街区。沿华盛顿街朝河走去，面前是一片从前的工商地带：我留意到前方一座工厂的废墟，又望见别的几座，以及右首河谷上游一座旧车站和带棚铁路桥的残迹。

===Original===

The uncertain bridge now before me was posted with a warning sign, but I took the risk and crossed again to the south bank where traces of life reappeared. Furtive, shambling creatures stared cryptically in my direction, and more normal faces eyed me coldly and curiously. Innsmouth was rapidly becoming intolerable, and I turned down Paine Street toward the Square in the hope of getting some vehicle to take me to Arkham before the still-distant starting time of that sinister bus.

It was then that I saw the tumbledown fire station on my left, and noticed the red-faced, bushy-bearded, watery-eyed old man in nondescript rags who sat on a bench in front of it talking with a pair of unkempt but not abnormal-looking firemen. This, of course, must be Zadok Allen, the half-crazed, liquorish nonagenarian whose tales of old Innsmouth and its shadow were so hideous and incredible.

===Chinese===

眼前这座摇摇欲坠的桥挂着告示，可我还是冒险过到南岸，那里又见人迹了。鬼祟的、拖着脚的家伙朝我这边谜样地瞪，几副较正常的面孔也冷冷地、好奇地打量我。印斯茅斯迅速变得叫人忍无可忍，我便拐下佩因街，朝广场走，指望在那班邪门的巴士还很远的发车时刻之前，找辆车送我去阿卡姆。

就在这时，我看见左边那座塌了架的消防站，注意到站前长凳上坐着个红脸膛、络腮胡、水汪汪眼睛的老头，穿着不成样子的破衣，正同一对邋遢但模样不算反常的消防员聊天。这当然必是扎多克·艾伦了，那个半疯半癫、嗜酒如命的九旬老人，他讲的老印斯茅斯和它的阴影，又骇人又难信。

### III /

### III /

### III / 
===Original===

I had been assured that the old man could do nothing but hint at wild, disjointed, and incredible legends, and I had been warned that the natives made it unsafe to be seen talking with him; yet the thought of this aged witness to the town’s decay, with memories going back to the early days of ships and factories, was a *lure* that no amount of reason could make me resist. Curiosity flared up beyond sense and caution, and in my youthful egotism I fancied I might be able to sift a nucleus of real history from the confused, extravagant outpouring I would probably extract with the aid of whiskey.

A quart bottle of such was easily, though not cheaply, obtained in the rear of a dingy variety-store just off the Square in Eliot Street.

Reentering the Square I saw that luck was with me; for﻿—shuffling out of Paine Street around the corner of the Gilman House﻿—I glimpsed nothing less than the tall, lean, tattered form of old Zadok Allen himself. In accordance with my plan, I attracted his attention by brandishing my newly-purchased bottle; and soon realized that he had begun to shuffle wistfully after me as I turned into Waite Street on my way to the most deserted region I could think of. Before I reached Main Street I could hear a faint and wheezy “Hey, Mister!” behind me, and I presently allowed the old man to catch up and take copious pulls from the quart bottle.

I began putting out feelers as we walked along to Water Street and turned southward amidst the omnipresent desolation and crazily tilted ruins, but found that the aged tongue did not loosen as quickly as I had expected. At length I saw a grass-grown opening toward the sea between crumbling brick walls, with the weedy length of an earth-and-masonry wharf projecting beyond. Piles of moss-covered stones near the water promised tolerable seats, and the scene was sheltered from all possible view by a ruined warehouse on the north.

===Chinese===

人家向我担保，这老头除了狂乱、语无伦次、难以置信的传说，什么也给不了；人家还警告我，叫本地人看见同他说话，是要担风险的；可想到这位镇子衰落的老年证人，记忆一直溯到船和工厂的早年，那是一枚多大的诱饵，多少理性也拦不住我。好奇心烧过了头，烧过了谨慎；凭年轻的自负，我竟觉得自己有本事从那笔糊涂的、狂言的倾倒里——多半得靠威士忌来引——筛出一核真实的历史来。

这样的一夸脱瓶酒，在广场边埃利奥特街上一家乌糟杂货铺的后头就弄到了，虽然不便宜。

回到广场，我一看，运气在我这边：从佩因街、吉尔曼旅馆墙角那边拖着脚步出来的，不是别人，正是扎多克·艾伦老头那高瘦褴褛的身影。按计划，我扬了扬新买的酒瓶来勾他的注意；我折上韦特街，朝我能想到的最僻静的地方走，很快觉察他已开始馋涎地跟了上来。还没到主街，我就听见背后一声气喘吁吁的“嘿，先生！”，我便让老头赶上，由着他抱住那夸脱瓶灌了个够。

我们一路向水街走去、再折向南，走在无所不在的荒凉和疯歪的废墟中间；我一路试探，却发现那把老舌头没有我想的开得快。终于，我望见崩裂的砖墙之间一个朝海的豁口，长草的土石码头探向海里。水边几堆生苔的石头，勉强可以坐人；北边一座仓库的残骸，把这一幕从一切可能的视线里遮了个严实。

===Original===

About four hours remained for conversation if I were to catch the eight o’clock coach for Arkham, and I began to dole out more liquor to the ancient tippler; meanwhile eating my own frugal lunch. In my donations I was careful not to overshoot the mark, for I did not wish Zadok’s vinous garrulousness to pass into a stupor. After an hour his furtive taciturnity showed signs of disappearing, and something or other had caused his wandering gaze to light on the low, distant line of Devil Reef, then showing plainly and almost fascinatingly above the waves. He bent toward me, took hold of my coat lapel, and hissed out some hints that could not be mistaken.

“Thar’s whar it all begun﻿—that cursed place of all wickedness whar the deep water starts. Gate o’ hell﻿—sheer drop daown to a bottom no saoundin’-line kin tech. Ol’ Cap’n Obed done it﻿—him that faound aout more’n was good fer him in the Saouth Sea islands.

“Never was nobody like Cap’n Obed﻿—old limb o’ Satan! Heh, heh! I kin mind him a-tellin’ abaout furren parts, an’ callin’ all the folks stupid fer goin’ to Christian meetin’ an’ bearin’ their burdens meek an’ lowly. Says they’d orter git better gods like some o’ the folks in the Injies﻿—gods as ud bring ’em good fishin’ in return fer their sacrifices, an’ ud reely answer folks’s prayers.

“Matt Eliot, his fust mate, talked a lot, too, only he was agin’ folks’s doin’ any heathen things. Told abaout an island east of Othaheite whar they was a lot o’ stone ruins older’n anybody knew anything abaout, kind o’ like them on Ponape, in the Carolines, but with carvin’s of faces that looked like the big statues on Easter Island. They was a little volcanic island near thar, too, whar they was other ruins with diff’rent carvin’s﻿—ruins all wore away like they’d ben under the sea onct, an’ with picters of awful monsters all over ’em.

===Chinese===

要是赶8点去阿卡姆的班车，还有大约四个钟头可谈；我开始一点一点往这老酒徒手里递酒，自己吃着随身的一点简单午饭。斟给他的分寸我很小心，不想叫扎多克酒后的话匣子变成一滩烂醉。一个钟头后，他那种鬼祟的沉默显出松动的迹象；不知什么东西引了他游移的目光，落到魔鬼礁那低低远远的一线上——此刻它正清清楚楚、几乎魅人地露在浪上。他朝我俯过身来，攥住我的衣领，嘶嘶地吐出几句错认不了的话：

“一切都是在那儿起的头——那个遭诅咒的、万恶的、深水开头的地方。地狱之门——笔直掉下去，测深绳都够不着底。是老奥贝德船长干下的——他呀，在南洋群岛打听着了些不好多知道的东西。

“从来没有谁比得上奥贝德船长——老撒旦的蹄子！嘿，嘿！我还记得他讲外洋地方，骂大伙儿都是傻瓜，傻呵呵上基督教的礼拜，温温顺顺地背自己的苦命。他说该换些好些的神，像印度那头一些人拜的——能用祭换回满网的鱼、当真会应人祷告的神。

“大副马特·埃利奥特话也多，只是他反对人干异教的营生。他讲过奥塔希提东边的一座岛，岛上有好些石头废墟，老得没人说得上来历，有点像卡罗琳群岛波纳佩那边的，可刻的脸，同复活节岛上的大石像一个模样。那附近还有座小小的火山岛，另有一批刻着别的花样的废墟——全磨蚀得像在水底待过一回，上头画满了狰狞的怪物。

===Original===

“Wal, Sir, Matt he says the natives araound thar had all the fish they cud ketch, an’ sported bracelets an’ armlets an’ head rigs made aout of a queer kind o’ gold an’ covered with picters o’ monsters jest like the ones carved over the ruins on the little island﻿—sorter fishlike frogs or froglike fishes that was drawed in all kinds o’ positions like they was human bein’s. Nobody cud git aout o’ them whar they got all the stuff, an’ all the other natives wondered haow they managed to find fish in plenty even when the very next islands had lean pickin’s. Matt he got to wonderin’ too, an’ so did Cap’n Obed. Obed, he notices, besides, that lots of the han’some young folks ud drop aout o’ sight fer good from year to year, an’ that they wan’t many old folk araound. Also, he thinks some of the folks looks durned queer even fer Kanakys.

“It took Obed to git the truth aout o’ them heathens. I dun’t know haow he done it, but he begun by tradin’ fer the gold-like things they wore. Ast ’em whar they come from, an’ ef they cud git more, an’ finally wormed the story aout o’ the old chief﻿—Walakea, they called him. Nobody but Obed ud ever a believed the old yeller devil, but the Cap’n cud read folks like they was books. Heh, heh! Nobody never believes me naow when I tell ’em, an I dun’t s’pose you will, young feller﻿—though come to look at ye, ye hev kind o’ got them sharp-readin’ eyes like Obed had.”

The old man’s whisper grew fainter, and I found myself shuddering at the terrible and sincere portentousness of his intonation, even though I knew his tale could be nothing but drunken fantasy.

===Chinese===

“唉，先生，马特说，那一带的土人有捕不完的鱼，还戴着古怪金子打的镯子、臂环、头面，上面錾的怪物，同小岛废墟上刻的一个模样——像鱼的蛙，又像蛙的鱼，各样姿势都有，跟人似的。没人能从他们嘴里问出那些东西是哪儿来的；旁边岛上的鱼打不上来，就他们鱼多得吃不完，旁的土人都纳闷。马特纳闷起来，奥贝德船长也纳闷起来。奥贝德还留意到，年年都有标致的年轻人不见了踪影，四下的老人也不多。他还觉得，有些人的模样，就算按卡拿基的标尺，也怪得出奇。

“弄清这帮异教徒的底细，全亏了奥贝德。他怎么弄成的我不知道，反正他开头是拿东西换他们戴的那种金货。问他们货是哪儿来的，还能不能弄到，末了从老酋长嘴里撬出了那段事——那酋长叫瓦拉基亚。要不是奥贝德，谁也不会信那黄皮老魔头的鬼话，可船长读人跟读书一样。嘿，嘿！如今我讲给人听也没人信，我看你也不会信，年轻人——不过瞧你这模样，倒有点奥贝德那双看透人的眼睛。”

老人的耳语愈来愈低，我发觉自己在他话音那可怕而诚恳的不祥里发着抖，虽然明知他的故事只可能是醉后的胡话。

===Original===

“Wal, Sir, Obed he larnt that they’s things on this arth as most folks never heard abaout﻿—an’ wouldn’t believe ef they did hear. It seems these Kanakys was sacrificin’ heaps o’ their young men an’ maidens to some kind o’ god-things that lived under the sea, an’ gittin’ all kinds o’ favors in return. They met the things on the little islet with the queer ruins, an’ it seems them awful picters o’ frogfish monsters was supposed to be picters o’ these things. Mebbe they was the kind o’ critters as got all the mermaids stories an’ sech started. They had all kinds o’ cities on the sea-bottom, an’ this island was heaved up from thar. Seems they was some of the things alive in the stone buildin’s when the island come up sudden to the surface. That’s haow the Kanakys got wind they was daown thar. Made sign-talk as soon as they got over bein’ skeert, an’ pieced up a bargain afore long.

“Them things liked human sacrifices. Had had ’em ages afore, but lost track o’ the upper world arter a time. What they done to the victims it ain’t fer me to say, an’ I guess Obed wa’n’t none too sharp abaout askin’. But it was all right with the heathens, because they’d ben havin’ a hard time an’ was desp’rate abaout everything. They give a sarten number o’ young folks to the sea-things twict every year﻿—May-Eve an’ Halloween﻿—reg’lar as cud be. Also give some o’ the carved knickknacks they made. What the things agreed to give in return was a plenty o’ fish﻿—they druv ’em in from all over the sea﻿—an’ a few gold-like things naow an’ then.

“When it come to matin’ with them toad-lookin’ fishes, the Kanakys kind o’ balked, but finally they larnt something as put a new face on the matter.
