Men of broader intellect know that there is no sharp distinction betwixt the real and the unreal; that all things appear as they do only by virtue of the delicate individual physical and mental media through which we are made conscious of them; but the prosaic materialism of the majority condemns as madness the flashes of supersight which penetrate the common veil of obvious empiricism.

My name is Jervas Dudley, and from earliest childhood I have been a dreamer and a visionary. Wealthy beyond the necessity of a commercial life, and temperamentally unfitted for the formal studies and social recreations of my acquaintances, I have dwelt ever in realms apart from the visible world; spending my youth and adolescence in ancient and little known books, and in roaming the fields and groves of the region near my ancestral home. I do not think that what I read in these books or saw in these fields and groves was exactly what other boys read and saw there; but of this I must say little, since detailed speech would but confirm those cruel slanders upon my intellect which I sometimes overhear from the whispers of the stealthy attendants around me. It is sufficient for me to relate events without analyzing causes.

===Chinese===

但求死后至少能安眠于平静的居所。

——维吉尔

在讲述把我关进这座疯人庇护所的种种情由时，我知道，我眼下的处境，自然会叫人怀疑我这叙述的真实。不幸的是，人类的多数，心眼太窄，对于只有心理敏感的少数人才看得见、感受得到的那些孤立现象——它们躺在共同经验之外——既无耐心掂量，也无智慧权衡。头脑更开阔的人知道，真实与不真实之间并没有截然的界线；万物之所以如我们所见，只是凭着我们赖以意识它们的、各人那套精微的身心媒介；可多数人那散文式的唯物主义，却把穿透庸常经验主义帷幕的超视闪光，判为疯狂。

我的名字叫杰瓦斯·达德利，从最早的童年起，我就是一个做梦的人、一个幻想家。家财殷实，无须经商度日，性情又不合我那些相识的正式功课和社交游乐，我便始终居住在可见世界之外的疆域里，把少年和青春都消磨在古老而少为人知的书里，消磨在祖宅近旁的田野和树丛间。我不认为我在这些书里读到、在这些田野树丛里看见的，同别的男孩读到、看见的分毫不差；但这我必须少说，因为细讲只会坐实那些残忍的谗言——说我的智力如何如何——那是我在身边那些鬼祟看护的窃语里，有时听得见的。对我来说，把事件讲出来就够了，不必分析缘由。

===Original===

I have said that I dwelt apart from the visible world, but I have not said that I dwelt alone. This no human creature may do; for lacking the fellowship of the living, he inevitably draws upon the companionship of things that are not, or are no longer, living. Close by my home there lies a singular wooded hollow, in whose twilight deeps I spent most of my time; reading, thinking, and dreaming. Down its moss-covered slopes my first steps of infancy were taken, and around its grotesquely gnarled oak trees my first fancies of boyhood were woven. Well did I come to know the presiding dryads of those trees, and often have I watched their wild dances in the struggling beams of a waning moon﻿—but of these things I must not now speak. I will tell only of the lone tomb in the darkest of the hillside thickets; the deserted tomb of the Hydes, an old and exalted family whose last direct descendant had been laid within its black recesses many decades before my birth.

The vault to which I refer is of ancient granite, weathered and discolored by the mists and dampness of generations. Excavated back into the hillside, the structure is visible only at the entrance. The door, a ponderous and forbidding slab of stone, hangs upon rusted iron hinges, and is fastened ajar in a queerly sinister way by means of heavy iron chains and padlocks, according to a gruesome fashion of half a century ago. The abode of the race whose scions are here inurned had once crowned the declivity which holds the tomb, but had long since fallen victim to the flames which sprang up from a stroke of lightning. Of the midnight storm which destroyed this gloomy mansion, the older inhabitants of the region sometimes speak in hushed and uneasy voices; alluding to what they call “divine wrath” in a manner that in later years vaguely increased the always strong fascination which I had felt for the forest-darkened sepulcher. One man only had perished in the fire. When the last of the Hydes was buried in this place of shade and stillness, the sad urnful of ashes had come from a distant land; to which the family had repaired when the mansion burned down. No one remains to lay flowers before the granite portal, and few care to brave the depressing shadows which seem to linger strangely about the water-worn stones.

===Chinese===

我说过我住在可见世界之外，但没有说过我独自居住。这是任何人都做不到的；因为缺少了活人的伙伴，他就不可避免地招来那些不是活物、或不再是活物的东西做伴。紧挨我家有一片古怪的林间洼地，它暮色似的深处，消磨了我大部分的时光：读书，思想，做梦。我幼年最初的脚步，就是踏着它生苔的斜坡迈出的；我少年最初的幻想，就是绕着它那些疙疙瘩瘩的古橡树编成的。那些树的守护树灵，我渐渐熟悉得很，也常在一弯残月挣扎的光线里看她们的狂舞——但这些事我现在不可多说。我只讲那座孤坟，在山坡灌木最密处的那座；被弃的海德家的坟——一个古老而显赫的家族，它最后一名直系后裔，在我出生前几十年就已安放在它幽黑的深处。

我说的这座地窟是古花岗岩的，被几代人的雾气和潮气风蚀得变了色。它凿进山坡，只有入口露在外面。那扇门，一块沉重而森然的石板，挂在锈铁铰链上，照半个世纪前一种阴惨的时样，用粗重的铁链和挂锁虚掩着，透着一股说不出的邪气。埋在这里的这族的宅邸，曾加冕在容纳这座坟的坡上，可早就毁于一道闪电燃起的大火。说到那场烧掉这座阴沉府邸的午夜风暴，当地的老住户有时还压低嗓音、不安地讲起，把它叫作“天谴”；这些年里，他们对它那种含糊的敬畏，隐隐添浓了我对这座林影笼罩的墓穴一直怀着的那股强烈的迷恋。火灾里只死了一个人。海德家最后一人葬进这片幽静之地时，那一瓮悲哀的骨灰，是来自一片遥远的国土；府邸焚毁后，那一家人就迁去了那里。再没有人到花岗岩的门前来献花，也少有人肯闯那片仿佛在渍水的石头四周怪异地徘徊不去的、压得人喘不过气的阴影。

===Original===

I shall never forget the afternoon when first I stumbled upon the half-hidden house of death. It was in midsummer, when the alchemy of nature transmutes the sylvan landscape to one vivid and almost homogeneous mass of green; when the senses are well-nigh intoxicated with the surging seas of moist verdure and the subtly indefinable odors of the soil and the vegetation. In such surroundings the mind loses its perspective; time and space become trivial and unreal, and echoes of a forgotten prehistoric past beat insistently upon the enthralled consciousness.

===Chinese===

我永远不会忘记我第一次撞见这座半掩的死者之家的那个下午。那是仲夏，自然的炼金术把林间景色熔成一片鲜亮而几乎匀质的绿；感官几乎被潮湿青翠的汹涌海面、被泥土和草木那微妙而无可名状的气味熏醉了。在这样的环境里，头脑失了透视；时间与空间变得琐碎而不实，一个被遗忘的史前往昔的回声，执拗地敲打着这颗被摄住的意识。

===Original===

All day I had been wandering through the mystic groves of the hollow; thinking thoughts I need not discuss, and conversing with things I need not name. In years a child of ten, I had seen and heard many wonders unknown to the throng; and was oddly aged in certain respects. When, upon forcing my way between two savage clumps of briars, I suddenly encountered the entrance of the vault, I had no knowledge of what I had discovered. The dark blocks of granite, the door so curiously ajar, and the funeral carvings above the arch, aroused in me no associations of mournful or terrible character. Of graves and tombs I knew and imagined much, but had on account of my peculiar temperament been kept from all personal contact with churchyards and cemeteries. The strange stone house on the woodland slope was to me only a source of interest and speculation; and its cold, damp interior, into which I vainly peered through the aperture so tantalizingly left, contained for me no hint of death or decay. But in that instant of curiosity was born the madly unreasoning desire which has brought me to this hell of confinement. Spurred on by a voice which must have come from the hideous soul of the forest, I resolved to enter the beckoning gloom in spite of the ponderous chains which barred my passage. In the waning light of day I alternately rattled the rusty impediments with a view to throwing wide the stone door, and essayed to squeeze my slight form through the space already provided; but neither plan met with success. At first curious, I was now frantic; and when in the thickening twilight I returned to my home, I had sworn to the hundred gods of the grove that *at any cost* I would some day force an entrance to the black, chilly depths that seemed calling out to me. The physician with the iron-gray beard who comes each day to my room, once told a visitor that this decision marked the beginning of a pitiful monomania; but I will leave final judgment to my readers when they shall have learnt all.

===Chinese===

那一整天，我都在洼地那些神秘的树丛间游荡；想着我不必讨论的念头，同我不必命名的物件交谈。论年纪我是个十岁的孩子，可我见过、听过许多众人不知道的奇事；在某些方面出奇地早熟。当我从两丛狰狞的荆棘间硬挤过去，猛然撞上地窟的入口时，我并不知道自己发现了什么。深色的花岗岩块，那扇古怪地虚掩的门，门楣上的丧仪雕刻，都没有在我心里唤起悲悼或恐怖的联想。坟墓和陵墓，我知道得、想象得很多；但因为性情的古怪，父母一直不许我亲身接触教堂墓园和坟场。林坡上这座古怪的石头房子，于我只是一个兴趣和揣测的源头；它冰冷潮湿的内部——我徒然从那道撩人地留着的缝隙往里张望——对我没有一丝死亡或朽烂的暗示。可就在好奇的那一瞬，生出了那股把我带进这座囚禁之地狱的、疯狂而不讲道理的欲望。被一个必定出自森林可憎灵魂的声音驱策着，我决意不管那拦路的重链，闯进那召唤的幽暗。在渐残的天光里，我时而哗啦哗啦摇那生锈的障碍，想把石门摇开，时而试图把我瘦小的身子从现成的缝隙里挤进去；两计都未得逞。起初是好奇，如今是狂乱；在愈来愈浓的暮色里回家时，我已向树丛的百神起誓：无论付出什么代价，总有一天我要闯进那仿佛在向我呼喊的、黑色阴寒的深处。那位天天到我房间里来的铁灰胡子的医生，曾对一位来访者说，这个决定标志了一场可悲的单向执迷的开端；但最后的裁断，我留给我的读者，等他们听完全部再说。

===Original===

The months following my discovery were spent in futile attempts to force the complicated padlock of the slightly open vault, and in carefully guarded inquiries regarding the nature and history of the structure. With the traditionally receptive ears of the small boy, I learned much; though an habitual secretiveness caused me to tell no one of my information or my resolve. It is perhaps worth mentioning that I was not at all surprised or terrified on learning of the nature of the vault. My rather original ideas regarding life and death had caused me to associate the cold clay with the breathing body in a vague fashion; and I felt that the great and sinister family of the burned-down mansion was in some way represented within the stone space I sought to explore. Mumbled tales of the weird rites and godless revels of bygone years in the ancient hall gave to me a new and potent interest in the tomb, before whose door I would sit for hours at a time each day. Once I thrust a candle within the nearly closed entrance, but could see nothing save a flight of damp stone steps leading downward. The odor of the place repelled yet bewitched me. I felt I had known it before, in a past remote beyond all recollection; beyond even my tenancy of the body I now possess.

---

The year after I first beheld the tomb, I stumbled upon a worm-eaten translation of Plutarch’s *Lives* in the book-filled attic of my home. Reading the life of Theseus, I was much impressed by that passage telling of the great stone beneath which the boyish hero was to find his tokens of destiny whenever he should become old enough to lift its enormous weight. This legend had the effect of dispelling my keenest impatience to enter the vault, for it made me feel that the time was not yet ripe. Later, I told myself, I should grow to a strength and ingenuity which might enable me to unfasten the heavily chained door with ease; but until then I would do better by conforming to what seemed the will of Fate.

===Chinese===

发现之后的几个月，都花在徒劳地撬那虚掩地窟的复杂挂锁上，花在小心守口地打探这建筑的来历与历史上。凭着一个男孩惯有的那种善于倾听的耳朵，我打听到许多；虽然习惯性的守密使我没有把自己的情报或决心告诉任何人。值得一提的也许是：得知地窟的性质时，我一点也不惊讶，也不害怕。我对生与死那些相当别致的观念，使我早已把冷冷的黏土同呼吸的身体含糊地联在一起；我觉着，那座焚毁府邸的伟大而阴森的一族，就以某种方式，代表在我要探索的这方石头空间里。古宅里往昔岁月的怪异仪式和渎神狂欢，那些咕咕哝哝的传说，给了我一个新的、有力的兴味；如今我每天都要在墓门前一坐几个钟头。有一回我把一支蜡烛从几乎关死的门里探进去，可什么也看不见，只看见一段潮湿的石阶通向下面。那地方的气味，又排斥我又蛊惑我。我觉得我从前认得它，在一个远过一切回忆的往昔；甚至远过我现在这具躯壳的租期。

---

初见坟墓的次年，我在家里堆满书的顶楼上翻出一部虫蛀的普鲁塔克《名人传》译本。读忒修斯的生平，我对那一段落印象极深：那位少年英雄，每当他长到搬得动那块巨石的年纪，就要在石下找到他命运的凭证。这个传说驱散了我最尖刻的、要进地窟的焦躁，因为它使我觉得时机未熟。我对自己说，往后我会长出一份力气和巧劲，轻易打开那扇锁着重链的门；在那之前，还是顺从天意的好。

===Original===

Accordingly my watches by the dank portal became less persistent, and much of my time was spent in other though equally strange pursuits. I would sometimes rise very quietly in the night, stealing out to walk in those churchyards and places of burial from which I had been kept by my parents. What I did there I may not say, for I am not now sure of the reality of certain things; but I know that on the day after such a nocturnal ramble I would often astonish those about me with my knowledge of topics almost forgotten for many generations. It was after a night like this that I shocked the community with a queer conceit about the burial of the rich and celebrated Squire Brewster, a maker of local history who was interred in 1711, and whose slate headstone, bearing a graven skull and crossbones, was slowly crumbling to powder. In a moment of childish imagination I vowed not only that the undertaker, Goodman Simpson, had stolen the silver-buckled shoes, silken hose, and satin small-clothes of the deceased before burial; but that the Squire himself, not fully inanimate, had turned twice in his mound-covered coffin on the day after interment.

But the idea of entering the tomb never left my thoughts; being indeed stimulated by the unexpected genealogical discovery that my own maternal ancestry possessed at least a slight link with the supposedly extinct family of the Hydes. Last of my paternal race, I was likewise the last of this older and more mysterious line. I began to feel that the tomb was *mine*, and to look forward with hot eagerness to the time when I might pass within that stone door and down those slimy stone steps in the dark. I now formed the habit of listening very intently at the slightly open portal, choosing my favorite hours of midnight stillness for the odd vigil. By the time I came of age, I had made a small clearing in the thicket before the mold-stained façade of the hillside, allowing the surrounding vegetation to encircle and overhang the space like the walls and roof of a sylvan bower. This bower was my temple, the fastened door my shrine, and here I would lie outstretched on the mossy ground, thinking strange thoughts and dreaming strange dreams.

===Chinese===

于是我在湿门前的守望不再那样执着，我的许多时光转投别的、却同样古怪的追求。有时我会在夜里悄悄起身，溜出去，到那些父母一直不许我去的教堂墓园和葬地间散步。我在那里做了什么，我不可说，因为某些事情如今我已不敢断定其真实；但我知道，这样的夜游之后的那天，我常常以谈论几代人间几乎被忘尽的话题，叫周围的人吃惊。就是这样的一夜之后，我以一个古怪的念头震惊了地方：说的是富有而显赫的布鲁斯特乡绅——一位地方史的制作家，1711年下葬，他那块刻着骷髅交叉骨的石板墓碑正慢慢碎成粉——的下葬。在孩童想象的一阵发作里，我咬定：不但承办殡葬的古德曼·辛普森在下葬前偷了死者的银扣鞋、真丝袜和缎子马裤；而且乡绅本人也未曾全然死透，下葬的次日，在覆土的棺材里翻了两回身。

但进坟墓的念头从不曾离开我的思想；一笔出乎意料的谱系发现，反而给它添了柴——我发现我自己的母系血统，同那据信已经绝嗣的海德家，至少有着一线微弱的关联。作为父系一族最后一人，我同样也是这条更古老、更神秘的支脉的最后一人。我开始觉得那坟墓是我的，开始火热地盼望那一天：穿过那道石门，在黑暗里走下那些黏滑的石阶。我养成了在那虚掩的门前凝神倾听的习惯，专挑子夜寂静的钟点作这古怪的守夜。到我成年时，我已在山坡那座霉渍斑驳的正面之前的灌木里清出一小片空地，任四周的草木环绕覆盖，像一座林间凉亭的墙与顶。这凉亭是我的神庙，那扇锁着的门是我的圣龛；在这里，我摊开手脚躺在生苔的地上，想着怪念头，做着怪梦。

===Original===

The night of the first revelation was a sultry one. I must have fallen asleep from fatigue, for it was with a distinct sense of awakening that I heard the voices. Of these tones and accents I hesitate to speak; of their quality I will not speak; but I may say that they presented certain uncanny differences in vocabulary, pronunciation, and mode of utterance. Every shade of New England dialect, from the uncouth syllables of the Puritan colonists to the precise rhetoric of fifty years ago, seemed represented in that shadowy colloquy, though it was only later that I noticed the fact. At the time, indeed, my attention was distracted from this matter by another phenomenon; a phenomenon so fleeting that I could not take oath upon its reality. I barely fancied that as I awoke, a *light* had been hurriedly extinguished within the sunken sepulcher. I do not think I was either astounded or panic-stricken, but I know that I was greatly and permanently *changed* that night. Upon returning home I went with much directness to a rotting chest in the attic, wherein I found the key which next day unlocked with ease the barrier I had so long stormed in vain.

---

It was in the soft glow of late afternoon that I first entered the vault on the abandoned slope. A spell was upon me, and my heart leaped with an exultation I can but ill describe. As I closed the door behind me and descended the dripping steps by the light of my lone candle, I seemed to know the way; and though the candle sputtered with the stifling reek of the place, I felt singularly at home in the musty, charnel-house air. Looking about me, I beheld many marble slabs bearing coffins, or the remains of coffins. Some of these were sealed and intact, but others had nearly vanished, leaving the silver handles and plates isolated amidst certain curious heaps of whitish dust. Upon one plate I read the name of Sir Geoffrey Hyde, who had come from Sussex in 1640 and died here a few years later. In a conspicuous alcove was one fairly well preserved and untenanted casket, adorned with a single name which brought to me both a smile and a shudder. An odd impulse caused me to climb upon the broad slab, extinguish my candle, and lie down within the vacant box.

===Chinese===

第一次启示降临的那一夜，闷热得很。我必定是疲乏得睡着了，因为听见那些声音时，我带着分明是醒来的感觉。那些腔调与口音，我迟疑不愿讲；它们的质地，我更不肯讲；但我可以说，它们在用语、发音和说话方式上带着某种不祥的差异。新英格兰方言的每一种层次，从清教殖民者粗鄙的音节，到五十年前考究的修辞，仿佛都聚在那场幽影的交谈里——虽然那是后来才留意到的。当时，我的注意力其实被另一桩现象岔开了；那现象倏忽得我不敢就它的真实性起誓。我恍惚觉得，就在我醒来的一刻，那下陷的墓穴里，一盏“光”被仓皇掐灭了。我不认为我惊愕了或慌了；但我知道，那一夜，我被巨大而永久地改变了。回到家，我径直奔向顶楼上一只朽烂的箱子，在里面找到了一把钥匙——第二天，它就轻易打开了那扇我久攻不下的门。

---

我头一回走进那废弃坡上的地窟，是在迟午柔和的光里。一道符咒罩着我，我的心跳着一种我拙于描摹的狂喜。我关上身后的门，就着一支孤烛的光走下滴水的石阶，我仿佛认得这条路；虽然蜡烛被那地方的窒息恶臭熏得噼啪作响，我在这股发霉的藏尸房气味里，却出奇地如归。环顾四周，我看见许多承着棺材、或棺材残骸的大理石板。有的封着、完好，有的几乎烂尽，只剩银把手和铭牌孤零零嵌在一堆堆古怪的白粉里。一块铭牌上，我读到杰弗里·海德爵士的名字，他1640年自萨塞克斯来，几年后死在这里。一处显眼的壁龛里，有一口保存尚好、无人占用的大棺，饰着唯一一个名字，它同时给了我一个微笑和一阵寒噤。一股古怪的冲动驱使我爬上那块宽石板，吹灭蜡烛，在那口空棺里躺了下去。

===Original===

In the gray light of dawn I staggered from the vault and locked the chain of the door behind me. I was no longer a young man, though but twenty-one winters had chilled my bodily frame. Early-rising villagers who observed my homeward progress looked at me strangely, and marveled at the signs of ribald revelry which they saw in one whose life was known to be sober and solitary. I did not appear before my parents till after a long and refreshing sleep.

Henceforward I haunted the tomb each night; seeing, hearing, and doing things I must never recall. My speech, always susceptible to environmental influences, was the first thing to succumb to the change; and my suddenly acquired archaism of diction was soon remarked upon. Later a queer boldness and recklessness came into my demeanor, till I unconsciously grew to possess the bearing of a man of the world despite my lifelong seclusion. My formerly silent tongue waxed voluble with the easy grace of a Chesterfield or the godless cynicism of a Rochester. I displayed a peculiar erudition utterly unlike the fantastic, monkish lore over which I had pored in youth; and covered the flyleaves of my books with facile impromptu epigrams which brought up suggestions of Gay, Prior, and the sprightliest of the Augustan wits and rimesters. One morning at breakfast I came close to disaster by declaiming in palpably liquorish accents an effusion of Eighteenth Century bacchanalian mirth a bit of Georgian playfulness never recorded in a book, which ran something like this:

Come hither, my lads, with your tankards of ale,

And drink to the present before it shall fail;

Pile each on your platter a mountain of beef,

For ’tis eating and drinking that bring us relief:

So fill up your glass,

For life will soon pass;

When you’re dead ye’ll ne’er drink to your king or your lass!

Anacreon had a red nose, so they say;

But what’s a red nose if ye’re happy and gay?

Gad split me! I’d rather be red whilst I’m here,

Than white as a lily﻿—and dead half a year!

So Betty, my miss,

Come give me a kiss;

In hell there’s no innkeeper’s daughter like this!

Young Harry, propp’d up just as straight as he’s able,

Will soon lose his wig and slip under the table;

But fill up your goblets and pass ’em around﻿—

Better under the table than under the ground!

So revel and chaff

As ye thirstily quaff:

===Chinese===

灰蒙蒙的晨光里，我踉跄走出地窟，把门上的链子在自己身后锁好。我不再是年轻人了，虽然不过二十一个寒冬侵蚀过我的肉身。早起的村民看见我回家的样子，奇怪地打量我，惊异于这样一个出了名的清苦独居的人身上，竟有纵酒狂欢的痕迹。直到睡了一长觉、缓过神来，我才在父母面前露面。

从此我每夜出没于那座坟墓；看见的、听见的、做下的，我永远不能追忆。我的谈吐，本就易受环境浸染，头一个向这变化屈服；我骤然习得的古奥措辞，很快惹人注目。随后我的举止里生出一股古怪的胆大与放浪，不知不觉间，我竟有了世家子弟走遍天下的风度，虽然我终身幽居。先前沉默的舌头，如今滔滔不绝，时而流着切斯特菲尔德式的从容雅致，时而流着罗切斯特式的渎神讥诮。我显露出一门古怪的博学，同我少年时埋头苦读的那种空幻的修院学问全然两样；我在书的前扉上写满即兴的隽语，叫人想起盖伊、普赖尔，和奥古斯都时代最轻灵的一班才子和诗客。一天早晨吃早饭时，我险些闯下大祸：用分明酒气熏熏的腔调，高声吟诵了一段十八世纪的酒神狂欢——一段任何书里都不曾记载的乔治王朝的谐谑——它大致是这样：

来吧，伙计们，端起你们的麦酒，
趁今天还没溜走，先为眼前干一口；
盘子里牛肉堆成山，
吃吃喝喝才解忧：
斟满你的杯，
人生快如飞；
死了可没法再敬你的国王和宝贝！

人家说阿那克里翁鼻子红；
可只要快活，红鼻子算什么毛病？
见鬼！我宁可活着当红鼻公，
也不做百合似的白脸——死了半年整！
所以贝蒂，我的小亲亲，
过来给我一个吻；
地狱里可找不着这样好的掌柜女儿！

小哈利硬撑着坐得笔直，
一会儿就要掉假发、溜到桌子底；
可先把酒杯斟满，传一圈——
桌子底下总比地底强得多！
所以放量喝吧，
边喝边笑骂：

===Original===

Under six feet of dirt ’tis less easy to laugh!

The fiend strike me blue! I’m scarce able to walk,

And damn me if I can stand upright or talk!

Here, landlord, bid Betty to summon a chair;

I’ll try home for a while, for my wife is not there!

So lend me a hand;

I’m not able to stand,

But I’m gay whilst I linger on top of the land!

About this time I conceived my present fear of fire and thunderstorms. Previously indifferent to such things, I had now an unspeakable horror of them; and would retire to the innermost recesses of the house whenever the heavens threatened an electrical display. A favorite haunt of mine during the day was the ruined cellar of the mansion that had burned down, and in fancy I would picture the structure as it had been in its prime. On one occasion I startled a villager by leading him confidently to a shallow sub-cellar, of whose existence I seemed to know in spite of the fact that it had been unseen and forgotten for many generations.

---

At last came that which I had long feared. My parents, alarmed at the altered manner and appearance of their only son, commenced to exert over my movements a kindly espionage which threatened to result in disaster. I had told no one of my visits to the tomb, having guarded my secret purpose with religious zeal since childhood; but now I was forced to exercise care in threading the mazes of the wooded hollow, that I might throw off a possible pursuer. My key to the vault I kept suspended from a cord about my neck, its presence known only to me. I never carried out of the sepulcher any of the things I came upon whilst within its walls.

===Chinese===

六尺土底下，可没这么好哈哈！

魔鬼掐死我！我几乎走不动，
该死的，我连站直、说话都不成！
喂，掌柜的，叫贝蒂搬把椅子来；
我要回家待一会儿，我老婆不在！
搭把手扶我一把；
我自己站不住啦，
可只要还在这地面上，我就乐哈哈！

大约在这前后，我生出了如今对火和雷雨的恐惧。从前我不把这些放在心上，如今却对它们怀着说不出的恐怖；天一有放电的征兆，我就退到宅子最里面的角落。白天我爱去的一处地方，是那座烧掉的府邸的破地窖；在幻想里，我会把它画成全盛时的模样。有一回，我领一个村民径直走到一处浅浅的地下暗窖，把他吓了一跳——它的存在我似乎了如指掌，虽然它已几代无人见过、无人记得。

---

我终于等到了我久已害怕的东西。父母为他们独子变了样的举止形容惊心，开始对我的行动施以一种慈爱的侦探，眼看要以灾祸收场。我从没对人讲过我到坟地去的事，自幼就怀着宗教的热忱守护我秘密的目的；如今我被迫小心在意地在林间洼地的迷宫里穿行，好甩掉可能的跟踪者。地窟的钥匙，我用一根带子挂在颈上，它的存在只有我知道。在墓穴围墙之内遇到的东西，我从来没有带出墓外一件。

===Original===

One morning as I emerged from the damp tomb and fastened the chain of the portal with none too steady hand, I beheld in an adjacent thicket the dreaded face of a watcher. Surely the end was near; for my bower was discovered, and the objective of my nocturnal journeys revealed. The man did not accost me, so I hastened home in an effort to overhear what he might report to my careworn father. Were my sojourns beyond the chained door about to be proclaimed to the world? Imagine my delighted astonishment on hearing the spy inform my parent in a cautious whisper *that I had spent the night in the bower outside the tomb;* my sleep-filmed eyes fixed upon the crevice where the padlocked portal stood ajar! By what miracle had the watcher been thus deluded? I was now convinced that a supernatural agency protected me. Made bold by this heaven-sent circumstance, I began to resume perfect openness in going to the vault; confident that no one could witness my entrance. For a week I tasted to the full the joys of that charnel conviviality which I must not describe, when the *thing* happened, and I was borne away to this accursed abode of sorrow and monotony.

===Chinese===

一天早晨，我走出潮湿的坟墓，用不怎么稳的手扣好门上的链子，忽见旁边的灌木丛里有一张盯梢者的脸，真叫人心惊。想来尽头近了；我的凉亭被发现了，我夜行的目的地也败露了。那人没有上前来问我，我便赶回家，想偷听他会向我忧劳的父亲报告什么。我在锁链之门后的那些逗留，眼看要被宣告给全世界了？可你想象我听见那密探压低了声向我父亲禀报时的狂喜吧——他说，我在坟外那座凉亭里过的夜，我蒙着睡意的眼睛，一直望着挂锁的门虚掩的那道缝！那盯梢的是被怎样的奇迹蒙蔽的？我这才确信，有一种超自然的力量护着我。这一上天送来的情势壮了我的胆，我去地窟重新恢复了完全的坦然，自信没人能看见我进门。有一个星期，我把那场不可描述的藏尸之欢尝了个够；随后，那“事情”发生了，我被带到了这座悲哀而单调的可诅咒的居所。

===Original===

I should not have ventured out that night; for the taint of thunder was in the clouds, and a hellish phosphorescence rose from the rank swamp at the bottom of the hollow. The call of the dead, too, was different. Instead of the hillside tomb, it was the charred cellar on the crest of the slope whose presiding demon beckoned to me with unseen fingers. As I emerged from an intervening grove upon the plain before the ruin, I beheld in the misty moonlight a thing I had always vaguely expected. The mansion, gone for a century, once more reared its stately height to the raptured vision; every window ablaze with the splendor of many candles. Up the long drive rolled the coaches of the Boston gentry, whilst on foot came a numerous assemblage of powdered exquisites from the neighboring mansions. With this throng I mingled, though I knew I belonged with the hosts rather than with the guests. Inside the hall were music, laughter, and wine on every hand. Several faces I recognized; though I should have known them better had they been shriveled or eaten away by death and decomposition. Amidst a wild and reckless throng I was the wildest and most abandoned. Gay blasphemy poured in torrents from my lips, and in my shocking sallies I heeded no law of God, man, or nature.

Suddenly a peal of thunder, resonant even above the din of the swinish revelry, clave the very roof and laid a hush of fear upon the boisterous company. Red tongues of flame and searing gusts of heat engulfed the house; and the roysterers, struck with terror at the descent of a calamity which seemed to transcend the bounds of unguided nature, fled shrieking into the night. I alone remained, riveted to my seat by a groveling fear which I had never felt before. And then a second horror took possession of my soul. Burnt alive to ashes, my body dispersed by the four winds, *I might never lie in the tomb of the Hydes*! Was not my coffin prepared for me? Had I not a right to rest till eternity amongst the descendants of Sir Geoffrey Hyde? Aye! I would claim my heritage of death, even though my soul go seeking through the ages for another corporeal tenement to represent it on that vacant slab in the alcove of the vault. *Jervas Hyde* should never share the sad fate of Palinurus!

===Chinese===

那一夜我本不该出门；云里带着雷的腥气，洼地底下的疯沼泽升起一片地狱的磷光。死者的召唤，也不同了。召唤我的，不是山坡上的坟墓，而是坡顶那座焦黑的地窖，它主宰的恶魔用看不见的手指朝我勾着。当我从中间的树林出来、走到废墟前的平地上，我在雾蒙蒙的月光里看见了那件我一直恍惚期待的东西。那座消失了一个世纪的府邸，再一次把它堂皇的高身影投进如痴如望的眼里；每一扇窗，都辉映着千百支蜡烛的华彩。长长的车道上，波士顿仕宦的马车辚辚而来；四邻府邸搽粉的纨绔们，成群结队地步行而至。我混进了这群人里，虽然我知道我属于主人一边，不属于宾客。大厅里，四面八方都是音乐、笑声和酒。有几张脸我认得；虽然，倘若它们被死亡和腐烂皱缩了、蛀空了，我本该认得更熟才对。在狂放的一群里，我是最狂放、最肆无忌惮的一个。快活的渎神从我唇间倾泻如注，我那惊世骇俗的妙语里，上帝的、人间的、自然的一切律法，我一概不理。

突然一声雷，响得盖过猪猡狂欢的喧腾，劈开了屋顶，把一阵恐惧的静默压在这吵闹的一堂头上。红的火舌和灼人的热浪吞没了宅子；寻欢的人们被这场仿佛越出了无导自然之界限的灾祸吓破了胆，尖叫着逃进夜色。只有我留下，被一种从未尝过的匍匐的恐惧钉在座位上。随后第二种恐怖攫住了我的灵魂。被活活烧成灰，身子被四风打散，我可能永远躺不进海德家的坟墓了！我的棺材不是早已为我备好？难道我没有权利，在杰弗里·海德爵士的后嗣中间安息到永恒？啊！我要认领我死亡的遗产，哪怕我的灵魂得穿过一个个世代，另寻一具有形的居所，到地窟壁龛里那块空石板上去代表它。杰瓦斯·海德，绝不该落得帕利努鲁斯那样的伤心下场！

===Original===

As the phantom of the burning house faded, I found myself screaming and struggling madly in the arms of two men, one of whom was the spy who had followed me to the tomb. Rain was pouring down in torrents, and upon the southern horizon were flashes of the lightning that had so lately passed over our heads. My father, his face lined with sorrow, stood by as I shouted my demands to be laid within the tomb; frequently admonishing my captors to treat me as gently as they could. A blackened circle on the floor of the ruined cellar told of a violent stroke from the heavens; and from this spot a group of curious villagers with lanterns were prying a small box of antique workmanship, which the thunderbolt had brought to light.

Ceasing my futile and now objectless writhing, I watched the spectators as they viewed the treasure-trove, and was permitted to share in their discoveries. The box, whose fastenings were broken by the stroke which had unearthed it, contained many papers and objects of value; but I had eyes for one thing alone. It was the porcelain miniature of a young man in a smartly curled bag-wig, and bore the initials “J. H.” The face was such that as I gazed, I might well have been studying my mirror.

---

===Chinese===

燃烧的宅子的幻影淡去时，我发觉自己正在两个男人怀里尖叫、疯狂挣扎，其中一个，就是跟到坟地去的那密探。大雨倾盆，南面的地平线上，闪电还在闪光——不久前它才从我们头顶过去。父亲满脸愁纹地立在一边，听我喊叫着把我葬进坟墓的要求；一面不断叮嘱抓我的人，尽量待我温柔些。废墟地窖的地面上一个焦黑的圆圈，讲着从天上落下的一记猛雷；就在这个点上，一群提灯的好奇村民，正撬着一只雷劈出来的、古做工的小盒子。

我停止了徒劳的、如今已无对象的扭动，看围观的人看这宗意外之财，也获准分享他们的发现。盒子被劈出它的那一击打坏了锁扣，里面是许多文书和值钱的物件；可我的眼睛只认一件东西。那是一幅瓷绘的袖珍画像，画一个少年，戴着卷得漂亮的袋状假发，落着两个花押：“J. H.”。那张脸——我凝望着它，简直像在照我的镜子。

---

===Original===

On the following day I was brought to this room with the barred windows, but I have been kept informed of certain things through an aged and simple-minded servitor, for whom I bore a fondness in infancy, and who, like me, loves the churchyard. What I have dared relate of my experiences within the vault has brought me only pitying smiles. My father, who visits me frequently, declares that at no time did I pass the chained portal, and swears that the rusted padlock had not been touched for fifty years when he examined it. He even says that all the village knew of my journeys to the tomb, and that I was often watched as I slept in the bower outside the grim façade, my half-open eyes fixed on the crevice that leads to the interior. Against these assertions I have no tangible proof to offer, since my key to the padlock was lost in the struggle on that night of horrors. The strange things of the past which I have learned during those nocturnal meetings with the dead he dismisses as the fruits of my lifelong and omnivorous browsing amongst the ancient volumes of the family library. Had it not been for my old servant Hiram, I should have by this time become quite convinced of my madness.

But Hiram, loyal to the last, has held faith in me, and has done that which impels me to make public at least a part of my story. A week ago he burst open the lock which chains the door of the tomb perpetually ajar, and descended with a lantern into the murky depths. On a slab in an alcove he found an old but empty coffin whose tarnished plate bears the single word: *Jervas*. In that coffin and in that vault they have promised me I shall be buried.

===Chinese===

第二天我被带进这间装着铁栏窗的房间；但有些事，我仍从一个年迈而头脑简单的老仆那里陆续得知——婴孩时我就喜欢他，他同我一样爱教堂墓园。我斗胆讲出的那些在地窟之内的经历，只换来怜悯的微笑。常来看我的父亲宣称，我从来不曾通过那道锁链的门，还赌咒说，他查验时，那把锈挂锁已经五十年没人碰过。他甚至说，全村人都知道我到坟地去，都知道我常睡在那狰狞门面外的凉亭里，半睁的眼固定在那条通向内部的缝隙上。对这些说法，我拿不出有形的反证，因为我的挂锁钥匙，在那恐怖之夜的挣扎里丢了。我从那些与死者的夜会里学来的往昔怪事，他一概归之于我终身在这座家宅藏书室的古书堆里无所不啃的果实。若不是我的老仆海勒姆，我到这时怕已完全相信自己疯了。

可海勒姆忠心到最后一刻，始终对我不失信心，还做下了一件事，促使我至少把这故事的一部分公之于众。一个星期前，他砸开了那条把墓门永远虚掩着的锁链，提着灯笼下到幽暗的深处。在一处壁龛的石板上，他找到一口旧而空的棺材，黯淡的铭牌上只有一个词：杰瓦斯。在那口棺材里、在那座地窟里，他们已经答应我：我将下葬。

## The Unnamable / 不可名状
===Original===

We were sitting on a dilapidated seventeenth-century tomb in the late afternoon of an autumn day at the old burying-ground in Arkham, and speculating about the unnamable. Looking toward the giant willow in the center of the cemetery, whose trunk has nearly engulfed an ancient, illegible slab, I had made a fantastic remark about the spectral and unmentionable nourishment which the colossal roots must be sucking in from that hoary, charnel earth; when my friend chided me for such nonsense and told me that since no interments had occurred there for over a century, nothing could possibly exist to nourish the tree in other than an ordinary manner. Besides, he added, my constant talk about “unnamable” and “unmentionable” things was a very puerile device, quite in keeping with my lowly standing as an author. I was too fond of ending my stories with sights or sounds which paralysed my heroes’ faculties and left them without courage, words, or associations to tell what they had experienced. We know things, he said, only through our five senses or our religious intuitions; wherefore it is quite impossible to refer to any object or spectacle which cannot be clearly depicted by the solid definitions of fact or the correct doctrines of theology﻿—preferably those of the Congregationalists, with whatever modifications tradition and Sir Arthur Conan Doyle may supply.

===Chinese===

一个秋日的傍晚，我们坐在阿卡姆古墓园里一座十七世纪的破墓上，谈论着那不可名状之物。我望着墓园中央那棵大柳树——树身几乎吞掉了一块字迹漫漶的古碑——随口发了一通奇谈，说那庞然的树根，必定正从这藏尸的太古泥土里，吮吸着幽魂的、不可提及的滋养；我的朋友当即斥我胡说，说那里一百多年不曾下过葬，树的营养除却寻常的路数，不可能有别的东西。何况，他补了一句，我张口闭口“不可名状”、“不可提及”，是一种非常幼稚的伎俩，同我作为作家的卑微地位正相称。我太喜欢拿一些景象或声响收尾了——它们瘫掉我主角的官能，叫他们没勇气、没言语、没联想去讲述自己的经历。我们认识事物，他说，只有凭五种感官或宗教的直觉；所以，指着任何一件不能由事实的坚实定义或神学的正确教义——最好是公理会的教义，再加传统和阿瑟·柯南·道尔爵士可能提供的若干修正——清楚描绘的对象或景象说话，是完全不可能的。

===Original===

With this friend, Joel Manton, I had often languidly disputed. He was principal of the East High School, born and bred in Boston and sharing New England’s self-satisfied deafness to the delicate overtones of life. It was his view that only our normal, objective experiences possess any aesthetic significance, and that it is the province of the artist not so much to rouse strong emotion by action, ecstasy, and astonishment, as to maintain a placid interest and appreciation by accurate, detailed transcripts of everyday affairs. Especially did he object to my preoccupation with the mystical and the unexplained; for although believing in the supernatural much more fully than I, he would not admit that it is sufficiently commonplace for literary treatment. That a mind can find its greatest pleasure in escapes from the daily treadmill, and in original and dramatic recombinations of images usually thrown by habit and fatigue into the hackneyed patterns of actual existence, was something virtually incredible to his clear, practical, and logical intellect. With him all things and feelings had fixed dimensions, properties, causes, and effects; and although he vaguely knew that the mind sometimes holds visions and sensations of far less geometrical, classifiable, and workable nature, he believed himself justified in drawing an arbitrary line and ruling out of court all that cannot be experienced and understood by the average citizen. Besides, he was almost sure that nothing can be really “unnamable.” It didn’t sound sensible to him.

===Chinese===

同这位朋友，乔尔·曼顿，我时常懒懒地争辩。他是东部中学的校长，生在长在波士顿，同新英格兰一样，对生活精微的泛音怀着自满的聋。他的见解是：只有我们正常的、客观的经验才有审美的意义；艺术家的职分，与其说是用行动、狂喜和惊骇唤起强烈的情感，不如说是靠日常事务的精确细致的记录，维持一种平静的兴趣与欣赏。他尤其反对我沉溺于神秘与不可解释；因为虽然对超自然的信，远比我信得彻底，他却不承认它平常得可以入文学。一颗心可以从日常的踏车里寻得最大的快乐，办法是逃出去，把习惯与疲劳通常抛进现实生活陈腐套路里的那些意象，作原创而戏剧性的重组——这对他那清晰、实际而有逻辑的头脑，简直是不可思议。在他那里，一切事物和情感都有固定的尺寸、属性、原因和结果；虽然他隐约知道，头脑有时持有一些远不那么几何、不那么可归类、不那么可驾驭性质的形象与感觉，他却相信，自己有权划一条任意的线，把一切普通公民经历不了、理解不了的东西，一概摈于法庭之外。何况他几乎确信，没有什么东西当真是“不可名状”的。在他听来，这不像话。

===Original===

Though I well realised the futility of imaginative and metaphysical arguments against the complacency of an orthodox sun-dweller, something in the scene of this afternoon colloquy moved me to more than usual contentiousness. The crumbling slate slabs, the patriarchal trees, and the centuried gambrel roofs of the witch-haunted old town that stretched around, all combined to rouse my spirit in defence of my work; and I was soon carrying my thrusts into the enemy’s own country. It was not, indeed, difficult to begin a counterattack, for I knew that Joel Manton actually half clung to many old wives’ superstitions which sophisticated people had long outgrown; beliefs in the appearance of dying persons at distant places, and in the impressions left by old faces on the windows through which they had gazed all their lives. To credit these whisperings of rural grandmothers, I now insisted, argued a faith in the existence of spectral substances on the earth apart from and subsequent to their material counterparts. It argued a capability of believing in phenomena beyond all normal notions; for if a dead man can transmit his visible or tangible image half across the world, or down the stretch of the centuries, how can it be absurd to suppose that deserted houses are full of queer sentient things, or that old graveyards teem with the terrible, unbodied intelligence of generations? And since spirit, in order to cause all the manifestations attributed to it, cannot be limited by any of the laws of matter; why is it extravagant to imagine psychically living dead things in shapes﻿—or absences of shapes﻿—which must for human spectators be utterly and appallingly “unnamable”? “Common sense” in reflecting on these subjects, I assured my friend with some warmth, is merely a stupid absence of imagination and mental flexibility.

---

===Chinese===

虽然我深知，拿想象和玄学的论证去攻一个正统的向阳而居者的自满，是徒劳的，这天下午谈话的场面，却激起了我异乎寻常的好斗。崩碎的石板，德高望重的古树，四面延伸出去的、巫魇缠身的老镇那几个世纪的复折屋顶，合力鼓起了我为自己的作品辩护的心气；不一会儿，我的矛头便刺进了敌人自己的国土。反击其实不难开头，因为我知道，乔尔·曼顿其实还半抱着许多老太婆的迷信——城里人早甩掉了的：信将死之人会在远处现身，信老脸会把自己一生的凝望留在窗玻璃上。如今我咬定：肯信乡下祖母们的这些絮语，就等于信幽魂的物质之外、之后，还在这世上存在。就等于信一种越出一切正常观念的现象；因为一个死人既能把可见可触的形象传过大半个世界，或穿过几个世纪传下来，那么，假设空屋子里挤满古怪的有知觉之物，假设古墓园里挤满一代代可怕的、无形的智能，又有什么荒唐？既然灵魂要造出归在它名下的一切显形，就不能受任何物质定律的限制；那么，想象一些心理上活着的死物，其形状——或者无形状——在人类旁观者眼里必定彻底地、骇人地“不可名状”，又算什么奢侈？“常识”在这些题目上打转，我带着几分热度向朋友保证，不过是愚蠢地缺了想象力和心智的弹性。

---

===Original===

Twilight had now approached, but neither of us felt any wish to cease speaking. Manton seemed unimpressed by my arguments, and eager to refute them, having that confidence in his own opinions which had doubtless caused his success as a teacher; whilst I was too sure of my ground to fear defeat. The dusk fell, and lights faintly gleamed in some of the distant windows, but we did not move. Our seat on the tomb was very comfortable, and I knew that my prosaic friend would not mind the cavernous rift in the ancient, root-disturbed brickwork close behind us, or the utter blackness of the spot brought by the intervention of a tottering, deserted seventeenth-century house between us and the nearest lighted road. There in the dark, upon that riven tomb by the deserted house, we talked on about the “unnamable,” and after my friend had finished his scoffing I told him of the awful evidence behind the story at which he had scoffed the most.

===Chinese===

暮色已近，我们却谁也不想住口。曼顿似乎没有被我的论证打动，急着要驳倒它们——他对自己的见解怀着那种自信，无疑正是这自信使他做教师一帆风顺；而我太有把握，不怕落败。黄昏落下来，远处几扇窗里透出微弱的光，我们没有动。坐在墓上的位置很舒服；我知道，我那位散文式的朋友，不会在意身后古砖被树根拱开的那道深豁的裂口，也不会在意这一点的全然的黑——一座摇摇欲坠的十七世纪空屋隔在我们和最近的有灯的街之间，把黑带来了。就在那里的黑暗中，在那空屋旁裂开的墓上，我们继续谈着“不可名状”；朋友讥笑完了，我便给他讲了我被他笑得最凶的那篇故事背后的可怕证据。

===Original===

My tale had been called “The Attic Window,” and appeared in the January, 1922, issue of *Whispers*. In a good many places, especially the South and the Pacific coast, they took the magazines off the stands at the complaints of silly milksops; but New England didn’t get the thrill and merely shrugged its shoulders at my extravagance. The thing, it was averred, was biologically impossible to start with; merely another of those crazy country mutterings which Cotton Mather had been gullible enough to dump into his chaotic *Magnalia Christi Americana*, and so poorly authenticated that even he had not ventured to name the locality where the horror occurred. And as to the way I amplified the bare jotting of the old mystic﻿—that was quite impossible, and characteristic of a flighty and notional scribbler! Mather had indeed told of the thing as being born, but nobody but a cheap sensationalist would think of having it grow up, look into people’s windows at night, and be hidden in the attic of a house, in flesh and in spirit, till someone saw it at the window centuries later and couldn’t describe what it was that turned his hair grey. All this was flagrant trashiness, and my friend Manton was not slow to insist on that fact. Then I told him what I had found in an old diary kept between 1706 and 1723, unearthed among family papers not a mile from where we were sitting; that, and the certain reality of the scars on my ancestor’s chest and back which the diary described. I told him, too, of the fears of others in that region, and how they were whispered down for generations; and how no mythical madness came to the boy who in 1793 entered an abandoned house to examine certain traces suspected to be there.

===Chinese===

我那篇东西叫《顶楼的窗》，登在1922年1月号的《低语》上。在好些地方，尤其是南方和太平洋沿岸，一班愚蠢的软骨头一抱怨，杂志就从书摊上撤了；新英格兰却没得到那种刺激，只对我夸张耸一耸肩。人们断言，这东西在生物学上首先就不可能；不过是又一桩疯疯癫癫的乡野呓语，科顿·马瑟轻信得可以，把它倒进了他那部杂乱无章的《美国基督行传》（Magnalia Christi Americana）；而且查证得这样糟，连他也不敢点出恐怖发生的地点。至于我把那位老神秘主义者的寥寥数语铺张成那个样子——那更是全无可能，是一个轻浮想当然的涂抹匠的做派！马瑟确实讲了那东西的出生，可是除了廉价的耸动家，谁会想到叫它长大，夜里窥人的窗，藏在一座房子的顶楼里，肉身和魂灵一齐藏着，直到几百年后有人在窗前看见它，吓得头发白了也讲不出那是什么。这一切都是明晃晃的滥俗，我的朋友曼顿毫不迟疑地强调这一点。于是我对他说了我在一本1706至1723年间的旧日记里发现的东西——那日记，就在离我们坐处不到一英里的家藏文书堆里出土；还说了我祖先胸口和背上那些疤痕确凿的真实，日记里正描写过它们。我还告诉他那地方旁人的恐惧，它们怎样被一代代咬着耳朵传下来；还告诉他，1793年那个走进一座废弃老屋、去查证疑心存在的某些痕迹的男孩，并没有落下什么传说中的疯病。

===Original===

It had been an eldritch thing﻿—no wonder sensitive students shudder at the Puritan age in Massachusetts. So little is known of what went on beneath the surface﻿—so little, yet such a ghastly festering as it bubbles up putrescently in occasional ghoulish glimpses. The witchcraft terror is a horrible ray of light on what was stewing in men’s crushed brains, but even that is a trifle. There was no beauty; no freedom﻿—we can see that from the architectural and household remains, and the poisonous sermons of the cramped divines. And inside that rusted iron straitjacket lurked gibbering hideousness, perversion, and diabolism. Here, truly, was the apotheosis of the unnamable.

---

Cotton Mather, in that demoniac sixth book which no one should read after dark, minced no words as he flung forth his anathema. Stern as a Jewish prophet, and laconically unamazed as none since his day could be, he told of the beast that had brought forth what was more than beast but less than man﻿—the thing with the blemished eye﻿—and of the screaming drunken wretch that they hanged for having such an eye. This much he baldly told, yet without a hint of what came after. Perhaps he did not know, or perhaps he knew and did not dare to tell. Others knew, but did not dare to tell﻿—there is no public hint of why they whispered about the lock on the door to the attic stairs in the house of a childless, broken, embittered old man who had put up a blank slate slab by an avoided grave, although one may trace enough evasive legends to curdle the thinnest blood.

===Chinese===

那原是一桩鬼怪的事——无怪敏感的学子们一想到马萨诸塞的清教时代就要发抖。表面底下进行过什么，我们知道得太少——太少，然而当它偶尔从食尸鬼似的一瞥里腐臭地冒泡时，又是那样一场可怕的溃烂。巫术恐怖是一线可怕的光，照见人们被压碎的脑子里焖着的东西；可就连它也只是小事。没有美，没有自由——从建筑和家居的遗物，从那些心胸狭窄的神职人员的毒布道里，我们看得出来。而在那件锈铁的紧身衣底下，潜伏着语无伦次的狰狞、乖戾和魔道。这里才真正是“不可名状”的登峰造极。

---

科顿·马瑟在他那本谁也不该在天黑后读的恶魔的第六卷书里，抛出诅咒时毫不吞吐。他严峻得像一位犹太先知，简洁得不动声色——他之后没有人能这样——他讲了那头生下比兽多、比人少之物的畜生——那长着一只浊眼的东西——也讲了那个又叫又闹、被他们绞死的醉汉，罪名就是长了这样一只眼。这些他直统统讲了，却没有一字暗示后事。或许他不知道，或许他知道而不敢讲。别人知道，也不敢讲——为什么人们咬耳朵，说一座无儿无女、家破心灰的老人家里的顶楼楼梯门上有一把锁，为什么老人在一座人人回避的坟旁立了一块无字石板，公开的线索一点没有；尽管循着那些躲躲闪闪的传说，已经足够叫最淡的血凝结。

===Original===

It is all in that ancestral diary I found; all the hushed innuendoes and furtive tales of things with a blemished eye seen at windows in the night or in deserted meadows near the woods. Something had caught my ancestor on a dark valley road, leaving him with marks of horns on his chest and of apelike claws on his back; and when they looked for prints in the trampled dust they found the mixed marks of split hooves and vaguely anthropoid paws. Once a post-rider said he saw an old man chasing and calling to a frightful loping, nameless thing on Meadow Hill in the thinly moonlit hours before dawn, and many believed him. Certainly, there was strange talk one night in 1710 when the childless, broken old man was buried in the crypt behind his own house in sight of the blank slate slab. They never unlocked that attic door, but left the whole house as it was, dreaded and deserted. When noises came from it, they whispered and shivered; and hoped that the lock on that attic door was strong. Then they stopped hoping when the horror occurred at the parsonage, leaving not a soul alive or in one piece. With the years the legends take on a spectral character﻿—I suppose the thing, if it was a living thing, must have died. The memory had lingered hideously﻿—all the more hideous because it was so secret.

---

During this narration my friend Manton had become very silent, and I saw that my words had impressed him. He did not laugh as I paused, but asked quite seriously about the boy who went mad in 1793, and who had presumably been the hero of my fiction. I told him why the boy had gone to that shunned, deserted house, and remarked that he ought to be interested, since he believed that windows retained latent images of those who had sat at them. The boy had gone to look at the windows of that horrible attic, because of tales of things seen behind them, and had come back screaming maniacally.

===Chinese===

这一切都在我找到的那本祖传日记里；全都是压低的暗讽和偷偷的传闻：说夜里在窗前、在林边荒草地里，看见过长着浊眼的东西。有什么东西在一条黑暗的山谷路上扑到过我祖先身上，在他胸口留下角的印子，背上留下类猿的爪痕；人们在践踏的尘土里找脚印，找到的是裂蹄和依稀类人脚掌混合的印。有一回，一个驿骑说，黎明前月色稀薄的时辰，他在草甸山上看见一个老人追着、喊着一样跑得蹿高蹿跳的无名东西，许多人信他。当然，1710年的一夜有过古怪的议论：那无儿无女、心灰意冷的老人，葬在他自家屋后的地宫里，正对着那块无字的石板。那扇顶楼门他们始终没有开，整座屋子原样留着，又怕又空。里面有动静时，他们咬耳朵，打寒噤，指望顶楼门上的锁结实。后来牧师住宅出了那场恐怖，没留一个活口、一个囫囵人，他们连指望也不指望了。随着岁月，传说添上了幽魂的色彩——我想那东西，倘若它是活物，必已死了。记忆狰狞地缠留下去——正因为它这样秘密，才愈发狰狞。

---

这番讲述之间，我的朋友曼顿变得很沉默，我看得出我的话打动了他。我停顿时他没有笑，反倒一本正经地问起1793年那个发疯的男孩——多半被我当作了那篇小说的主角。我告诉他男孩为什么去那座人人回避的空屋，还说，既然他相信窗子会留住坐在窗前的人的潜影，他就该感兴趣。那男孩去，正是为看那可怕顶楼的窗，因为传说窗户后头有东西；他回来时已尖叫着疯了。

===Original===

Manton remained thoughtful as I said this, but gradually reverted to his analytical mood. He granted for the sake of argument that some unnatural monster had really existed, but reminded me that even the most morbid perversion of Nature need not be *unnamable* or scientifically indescribable. I admired his clearness and persistence, and added some further revelations I had collected among the old people. Those later spectral legends, I made plain, related to monstrous apparitions more frightful than anything organic could be; apparitions of gigantic bestial forms sometimes visible and sometimes only tangible, which floated about on moonless nights and haunted the old house, the crypt behind it, and the grave where a sapling had sprouted beside an illegible slab. Whether or not such apparitions had ever gored or smothered people to death, as told in uncorroborated traditions, they had produced a strong and consistent impression; and were yet darkly feared by very aged natives, though largely forgotten by the last two generations﻿—perhaps dying for lack of being thought about. Moreover, so far as aesthetic theory was involved, if the psychic emanations of human creatures be grotesque distortions, what coherent representation could express or portray so gibbous and infamous a nebulosity as the spectre of a malign, chaotic perversion, itself a morbid blasphemy against Nature? Moulded by the dead brain of a hybrid nightmare, would not such a vaporous terror constitute in all loathsome truth the exquisitely, the shriekingly *unnamable*?

---

The hour must now have grown very late. A singularly noiseless bat brushed by me, and I believe it touched Manton also, for although I could not see him I felt him raise his arm. Presently he spoke.

“But is that house with the attic window still standing and deserted?”

“Yes,” I answered. “I have seen it.”

“And did you find anything there﻿—in the attic or anywhere else?”

===Chinese===

我说话时曼顿一直沉思，可渐渐又回到他分析的心境。他为辩论起见，承认某个反自然的怪物或许真的存在过，却提醒我：连自然最病态的乖戾，也未必就“不可名状”、就科学地不可描述。我佩服他的清晰和坚持，又添了几件我从老人那里搜罗来的披露。那些后来的幽魂传说，我讲明白，说的是比任何有机物都更可怕的怪物显形：巨兽般的形体，有时看得见，有时只摸得着，无月的夜里四处飘荡，出没在那老屋、屋后的地宫、和一块字迹漫漶的石板旁抽出小树的那座坟。这样的显形是否真像无从证实的传说讲的那样顶死过、闷死过人，它们都留下了一种强烈而一贯的印象；很老很老的本地人至今还在暗暗地怕它们，虽然最近两代人大都忘了——也许因为没人惦记，正在死去。再说，就审美理论而论，如果人的心理流溢物已是怪诞的扭曲，那么，一个恶毒的、混乱的乖戾之幽魂——它本身就是对自然的一场病态渎神——这样一团凸凹而恶名昭彰的星云，又有什么连贯的再现能够表达或描画？由一个杂交梦魇的死脑筋塑成，这样一团雾似的恐怖，岂不就在一切可憎的真实里，构成那精微的、尖叫着的“不可名状”？

---

此刻时候必定很晚了。一只悄然无声的蝙蝠擦过我身边，我相信它也擦到了曼顿，因为虽然我看不见他，却觉出他抬起了手臂。过了片刻他开口了。

“可是那座带顶楼窗的房子，还立着、还空着么？”

“是，”我答，“我见过它。”

“你在那儿发现什么没有——顶楼上，或者随便哪儿？”

===Original===

“There were some bones up under the eaves. They may have been what that boy saw﻿—if he was sensitive he wouldn’t have needed anything in the window-glass to unhinge him. If they all came from the same object it must have been an hysterical, delirious monstrosity. It would have been blasphemous to leave such bones in the world, so I went back with a sack and took them to the tomb behind the house. There was an opening where I could dump them in. Don’t think I was a fool﻿—you ought to have seen that skull. It had four-inch horns, but a face and jaw something like yours and mine.”

At last I could feel a real shiver run through Manton, who had moved very near. But his curiosity was undeterred.

“And what about the windowpanes?”

“They were all gone. One window had lost its entire frame, and in the other there was not a trace of glass in the little diamond apertures. They were that kind﻿—the old lattice windows that went out of use before 1700. I don’t believe they’ve had any glass for an hundred years or more﻿—maybe the boy broke ’em if he got that far; the legend doesn’t say.”

Manton was reflecting again.

“I’d like to see that house, Carter. Where is it? Glass or no glass, I must explore it a little. And the tomb where you put those bones, and the other grave without an inscription﻿—the whole thing must be a bit terrible.”

“You did see it﻿—until it got dark.”

My friend was more wrought upon than I had suspected, for at this touch of harmless theatricalism he started neurotically away from me and actually cried out with a sort of gulping gasp which released a strain of previous repression. It was an odd cry, and all the more terrible because it was answered. For as it was still echoing, I heard a creaking sound through the pitchy blackness, and knew that a lattice window was opening in that accursed old house beside us. And because all the other frames were long since fallen, I knew that it was the grisly glassless frame of that demoniac attic window.

===Chinese===

“屋檐底下有几块骨头。多半就是那男孩看见的——他要是敏感，用不着窗玻璃里有什么，就够叫他失魂。要是这些骨头全出自同一个东西，那必定是个歇斯底里的、谵狂的怪物。这样的骨头留在世上是渎神，所以我带着一只口袋回去，把它们搬到屋后的墓里。那儿有个口子，我把它们倒了进去。别当我是傻子——你真该看看那颗颅骨。长着四英寸的角，可那张脸和下颌，有点像你我的。”

我终于觉出曼顿真的打了个寒噤，他挨得我很近了。可他的好奇没有退。

“那窗玻璃呢？”

“全没了。一扇窗连整个框子都掉了，另一扇的菱形小格里，玻璃一丝也不剩。就是那种窗——1700年前就废弃的老菱格窗。我看它们有一百年甚至更久没安过玻璃了——也许那男孩走得那么远，是他砸的；传说没说。”

曼顿又沉思了。

“我想看看那座房子，卡特。它在哪儿？有没有玻璃我都要去探一探。还有你放骨头的墓，还有那座没有碑文的坟——这整个事情必定有几分可怕。”

“你已经见过了——在天黑之前。”

我的朋友被搅动的程度超出了我的料想，因为这一手无害的戏法，竟叫他神经质地从我身边跳开，真的喊出了声——一种吞咽式的抽气，泄出了先前的压抑。那喊声古怪，更可怕的是，它得到了回答。因为它还在回响，我听见一阵吱嘎声穿过漆黑，知道我们旁边那座受诅咒的老屋里，一扇菱格窗正被推开。因为其余的窗框早已落尽，我知道，那是顶楼那扇恶魔之窗的无玻璃的狰狞框子。

===Original===

Then came a noxious rush of noisome, frigid air from that same dreaded direction, followed by a piercing shriek just beside me on that shocking rifted tomb of man and monster. In another instant I was knocked from my gruesome bench by the devilish threshing of some unseen entity of titanic size but undetermined nature; knocked sprawling on the root-clutched mould of that abhorrent graveyard, while from the tomb came such a stifled uproar of gasping and whirring that my fancy peopled the rayless gloom with Miltonic legions of the misshapen damned. There was a vortex of withering, ice-cold wind, and then the rattle of loose bricks and plaster; but I had mercifully fainted before I could learn what it meant.

---

Manton, though smaller than I, is more resilient; for we opened our eyes at almost the same instant, despite his greater injuries. Our couches were side by side, and we knew in a few seconds that we were in St. Mary’s Hospital. Attendants were grouped about in tense curiosity, eager to aid our memory by telling us how we came there, and we soon heard of the farmer who had found us at noon in a lonely field beyond Meadow Hill, a mile from the old burying ground, on a spot where an ancient slaughterhouse is reputed to have stood. Manton had two malignant wounds in the chest, and some less severe cuts or gougings in the back. I was not so seriously hurt, but was covered with welts and contusions of the most bewildering character, including the print of a split hoof. It was plain that Manton knew more than I, but he told nothing to the puzzled and interested physicians till he had learned what our injuries were. Then he said we were the victims of a vicious bull﻿—though the animal was a difficult thing to place and account for.

After the doctors and nurses had left, I whispered an awestruck question:

“Good God, Manton, but *what was it*? Those scars﻿—*was it like that?*”

And I was too dazed to exult when he whispered back a thing I had half expected﻿—

“*No﻿—it wasn’t that way at all.* It was everywhere﻿—a gelatin﻿—a slime﻿—yet it had shapes, a thousand shapes of horror beyond all memory. There were eyes﻿—and a blemish. It was the pit﻿—the maelstrom﻿—the ultimate abomination. Carter, *it was the unnamable*!”

===Chinese===

随后，从那同一个可怕的方向，涌来一股有毒的、恶臭的冷风；跟着，就在我旁边，在那裂开的葬着人与怪物之墓上，响起一声刺穿一切的尖叫。又一瞬间，我被某个看不见的、巨物般大小而本性不明的实体恶魔似的抽打，从那可怕的座位上撞下来，撞得四仰八叉，倒在可憎墓园那被树根攥住的泥土上；而墓里传出一阵捂住的、喘息与呼呼作响的大乱，我的幻想给这无光的幽暗，住满了弥尔顿式的、畸形受诅者的军团队列。一阵冰冷的枯萎之风打着旋，随后是松动的砖和灰泥的哗啦声；可庆幸的是，不等我明白这一切意味着什么，我已晕了过去。

---

曼顿个子比我小，却更有韧性；因为我们几乎在同一瞬间睁开眼，尽管他伤得更重。两张病床并排，几秒钟里我们就知道，我们在圣玛丽医院。看护们聚在一旁，紧张地好奇，急着想用讲述我们的来历帮我们恢复记忆；我们很快听说了那个农夫——中午时分，他在草甸山那边一片偏僻的田野里发现了我们，离古墓园一英里，那地方据说立过一座古老的屠宰场。曼顿胸口有两处恶性伤，背上另有几处轻些的割伤剜伤。我伤得没那么重，可浑身是莫名其妙性质的鞭痕和挫伤，包括一只裂蹄的印子。分明曼顿知道的比我多；但在弄清我们的伤势之前，他对又困惑又感兴趣的医生们一字不吐。然后他说，我们是一头凶牛的受害者——尽管这牲口是个难安顿、难解释的东西。

医生护士们出去后，我敬畏地低声问了一句：

“老天爷，曼顿，那到底是什么？那些疤——就是那样子么？”

当他低声答出一句我半已料到的话时，我已晕得顾不上雀跃——

“不——全不是那个样子。它哪儿都是——一团胶——一层黏液——可它有形状，一千种形状，恐怖得超出一切记忆。有眼睛——还有一块浊斑。它是深渊——是漩涡——是至极的憎物。卡特，那就是不可名状！”

## The White Ship / 白船
===Original===

I am Basil Elton, keeper of the North Point light that my father and grandfather kept before me. Far from the shore stands the grey lighthouse, above sunken slimy rocks that are seen when the tide is low, but unseen when the tide is high. Past that beacon for a century have swept the majestic barques of the seven seas. In the days of my grandfather there were many; in the days of my father not so many; and now there are so few that I sometimes feel strangely alone, as though I were the last man on our planet.

From far shores came those white-sailed argosies of old; from far Eastern shores where warm suns shine and sweet odours linger about strange gardens and gay temples. The old captains of the sea came often to my grandfather and told him of these things, which in turn he told to my father, and my father told to me in the long autumn evenings when the wind howled eerily from the East. And I have read more of these things, and of many things besides, in the books men gave me when I was young and filled with wonder.

But more wonderful than the lore of old men and the lore of books is the secret lore of ocean. Blue, green, grey, white or black; smooth, ruffled, or mountainous; that ocean is not silent. All my days have I watched it and listened to it, and I know it well. At first it told to me only the plain little tales of calm beaches and near ports, but with the years it grew more friendly and spoke of other things; of things more strange and more distant in space and in time. Sometimes at twilight the grey vapours of the horizon have parted to grant me glimpses of the ways beyond; and sometimes at night the deep waters of the sea have grown clear and phosphorescent, to grant me glimpses of the ways beneath. And these glimpses have been as often of the ways that were and the ways that might be, as of the ways that are; for ocean is more ancient than the mountains, and freighted with the memories and the dreams of Time.

===Chinese===

我是巴兹尔·埃尔顿，北角灯塔的看守，我父亲和我祖父在我之前看守着它。灰色的灯塔远远立在海上，脚下是滑腻的沉礁，潮落时露出来，潮涨时看不见。一个世纪以来，七大洋庄严的三桅船从那座标旁掠过。我祖父的时代还有许多；我父亲的时代少了些；如今这样少，我有时古怪地觉得自己孤单，仿佛是我们这颗行星上的最后一个人。

那些白帆的古老船队来自遥远的彼岸；来自遥远的东方海岸，那里暖阳照耀，异香的花园和欢快的神庙萦绕着甜香。旧日的老船长们常来找我祖父，把这些讲给他；他转讲给我父亲；我父亲又在长长的秋夜里讲给我，那时风从东方凄声号啸。这些，还有此外的许多，我少年时——满心惊奇的时候——又从人们给我的书里读到更多。

可比老人的掌故和书里的掌故更奇妙的，是海洋的秘密的掌故。蓝的，绿的，灰的，白的，黑的；平的，皱的，山立的；那海洋不沉默。我一生望着它、听着它，我知道它。起初它只对我讲些平静海滩和邻近港口的朴素小故事；可随着年头，它越来越友好，讲起别的；讲起空间和时间上更陌生、更遥远的事。有时在暮色里，天际的灰雾分开，许我一瞥彼界之路；有时在夜里，深海水变得清亮发光，许我一瞥此下之路。而这些一瞥，往往不是今之路，而是昔之路和或将之路；因为海洋比群山更古老，满载着时间的记忆与梦。

===Original===

Out of the South it was that the White Ship used to come when the moon was full and high in the heavens. Out of the South it would glide very smoothly and silently over the sea. And whether the sea was rough or calm, and whether the wind was friendly or adverse, it would always glide smoothly and silently, its sails distent and its long strange tiers of oars moving rhythmically. One night I espied upon the deck a man, bearded and robed, and he seemed to beckon me to embark for fair unknown shores. Many times afterward I saw him under the full moon, and ever did he beckon me.

Very brightly did the moon shine on the night I answered the call, and I walked out over the waters to the White Ship on a bridge of moonbeams. The man who had beckoned now spoke a welcome to me in a soft language I seemed to know well, and the hours were filled with soft songs of the oarsmen as we glided away into a mysterious South, golden with the glow of that full, mellow moon.

And when the day dawned, rosy and effulgent, I beheld the green shore of far lands, bright and beautiful, and to me unknown. Up from the sea rose lordly terraces of verdure, tree-studded, and showing here and there the gleaming white roofs and colonnades of strange temples. As we drew nearer the green shore the bearded man told me of that land, the Land of Zar, where dwell all the dreams and thoughts of beauty that come to men once and then are forgotten. And when I looked upon the terraces again I saw that what he said was true, for among the sights before me were many things I had once seen through the mists beyond the horizon in the phosphorescent depths of ocean. There too were forms and fantasies more splendid than I had ever known; the visions of young poets who died in want before the world could learn of what they had seen and dreamed. But we did not set foot upon the sloping meadows of Zar, for it is told that he who treads them may nevermore return to his native shore.

===Chinese===

白船惯于从南方来，当月亮圆满高悬的时候。它从南方来，非常平滑、非常无声地滑过海面。不论海是狂是静，不论风是顺风是逆风，它总是那样平滑而无声地滑行，帆吃饱着风，一长列古怪的桨有节奏地动着。一天夜里，我望见甲板上有一个人，有须，着袍，他似乎在招我上船，去美丽未知的彼岸。此后许多次，我在满月下看见他，他总是向我招手。

我应召的那一夜，月光亮极了；我踏着一道月光的桥，走出水面，走向白船。招我的那人用一种我仿佛熟稔的软语向我道了欢迎；我们滑进一片神秘的南方——浸着那轮饱满、醇熟的月的金光——钟点里满是桨手们轻柔的歌。

白日升起，红润而辉煌，我望见远方陆地青绿的海岸，明亮，美丽，我不识。青翠的大台地从海上隆起，缀满树木，处处闪着异样神庙的白顶和柱廊。我们驶近青岸时，有须的人对我讲起那地方，扎尔之地，凡是来过人身上一次随即被忘却的一切美的梦和思，都住在那里。我再望那些台地，便知他说的不虚，因为眼前的景物里，有许多我曾隔着天际的雾、在海洋的磷光深处见过的。那里还有比我历来所知更华美的形与幻；是夭亡的少年诗人们看的梦——他们死于穷愁，世人还不及知道他们看见了什么、梦见了什么。可我们没有踏上扎尔倾斜的草甸，因为据说踏了那土地的人，再不能回到他本乡的海岸。

===Original===

As the White Ship sailed silently away from the templed terraces of Zar, we beheld on the distant horizon ahead the spires of a mighty city; and the bearded man said to me, “This is Thalarion, the City of a Thousand Wonders, wherein reside all those mysteries that man has striven in vain to fathom.” And I looked again, at closer range, and saw that the city was greater than any city I had known or dreamed of before. Into the sky the spires of its temples reached, so that no man might behold their peaks; and far back beyond the horizon stretched the grim, grey walls, over which one might spy only a few roofs, weird and ominous, yet adorned with rich friezes and alluring sculptures. I yearned mightily to enter this fascinating yet repellent city, and beseeched the bearded man to land me at the stone pier by the huge carven gate Akariel; but he gently denied my wish, saying, “Into Thalarion, the City of a Thousand Wonders, many have passed but none returned. Therein walk only dæmons and mad things that are no longer men, and the streets are white with the unburied bones of those who have looked upon the eidolon Lathi, that reigns over the city.” So the White Ship sailed on past the walls of Thalarion, and followed for many days a southward-flying bird, whose glossy plumage matched the sky out of which it had appeared.

Then came we to a pleasant coast gay with blossoms of every hue, where as far inland as we could see basked lovely groves and radiant arbours beneath a meridian sun. From bowers beyond our view came bursts of song and snatches of lyric harmony, interspersed with faint laughter so delicious that I urged the rowers onward in my eagerness to reach the scene. And the bearded man spoke no word, but watched me as we approached the lily-lined shore. Suddenly a wind blowing from over the flowery meadows and leafy woods brought a scent at which I trembled. The wind grew stronger, and the air was filled with the lethal, charnel odour of plague-stricken towns and uncovered cemeteries. And as we sailed madly away from that damnable coast the bearded man spoke at last, saying, “This is Xura, the Land of Pleasures Unattained.”

===Chinese===

白船无声地驶离扎尔的神庙台地时，我们望见前方远天上一座巨城的尖塔；有须的人对我说：「这是萨拉里昂，千奇之城，人枉自穷究而不得的一切奥秘，都住在里面。」我再贴近些看，见那城比我识得的或梦过的任何城都大。神庙的尖塔直插天穹，没人望得见塔尖；灰色狰狞的大墙远远伸过天际，墙头只窥得见几座屋顶，怪异而凶险，却缀着华美的雕带和迷人的雕像。我热切地想进这座迷人又叫人却步的城，恳求有须的人送我在巨雕门阿卡里尔旁的石埠登岸；他却温和地回绝了我，说：「进萨拉里昂、进千奇之城的，多了，没有一个回来。里面走动的只有魔和不再是人的疯物；街道刷得雪白，用的是不曾下葬的白骨——那些望见过统治此城的神像拉西的人的骨。」于是白船驶过萨拉里昂的城墙，一连许多天，追着一只向南飞的鸟，鸟的羽色同它所自来的一般天色一模一样。

随后我们到了一片宜人的海岸，开满各色的花，目力所及，梅日的太阳下尽是可爱的树丛和明亮的凉棚。看不见的棚架外飘来一阵阵歌和抒情曲的断片，夹着一缕缕甜得叫人酥软的轻笑；我急切地催桨手们快划。有须的人一言不发，只望着我们驶近那百合镶边的海岸。骤然，一阵风从花田林梢吹来，带来一缕叫我发抖的香。风越刮越大，空气里灌满了致死的、藏尸所的气味——瘟城的气味和掘开的墓园的气味。我们发疯似的逃离那该咒的海岸时，有须的人终于开口：「这是修拉，未得之乐之地。」

===Original===

So once more the White Ship followed the bird of heaven, over warm blessed seas fanned by caressing, aromatic breezes. Day after day and night after night did we sail, and when the moon was full we would listen to soft songs of the oarsmen, sweet as on that distant night when we sailed away from my far native land. And it was by moonlight that we anchored at last in the harbour of Sona-Nyl, which is guarded by twin headlands of crystal that rise from the sea and meet in a resplendent arch. This is the Land of Fancy, and we walked to the verdant shore upon a golden bridge of moonbeams.

In the Land of Sona-Nyl there is neither time nor space, neither suffering nor death; and there I dwelt for many æons. Green are the groves and pastures, bright and fragrant the flowers, blue and musical the streams, clear and cool the fountains, and stately and gorgeous the temples, castles, and cities of Sona-Nyl. Of that land there is no bound, for beyond each vista of beauty rises another more beautiful. Over the countryside and amidst the splendour of cities can move at will the happy folk, of whom all are gifted with unmarred grace and unalloyed happiness. For the æons that I dwelt there I wandered blissfully through gardens where quaint pagodas peep from pleasing clumps of bushes, and where the white walks are bordered with delicate blossoms. I climbed gentle hills from whose summits I could see entrancing panoramas of loveliness, with steepled towns nestling in verdant valleys, and with the golden domes of gigantic cities glittering on the infinitely distant horizon. And I viewed by moonlight the sparkling sea, the crystal headlands, and the placid harbour wherein lay anchored the White Ship.

===Chinese===

于是白船再度跟着天上的鸟，行在温暖蒙福的海上，拂着爱抚的、含香的风。我们日复一日、夜复一夜地航行；满月的夜里，便听桨手们轻柔的歌，甜美如那个遥远的夜——我们驶离我遥远故乡的那个夜。也是借着月光，我们最后抛锚在索纳-尼尔的港里；两道水晶的海岬从海中拔起，合成一道辉煌的拱，守着港门。这是幻想之地；我们踏着一道月光的金桥，走上青绿的岸。

索纳-尼尔之地没有时间也没有空间，没有苦难也没有死亡；我在那里住了许多大纪。树丛和牧野青青，花明亮而芬芳，溪水蔚蓝而如乐，泉水清冽，神庙、城堡和城池庄严而绚烂。那地方没有边界，因为每一幅美的远景之后，又升起一幅更美的。快乐的民众随意行于乡野、行于城的华彩之间，个个天赋无瑕的优雅和纯粹的欢愉。住在那里的那些大纪，我有福地漫游在花园里，古雅的宝塔从宜人的灌木丛里探出头来，白色的小径镶着纤巧的花边。我攀登温柔的山，从山顶望见迷人的美的全景：尖塔的小城偎在青谷里，巨城的金穹在无穷远的天际闪光。月光下我看闪闪的海、水晶的海岬和平静的港——白船就锚泊在那里。

===Original===

It was against the full moon one night in the immemorial year of Tharp that I saw outlined the beckoning form of the celestial bird, and felt the first stirrings of unrest. Then I spoke with the bearded man, and told him of my new yearning to depart for remote Cathuria, which no man hath seen, but which all believe to lie beyond the basalt pillars of the West. It is the Land of Hope, and in it shine the perfect ideals of all that we know elsewhere; or at least so men relate. But the bearded man said to me, “Beware of those perilous seas wherein men say Cathuria lies. In Sona-Nyl there is no pain nor death, but who can tell what lies beyond the basalt pillars of the West?” Natheless at the next full moon I boarded the White Ship, and with the reluctant bearded man left the happy harbour for untravelled seas.

===Chinese===

在太古的塔普之年的一夜，衬着满月，我望见了那只天鸟招引的剪影，初次觉出了不安的悸动。于是我问有须的人，同他说起我新的渴望：动身去遥远的卡图利亚——没有人见过，但人人都信它在西方玄武岩石柱之外的希望之地。据说，我们在此世所知的一切完美的理想，都在那里发光；至少人们这样说。可有须的人对我说：「当心那些凶海，人说卡图利亚就躺在里面。索纳-尼尔没有苦痛也没有死亡，可谁能说，西方玄武岩石柱之外躺着什么？」下一个满月，我还是登上了白船，带着不情愿的有须的人，离开了幸福的港，驶向无人航过的海。

===Original===

And the bird of heaven flew before, and led us toward the basalt pillars of the West, but this time the oarsmen sang no soft songs under the full moon. In my mind I would often picture the unknown Land of Cathuria with its splendid groves and palaces, and would wonder what new delights there awaited me. “Cathuria,” I would say to myself, “is the abode of gods and the land of unnumbered cities of gold. Its forests are of aloe and sandalwood, even as the fragrant groves of Camorin, and among the trees flutter gay birds sweet with song. On the green and flowery mountains of Cathuria stand temples of pink marble, rich with carven and painted glories, and having in their courtyards cool fountains of silver, where purl with ravishing music the scented waters that come from the grotto-born river Narg. And the cities of Cathuria are cinctured with golden walls, and their pavements are also of gold. In the gardens of these cities are strange orchids, and perfumed lakes whose beds are of coral and amber. At night the streets and the gardens are lit with gay lanterns fashioned from three-coloured shell of the tortoise, and here resound the soft notes of the singer and the lutanist. And the houses of the cities of Cathuria are all palaces, each built over a fragrant canal bearing the waters of the sacred Narg. Of marble and porphyry are the houses, and roofed with glittering gold that reflects the rays of the sun and enhances the splendour of the cities as blissful gods view them from the distant peaks. Fairest of all is the palace of the great monarch Dorieb, whom some say to be a demigod and others a god. High is the palace of Dorieb, and many are the turrets of marble upon its walls. In its wide halls may multitudes assemble, and here hang the trophies of the ages. And the roof is of pure gold, set upon tall pillars of ruby and azure, and having such carven figures of gods and heroes that he who looks up to those heights seem to gaze upon the living Olympus. And the floor of the palace is of glass, under which flow the cunningly lighted waters of the Narg, gay with gaudy fish not known beyond the bounds of lovely Cathuria.”

Thus would I speak to myself of Cathuria, but ever would the bearded man warn me to turn back to the happy shores of Sona-Nyl; for Sona-Nyl is known of men, while none hath ever beheld Cathuria.

===Chinese===

天鸟在前引路，领我们朝西方的玄武岩石柱去；可这一次，满月之下，桨手们不再轻柔地唱。我心里常常描画那未知的卡图利亚之地，它华美的树丛和宫殿，纳罕那里有什么新的欢愉等我。「卡图利亚，」我对自己说，「是众神的居所，是数不清的黄金之城之地。它的森林是芦荟和檀香，正如卡莫林芬芳的树丛；树间翻飞着歌声甜美的欢鸟。卡图利亚青青的、开花的山上，立着粉色大理石的神庙，满布雕绘的华彩，庭院里有清凉的银泉，洞生的纳尔格河的水带着醉人的音乐在那里淙淙。卡图利亚的城围着金墙，街道也铺着金。这些城的花园里有奇兰，有香湖，湖床是珊瑚和琥珀。夜里，街道和花园点着欢快的灯，用三色龟壳做成；歌者和鲁特琴手的软音在这里回响。卡图利亚诸城的房屋座座是宫，每座架在一条香运河上，载着神圣纳尔格的水。房屋是大理石和斑岩造的，覆着闪光的金顶，映着日光，更增城的辉煌——幸福的众神从远峰上望下来。最美的是大王多里布的宫殿，有人说他是半神，有人说他是神。多里布的宫殿高，墙上的大理石塔楼多。宽阔的厅堂里容得下大众，历代战利悬在四壁。宫顶是纯金，架在红玉和青金石的高柱上，雕着众神和英雄，抬头仰望的人仿佛在望活的奥林波斯。宫的地板是玻璃的，底下流着纳尔格巧妙照明的水，游着可爱的卡图利亚界外无人识的艳鱼。」

我便这样对自己说卡图利亚；可有须的人总警告我折回索纳-尼尔幸福的岸；因为索纳-尼尔是人识得的，而卡图利亚，没有人望见过。

===Original===

And on the thirty-first day that we followed the bird, we beheld the basalt pillars of the West. Shrouded in mist they were, so that no man might peer beyond them or see their summits﻿—which indeed some say reach even to the heavens. And the bearded man again implored me to turn back, but I heeded him not; for from the mists beyond the basalt pillars I fancied there came the notes of singer and lutanist; sweeter than the sweetest songs of Sona-Nyl, and sounding mine own praises; the praises of me, who had voyaged far under the full moon and dwelt in the Land of Fancy.

So to the sound of melody the White Ship sailed into the mist betwixt the basalt pillars of the West. And when the music ceased and the mist lifted, we beheld not the Land of Cathuria, but a swift-rushing resistless sea, over which our helpless barque was borne toward some unknown goal. Soon to our ears came the distant thunder of falling waters, and to our eyes appeared on the far horizon ahead the titanic spray of a monstrous cataract, wherein the oceans of the world drop down to abysmal nothingness. Then did the bearded man say to me with tears on his cheek, “We have rejected the beautiful Land of Sona-Nyl, which we may never behold again. The gods are greater than men, and they have conquered.” And I closed my eyes before the crash that I knew would come, shutting out the sight of the celestial bird which flapped its mocking blue wings over the brink of the torrent.

Out of that crash came darkness, and I heard the shrieking of men and of things which were not men. From the East tempestuous winds arose, and chilled me as I crouched on the slab of damp stone which had risen beneath my feet. Then as I heard another crash I opened my eyes and beheld myself upon the platform of that lighthouse from whence I had sailed so many æons ago. In the darkness below there loomed the vast blurred outlines of a vessel breaking up on the cruel rocks, and as I glanced out over the waste I saw that the light had failed for the first time since my grandfather had assumed its care.

===Chinese===

跟着鸟的第三十一天，我们望见了西方的玄武岩石柱。它们裹在雾里，没人能望穿它们，也没人望得见柱顶——有人说柱顶直抵天。有须的人再次恳求我折回，我不听；因为石柱之外的雾里，我恍惚听见歌者和鲁特琴手的乐音；比索纳-尼尔最甜的歌还甜，唱的且是我自己的颂词——赞我这个满月下远航过、住过幻想之地的人。

就这样，和着乐音，白船驶进了西方玄武岩石柱之间的雾。乐音停了，雾散了：我们望见的不是卡图利亚之地，而是一片疾奔的、无可抗拒的海，我们无助的船被载向某个未知的目标。不久，耳中传来远处落水的雷声，眼前远远的天际上，出现一道巨瀑的泰坦水沫——世界的海洋就从那里跌入深渊的无。有须的人颊上带着泪对我说：「我们抛掉了美丽的索纳-尼尔之地，再也不能望见它了。众神比人大，他们胜了。」我闭上了眼睛，等我知道必来的那一撞，遮住了那只天鸟——它在激流的崖口上，扑着嘲弄的蓝翅膀。

那一撞里出来黑暗，我听见人和不是人的东西的尖叫。东方刮起狂暴的风，冻着我——我伏在脚下升起的那块湿石板上。又一声崩响，我睁开眼，看见自己立在那座灯塔的平台上——不知多少大纪前，我从那里启航。下面的黑暗里，隐着一艘船的巨大模糊的轮廓，正在狰狞的礁石上碎掉；我朝那片荒水外一望，看见灯灭了——自我祖父接手看守以来，头一回熄了。

===Original===

And in the later watches of the night, when I went within the tower, I saw on the wall a calendar which still remained as when I had left it at the hour I sailed away. With the dawn I descended the tower and looked for wreckage upon the rocks, but what I found was only this: a strange dead bird whose hue was as of the azure sky, and a single shattered spar, of a whiteness greater than that of the wave-tips or of the mountain snow.

And thereafter the ocean told me its secrets no more; and though many times since has the moon shone full and high in the heavens, the White Ship from the South came never again.

===Chinese===

夜最深的时辰，我走进塔里，看见墙上一本日历，还停在我启航那刻离开时的样子。拂晓我下了塔，到礁石间寻找残骸，可找到的只有这些：一只古怪的死鸟，毛色如蔚蓝的天；一根折断的船桅，白得赛过浪尖，赛过高山之雪。

此后，海洋再没有对我讲过它的秘密；虽然从那以后，许多回月亮圆满高悬在天上，南方的白船，再没有来过。
